Designing Data-Intensive Applications

A chapter-by-chapter guide

Designing data-intensive applications

The big ideas behind reliable, scalable and maintainable systems: how data is stored, copied, split, transacted and processed, explained in plain English with the book’s examples and diagrams.

Based on Martin Kleppmann’s Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O’Reilly, first edition, March 2017).

12 chapters772 min readPreface to glossary, nothing skipped

This is an independent retelling written for readers, not the book itself. It follows every chapter in order, keeps the book’s own examples, and quotes only short lines. The diagrams are redrawn from scratch. Kleppmann’s writing is more careful and detailed than a summary can be, so read the book too.

Front matter

Preface

The big idea: the tools for storing and processing data change quickly, but the principles behind them last longer. Learn those principles, and you can judge any tool, see where it fits, and spot its pitfalls before they hurt you.

If you have worked in software in recent years, especially on servers and backends, you have probably been hit by a flood of buzzwords about data. The preface lists NoSQL, Big Data, web-scale, sharding, eventual consistency, ACID, the CAP theorem, cloud services, MapReduce, and real-time. Several of these come up again later in the book. Here is what some of them mean in plain words:

  • NoSQL is a loose label for newer database types that do not follow the traditional table model of SQL databases.
  • Sharding means splitting a large dataset into parts that live on different machines.
  • Eventual consistency means copies of the data may disagree for a while, but they settle down over time.
  • ACID is the set of guarantees a database gives for transactions, which are groups of changes that must succeed or fail together.
  • The CAP theorem says a distributed system, which is one spread across several machines, cannot fully guarantee both consistency and availability when the network splits.
  • MapReduce is a way of processing large batches of data across many machines.

In the last decade there have been many developments in databases, in distributed systems, and in how we build applications on top of them. Several forces drive these developments. The preface names six:

  • Internet companies such as Google, Yahoo!, Amazon, Facebook, LinkedIn, Microsoft, and Twitter handle huge volumes of data and traffic. They have had to build new tools to handle that scale.
  • Businesses need to be agile. That means testing ideas cheaply, responding quickly to new market insights, and keeping development cycles short and data models flexible.
  • Free and open source software is now often preferred over commercial or in-house software.
  • CPU clock speeds are barely rising, but multi-core processors (chips with several processing cores) are standard, and networks are getting faster. So parallelism, doing many things at once, will only increase.
  • Even a small team can now build systems spread across many machines and regions, thanks to infrastructure as a service (IaaS), such as Amazon Web Services.
  • Many services are now expected to be highly available, meaning they stay up. Long downtime, whether from outages or maintenance, is becoming less and less acceptable.

The preface calls an application data-intensive when data is its main challenge. The challenge might be the quantity of data, its complexity, or how fast it changes. The opposite is compute-intensive work, where the processor’s raw speed is the bottleneck. Data-intensive applications are pushing the limits of what is possible, using these new technologies to do it.

The tools that help such applications store and process data are adapting too. NoSQL databases get a lot of attention. But message queues (where one part of a program sends messages that another part handles later), caches, search indexes, and frameworks for batch and stream processing are just as important. Many applications use some combination of these.

The buzzwords are a sign of enthusiasm for new possibilities, and that is a good thing. But engineers and architects also need a precise, technically accurate understanding of each technology and its trade-offs. To get that, you have to dig deeper than the buzzwords.

Key idea

Tools come and go, but the principles and trade-offs behind them stay true whatever version you use. Learn those, and each new tool becomes easier to place.

The book’s goal is to help you find your way through a diverse, fast-changing set of tools for processing and storing data. It is not a tutorial for one tool, and it is not a dry textbook of theory. It looks at successful data systems, the technologies under many popular applications that must meet demands for scale, speed, and reliability every day. It digs into their internals and key algorithms, and asks not only how each one works but why it works that way.

After reading, you should be able to decide which kind of technology suits which purpose, and see how tools combine into the foundation of a good application. You will not be ready to build your own storage engine (the part of a database that lays data out on disk) from scratch, and that is rarely needed. You will, however, understand what your systems do under the hood, so you can reason about their behavior, make good design decisions, and track down problems.

Who Should Read This Book?

If you build applications that have a server or backend for storing or processing data, and those applications use the internet (for example, web applications, mobile apps, or internet-connected sensors), this book is for you.

It is written for software engineers, software architects, and technical managers who love to code. It is especially useful if you make decisions about the architecture of your systems, such as choosing tools for a problem and working out how to apply them. Even if you have no choice over your tools, the book will help you understand their strengths and weaknesses.

You should have some experience building web applications or network services, and be familiar with relational databases and SQL. Experience with non-relational databases and other data tools is a bonus, but not required. A general understanding of network protocols such as TCP and HTTP helps. Your choice of programming language or framework makes no difference.

The book will be valuable to you if any of these are true:

  • You want to learn how to make data systems scalable, for example to support web or mobile apps with millions of users.
  • You need to make applications highly available, minimizing downtime, and operationally robust.
  • You want to make systems easier to maintain in the long run, even as they grow and as requirements and technologies change.
  • You have a natural curiosity for the way things work, and want to know what goes on inside major websites and online services. The book breaks down the internals of many databases and data processing systems.

Sometimes people say, “You’re not Google or Amazon. Stop worrying about scale and just use a relational database.” The preface agrees in part. Building for scale you do not need is wasted effort, and it may lock you into an inflexible design. That is a form of premature optimization, which means solving a speed or scale problem before you actually have it.

But choosing the right tool for the job still matters, and each technology has its own strengths and weaknesses. Relational databases are important, but they are not the final word on handling data.

Watch out

Do not build for scale you do not need, because that effort is wasted and can lock you into a rigid design. Still, pick each tool with its strengths and weaknesses in mind.

Scope of This Book

The book does not give step-by-step instructions for installing or using specific software packages or APIs (the interfaces programs use to talk to each other). Plenty of documentation already exists for those. Instead, it discusses the principles and trade-offs that are fundamental to data systems, and the different design decisions that different products take.

The book looks mainly at the architecture of data systems and at how they are combined into data-intensive applications. It does not have space to cover deployment, operations, security, management, and other areas. The preface says these are complex and important topics, and covering them as side notes would do them no justice. They deserve books of their own.

The book also avoids the term Big Data. The preface says it is so overused and underdefined that it is not useful in serious engineering talk. The book uses clearer terms instead, such as single-node versus distributed systems, or online versus offline (batch) processing systems.

The book has a bias toward free and open source software (FOSS). Reading, changing, and running source code is a good way to understand how something works in detail. Open platforms also reduce the risk of vendor lock-in, which is being stuck with one company’s product. Where it fits, though, the book also discusses proprietary software: closed-source products, software sold as a service, and in-house systems that companies have described in the literature but never released.

Outline of This Book

The book is arranged into three parts.

  • Part I: the fundamental ideas that underpin the design of data-intensive applications.
    • Chapter 1 asks what we are trying to achieve: reliability, scalability, and maintainability. It covers how to think about each one and how to achieve them.
    • Chapter 2 compares several data models and query languages, and shows which suit which situations.
    • Chapter 3 covers storage engines, which arrange data on disk so that it can be found again efficiently.
    • Chapter 4 covers formats for data encoding (also called serialization) and how schemas change over time.
  • Part II: distributed data. This moves from data on one machine to data spread across many. That is often needed for scalability, but it brings unique challenges.
    • Chapter 5 covers replication, which keeps copies of data on several machines.
    • Chapter 6 covers partitioning, also called sharding.
    • Chapter 7 covers transactions.
    • Chapter 8 covers the problems that come up in distributed systems.
    • Chapter 9 covers what it takes to achieve consistency and consensus (getting several machines to agree) in a distributed system.
  • Part III: derived data. This covers systems that build some datasets from other datasets. Derived data often appears in heterogeneous systems, meaning systems made of several different tools. When no single database does everything well, applications integrate several databases, caches, indexes, and more.
    • Chapter 10 starts with a batch processing approach to derived data.
    • Chapter 11 builds on that with stream processing.
    • Chapter 12 puts everything together and discusses how to build reliable, scalable, and maintainable applications in the future.

References and Further Reading

Most of what the book discusses has been said elsewhere, in conference talks, research papers, blog posts, code, mailing lists, and engineering folklore. The book summarizes those ideas and points to the original literature throughout. The references at the end of each chapter are a good place to go deeper, and most are freely available online.

Part I

Foundations of Data Systems

Chapters 1 to 4 cover the ideas that apply to every data system, from reliability and scaling to data models, storage engines, and data encoding.

A paraphrase of Kleppmann’s part introduction: the first four chapters apply whether a system runs on one machine or many, and Part II then turns to distributed systems.

Part I · Chapter 1

Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Applications

The big idea: a good data system keeps working correctly when things go wrong, copes with growth in load, and stays easy for people to run and change. Each of these goals has a price, and there are no free wins.

Most applications today are data-intensive rather than compute-intensive. A compute-intensive program is held back by how fast the processor is. A data-intensive one is held back by how much data it has, how complicated that data is, and how fast it changes. Raw CPU power is rarely the real limit.

Such applications are usually built from a few standard building blocks, each giving a common kind of help:

  • A database stores data so that the application, or another one, can find it again later.
  • A cache remembers the result of an expensive operation so that the next read is faster.
  • A search index lets users find data by keyword or filter it in different ways.
  • Stream processing sends a message to another process to be handled asynchronously, which means the sender does not wait for it.
  • Batch processing periodically crunches a large amount of data that has built up.

If that sounds obvious, it is because these data systems are such a successful idea. Almost nobody writes a new storage engine (the part of a database that lays data out on disk) from scratch. A database is a perfectly good tool for the job.

But reality is not that simple. There are many database systems with different strengths, because applications have different needs. There are several approaches to caching and several ways to build search indexes. An engineer still has to pick the tools and approaches that fit the task, and it can be hard to combine tools when one tool alone cannot do the whole job.

This chapter starts with the basics. It defines what we mean by reliable, scalable, and maintainable data systems, gives some ways of thinking about each goal, and sets up vocabulary that the later chapters will use. Those later chapters go layer by layer through the design decisions that come up when building a data-intensive application.

Thinking About Data Systems

We usually put databases, queues, and caches into different categories. A database and a message queue (a system where one part of a program puts messages in, and another takes them out to process) both hold data for some time. Even so, they have very different access patterns, which means different performance characteristics, and so very different implementations.

So why lump them all together under the umbrella term data systems? The book gives two reasons.

The first is that the boundaries between categories are blurring. Some datastores are also used as message queues, such as Redis. Some message queues have database-like durability, which means a promise that written data is not lost, such as Apache Kafka. The old labels no longer fit neatly.

The second reason is that many applications now have requirements that a single tool cannot meet. The work is broken into tasks that one tool can do efficiently, and application code stitches those tools together. For example, a team may run an application-managed cache (using a server such as Memcached, which keeps data in memory for fast reads) or a full-text search server (such as Elasticsearch or Solr) next to the main database. In that setup, the application code is responsible for keeping the caches and indexes in sync with the main database.

When you combine several tools to provide a service, the service’s interface, or application programming interface (API), usually hides those details from clients. The result is effectively a new, special-purpose data system built from smaller general-purpose parts. That composite system may promise certain guarantees, such as that the cache is correctly updated or invalidated (removed as stale) on writes, so that outside clients always see consistent results. The book’s point is that once you do this, you are not only an application developer. You are also a data system designer.

Designing a data system raises hard questions. How do you keep the data correct and complete when parts of the system fail? How do you keep performance steady for clients when parts of the system are degraded? How do you scale up to handle more load? What should a good API look like? Other factors also shape the design, including the skills and experience of the team, dependencies on older systems, the time available for delivery, how much risk the organization accepts, and legal rules. These factors depend a lot on the situation.

The book focuses on three concerns that matter in most software systems:

  • Reliability: the system keeps working correctly, at the expected level of performance, even when things go wrong.
  • Scalability: as the system grows in data, traffic, or complexity, there are reasonable ways to deal with that growth.
  • Maintainability: many different people work on the system over the years, and all of them can work on it productively.

These words are often used loosely, so the rest of the chapter defines them more carefully.

Reliability

Everyone has an intuitive sense of what reliable means. For software, typical expectations include:

  • The application performs the function the user expected.
  • It can tolerate the user making mistakes or using the software in unexpected ways.
  • Its performance is good enough for the use case, under the expected load and data volume.
  • The system prevents unauthorized access and abuse.

Taken together, these mean something like continuing to work correctly, even when things go wrong.

The things that go wrong are called faults. A system that anticipates faults and copes with them is called fault-tolerant or resilient. The book notes that the term fault-tolerant is a little misleading. It suggests that a system could be made tolerant of every possible fault, and that is not realistic. If the whole planet, with every server on it, were swallowed by a black hole, the only protection would be hosting in space, which is not a budget item anyone would approve. So it only makes sense to talk about tolerating certain kinds of faults.

A fault is usually one component of the system deviating from its specification (the agreed behavior). A failure is when the system as a whole stops giving the service the user needs. The two are different. A fault can happen without a failure, if the system is built to absorb it. The probability of a fault can never be reduced to zero, so the book suggests designing fault-tolerance mechanisms that stop faults from turning into failures. Later chapters cover many techniques for building reliable systems from unreliable parts.

It may sound odd, but a fault-tolerant system can benefit from causing faults on purpose. For example, you can randomly kill individual processes without warning. Many critical bugs come from poor error handling. If you trigger faults deliberately, the fault-handling code runs all the time, so you can be more confident it will work when a real fault happens. Netflix’s Chaos Monkey is an example of this approach.

Prevention is sometimes better than cure. Security is one example. If an attacker has already broken in and read sensitive data, that cannot be undone. The book, however, mostly deals with faults that can be cured.

Hardware Faults

When people think about why systems fail, hardware usually comes to mind first. Hard disks crash, memory goes bad, the power grid has a blackout, and someone unplugs the wrong network cable. Anyone who has run a large datacenter knows these things happen all the time once you have many machines.

Hard disks have a mean time to failure (MTTF, the average expected lifetime) of about 10 to 50 years. That sounds reassuring until you do the arithmetic. On a storage cluster with 10,000 disks, the book says you should expect about one disk to die per day.

The usual first response is to add redundancy to each hardware component, which means keeping a spare that can take over. Disks can be set up in a RAID configuration (several disks wired together so that one can fail without losing data). Servers can have two power supplies and CPUs that can be swapped while the machine runs. Datacenters can have batteries and diesel generators for backup power. When one part dies, its spare takes over while the broken part is replaced. Redundancy cannot stop every hardware problem from causing a failure, but it is well understood and can often keep one machine running for years without interruption.

Until recently, this was enough for most applications. As long as you could restore a backup onto a new machine fairly quickly, downtime after a failure was not a disaster for most applications. Only a small number of applications, where high availability was essential, needed multi-machine redundancy.

That has changed. Data volumes and computing demands have grown, so more applications run on large numbers of machines. More machines means a higher rate of hardware faults. Cloud platforms such as Amazon Web Services (AWS) also make it fairly common for virtual machines to become unavailable without warning. Those platforms are designed to favor flexibility and elasticity (the ability to add or remove capacity quickly) over the reliability of any single machine.

This is why there is a move toward systems that can survive the loss of an entire machine, using software fault-tolerance techniques instead of, or in addition to, hardware redundancy. These systems also make operations easier. A single-server system needs planned downtime to reboot, for example to apply operating system security patches. A system that tolerates machine failure can be patched one node (one machine in the cluster) at a time, while the rest keep serving users. This is called a rolling upgrade, and Chapter 4 covers it further.

Software Errors

We usually think of hardware faults as random and independent. One machine’s disk failing does not mean another machine’s disk will fail soon. There can be weak links, such as several servers in one rack all getting too hot, but in general a large number of hardware parts are unlikely to fail at the same time.

Software faults are different. They are systematic errors, which are bugs that show up the same way wherever the same condition appears. They are harder to anticipate, and because they are correlated across nodes, they tend to cause many more failures than random hardware faults. Examples include:

  • A bug that makes every instance of an application server crash when it receives a particular bad input. The book gives the leap second added on June 30, 2012, as an example. A bug in the Linux kernel made many applications hang at the same moment.
  • A runaway process that uses up a shared resource, such as CPU time, memory, disk space, or network bandwidth.
  • A service that the system depends on becomes slow, unresponsive, or starts returning corrupted responses.
  • Cascading failures, where a small fault in one component triggers a fault in another, which triggers further faults.

The bugs behind these faults often lie dormant for a long time. They appear only when an unusual set of circumstances comes together. Usually, the software is making some assumption about its environment. That assumption is true most of the time, but eventually it stops being true for some reason.

There is no quick fix for systematic faults in software. The book lists several things that help: think carefully about assumptions and interactions in the system, test thoroughly, isolate processes from one another, let processes crash and restart, and measure, monitor, and analyze behavior in production. A system can also check itself while it runs. If it is supposed to guarantee something, such as that the number of messages coming out of a queue equals the number going in, it can verify that continuously and raise an alert when the numbers do not match.

Human Errors

Humans design and build software, and humans run it. Even people with the best intentions are unreliable. The book cites one study of large internet services, which found that configuration errors by operators were the leading cause of outages. Hardware faults, in servers or the network, played a role in only 10 to 25 percent of outages.

How do we make a system reliable when the people working on it are not? The book suggests combining several approaches.

  • Make mistakes hard to make. Well-designed abstractions, APIs, and admin tools make the right thing easy and the wrong thing unlikely. But if the interfaces are too restrictive, people work around them, which cancels the benefit. Getting that balance right is tricky.
  • Separate the places where people err from the places where errors cause failures. Provide fully featured sandbox environments that are not production. People can then explore and experiment with realistic data without affecting real users.
  • Test at every level. That includes unit tests, whole-system integration tests, and manual tests. Automated testing is widely used and is especially good at covering rare corner cases.
  • Make recovery quick and easy. Roll back configuration changes fast. Release new code gradually, so that any unexpected bug hits only a small group of users. Provide tools to recompute data if an old computation turns out to be wrong.
  • Monitor in detail. Watch performance metrics and error rates. Other engineering fields call this telemetry. Once a rocket leaves the ground, telemetry is how you track it and understand a failure. Monitoring gives early warnings and checks whether assumptions still hold, and metrics are invaluable when diagnosing a problem.
  • Good management and training. The book calls this an important part of the picture, but it is beyond the scope of the book.

How Important Is Reliability?

Reliability is not only for nuclear power stations and air traffic control software. Ordinary business applications also need to work. Bugs in them cost productivity, and wrong figures in reports can create legal risk. Outages at an e-commerce site can cost a great deal in lost revenue and damaged reputation.

Example

The book asks you to picture a parent who stores every photo and video of their children in your photo application. If that database suddenly became corrupted, how would they feel? Would they know how to restore it from a backup? The application may be a noncritical product for the company, but it is critical to that parent.

There are times when reliability can be sacrificed to save money. A team building a prototype for a market that has not been proven might accept more risk to cut development costs. A service with a very thin profit margin might accept more risk to cut operating costs. The book’s advice is to be very aware when you are cutting corners.

Key idea

Reliability means continuing to work correctly even when things go wrong. Expect faults from hardware, software, and people, and design so that faults do not become failures.

Scalability

A system that works reliably today may not work reliably tomorrow. A common reason for decline is increased load. Perhaps the system grew from 10,000 concurrent users (people using it at the same time) to 100,000, or from 1 million to 10 million. Perhaps it now processes far more data than before.

Scalability is the word for a system’s ability to cope with increased load. It is not a simple yes or no label. Saying “X is scalable” or “Y doesn’t scale” means very little. A better question is: if the system grows in a particular way, what are our options, and how can we add computing resources to handle the extra load?

Describing Load

Before you can discuss growth, you need a short, precise way to describe the current load. The book calls the few numbers that describe it load parameters. The right choice depends on the architecture. It might be requests per second to a web server, the ratio of reads to writes in a database, the number of people active at once in a chat room, or the hit rate on a cache (the share of lookups that the cache can answer). You also need to decide whether the average case matters most, or whether a small number of extreme cases dominates the bottleneck.

The book uses Twitter as its example, with data it published in November 2012. Two of Twitter’s main operations were:

  • Post tweet: a user publishes a new message to their followers. This ran at 4.6k requests per second on average, and over 12k at peak.
  • Home timeline: a user views the tweets posted by the people they follow. This ran at 300k requests per second.

Handling 12,000 writes per second, the peak rate for posting tweets, would be fairly easy. Twitter’s real scaling challenge is not tweet volume. It is fan-out, which means that each user follows many people and is followed by many people. The term is borrowed from electronics, where it counts how many inputs one output must drive. In transaction processing systems, it means the number of requests to other services that you must make to serve one incoming request. Here it describes how many timelines a single tweet has to reach.

There are broadly two ways to build the two operations.

Example

Approach 1: work at read time. Posting a tweet simply inserts it into one global collection of tweets. When a user asks for their home timeline, the system does the following steps:

  1. Look up all the people this user follows.
  2. Find all the tweets written by each of those people.
  3. Merge them into one list, sorted by time.

In a relational database, the book says the read could be a query like this:

SELECT tweets.*, users.*
FROM tweets
JOIN users ON tweets.sender_id = users.id
JOIN follows ON follows.followee_id = users.id
WHERE follows.follower_id = current_user
Example

Approach 2: work at write time. The system keeps a cache for each user’s home timeline, which works like a mailbox of tweets for that user. When a user posts a tweet, the system does the following steps:

  1. Look up everyone who follows that user.
  2. Insert the new tweet into the home timeline cache of each of those followers.

Reading a home timeline is then cheap, because the result was already computed ahead of time. The book’s own figures show the relational schema for approach 1 and the data pipeline for approach 2. The diagram below is a simplified picture of approach 2.

The first version of Twitter used approach 1. The systems struggled to keep up with home timeline queries, so the company switched to approach 2. The reason is a trade-off the book makes clear. The average rate of published tweets is almost two orders of magnitude lower than the rate of home timeline reads. That makes it better to do more work when a tweet is written and less work when a timeline is read.

Approach 2 has a cost, though. Posting a tweet now takes a lot of extra work. On average a tweet is delivered to about 75 followers. So 4.6k tweets per second become about 345k writes per second to the home timeline caches. The average hides a bigger problem. The number of followers per user varies wildly, and some users have over 30 million followers. A single tweet from one of those users can cause over 30 million writes. Twitter tries to deliver tweets to followers within five seconds, so doing this on time is a major engineering challenge.

In this example, the spread of follower counts (perhaps weighted by how often each user tweets) is a key load parameter, because it determines the fan-out load. Your own application will have different numbers, but the same reasoning applies.

The last twist is that Twitter is moving to a hybrid of both approaches. Most users’ tweets are still fanned out to home timelines when they are posted. A small number of users with very many followers, the celebrities, are left out of that fan-out. When a user reads their timeline, tweets from any celebrities they follow are fetched separately and merged in, the way approach 1 works. This hybrid delivers consistently good performance. The book returns to this example in Chapter 12, after it has covered more technical ground.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
Approach 1: combine at read timeWrites are cheap, since a tweet is one insertEvery timeline read does heavy work. The first Twitter version struggled with this load.
Approach 2: fan out at write timeTimeline reads are cheap, because the result is ready ahead of timeEach tweet causes many writes. A celebrity tweet can cause over 30 million.
Hybrid (Twitter’s direction)Consistently good performance, with fan-out for most users and read-time merging for celebritiesTwo mechanisms to build and run, and the read path must merge both sets of tweets correctly.
Try it

The book says the average tweet reaches about 75 followers, but some users have over 30 million. Imagine you run a timeline service with approach 2. Which accounts would you watch most closely, and what would the hybrid design change for them?

Describing Performance

Once you have described the load, you can ask what happens when the load increases. There are two ways to look at it:

  • If you increase a load parameter and keep the system’s resources (CPU, memory, network bandwidth, and so on) the same, how does performance change?
  • If you increase a load parameter, how much must you add to the resources to keep performance the same?

Both questions need performance numbers, so the book looks at how to describe performance first.

In a batch processing system such as Hadoop, the key measure is usually throughput. That is the number of records processed per second, or the total time to run a job on a dataset of a given size. In an ideal world, a batch job’s running time is the dataset size divided by the throughput. In practice it is often longer, because data is not spread evenly across workers (this is called skew), and the job has to wait for its slowest task to finish.

In online systems, what usually matters more is the response time. That is the time between a client sending a request and receiving a response.

Watch out

Latency and response time are often used to mean the same thing, but they are not the same. Response time is what the client sees. It includes the actual time to process the request (the service time), plus network delays and queueing delays. Latency is the time a request spends waiting to be handled, while it is latent, or waiting for service.

Response time is not one fixed number. Even if you send the same request again and again, each reply takes a slightly different time. In a system handling many kinds of requests, the variation can be large. So response time should be treated as a distribution of values that you measure, not as a single number.

Measuring response times

The book’s Figure 1-4 shows the response times of 100 requests to one service as a row of bars, one per request. Most requests are reasonably fast, but there are occasional outliers that take much longer. Some slow requests are intrinsically more expensive, because they process more data. But even when all requests should take the same time, you still see variation. Random extra delay can come from a context switch to a background process, the loss of a network packet and the TCP retransmission that follows, a garbage collection pause (when the language runtime pauses the program to clean up memory), a page fault that forces a read from disk, or even mechanical vibrations in the server rack.

It is common to see the average response time of a service reported. Strictly speaking, “average” does not name one formula, but in practice it means the arithmetic mean: add up all the values and divide by how many there are. The mean is not a good measure of a typical response time, because it does not tell you how many users actually experienced that delay.

Percentiles are usually better. Take your list of response times and sort it from fastest to slowest. The median is the halfway point. If the median is 200 ms (milliseconds), then half the requests return in less than 200 ms and half take longer. That makes the median a good answer to “how long do users typically wait?” It is also called the 50th percentile, or p50.

The median describes a single request. A user who loads a page with several resources, or who makes several requests during a session, is much more likely to hit at least one slow request. The probability that at least one of several requests is slower than the median is far greater than 50 percent.

To see how bad the outliers are, look at higher percentiles. The 95th, 99th, and 99.9th percentiles are common, written p95, p99, and p999. Each one is the response time at which 95, 99, or 99.9 percent of requests are faster. For example, if the 95th percentile is 1.5 seconds, then 95 out of 100 requests take less than 1.5 seconds, and 5 out of 100 take 1.5 seconds or more.

Key idea

Do not judge a service by its average alone. Look at percentiles such as the median, p95, and p99, because they show how many users actually had the slow experience.

Tail latency and why it matters

The highest percentiles are called tail latencies, and they matter because they shape users’ experience. Amazon describes response time requirements for internal services using the 99.9th percentile, even though that affects only 1 in 1,000 requests. The reason is that customers with the slowest requests are often the ones with the most data in their accounts, because they have made many purchases. They are also the most valuable customers, so keeping their experience fast matters.

The book gives two other figures about the cost of slowness. Amazon found that a 100 ms increase in response time reduces sales by 1 percent. Other reports say that a 1-second slowdown reduces a customer satisfaction measure by 16 percent. Amazon, however, chose not to optimize the 99.99th percentile, the slowest 1 in 10,000 requests, because it was too expensive for the benefit. At very high percentiles, response times are easily affected by random events outside your control, and each extra improvement brings less benefit.

Percentiles are used in service level objectives (SLOs), which are internal targets, and in service level agreements (SLAs), which are contracts that define the expected performance and availability of a service. An SLA might say that the service is considered up if its median response time is under 200 ms and its 99th percentile is under 1 second. (If responses take longer, the service might as well be down.) The same SLA could require the service to be up at least 99.9 percent of the time. These numbers set expectations for clients, and they let customers demand a refund if the SLA is not met.

Queueing and head-of-line blocking

Queueing delays often make up a large part of the response time at high percentiles. A server can only process a small number of things in parallel, limited by its number of CPU cores, for example. So a small number of slow requests can hold up the requests behind them. This is called head-of-line blocking. Even if the later requests are quick to process on the server, the client sees a slow overall response, because it waited for the earlier request to finish.

For this reason, the book says it is important to measure response times on the client side. The server’s own timing misses the time spent waiting in the queue.

The same issue affects load testing. When you generate artificial load to test scalability, the load-generating client must keep sending requests regardless of how fast the responses come back. If the client waits for each response before sending the next request, the queues in the test stay shorter than they would be in real life. That skews the measurements.

Percentiles in Practice

High percentiles become especially important in backend services that are called several times to serve one end-user request. Even if the calls are made in parallel, the end-user request must wait for the slowest of them to finish. One slow call is enough to make the whole request slow.

This is shown in the book’s Figure 1-5. A small share of slow backend calls can still cause a larger share of slow end-user requests, because the chance of meeting at least one slow call grows with the number of calls. The book calls this tail latency amplification.

If you want to add response time percentiles to the monitoring dashboards for your services, you need to calculate them efficiently and continuously. For example, you might keep a rolling window of the response times of requests in the last 10 minutes. Every minute, you calculate the median and the other percentiles over the values in that window, and plot them on a graph.

The naive way is to keep a list of all response times in the window and sort it every minute. If that is too slow or uses too much memory, there are algorithms that approximate percentiles with little CPU and memory cost. The book names forward decay, t-digest, and HdrHistogram as examples.

A common mistake to avoid: averaging percentiles is mathematically meaningless, whether you do it to reduce time resolution or to combine data from several machines. Instead, add up the histograms (counts of how many requests fell into each time range) and compute the percentile from the total.

Approaches for Coping with Load

Now that the book has covered how to describe load and measure performance, it turns to scalability itself. How do you keep performance good when your load parameters increase?

An architecture that suits one level of load is unlikely to cope with ten times that load. If you work on a fast-growing service, you will probably need to rethink the architecture every time the load grows by an order of magnitude (a factor of ten), or even more often.

People often talk about a choice between two approaches:

  • Scaling up (vertical scaling) means moving to a more powerful machine.
  • Scaling out (horizontal scaling) means spreading the load across several smaller machines. Spreading load over many machines is also called a shared-nothing architecture, because the machines do not share memory or disks.

A system that runs on one machine is often simpler. But high-end machines become very expensive, so very demanding workloads often cannot avoid scaling out. In practice, good architectures usually mix the two. For example, several fairly powerful machines can be simpler and cheaper than a large number of small virtual machines.

The book also contrasts two ways of adding capacity. An elastic system adds computing resources automatically when it detects a load increase. A manually scaled system waits for a person to analyze capacity and decide to add machines. Elastic systems help when load is hard to predict. Manually scaled systems are simpler and may have fewer surprises in operation. The book returns to this in its later discussion of rebalancing partitions.

Distributing stateless services (services that keep no data of their own between requests) across machines is fairly straightforward. Stateful data systems are different. Moving a database from a single node (one machine) to a distributed setup adds a lot of complexity. Until recently, the common wisdom was to keep your database on one node, scaling up, until the cost of scaling or the need for high availability forced you to distribute it. The book notes that this may change as tools for distributed systems improve. Distributed data systems might even become the default one day, including for applications that do not handle large volumes of data. The rest of the book covers many kinds of distributed data systems and looks at how they fare in ease of use and maintainability, not only in scalability.

There is no one-size-fits-all scalable architecture. The problem might be the volume of reads, the volume of writes, the volume of data to store, the complexity of the data, the response time requirements, the access patterns, or, usually, a mixture of all of these. A system built to handle 100,000 requests per second, each 1 kB in size, looks very different from one built for 3 requests per minute, each 2 GB in size. Even so, the two have the same data throughput.

An architecture that scales well for a particular application is built around assumptions about which operations will be common and which will be rare. These assumptions are the load parameters. If they turn out to be wrong, the effort spent on scaling is wasted at best, and counterproductive at worst. For an early-stage startup or an unproven product, it is usually more important to iterate quickly on features than to prepare for a hypothetical future load.

Even though each scalable architecture is specific to its application, it is usually built from general-purpose building blocks arranged in familiar patterns. The rest of the book covers those building blocks and patterns.

Try it

Two systems have the same data throughput. One handles 100,000 requests per second, each 1 kB. The other handles 3 requests per minute, each 2 GB. Which one would be harder to run, and why? Think about how many requests each server must handle and how big each request is.

Maintainability

Most of the cost of software is not in its first version. It is in ongoing maintenance: fixing bugs, keeping the system running, investigating failures, adapting it to new platforms, changing it for new use cases, paying off technical debt (shortcuts that make later work slower), and adding features.

Many people dislike maintaining so-called legacy systems, which are older systems that are hard to change. Perhaps the work involves fixing other people’s mistakes, working with platforms that are now outdated, or dealing with systems forced to do things they were never designed for. Every legacy system is unpleasant in its own way, so general advice for them is hard to give.

We can, however, design software so that maintenance hurts less, and so that we do not create new legacy systems. The book pays particular attention to three design principles.

  • Operability: make it easy for operations teams to keep the system running smoothly.
  • Simplicity: make it easy for new engineers to understand the system, by removing as much complexity as possible. This is not the same as simplicity of the user interface.
  • Evolvability: make it easy for engineers to change the system later, as requirements change. It is also called extensibility, modifiability, or plasticity.

As with reliability and scalability, there are no easy solutions. The book instead asks you to think about systems with operability, simplicity, and evolvability in mind.

Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations

The book quotes an idea that good operations can often work around the limits of bad software, but good software cannot run reliably with bad operations. Some parts of operations can be automated. But people still have to set up the automation and make sure it keeps working.

A good operations team is responsible for many things, including:

  • Monitoring the health of the system and quickly restoring service when it goes into a bad state.
  • Tracking down the cause of failures or slow performance.
  • Keeping software and platforms up to date, including security patches.
  • Watching how systems affect each other, so that a risky change can be avoided before it causes damage.
  • Anticipating problems before they happen, for example through capacity planning.
  • Setting up good practices and tools for deployment and configuration management.
  • Carrying out complex tasks, such as moving an application from one platform to another.
  • Keeping the system secure as configuration changes are made.
  • Defining processes that make operations predictable and the production environment stable.
  • Keeping the organization’s knowledge of the system, even as people come and go.

Good operability means making routine tasks easy, so that the team can spend its effort on high-value work. Data systems can help in several ways:

  • Give visibility into runtime behavior and internals, through good monitoring.
  • Support automation and integrate well with standard tools.
  • Avoid depending on any one machine, so that machines can be taken down for maintenance while the whole system keeps running.
  • Provide good documentation and an easy-to-understand operational model, so people can predict the result of an action (“if I do X, Y will happen”).
  • Provide good default behavior, while still letting administrators override the defaults when needed.
  • Heal themselves where appropriate, while still letting administrators take manual control of the system state when needed.
  • Behave predictably and minimize surprises.

Simplicity: Managing Complexity

Small software projects can have delightfully simple and expressive code. As projects grow, they often become very complex and hard to understand. That complexity slows down everyone who works on the system and raises the cost of maintenance. A project mired in complexity is sometimes called a big ball of mud.

Complexity has many symptoms. The state space can explode, modules can be tightly coupled, dependencies can be tangled, names and terms can be inconsistent, performance hacks pile up, and special cases appear to work around problems elsewhere. When maintenance is hard, budgets and schedules overrun. In a complex system, a developer making a change is also more likely to introduce a bug, because hidden assumptions, unintended consequences, and unexpected interactions are easy to miss when the system is hard to reason about. Reducing complexity therefore greatly improves maintainability, and simplicity should be a key goal.

Simplicity does not always mean fewer features. It can also mean removing accidental complexity. The book uses Moseley and Marks’s definition: complexity is accidental if it is not inherent in the problem the software solves, as the users see it, and arises only from the way the software was implemented.

One of the best tools for removing accidental complexity is abstraction. A good abstraction hides a great deal of implementation detail behind a clean, simple façade (a simple outer face). It can also be reused across many applications. Reuse is more efficient than rebuilding the same thing several times, and it improves quality, because every improvement to the shared component benefits all the applications that use it.

Two examples from the book. High-level programming languages hide machine code, CPU registers, and system calls. SQL hides complex on-disk and in-memory data structures, concurrent requests from other clients, and inconsistencies after a crash. You are still running machine code in a high-level language, but you do not have to think about it.

Finding good abstractions is very hard. In distributed systems there are many good algorithms, but it is much less clear how to package them into abstractions that keep the system manageable. The book promises to look for good abstractions throughout, so that parts of a large system can be pulled out as well-defined, reusable components.

Evolvability: Making Change Easy

Your system’s requirements will almost certainly not stay the same. They are in constant flux. You learn new facts, unanticipated use cases appear, business priorities change, users ask for new features, new platforms replace old ones, legal rules change, and growth forces architectural changes.

Agile working patterns provide a way to handle change at the level of an organization. The Agile community has also developed technical tools, such as test-driven development (TDD, writing tests before the code) and refactoring (improving a program’s structure without changing what it does). These are useful when software changes often.

Most discussions of these techniques focus on a fairly small scale, such as a few source files in the same application. The book looks for ways to increase agility on the level of a whole data system, which may consist of several applications or services. For example, how would you refactor Twitter’s architecture for assembling home timelines from approach 1 to approach 2? That is a change to the whole design, not to a single file.

How easily you can modify a data system depends closely on its simplicity and its abstractions. Simple, easy-to-understand systems are usually easier to change than complex ones. Because this idea is so important, the book uses a separate word for agility at the level of a data system: evolvability.

Rule of thumb

Simple systems with good abstractions are easier to run and easier to change. Every extra piece of accidental complexity is a cost that your future self and your colleagues will pay.

Summary

Summary
  • Requirements. An application has functional requirements (what it should do, such as storing, retrieving, searching, and processing data) and nonfunctional requirements (such as security, reliability, compliance, scalability, compatibility, and maintainability). This chapter focused on reliability, scalability, and maintainability.
  • Reliability means making systems work correctly even when faults occur. Faults can come from hardware (typically random and uncorrelated), from software (bugs are typically systematic and hard to handle), and from humans (who inevitably make mistakes from time to time). Fault-tolerance techniques can hide some faults from the end user.
  • Scalability means having strategies to keep performance good as load increases. To discuss it, you first need quantitative ways to describe load and performance. The chapter used Twitter’s home timelines as an example of describing load, and response time percentiles as a way of measuring performance. A scalable system lets you add processing capacity to stay reliable under high load.
  • Maintainability has many facets, but at heart it is about making life better for the engineering and operations teams who work with the system. Good abstractions reduce complexity and make a system easier to modify for new uses. Good operability means having visibility into the system’s health and effective ways of managing it.

There is no easy fix for making applications reliable, scalable, or maintainable. But certain patterns and techniques keep reappearing across different kinds of applications. The next few chapters look at examples of data systems and analyze how they work toward those goals. Part III then looks at patterns for systems made of several components working together, such as the composite system shown earlier in this chapter.

The chapter ends with a numbered list of 34 references to papers, blog posts, and talks that support its claims, such as the Chaos Monkey post and the paper The Tail at Scale. This retelling does not reproduce that list.

Check yourself

  1. Twitter’s first design built each home timeline at read time. Why did it move to copying each tweet into followers’ timeline caches at write time?

    Show answer

    Home timeline reads are far more frequent than tweet posts, almost two orders of magnitude more. Doing more work at write time and less at read time was the better trade for that load.

  2. The 95th percentile response time of a service is 1.5 seconds. Out of every 100 requests, how many take 1.5 seconds or longer?

    Show answer

    Five. The 95th percentile means 95 of 100 requests are faster than 1.5 seconds, so the remaining 5 take 1.5 seconds or more.

  3. An end-user request calls five backend services in parallel. Why can one slow backend call make the whole request slow, and why does the problem get worse as the number of calls grows?

    Show answer

    The end-user request has to wait for the slowest of the parallel calls. With more calls, the chance that at least one is slow rises, so a larger share of end-user requests end up slow. The book calls this tail latency amplification.

  4. In a RAID set, one disk fails, but the system keeps serving users without interruption. Is this a fault, a failure, or both?

    Show answer

    It is a fault, because one component deviated from its specification. It is not a failure, because the system as a whole still provides the service. Redundancy kept the fault from becoming a failure.

Part I · Chapter 2

Data Models and Query Languages

The big idea: a data model is the lens through which you see your data. It shapes what is easy to write, what is slow, and how you think about the problem. Relational, document, and graph models each suit a different shape of data, and each is awkward for the others.

A data model is the way information is described, stored, and asked about. Choosing one is among the most important decisions in building software. It affects how the code is written, and also how the people building it think about the problem.

Most applications are built by stacking one data model on top of another. At each layer the question is the same: how is this layer represented in terms of the layer below? The book describes four levels:

  1. An application developer looks at the real world (people, organizations, goods, actions, money flows, sensors) and models it as objects or data structures, along with the APIs that work on them.
  2. To store those structures, the developer expresses them in a general-purpose data model, such as JSON or XML documents, tables in a relational database, or a graph.
  3. The engineers who built the database decide how that data is represented as bytes in memory, on disk, or on a network. The representation determines how the data can be queried and processed.
  4. Hardware engineers represent those bytes as electrical currents, pulses of light, or magnetic fields.

Real systems can have more layers, such as APIs built on other APIs, but the idea is the same. Each layer hides the complexity below it behind a clean model. That lets different groups work together. The engineers at a database vendor and the developers who use that database do not need to share every detail.

Every data model carries assumptions about how it will be used. Some uses are easy and some are not supported at all. Some operations are fast and others perform badly. The book notes that you could fill many books just on relational data modeling, so mastering one model takes real effort. Because the model has such a deep effect on what the software can do, it is worth choosing one that fits the application.

This chapter covers the second level in the list: general-purpose models for storing and querying data. It compares the relational model, the document model, and several graph models, and it looks at the query languages that go with each. Chapter 3 covers the third level, which is how these models are actually implemented as storage engines.

The chapter opens with a line from the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein: “The limits of my language mean the limits of my world.” The models you know shape what you can easily think to ask.

Relational Model Versus Document Model

The best-known data model today is the one behind SQL. It is based on the relational model, which Edgar Codd proposed in 1970. In this model, data is organized into relations, called tables in SQL. Each relation is an unordered collection of tuples, called rows in SQL.

When the idea appeared, many people doubted it could be built efficiently. By the mid-1980s, though, relational database management systems (RDBMSes, the software that runs a relational database) and SQL had become the usual tools for anyone storing data with a regular structure. Relational databases have dominated for about 25 to 30 years, which is a very long time in computing.

Their roots are in business data processing on mainframe computers in the 1960s and 1970s. The jobs look mundane today: transaction processing, which means recording sales, bank transactions, airline reservations, and warehouse stock, and batch processing, which means running jobs such as customer invoicing, payroll, and reports on large amounts of data at once. Earlier databases forced developers to think hard about how data was laid out internally. The relational model aimed to hide that detail behind a cleaner interface.

In the 1970s and early 1980s the network and hierarchical models were the main rivals, but the relational model came to dominate them. Object databases came and went in the late 1980s and early 1990s. XML databases appeared in the early 2000s but found only niche use. Each challenger generated hype and then faded. Relational databases, though, turned out to generalize well beyond business data. Much of what is on the web today still runs on them, including online publishing, discussion sites, social networks, e-commerce, games, and software-as-a-service products.

The Birth of NoSQL

NoSQL is the name for the newer wave of databases that try to overturn the relational model’s dominance. The name is unfortunate, because it does not refer to any one technology. It began as a catchy hashtag for a 2009 meetup about open source, distributed, nonrelational databases. The label spread quickly through the web startup community, and it was later reinterpreted as Not Only SQL.

The book lists four forces behind the adoption of NoSQL databases:

  • A need for more scalability than relational databases can easily reach, such as very large datasets or very high rates of writes.
  • A widespread preference for free and open source software over commercial products.
  • Specialized query operations that the relational model does not support well.
  • Frustration with strict relational schemas, meaning the fixed description of which tables and columns exist and what they hold, and a wish for a more dynamic and expressive model.

Different applications have different needs, so the best tool for one job may not be the best for another. The book expects relational databases to keep running alongside a wide variety of nonrelational datastores. This mix is called polyglot persistence: several storage technologies used together, each for the job it does best.

The Object-Relational Mismatch

Most application code is written in object-oriented languages. A common criticism of SQL is that if data is stored in relational tables, an awkward translation layer is needed between the objects in the code and the tables, rows, and columns in the database. The gap between the two models is called an impedance mismatch. The term comes from electronics, where a poor match between two circuits wastes power and causes signal reflections.

Object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks, such as ActiveRecord and Hibernate, cut down the boilerplate in that translation layer. But they cannot hide all the differences between the two models.

The book uses a résumé, such as a LinkedIn profile, to show the problem. Its Figure 2-1 represents one in a relational schema. The profile as a whole is identified by a user_id. Fields like first name and last name appear once per person, so they can be columns on a users table. But most people have had several jobs, several periods of education, and any number of pieces of contact information. Each of those is a one-to-many relationship: one user has many positions. The book describes three ways to represent that in a database:

  • The traditional normalized way, before SQL:1999: put positions, education, and contact information in separate tables. Each table has a foreign key, a column holding the ID of a row in another table, pointing back to the users table.
  • Later SQL standards added structured types and XML support. These allow several values to sit inside one row, and they can be queried and indexed. Several major databases support this to varying degrees, and several support a JSON type as well.
  • Encode the jobs and education as one JSON or XML document, store it in a text column, and let the application interpret it. In this setup the database usually cannot query values inside that text.
Example

For a self-contained document like a résumé, the book says a JSON representation can be quite appropriate. JSON is much simpler than XML. Document databases such as MongoDB, RethinkDB, CouchDB, and Espresso store data in this model. The book’s Example 2-1 shows a profile for Bill Gates, shortened here:

{
  "user_id": 251,
  "first_name": "Bill",
  "last_name": "Gates",
  "positions": [
    {"job_title": "Co-chair", "organization": "Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation"},
    {"job_title": "Co-founder, Chairman", "organization": "Microsoft"}
  ],
  ...
}

Read step by step, the document works like this. The user_id of 251 identifies the profile. The top-level fields hold the name, a short summary, a region ID and an industry ID, and a photo URL. positions is a list of two objects: Co-chair at the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and Co-founder and Chairman at Microsoft. education is a list with Harvard University (1973 to 1975) and Lakeside School, Seattle, which has no dates. contact_info is a nested object holding a blog link and a Twitter link. Everything about this person sits in one document.

Some developers feel that JSON reduces the impedance mismatch, because the document looks like the object in the code. The book adds two cautions. JSON has problems of its own as an encoding format, which Chapter 4 covers. And the lack of a schema, often cited as an advantage, is a topic the chapter returns to later.

The JSON form also has better locality, meaning related data is stored close together. To fetch a profile in the relational layout, you either query each table by user_id, or write a messy multi-way join across the users table and its related tables. In the JSON form, all the relevant information is in one place, and one query is enough. The one-to-many links form a tree: the profile is the root, and the positions, schools, and contacts are branches. The diagram below shows the two layouts side by side.

Many-to-One and Many-to-Many Relationships

In Example 2-1, region_id and industry_id are IDs, not plain text such as “Greater Seattle Area” or “Philanthropy”. Why? If the page had free-text boxes for region and industry, plain strings would work. But a standard list of regions and industries, chosen from a drop-down menu or an autocomplete box, has several advantages:

  • Consistent style and spelling across profiles.
  • No ambiguity, for example when several cities share the same name.
  • Easy updates, because the name is stored in only one place. If a city is renamed, one change fixes it everywhere.
  • Localization. When the site is translated, the list can be translated too, so each region is shown in the viewer’s language.
  • Better search. A search for philanthropists in Washington State can match this profile, because the list of regions can record that Seattle is in Washington. That fact is not visible in the text “Greater Seattle Area”.
Example

Take the profile with region_id set to us:91, as in the book. The region’s name lives in one row of a regions list. Suppose a city is renamed after a political change. You update that one row, and every profile that points to it is correct at once. If each profile had stored the text instead, every profile with that text would need its own update. Some of those updates might be missed, and the copies would then disagree.

Whether you store an ID or a text string is a question of duplication. With an ID, the human-meaningful information (such as the word Philanthropy) is stored in one place, and everything else refers to it with an ID. The ID means nothing to people, so it never needs to change, even when the thing it names changes. With text, the information is copied into every record that uses it. Any future change then means updating every copy, which costs writes and risks copies that disagree. Removing this duplication is the key idea behind normalization, the practice of organizing a database so each fact is stored once.

Rule of thumb

If you are duplicating values that could be stored in just one place, the schema is not normalized. The book notes that the formal normal forms in the literature matter less in practice than this rule.

Database administrators and developers like to argue about normalization and its opposite, denormalization, which means copying data on purpose to make reads faster. The book suspends judgment here. It returns to the topic in Part III, which covers caching, denormalization, and derived data.

Normalizing this data needs many-to-one relationships: many people live in one region, and many people work in one industry. These do not fit the document model neatly. In relational databases it is normal to refer to rows in other tables by ID, because a join, which combines rows from two tables in one query, is easy. In document databases, joins are not needed for one-to-many tree structures, and support for joins is often weak. The book notes that at the time of writing, RethinkDB supported joins, MongoDB did not, and CouchDB supported them only in predeclared views.

If the database cannot join, the application has to emulate a join with several queries and combine the results itself. For the region and industry lists, which are small and change slowly, the application could keep them in memory. Even so, the work of the join has moved from the database into the application code.

Data also tends to become more connected as features are added. The book gives two changes to the résumé example:

Organizations and schools as entities. At the moment, the company and the school are just strings. Perhaps each should be a reference to its own entity, with its own page, logo, and news feed. Then a résumé could link to the organizations and schools it mentions and show their logos. Figure 2-3 in the book shows LinkedIn doing this for company names.

Recommendations. One user can write a recommendation for another. It appears on the recommended person’s résumé, together with the name and photo of the person who wrote it. If the author changes their photo, the recommendations they wrote should show the new one. So the recommendation should hold a reference to the author’s profile, not a copy of their name and photo.

Figure 2-4 in the book shows that these features need many-to-many relationships. The data inside each dotted box can be grouped into one document. But the references to organizations, schools, and other users must be stored as references, and they require joins when queried.

Are Document Databases Repeating History?

Many-to-many relationships are routine in relational databases. Document databases and NoSQL reopened the debate about how best to represent them. That debate is older than NoSQL, and it goes back to the very earliest computerized databases.

The most popular business database of the 1970s was IBM’s Information Management System (IMS). It was developed for stock-keeping in the Apollo space program and first released commercially in 1968. It is still maintained and runs on IBM mainframes. IMS used the hierarchical model, which stores all data as a tree of records nested inside records, much like the JSON in Figure 2-2. The book notes that this has remarkable similarities to the JSON model used by document databases.

Like document databases, IMS worked well for one-to-many relationships. It made many-to-many relationships difficult, and it had no joins. Developers had to choose between duplicating data (denormalizing it) and resolving references from one record to another by hand. The book says these problems of the 1960s and 1970s are much like the ones developers meet with document databases today.

Two solutions were proposed. The first was the relational model, which became SQL and took over the world. The second was the network model, which had a large following at first and then faded away. The debate between these two camps lasted much of the 1970s. Since the problem is still so relevant, the book revisits the debate in today’s light.

The network model. The network model was standardized by a committee called CODASYL (the Conference on Data Systems Languages), and several vendors implemented it. It generalized the hierarchical model. In a tree, each record has exactly one parent. In the network model, a record can have several parents. For example, one record for the Greater Seattle Area region could be linked to every user who lives there. That made many-to-one and many-to-many relationships possible.

The links in the network model were not foreign keys. They were more like pointers in a programming language, stored on disk. The only way to reach a record was to follow an access path, a chain of links starting at a root record. In the simplest case that is like walking a linked list, looking at one record at a time. With many-to-many links, several paths can lead to the same record, and the programmer had to keep all of them in mind. Even the committee’s members admitted that this was like navigating an n-dimensional data space.

Queries worked by moving a cursor through lists of records and following access paths. Choosing paths by hand made good use of the slow hardware of the 1970s, such as tape drives. But it made the query and update code complicated and inflexible. If you needed data that had no path, you were stuck. You had to change the access paths and then rewrite a lot of handwritten query code.

The relational model. The relational model laid all the data out in the open. A relation is simply a collection of tuples, and that is it. There are no nested structures and no access paths to follow. You can read any or all of the rows in a table, selecting those that match any condition. You can read a particular row by naming some columns as a key and matching on them. You can insert a new row into any table without worrying about foreign key links to and from other tables. (Foreign key constraints are optional. The relational model does not require them. In CODASYL, the link was effectively made at insert time, while in a relational database a join on a foreign key happens at query time.)

In a relational database, a query optimizer, which is the part of the database that decides how to run each query, automatically chooses the order of the steps and which indexes to use. (An index is a separate structure that helps the database find rows quickly.) Those choices are effectively the access path, but the database makes them, not the application developer, so we rarely need to think about them. If you want to query your data in a new way, you can declare a new index, and queries will use it automatically. You do not change the queries. The relational model made it much easier to add new features to applications.

Query optimizers are complicated, and they consumed many years of research and development. The key insight is that you only need to build one optimizer, and then every application that uses the database benefits from it. Without an optimizer, it can seem easier to hand-code the access path for one particular query. But the general-purpose solution wins in the long run.

Comparison to document databases. Document databases went back to the hierarchical model in one respect: they store nested records, such as the positions, education, and contact info in Figure 2-1, inside their parent record rather than in a separate table. For many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, though, relational and document databases are not fundamentally different. In both, the related item is referenced by a unique identifier. In the relational model that identifier is a foreign key. In the document model it is a document reference. Either way, the reference is resolved at read time, using a join or follow-up queries. So far, document databases have not followed the path of CODASYL.

Relational Versus Document Databases Today

Relational and document databases differ in many ways, including fault tolerance (Chapter 5) and how they handle concurrency (Chapter 7). This chapter looks only at the data model. The main arguments for the document model are schema flexibility, better performance from locality, and a closer match to the data structures used in application code. The relational model answers with better support for joins and for many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.

Which data model leads to simpler application code? If your data has a document-like structure, meaning a tree of one-to-many relationships that is usually loaded all at once, a document model is probably a good idea. The relational technique of shredding, which splits such a structure across several tables, can lead to cumbersome schemas and unnecessarily complicated application code.

The document model has its limits. You cannot refer directly to a nested item within a document. Instead you must point to it by position, as in the second entry in user 251’s list of positions. That is much like an access path in the hierarchical model. As long as documents are not too deeply nested, that is usually not a problem.

Poor support for joins may or may not matter. An analytics application that uses a document database to record which events happened at which times may never need many-to-many relationships. But if your application does use them, the document model becomes less appealing. You can reduce the need for joins by denormalizing, but then the application code must work to keep the copies consistent. You can emulate joins by making several requests, but that moves complexity into the application and is usually slower than a join done by specialized code inside the database. In such cases a document model can lead to much more complex application code and worse performance.

So the book says it is impossible to say in general which model gives simpler code. It depends on the relationships between data items. For highly interconnected data, the document model is awkward, the relational model is acceptable, and graph models are the most natural.

Schema flexibility in the document model. Most document databases, and the JSON support in relational databases, do not enforce any schema on the data in documents. XML support in relational databases usually comes with optional schema validation. With no schema, arbitrary keys and values can be added to a document, and when reading, clients have no guarantee about which fields a document contains.

Watch out

Document databases are often called schemaless, but the book says that name is misleading. The code that reads the data usually assumes some structure, so there is an implicit schema. It is just not enforced by the database.

A more accurate term is schema-on-read. The structure is implicit, and it is only interpreted when the data is read. This contrasts with schema-on-write, the traditional relational approach, where the schema is explicit and the database makes sure every written record conforms to it. The first is similar to dynamic type checking in a programming language, and the second is similar to static, compile-time type checking. Programmers argue about the merits of each, and the book says the same is true of database schemas. There is no clear right or wrong answer.

The difference shows most clearly when an application wants to change the format of its data. Say you currently store each user’s full name in one field, and you want first and last names stored separately. In a document database, you start writing new documents with the new fields, and you add code that handles old documents when they are read. The book’s example is this:

if (user && user.name && !user.first_name) {
  // Documents written before Dec 8, 2013 don't have first_name
  user.first_name = user.name.split(" ")[0];
}

In a statically typed relational schema, you would run a migration instead:

ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN first_name text;
UPDATE users SET first_name = split_part(name, ' ', 1);  -- PostgreSQL
UPDATE users SET first_name = substring_index(name, ' ', 1);  -- MySQL
Example
