The book walks through the cost of each route. Schema changes have a bad reputation for being slow and requiring downtime, and the book says this is not entirely deserved. Most relational systems run ALTER TABLE in a few milliseconds. MySQL is the notable exception. It copies the entire table during ALTER TABLE, which can mean minutes or even hours of downtime on a large table, although tools exist to work around this.

The UPDATE is a different matter. It is likely to be slow on any database, because every row must be rewritten. If that is not acceptable, the application can leave first_name set to its default of NULL (meaning no value) and fill it in at read time, the same way it would with a document database.

Schema-on-read is an advantage when the items in a collection do not all share the same structure. That happens when there are many different types of objects, and putting each type in its own table is impractical. It also happens when the structure is set by external systems that you do not control and that may change at any time. In those situations a schema may hurt more than it helps, and schemaless documents can be a more natural model. But when all records are expected to have the same structure, a schema is a useful way to document and enforce it. Chapter 4 discusses schemas and how they change over time.

Try it

Think of an application you know. Which of its data is a tree of one-to-many items that is always read together, such as a profile and its list of addresses? Which data is shared, such as a region or product category that many records point to? Where would you put the boundary between documents and references?

Data locality for queries. A document is usually stored as a single continuous string, encoded as JSON, XML, or a binary variant such as MongoDB’s BSON. If your application often needs the whole document, for example to render a web page, storing it as one unit is a performance advantage. Data split across tables, as in Figure 2-1, needs several index lookups to gather, which can mean more disk seeks and more time.

The locality advantage only helps if you need large parts of the document at the same time. The database typically loads the entire document even if you need only a small part of it, which is wasteful for large documents. When a document is updated, the whole thing is usually rewritten. Only changes that do not alter the encoded size can easily be made in place. For these reasons the book recommends keeping documents fairly small and avoiding writes that make a document grow. These limits reduce the set of situations in which document databases are useful.

Grouping related data together for locality is not limited to the document model. Google’s Spanner lets a relational schema declare that one table’s rows should be interleaved, or nested, inside a parent table. Oracle offers the same with a feature called multi-table index cluster tables. The column-family concept in the Bigtable data model, used in Cassandra and HBase, also serves to manage locality. Chapter 3 says more about locality.

Convergence of document and relational databases. Most relational database systems, other than MySQL, have supported XML since the mid-2000s. This includes functions to make local changes to XML documents, and the ability to index and query inside them. Applications can therefore use data models very similar to those of a document database. PostgreSQL since version 9.3, MySQL since version 5.7, and IBM DB2 since version 10.5 offer a similar level of support for JSON documents. Given how popular JSON is for web APIs, the book expects other relational databases to follow.

On the document side, RethinkDB supports relational-like joins in its query language. Some MongoDB drivers automatically resolve database references. That is effectively a join done on the client side. It is likely to be slower than a join done inside the database, because it needs extra network round trips and is less optimized.

The book also points out that relational pioneer Edgar Codd’s original description of the relational model allowed something close to JSON documents inside a relational schema. A value in a row did not have to be a simple number or string. It could be a nested table, giving an arbitrarily nested tree structure. That kind of support was added to SQL over 30 years later, in the form of JSON and XML.

The book sees the two kinds of database becoming more similar over time, and it considers that a good thing, because the data models complement each other. If one database can handle document-like data and also run relational queries on it, applications can use the combination of features that best fits their needs. The book’s conclusion is that a hybrid of the relational and document models is a good route for databases to take in the future.

Query Languages for Data

When the relational model arrived, it brought a new way of asking for data. SQL is a declarative query language, while IMS and CODASYL queried their databases with imperative code. What is the difference?

Most common programming languages are imperative. They tell the computer to perform certain steps in a certain order. Suppose you have a list of animal species and want only the sharks. You might write a function like this in JavaScript:

function getSharks() {
  var sharks = [];
  for (var i = 0; i < animals.length; i++) {
    if (animals[i].family === "Sharks") {
      sharks.push(animals[i]);
    }
  }
  return sharks;
}

The function creates an empty list. It loops over every animal. For each one, it checks whether the family is Sharks, and if so, adds the animal to the list. Finally it returns the list. You can picture stepping through it line by line, checking conditions, updating variables, and deciding whether to go around the loop once more.

In relational algebra, the same result is written as a single expression, where σ (the Greek letter sigma) is the selection operator. It returns only the animals that match the condition family = Sharks. SQL was designed to follow the structure of relational algebra fairly closely. The equivalent SQL is one line:

SELECT * FROM animals WHERE family = 'Sharks';

A declarative language does not give the steps. You specify the pattern of the data you want: the conditions the results must meet, and how the results should be transformed, such as sorted, grouped, or added up. You do not say how to get there. The database system’s query optimizer decides which indexes and which join methods to use, and in what order to run the parts of the query.

Declarative queries have two main advantages:

  • They are usually more concise and easier to work with than an imperative API.
  • They hide the details of the database engine. That means the database can add performance improvements without any change to the queries.

Consider the ordering of the animals in the imperative example. The list comes back in a particular order, and the code may depend on that order. If the database wants to reclaim unused disk space, it might need to move records around, which would change that order. Can it do so safely? With the SQL version, yes. SQL does not promise any particular order, so the database is free to rearrange the rows. With imperative code, the database cannot be sure whether the program relies on the order. The fact that SQL offers less functionality gives the database much more room for automatic optimization.

Declarative languages also suit parallel execution. The book notes that CPUs are getting faster by adding more cores, not by running at much higher clock speeds. Imperative code is very hard to parallelize across cores and machines, because it spells out instructions that must run in a particular order. A declarative query states only the pattern of the results, not the algorithm for producing them. So the database is free to run it in parallel if that is appropriate.

Declarative Queries on the Web

The advantages of declarative languages are not limited to databases. The book compares the two styles in a web browser. Suppose you have a page about ocean animals with a navigation list. The Sharks item is the page currently shown, so its list item carries the CSS class selected, and its title sits in a paragraph inside that item. Now you want the title of the selected page to have a blue background. With CSS, that is one rule:

li.selected > p {
  background-color: blue;
}

The selector li.selected > p describes a pattern: every paragraph whose direct parent is a list item with the class selected. The Sharks title matches. The Whales title does not, because its list item lacks the class. The browser does the matching for you. XSL, a stylesheet language for XML, can express the same idea with the XPath expression li[@class='selected']/p. Both CSS and XSL are declarative styling languages.

Doing the same thing imperatively in JavaScript, using the core DOM API, means looping over every list item, checking its class, looping over its children, checking which are paragraphs, and then setting a style on the matching ones. It works, but it is much longer and harder to read. It also has two serious problems:

  • If the selected class is removed, say because the user clicked a different page, the blue stays. Rerunning the code does not remove it, so the item stays highlighted until the whole page reloads. With CSS, the browser notices by itself when the rule no longer applies and removes the blue as soon as the class goes.
  • If you want to use a newer API, such as getElementsByClassName or document.evaluate, which may be faster, you must rewrite the code. Browser vendors, on the other hand, can speed up CSS and XPath without breaking compatibility.

The book’s conclusion is that declarative CSS is much better than imperative style manipulation in JavaScript. In the same way, declarative query languages such as SQL turned out to be much better than imperative query APIs for databases. (IMS and CODASYL both used imperative APIs. Applications typically used COBOL code to step through the records one at a time.)

MapReduce Querying

MapReduce is a programming model, popularized by Google, for processing large amounts of data in bulk across many machines. Some NoSQL datastores, including MongoDB and CouchDB, support a limited form of it as a way to run read-only queries across many documents. Chapter 10 covers MapReduce in general. Here the book briefly looks at how MongoDB uses it.

MapReduce is neither a declarative query language nor a fully imperative query API. It sits somewhere in between. The query logic is written as snippets of code, and the processing framework calls those snippets repeatedly. The model is based on two functions found in many functional programming languages: map, which is also called collect, and reduce, which is also called fold or inject.

Example

Imagine you are a marine biologist. Every time you see animals in the ocean, you add an observation record to your database. You now want a report of how many sharks you have sighted each month. In PostgreSQL you could write:

SELECT date_trunc('month', observation_timestamp) AS observation_month,
       sum(num_animals) AS total_animals
FROM observations
WHERE family = 'Sharks'
GROUP BY observation_month;

Step by step, this query first keeps only the observations in the Sharks family. The function date_trunc('month', timestamp) finds the calendar month containing a timestamp and returns the start of that month, which rounds the timestamp down to the nearest month. The query then groups the observations by month and adds up the number of animals in each group.

The same report can be written with MongoDB’s MapReduce feature. The call takes three things: a map function, a reduce function, and options. The options include a query that keeps only documents where the family is Sharks, and an out setting that names the output collection, monthlySharkReport. The filter is a declarative part of the call, and it is a MongoDB-specific extension to MapReduce. Then the two functions do the work:

  • The map function runs once for each matching document, with this set to that document. It builds a key from the year and month of the observation, such as “2013-12”, and emits that key with the number of animals as the value.
  • The emitted key-value pairs are grouped by key. For each key, that is, each month, the reduce function runs once and adds up the values, giving the total number of animals for that month.

Here is how it works on two example documents. Both are sharks. The first records a sighting on 25 December 1995 of 3 animals of the species Carcharodon carcharias. The second records a sighting on 12 December 1995 of 4 animals of the species Carcharias taurus. The map function runs once for each document and emits ("1995-12", 3) and then ("1995-12", 4). Both pairs have the same key, so the reduce function runs once with the key "1995-12" and the values 3 and 4. It returns 7.

The map and reduce functions are restricted. They must be pure functions: they use only the data passed to them as input, they cannot run additional database queries, and they must not have side effects. These rules let the database run the functions anywhere, in any order, and rerun them if a failure happens. Even so, they are powerful. They can parse strings, call library functions, perform calculations, and more.

MapReduce is a fairly low-level model for distributed execution on a cluster of machines. Higher-level query languages such as SQL can be built as a pipeline of MapReduce operations (Chapter 10 explains this). But there are also many distributed implementations of SQL that do not use MapReduce. Nothing in SQL requires a single machine, and MapReduce does not have a monopoly on distributed query execution.

Using JavaScript in the middle of a query is a great feature for advanced queries, and it is not limited to MapReduce. Some SQL databases can be extended with JavaScript functions too.

MapReduce has a usability problem. You have to write two carefully coordinated functions, which is often harder than writing a single query. A declarative query also gives the optimizer more room to improve performance. For these reasons MongoDB 2.2 added a declarative query language called the aggregation pipeline. The shark report looks like this in that language:

db.observations.aggregate([
  { $match: { family: "Sharks" } },
  { $group: {
      _id: {
        year: { $year: "$observationTimestamp" },
        month: { $month: "$observationTimestamp" }
      },
      totalAnimals: { $sum: "$numAnimals" }
  } }
]);

The first stage keeps only the shark documents. The second stage groups them by the year and month of the timestamp, and adds up numAnimals within each group. The aggregation pipeline is about as expressive as a subset of SQL. It uses a JSON-based syntax instead of SQL’s English-like sentences, which the book treats as a matter of taste. Its moral is that a NoSQL system may end up reinventing SQL, in disguise.

Graph-Like Data Models

Many-to-many relationships are an important way to tell data models apart. If your application has mostly one-to-many relationships, such as tree-structured data, or almost no relationships between records, the document model fits. But if many-to-many relationships are very common, the picture changes. The relational model handles simple cases of them well. As the connections in your data grow more complex, it becomes more natural to model the data as a graph.

A graph has two kinds of objects. Vertices (also called nodes or entities) are the things, and edges (also called relationships or arcs) are the connections between them. Many kinds of data fit this shape:

  • Social graphs: vertices are people, and edges show which people know each other.
  • The web graph: vertices are web pages, and edges are the HTML links between them.
  • Road or rail networks: vertices are junctions, and edges are the roads or railway lines between them.

Well-known algorithms run on these graphs. A car navigation system searches for the shortest path between two points in a road network. PageRank runs on the web graph to measure how popular a page is, which feeds into its ranking in search results.

In these examples, all the vertices are the same kind of thing. Graphs do not have to be that uniform, though. They can store completely different types of objects in one datastore with one consistent model. The book gives Facebook as an example. It keeps a single graph with many types of vertices, for people, locations, events, check-ins, and comments. Its edges say which people are friends, which check-in happened at which location, who commented on which post, and who attended which event.

The book uses one example throughout this part of the chapter, shown in its Figure 2-5. It could come from a social network or a family tree. It describes two people: Lucy, from Idaho, and Alain, from Beaune in France. They are married and live in London.

Several related ways of structuring and querying graphs exist. The chapter covers the property graph model, used by Neo4j, Titan, and InfiniteGraph, and the triple-store model, used by Datomic, AllegroGraph, and others. For querying, it covers three declarative languages: Cypher, SPARQL, and Datalog. There are also imperative graph query languages, such as Gremlin, and graph processing frameworks, such as Pregel, which Chapter 10 covers.

Property Graphs

In the property graph model, each vertex consists of:

  • A unique identifier.
  • A set of outgoing edges.
  • A set of incoming edges.
  • A collection of properties, which are key-value pairs.

Each edge consists of:

  • A unique identifier.
  • The vertex where the edge starts, called the tail vertex.
  • The vertex where the edge ends, called the head vertex.
  • A label that describes the kind of relationship between the two vertices.
  • A collection of properties, which are key-value pairs.

You can store a graph in two relational tables, one for vertices and one for edges. The book’s Example 2-2 does this and uses PostgreSQL’s json type for the properties. Each edge row records its tail and head vertex, and two indexes, one on each, let you find the incoming or outgoing edges of any vertex quickly. Three features matter most:

  1. Any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex. No schema limits which kinds of things can be connected.
  2. Given any vertex, you can efficiently find both its incoming and its outgoing edges, and so traverse the graph, meaning follow a path through a chain of vertices, forward and backward.
  3. By using different labels for different kinds of relationships, one graph can hold several kinds of information while keeping a clean data model.

These features give graphs a lot of flexibility, as the book’s Figure 2-5 shows. It includes things that would be hard to express in a traditional relational schema. Different countries have different regional structures: France has départements and régions, while the US has counties and states. A country can sit inside another region, which is a quirk of history. The data also has varying granularity. Lucy’s current residence is recorded as a city, while her birthplace is recorded only at the level of a state.

The graph could be extended with much more. For example, you could add a vertex for each food allergen, an edge from a person to each allergen they react to, and vertices for foods, linked to the substances they contain. A query could then find what is safe for each person to eat. The book notes that graphs are good for evolvability: as the application gains features, the graph can be extended to fit the changing data.

The Cypher Query Language

Cypher is a declarative query language for property graphs. It was created for the Neo4j graph database. Its name comes from a character in the film The Matrix, and it is not related to ciphers in cryptography.

Example 2-3 in the book shows a Cypher statement that inserts part of Figure 2-5 into a graph database. Each vertex gets a symbolic name, such as USA or Idaho, and later parts of the statement use those names to make edges with an arrow notation. The notation (Idaho) -[:WITHIN]-> (USA) creates an edge labeled WITHIN, with Idaho as the tail and USA as the head. The last lines of the statement read:

(Idaho) -[:WITHIN]-> (USA) -[:WITHIN]-> (NAmerica),
(Lucy) -[:BORN_IN]-> (Idaho)
Example

Now the book asks a real question: find the names of all people who emigrated from the United States to Europe. To be precise, find every vertex that has a BORN_IN edge to a location within the US, and also a LIVES_IN edge to a location within Europe, then return the name of each one. Example 2-4 expresses this in Cypher:

MATCH
  (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (us:Location {name:'United States'}),
  (person) -[:LIVES_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (eu:Location {name:'Europe'})
RETURN person.name

The arrow notation in the MATCH clause finds patterns in the graph. The pattern (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () matches any two vertices joined by a BORN_IN edge. The tail vertex is bound to the variable person, and the head is left unnamed. The query then reads as two conditions on the same person vertex:

  1. The person has an outgoing BORN_IN edge to some vertex. From that vertex you can follow a chain of outgoing WITHIN edges until you reach a Location vertex whose name is “United States”.
  2. The same person also has an outgoing LIVES_IN edge. Following it, and then a chain of outgoing WITHIN edges, you eventually reach a Location vertex whose name is “Europe”.

For each person who meets both conditions, the query returns the name property. The syntax :WITHIN*0.. means that a WITHIN edge may be followed zero or more times. It works like the * operator in a regular expression. Zero hops covers the case where the birthplace or residence is the country or continent itself.

There are several ways to run this query. One reading suggests starting by scanning all the people, checking each one’s birthplace and residence, and keeping those who match. But the database could work backward instead. If there is an index on the name property, it can find the US and Europe vertices quickly. From each of them it follows all incoming WITHIN edges to collect every location inside. Finally it looks for people with an incoming BORN_IN or LIVES_IN edge to one of those locations.

As is typical for a declarative language, you do not specify this choice when writing the query. The optimizer picks the strategy that is predicted to be fastest, so you can get on with the rest of the application.

Graph Queries in SQL

Example 2-2 showed that graph data can be stored in a relational database. But can you query it with SQL too? Yes, though with some difficulty. In a relational database you usually know in advance which joins a query needs. In a graph query, you may have to follow a variable number of edges before you find the vertex you want. The number of joins is not fixed in advance.

That happens in the (...) -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (...) part of the Cypher query. A person’s LIVES_IN edge may point at any kind of location: a street, a city, a district, a region, a state, and so on. A city may sit within a region, a region within a state, and a state within a country. The LIVES_IN edge may point directly at the location being searched for, or it may be several levels away in the hierarchy. Cypher’s :WITHIN*0.. covers all of these cases in one short expression.

Since SQL:1999, a similar idea can be written with recursive common table expressions, using the WITH RECURSIVE syntax. This lets a query repeat a step until nothing new is found. Example 2-5 in the book runs the same emigration query in SQL. It works in PostgreSQL, IBM DB2, Oracle, and SQL Server, but the syntax is clumsy compared with Cypher.

Example

The SQL version builds up four sets of vertex IDs, then joins them. Step by step:

  1. in_usa. Find the vertex whose name is “United States”, and make it the first member of the set in_usa. Follow all incoming within edges from vertices already in the set, and add their tails to the set. Repeat until no more incoming within edges remain.
  2. in_europe. Do the same, starting from the vertex named “Europe”, to build the set in_europe.
  3. born_in_usa. For each vertex in in_usa, follow the incoming born_in edges. That gives the people born somewhere within the United States.
  4. lives_in_europe. For each vertex in in_europe, follow the incoming lives_in edges. That gives the people who live somewhere in Europe.
  5. The final join. Intersect the two sets of people by joining them on vertex ID, and return the names of the people who appear in both.

The book points out that the same query takes 4 lines in one language and 29 lines in the other. That shows that different data models are designed for different use cases, and that it matters to pick one that suits your application.

Triple-Stores and SPARQL

The triple-store model is mostly equivalent to the property graph model, using different words for the same ideas. It is still worth discussing, because the tools and languages built for triple-stores can be valuable additions to your toolbox.

In a triple-store, all information is stored as very simple three-part statements: (subject, predicate, object). In the triple (Jim, likes, bananas), Jim is the subject, likes is the predicate (the verb), and bananas is the object.

The subject of a triple corresponds to a vertex in a graph. The object is one of two things:

  1. A value of a primitive type, such as a string or a number. Then the predicate and object together act like the key and value of a property on the subject vertex. For example, (lucy, age, 33) is like a vertex called lucy with the properties {"age":33}.
  2. Another vertex in the graph. Then the predicate is an edge, the subject is its tail vertex, and the object is its head vertex. For example, in (lucy, marriedTo, alain), both lucy and alain are vertices, and marriedTo is the label of the edge between them.

Example 2-6 in the book writes the same data as Example 2-3 using Turtle, a human-readable format that is a subset of Notation3 (N3). Vertices are written as names starting with _:. These names mean nothing outside the file. They exist only so the file can say which triples refer to the same vertex. When the predicate is an edge, the object is a vertex, as in _:idaho :within _:usa. When the predicate is a property, the object is a string, as in _:usa :name "United States".

Repeating the same subject for every fact is tiresome, so Turtle lets you use semicolons to say several things about one subject. Example 2-7 shows the same data written more concisely:

@prefix : <urn:example:>.
_:lucy a :Person; :name "Lucy"; :bornIn _:idaho.
_:idaho a :Location; :name "Idaho"; :type "state"; :within _:usa.
_:usa a :Location; :name "United States"; :type "country"; :within _:namerica.
_:namerica a :Location; :name "North America"; :type "continent".

The Semantic Web

If you read about triple-stores, you may get pulled into a large body of writing about the semantic web. The triple-store data model is completely independent of the semantic web. For example, Datomic is a triple-store that does not claim any connection to it. (Technically, Datomic stores 5-tuples rather than triples. The two extra fields hold metadata for versioning.) But the two are closely linked in many people’s minds, so the book discusses them briefly.

The semantic web is a simple and reasonable idea at its core. Websites already publish information as text and pictures for humans to read. Why not also publish it as machine-readable data for computers? The Resource Description Framework (RDF) was intended as a mechanism for different websites to publish data in a consistent format. Data from different sites could then be combined automatically into a web of data, a kind of internet-wide database of everything.

Unfortunately, the semantic web was overhyped in the early 2000s and has not yet been realized in practice. That has made many people cynical. It has also suffered from a crowd of acronyms, overly complex standards proposals, and a lot of hubris. But the project has also produced good work, and triples can be a good internal data model for an application, even if you have no interest in publishing RDF data on the web.

The RDF Data Model

The Turtle language used in Example 2-7 is a human-readable format for RDF data. RDF is also sometimes written in an XML format, which says the same thing much more verbosely. Example 2-8 shows the data from Example 2-7 in RDF/XML. Each location becomes a nested element, and Lucy is a Person element with a bornIn element pointing at Idaho. The book prefers Turtle or N3 because it is much easier to read, and tools such as Apache Jena can convert between RDF formats when needed.

RDF has some quirks because it was designed for data exchange across the whole internet. The subject, predicate, and object of a triple are often URIs (web addresses used as unique names). For example, a predicate might be a URI such as a namespace on a company’s domain followed by within or lives_in, rather than the plain words WITHIN or LIVES_IN. The reason is that you should be able to combine your data with someone else’s. If another organization gives the word within a different meaning, its predicates are different URIs, so there is no clash. A namespace URL does not need to lead to a real web page. Only the naming matters. The book’s examples use non-resolvable URIs such as urn:example:within to avoid confusion, and they declare the prefix once at the top of the file.

The SPARQL Query Language

SPARQL is a query language for triple-stores that use the RDF data model. Its name is an acronym for SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language, pronounced “sparkle”. It came before Cypher. Cypher’s pattern matching borrows from SPARQL, so the two look quite similar.

Example

The same emigration question, asking for people who moved from the US to Europe, is even more concise in SPARQL. Example 2-9 reads:

PREFIX : <urn:example:>
SELECT ?personName WHERE {
  ?person :name ?personName.
  ?person :bornIn / :within* / :name "United States".
  ?person :livesIn / :within* / :name "Europe".
}

Read step by step, the query has one SELECT and three patterns about the same person. Variables start with a question mark. The first pattern binds the person’s name to ?personName. The second says the person was born in something, from which a chain of :within steps (zero or more) leads to a thing named United States. The third says the person lives in something whose chain of :within steps reaches a thing named Europe.

The structure matches the Cypher query closely. The Cypher pattern (person) -[:BORN_IN]-> () -[:WITHIN*0..]-> (location) corresponds to the SPARQL pattern ?person :bornIn / :within* ?location.. Because RDF does not distinguish between properties and edges, and uses predicates for both, the same syntax also matches properties. The Cypher pattern (usa {name:'United States'}) is written ?usa :name "United States". in SPARQL, binding the variable to any vertex whose name is the string “United States”. The book concludes that SPARQL is a nice query language. Even if the semantic web never happens, it can be a powerful tool for applications to use internally.

Graph Databases Compared to the Network Model

Earlier in the chapter, CODASYL and the relational model competed to handle many-to-many relationships. At first glance CODASYL’s network model looks like the graph model. Are graph databases the second coming of CODASYL in disguise? The book says no, and gives four differences:

  • In CODASYL, the database had a schema that specified which record type could be nested inside which other type. In a graph database there is no such restriction. Any vertex can have an edge to any other vertex, which makes it much easier to adapt as requirements change.
  • In CODASYL, the only way to reach a record was to traverse one of the access paths to it. In a graph database you can refer directly to any vertex by its unique ID, or use an index to find vertices with a particular value.
  • In CODASYL, the children of a record were an ordered set. The database had to maintain that order, which affected storage layout, and applications inserting records had to worry about their positions. In a graph database, vertices and edges are not ordered. You can sort the results only when you run a query.
  • In CODASYL, all queries were imperative. They were hard to write and easily broke when the schema changed. In a graph database you can write a traversal in imperative code if you want, but most graph databases also support high-level declarative languages such as Cypher or SPARQL.

The Foundation: Datalog

Datalog is much older than SPARQL or Cypher. Academics studied it extensively in the 1980s. It is less well known among software engineers, but it provides the foundation that later query languages build upon. It is the query language of Datomic, and Cascalog is a Datalog implementation for querying large datasets in Hadoop. (Datomic and Cascalog use a Clojure S-expression syntax for Datalog. This chapter uses the Prolog syntax, which is a little easier to read. The difference is only in notation.)

Datalog’s data model is similar to the triple-store model, generalized a little. Instead of writing a triple as (subject, predicate, object), you write it as predicate(subject, object). Example 2-10 writes the data from the earlier examples in this form:

name(namerica, 'North America').
type(namerica, continent).
name(usa, 'United States').
type(usa, country).
within(usa, namerica).
name(idaho, 'Idaho').
type(idaho, state).
within(idaho, usa).
name(lucy, 'Lucy').
born_in(lucy, idaho).

Example 2-11 writes the emigration query in Datalog. Unlike Cypher and SPARQL, which begin with a SELECT, Datalog takes small steps. It first defines rules that tell the database about new predicates. The rules are:

within_recursive(Location, Name) :- name(Location, Name).
within_recursive(Location, Name) :- within(Location, Via), within_recursive(Via, Name).
migrated(Name, BornIn, LivingIn) :- name(Person, Name),
    born_in(Person, BornLoc), within_recursive(BornLoc, BornIn),
    lives_in(Person, LivingLoc), within_recursive(LivingLoc, LivingIn).
?- migrated(Who, 'United States', 'Europe').

The first rule, which the book numbers rule 1, says that a location with a name is within itself. The second, rule 2, says that if a location is within some place, and that place is within a named location, then the location is within that named location too. Rule 3 defines migrated: a person with a given name was born in some place and lives in some place, and each of those places is within the named regions. The last line is the question. It asks for every value of Who when the birthplace is within the United States and the residence is within Europe. The answer is Lucy.

Uppercase words are variables, and predicates match in the same way as in Cypher and SPARQL. For example, name(Location, Name) matches the fact name(namerica, 'North America'), binding Location to namerica and Name to 'North America'. A rule applies when the system can match every predicate on the right of the :- symbol. When it applies, it is as though the left side were added to the database, with the variables replaced by the values they matched. The rules can refer to other rules, just as functions call functions or call themselves recursively. So complex queries can be built a small piece at a time.

The book walks through one way the rules are applied to the example data:

  1. name(namerica, 'North America') exists, so rule 1 applies. It generates within_recursive(namerica, 'North America').
  2. within(usa, namerica) exists, and the previous step produced within_recursive(namerica, 'North America'). So rule 2 applies and generates within_recursive(usa, 'North America').
  3. within(idaho, usa) exists, and the previous step produced within_recursive(usa, 'North America'). So rule 2 applies again and generates within_recursive(idaho, 'North America').

By repeatedly applying rules 1 and 2, the within_recursive predicate can list every location in North America, or in any other named location, that the database contains. The diagram below shows this chain of derivations.

Rule 3 then uses the same derived facts. It finds people born in some location, and living in some location, that falls within the two named regions. Querying with United States and Europe leaves the person as the variable Who, so the system finds which values can fill it. The answer is the same as in the Cypher and SPARQL queries.

Datalog needs a different way of thinking from the other languages in this chapter. But it is powerful, because rules can be combined and reused across many queries. It is less convenient for simple one-off queries, and it copes better as the data becomes more complex.

Key idea

Choose the model that fits the shape of your data. Tree-shaped, self-contained data suits documents. Shared, many-to-one links suit relational tables. Highly connected data, where anything can relate to anything, suits graph models, which are the most natural fit for it.

Try it

Suppose you add a new vertex for a city inside Idaho. Which new facts would you add to the Datalog database for that city? Which existing rule would then let you find the city when you ask what is within North America? Check that the chain of rule applications reaches the new city.

Trade-offs
ModelGood atCosts
Relational (SQL)Joins, many-to-one and many-to-many links, declarative queries, and an optimizer that chooses indexes and join orderOne-to-many data is split across tables, which needs a translation layer between code objects and rows. Schema changes are explicit, and some databases, such as MySQL, copy the whole table on ALTER TABLE.
Document (JSON or XML)Self-contained trees that are loaded in one read, flexible structure, close to the objects in application codeJoins are weak, so links are resolved in application code or with extra queries. The whole document is loaded and rewritten on change, and nested items cannot be referred to directly.
Graph (property graph, triple-store)Highly connected data, any vertex linked to any other, traversals of unknown depth, and several kinds of objects in one storeMulti-level traversals are clumsy in SQL (29 lines against 4 in the book’s example). Datalog takes more thought for one-off queries. No schema restricts the connections.

Summary

Summary
  • History. Data started out as one big tree in the hierarchical model. That was poor at representing many-to-many relationships, so the relational model was invented to solve that problem. Later, developers found that some applications did not fit the relational model well either. New nonrelational “NoSQL” datastores then split in two main directions.
  • Document databases target use cases where data comes in self-contained documents, and relationships between one document and another are rare.
  • Graph databases go the other way. They target use cases where anything is potentially related to everything.
  • Each model is good in its own domain. Document, relational, and graph models are all widely used. One model can be emulated in another, such as storing graph data in a relational database, but the result is often awkward. That is why there are different systems for different purposes, and no single one-size-fits-all solution.
  • Schemas. Document and graph databases typically do not enforce a schema, which can make it easier to adapt applications to changing requirements. Applications still assume the data has some structure. The real question is whether the schema is explicit (enforced on write) or implicit (handled on read).
  • Query languages. Each model has its own query language or framework. The chapter covered SQL, MapReduce, MongoDB’s aggregation pipeline, Cypher, SPARQL, and Datalog. It also touched on CSS and XSL/XPath, which are not database query languages but have interesting parallels.

Many data models were left out. Three examples follow.

  • Genome data needs sequence-similarity searches, which take one very long string, a DNA molecule, and match it against a large database of strings that are similar but not identical. None of the databases described here can do this, which is why researchers have written specialized genome software such as GenBank.
  • Particle physics has done large-scale, big-data-style analysis for decades. Projects such as the Large Hadron Collider now work with hundreds of petabytes. At that scale, custom solutions are needed to keep hardware costs from spiraling out of control.
  • Full-text search is often used alongside databases. It is a large specialist field that the book does not cover in depth. Chapter 3 and Part III touch on search indexes.

The next chapter discusses some of the trade-offs that come into play when implementing the data models described here.

The chapter ends with a long reference list of 49 numbered sources, covering papers, books, and documentation. This retelling does not reproduce that list.

Check yourself

  1. A profile stores its region as a copy of the text “Greater Seattle Area” rather than as an ID. What does the book say this costs, and what should be stored instead?

    Show answer

    The human-meaningful text is duplicated in every record. If the name ever changes, every copy must be updated, and missed copies leave the data inconsistent. Storing an ID that points to one region record means a change is made in only one place.

  2. Adding a first_name field can be done in two ways. One writes new documents with the field and has application code fill in old documents when they are read. The other runs ALTER TABLE and then an UPDATE once. Which one is schema-on-read, and which is schema-on-write?

    Show answer

    Writing new documents and handling old ones in the application is schema-on-read, because the structure is only interpreted when the data is read. The ALTER TABLE and UPDATE approach is schema-on-write, because the schema is explicit and the database enforces it on every write.

  3. Why can a database reorder rows or add a new index without breaking SQL queries, while the same change might break an imperative program?

    Show answer

    SQL declares which results are wanted, not the steps to get them. It does not promise any row order, and the optimizer chooses indexes and join order. Imperative code spells out steps and may depend on a particular order, which the database cannot check.

  4. The Cypher query for people who emigrated from the US to Europe could be run in two ways. What are they?

    Show answer

    One way scans all the people, checks each one’s birthplace and residence, and keeps the matches. The other starts from the US and Europe Location vertices, which an index on name can find quickly. It follows incoming WITHIN edges to collect all the locations inside each region, then finds people with incoming BORN_IN or LIVES_IN edges to those locations. The optimizer picks the strategy.

Part I · Chapter 3

Storage and Retrieval

The big idea: log-structured engines only add to files and clean up later, while B-trees overwrite fixed-size pages on disk. Analytic systems need a third layout, column storage, because they read a few columns from huge tables. Each design makes some work fast and some work slow.

A database has two basic jobs. When you give it some data, it must store that data. When you ask for it later, it must give the data back. Chapter 2 looked at this from the application side, through data models and query languages. This chapter looks at the same problem from the database’s side: how the data is laid out on disk, and how it is found again.

Why should an application developer care? Most of us will never write a storage engine (the part of a database that decides how bytes are arranged in memory and on disk). But we still have to choose one from many options, and to tune it we need a rough picture of what happens under the hood. The chapter opens with a German proverb, which says that people who keep things tidily ordered are just too lazy to go searching. That captures the central problem. Keeping data in order makes reads easier, but ordering costs work when you write.

The chapter starts with the storage engines used in most traditional relational databases and many NoSQL databases. These engines fall into two families: log-structured engines, which only append to files, and page-oriented engines such as B-trees, which overwrite fixed-size blocks of disk. Later the chapter turns to engines built for analytics, which have very different needs.

Data Structures That Power Your Database

The book starts with the simplest database it can think of. It is built from two Bash functions (Bash is a command-line shell for running scripts). Together they form a key-value store, which keeps a value under a name, called the key. The value can be almost anything, such as a JSON document (a text format for structured data).

Example

The first function, db_set, appends one line to a file called database. The line holds the key, a comma, and the value. The second function, db_get, searches the file for lines that start with the key, keeps the last one, and prints its value. Here is a session, step by step:

  1. Run db_set 123456 with a JSON value about London. The file gets one line.
  2. Run db_set 42 with a value about San Francisco. The file gets a second line.
  3. Run db_get 42. The function finds the line that starts with 42, and prints the San Francisco value.
  4. Run db_set 42 again, this time with a value about the Exploratorium. The file gets a third line. The old line for key 42 is still there.
  5. Run db_get 42 again. Now the function finds two matching lines, keeps the last one, and prints the Exploratorium value.
db_set () {
  echo "$1,$2" >> database
}
db_get () {
  grep "^$1," database | sed -e "s/^$1,//" | tail -n 1
}

The storage format is a plain text file, with one key-value pair per line. Nothing is ever overwritten. Each write adds a line at the end, and the newest value for a key is the last line that mentions it. The book points out that this is roughly the same as a CSV file, ignoring escaping problems.

The write side is fast. Adding to the end of a file is one of the cheapest things a disk can do. Many real databases use a log internally for the same reason. A log here means an append-only sequence of records. It does not mean an application log of human-readable messages, and it does not have to be readable by people at all. Real databases also have to handle concurrent writers, reclaim disk space so the file does not grow forever, and deal with records that were only partly written. The basic idea is the same, though, and logs come up again and again in the rest of the book.

The read side is the problem. Every db_get scans the whole file from start to finish. In algorithm terms, the cost grows with the number of records, which is written O(n). If you double the records, a lookup takes twice as long. That does not scale.

To find a value quickly, the database needs an index. An index is extra metadata kept on the side, a bit like a signpost, that helps the database locate data without reading everything. An index is derived from the primary data, so you can add or remove one without changing what the database stores. It only changes how fast queries run. If you want to search the same data in several ways, you may need several indexes.

There is a catch. Every index has to be updated whenever data is written, so it slows writes down. Nothing beats the speed of simply appending to a file. Well-chosen indexes speed up reads, but each one costs something on every write. For this reason, databases usually do not index everything by default. The application developer or database administrator picks the indexes, using knowledge of the common queries, so that the benefit outweighs the overhead.

Hash Indexes

Hash indexes are for key-value data. This is not the only kind of data you can index, but it is common, and it is a useful building block for more complex indexes.

A key-value store is much like the dictionary type found in most programming languages, which is usually built as a hash map (also called a hash table). A hash map jumps straight to the place where a key lives. So why not use one to index data on disk?

Suppose the storage is just the append-only file from the last section. The simplest index is this: keep a hash map in memory that maps every key to a byte offset, which is the position in the file where that key’s latest value starts. When you append a new key-value pair, you also update the hash map so it points at the new line. This works for new keys and for updated keys alike. To read a value, look up the offset in the hash map, seek to that position in the file (move the read point directly there), and read the value.

This may sound too simple, but it is a workable design. It is essentially what Bitcask does. Bitcask is the default storage engine in Riak, a distributed database. Bitcask gives fast reads and writes, with one important condition: all the keys must fit in memory, because the whole hash map lives there. The values do not have to fit. A value can be read from disk with a single seek. If that part of the file is already in the operating system’s file cache, the read needs no disk input or output at all.

A design like Bitcask suits workloads where each key is updated often, but there are not many distinct keys. The book’s example is a count of how many times each cat video has been played. Each click writes a new count, so there are many writes. But the number of video URLs is small enough that all of them fit in memory.

This raises an obvious question. The file only ever grows, so how do we avoid running out of disk space? The answer is to split the log into segments. When a segment file reaches a set size, it is closed, and new writes go to a new segment. Closed segments are never changed again. Then you run compaction on them. Compaction throws away duplicate keys and keeps only the most recent value for each key.

Example

Imagine the play-count log for one cat video. Suppose a closed segment contains the count for that video written five times. Compaction reads the segment, keeps only the last of the five counts, and writes out a smaller segment. This works best when a key is overwritten many times within one segment, because then compaction shrinks the segment a lot.

Compaction makes segments smaller, so you can also merge several segments in the same pass. Merged output is written to a new file. Frozen segments are never modified, which makes this safe. The merge can run in a background thread while the database keeps serving reads and writes from the old segment files. When the merge finishes, reads switch to the new merged segment, and the old files are deleted.

Each segment has its own in-memory hash map. To find a key, check the newest segment’s hash map first. If the key is not there, check the second-newest segment, and so on back in time. Merging keeps the number of segments small, so a lookup rarely has to check many maps.

Many details matter in a real implementation. The book lists these:

  • File format. CSV is not the best format for a log. A binary format is faster and simpler. It stores the length of each string in bytes, followed by the raw bytes, so no escaping is needed.
  • Deleting records. To delete a key, the database appends a special deletion record, called a tombstone. When segments are merged, a tombstone tells the merge to throw away every earlier value for that key.
  • Crash recovery. The hash maps live only in memory, so they are lost on a restart. You could rebuild them by reading each segment from beginning to end and noting the latest offset for each key. But for large segments that could take a long time. Bitcask speeds this up by saving a snapshot of each segment’s hash map to disk, which loads much faster.
  • Partly written records. A crash can happen halfway through appending a record. Bitcask files include checksums (a value computed from the data, used to spot corruption), so damaged parts of the log can be found and ignored.
  • Concurrency. Writes are appended in strict order, so a common choice is to have just one writer thread. Segments are append-only and never changed, so many reader threads can read them at the same time.

An append-only log may look wasteful. Why not update the file in place, overwriting the old value? The book gives three reasons the append-only design is good:

  • Appending and merging are sequential writes, meaning they write one place after another. These are much faster than random writes, which jump around the disk. The gap is especially big on spinning hard drives. Sequential writes are also preferred on flash-based solid state drives (SSDs), to some extent.
  • Concurrency and crash recovery are simpler when files are never changed. You do not have to worry about a crash that happened halfway through overwriting a value, which could leave part of the old value and part of the new one spliced together.
  • Merging old segments stops data files from becoming fragmented (scattered in small leftover pieces) over time.

The hash index also has two limits:

  • The hash map must fit in memory. With a very large number of keys, you are out of luck. You could keep a hash map on disk, but it is hard to make one perform well there. It needs many random reads and writes, it is expensive to grow when full, and collisions (two keys landing in the same slot) need fiddly logic.
  • Range queries are slow. You cannot easily scan all keys between kitty00000 and kitty99999. You would have to look up each possible key one at a time in the hash map.

The next section looks at an indexing structure that does not have these limits.

SSTables and LSM-Trees

In the segments above, each segment is a list of key-value pairs in the order they were written. Later entries win over earlier ones for the same key. Now make one simple change: require each segment’s pairs to be sorted by key. The book calls this format a Sorted String Table, or SSTable. Each key appears only once in a merged segment, which compaction already guarantees.

At first glance, sorting seems to break the sequential-write idea. The book says it does not, and explains why. SSTables have three big advantages over the log segments with hash indexes.

1. Merging is simple and efficient, even when files are bigger than memory. The merge works like the merge step of the mergesort algorithm. You open the input files side by side and look at the first key in each. You copy the lowest key to the output and move forward in that file. Repeat until done. The result is a new sorted segment.

Example

Suppose two segments both contain the key kiwi. Each segment holds all the writes from some period of time, and the segments are merged in time order. So every value in the newer segment is more recent than every value in the older one. When a key shows up in both, keep the value from the newer segment and drop the older one. The figure below shows this with simple made-up keys.

2. You no longer need to keep an index of every key in memory. Suppose you are looking for the key handiwork, but you do not know its exact offset in the segment file. You do know the offsets of handbag and handsome. Because the file is sorted, handiwork must sit between them. So you jump to the offset of handbag and scan forward until you find handiwork, or pass where it would be and conclude it is absent.

You still need an in-memory index to know some of the offsets. But it can be sparse, meaning it holds one key for every few kilobytes of the file, rather than every key. A few kilobytes can be scanned very quickly. (If all keys and values had a fixed size, you could skip the index and use binary search on the file. In practice they vary in length, so you cannot tell where one record ends without an index.)

3. Reads can be compressed in blocks. A read of a range of keys has to scan several records anyway. So the records can be grouped into a block and compressed before being written to disk. Each entry in the sparse index then points to the start of a compressed block. This saves disk space and also reduces the amount of data read from disk.

Constructing and maintaining SSTables

Sorted files are useful, but how do you get data sorted in the first place? Writes arrive in any order. Keeping a sorted structure on disk is possible (the B-tree section covers one way). It is much easier to keep one in memory. Standard balanced trees, such as red-black trees or AVL trees, let you insert keys in any order and read them back in sorted order.

The storage engine then works in four steps:

  • When a write arrives, add it to an in-memory balanced tree. This tree is called a memtable.
  • When the memtable grows past a threshold, typically a few megabytes, write it to disk as an SSTable. This is cheap, because the tree already holds the pairs in sorted order. The new SSTable becomes the newest segment. Writes can carry on into a fresh memtable while the old one is being written.
  • To serve a read, check the memtable first, then the newest on-disk segment, then the next older one, and so on.
  • From time to time, run a merge and compaction in the background. This combines segments and throws away overwritten or deleted values.

There is one weakness. If the database crashes, the most recent writes are lost. They were in the memtable but had not yet been written to disk. To prevent this, keep a separate log on disk, and append every write to it immediately, just as in the earlier log design. This log is not sorted, and it does not need to be. Its only job is to rebuild the memtable after a crash. Once the memtable has been saved as an SSTable, the matching log can be discarded.

Making an LSM-tree out of SSTables

This algorithm is essentially what LevelDB and RocksDB use. Both are key-value storage libraries designed to be built into other applications. LevelDB can be used in Riak as an alternative to Bitcask. Similar engines are used in Cassandra and HBase, which were both inspired by Google’s Bigtable paper. That paper introduced the terms SSTable and memtable.

The index structure was first described by Patrick O’Neil and colleagues, who named it the Log-Structured Merge-Tree, or LSM-tree. It builds on earlier work on log-structured filesystems. Storage engines based on this idea of merging and compacting sorted files are often called LSM storage engines.

Lucene, the full-text search library used by Elasticsearch and Solr, uses a similar method for its term dictionary. Full-text search is harder than key-value lookup, but it rests on a similar idea. Given a word in a search, find all the documents that contain it. The index maps each word (a term) to a postings list, which is the list of IDs of documents that contain the word. In Lucene, that mapping is kept in SSTable-like sorted files, which are merged in the background as needed.

Performance optimizations

As always, a lot of detail goes into making a storage engine fast. The LSM-tree is slow for keys that do not exist. You must check the memtable, then every segment back to the oldest, possibly reading from disk for each one, before you can be sure a key is absent. To speed this up, storage engines often add Bloom filters. A Bloom filter is a compact structure that approximates which items are in a set. It can say that a key is definitely not in the database, which saves many unnecessary disk reads.

There are also different rules for when and how segments are merged. The two most common are size-tiered and leveled compaction. LevelDB and RocksDB use leveled compaction, which is where LevelDB’s name comes from. HBase uses size-tiered compaction, and Cassandra supports both. In size-tiered compaction, newer and smaller SSTables are merged into older and larger ones. In leveled compaction, the key range is split into smaller SSTables, and older data is moved into separate “levels.” This lets compaction proceed in smaller steps and use less disk space.

Even with these details, the core idea is simple: keep a cascade of SSTables and merge them in the background. It works well even when the data is much bigger than memory. Because data is stored in sorted order, range queries are efficient. Because disk writes are sequential, an LSM-tree can sustain remarkably high write throughput.

B-Trees

Log-structured indexes are gaining acceptance, but they are not the most common index. The most widely used structure is the B-tree. It was introduced in 1970, and less than ten years later it was already described as ubiquitous. B-trees remain the standard index in almost all relational databases, and many nonrelational databases use them too.

Like SSTables, B-trees keep key-value pairs sorted by key, so they support fast lookups and range queries. Beyond that, the designs are very different. Log-structured indexes split the database into variable-size segments, usually several megabytes or more, and always write a segment in one sequential pass. B-trees split the database into fixed-size blocks called pages. A page is traditionally 4 KB (kilobytes), sometimes more. The database reads or writes one page at a time. This matches the hardware better, because disks are also laid out in fixed-size blocks.

Each page has an address, which lets one page refer to another. This is like a pointer, but it points to a place on disk rather than in memory. Page references form a tree of pages. One page is the root. To find a key, you start at the root. The root holds several keys and references to child pages. Each child covers a continuous range of keys, and the keys between the references mark where the boundaries between ranges lie.

Example

The book looks up the key 251 in a B-tree. The steps are:

  1. Start at the root. Its boundaries say which child covers each range. Key 251 falls between the boundaries 200 and 300, so follow the reference in that range.
  2. That child page breaks the 200 to 300 range into smaller subranges. Find the subrange that holds 251 and follow its reference.
  3. Keep going until you reach a leaf page, the bottom level, which holds the individual keys. The leaf either stores each value inline or stores references to where the values are.

To update the value for an existing key, search for the leaf page holding it, change the value there, and write the page back. Page references stay valid because the page keeps its address. To add a new key, find the page whose range covers it and add it there. If the page is too full, it is split into two half-full pages. The parent page is then updated to point at both halves, which may in turn split the parent.

This keeps the tree balanced. A B-tree with n keys always has a depth of O(log n), which means the depth grows very slowly as the data grows. Most databases fit into a B-tree that is three or four levels deep, so you rarely need to follow many references to reach a page. The book’s example: a four-level tree of 4 KB pages with a branching factor of 500 can store up to 256 TB. The branching factor is the number of child references in one page. In the figure above it is three, and in practice it is typically several hundred. (Inserting into a B-tree is fairly intuitive. Deleting while keeping the tree balanced is more involved.)

Making B-trees reliable

The basic write operation of a B-tree is to overwrite a page on disk with new data, keeping its location unchanged so that all references to it remain valid. This is very different from log-structured indexes, which only append to files and delete obsolete ones.

Overwriting a page is a real hardware action. On a magnetic hard drive, the disk head must move to the right place, wait for the platter to spin the right spot under it, and then overwrite the sector. SSDs are more complicated, because they must erase and rewrite fairly large blocks of the storage chip at a time.

Some operations need several pages changed together. When a page is split, you must write the two new pages and also overwrite the parent so it points at both. If the database crashes after only some of these writes, the index is corrupted. You might end up with an orphan page, one that no parent points to.

To make B-trees crash-resistant, most implementations add a write-ahead log, also called a redo log. This is an append-only file. Every change to the B-tree must be written to this log before it is applied to the tree’s pages. If the database crashes, the log is replayed to bring the tree back to a consistent state. This is the same idea used for the memtable log above, but the log protects the tree’s pages instead.

Updating pages in place also needs careful concurrency control, the rules that keep several threads from getting in each other’s way. If several threads use the tree at once, one may see it in an inconsistent state. The usual fix is to protect the tree with latches, which are lightweight locks. Log-structured designs are simpler here. They do their merging in the background, without interfering with incoming queries, and swap old segments for new ones at once.

B-tree optimizations

B-trees have been around for decades, and many optimizations have been developed. The book mentions a few:

  • Copy-on-write. Some databases, such as LMDB, avoid overwriting pages and the write-ahead log. A changed page is written to a new location, and new versions of its parent pages are created to point to it. This also helps concurrency control, which the book covers later.
  • Abbreviated keys. Pages do not need to store entire keys. Keys inside the tree only have to act as boundaries between ranges, so they can be shortened. That packs more keys into each page, which raises the branching factor and reduces the number of levels.
  • Layout on disk. Pages can sit anywhere on disk. Nearby key ranges are not stored near each other. A scan over a large part of the key range may then need a disk seek for every page. Some implementations try to keep leaf pages in sequential order, but this is hard to maintain as the tree grows. LSM-trees find this easier, because merges rewrite large chunks of storage in one go and keep neighboring keys close together.
  • Sibling pointers. Each leaf page can point to its left and right neighbors. This lets a scan move along the keys in order without climbing back up to parent pages.
  • Fractal trees. Some B-tree variants borrow ideas from log-structured designs to reduce disk seeks. Despite the name, they have nothing to do with fractals.

Comparing B-Trees and LSM-Trees

B-tree implementations are generally more mature than LSM-tree implementations. Even so, LSM-trees are interesting because of their performance. As a rule of thumb, LSM-trees are typically faster for writes, and B-trees are thought to be faster for reads. Reads are slower on LSM-trees because they may have to check several structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction.

The book adds a warning. Benchmarks are often inconclusive and depend on the details of the workload. To make a valid comparison, test each system with your own workload. The book then lists several things worth considering when measuring a storage engine.

Advantages of LSM-trees

A B-tree must write each piece of data at least twice. Once is to the write-ahead log, and once is to the tree page itself. Pages may be written again when they split. There is also overhead from writing a whole page even if only a few bytes in it changed. Some storage engines overwrite the same page twice, so that a power failure cannot leave a page half updated.

LSM-trees also rewrite data several times, because compaction and merging copy SSTables again and again. Over the life of the database, one logical write can lead to many physical disk writes. This is called write amplification. It matters most on SSDs, which can only overwrite blocks a limited number of times before they wear out.

In a write-heavy application, the bottleneck can be how fast the database can write to disk. Here write amplification costs directly. The more the storage engine writes, the fewer writes per second it can handle within the available disk bandwidth. LSM-trees usually sustain higher write throughput than B-trees. This is partly because they sometimes have lower write amplification, though it depends on configuration and workload. It is also because they write compact SSTable files in sequence, rather than overwriting several scattered pages. That difference is large on magnetic disks, where sequential writes are much faster than random ones.

LSM-trees can also be compressed better, so they often produce smaller files than B-trees. B-tree storage leaves some disk space unused. When a page splits, or a row does not fit into a page with room left, part of the page stays empty. LSM-trees are not page-oriented, and they periodically rewrite SSTables to remove this fragmentation. So their storage overhead is lower, especially with leveled compaction.

On many SSDs, the firmware internally uses a log-structured method to turn random writes into sequential writes on the chips. So the storage engine’s write pattern matters less there. Even so, lower write amplification and less fragmentation still help on SSDs, because compact data lets more reads and writes fit into the available I/O bandwidth. (I/O means input and output, the traffic between the CPU and storage.)

Downsides of LSM-trees

The downside of log-structured storage is that compaction can interfere with ongoing reads and writes. Storage engines try to compact in small steps without affecting concurrent access. But disks have limited resources, so a request may have to wait while the disk finishes a large compaction. The effect on average response time is usually small. But at higher percentiles (the slowest requests, as described in Chapter 1), queries to log-structured engines can be quite slow, and B-trees are more predictable.

A second issue appears at high write throughput. A disk has finite write bandwidth, which must be shared between new writes (logging them and flushing the memtable) and background compaction. A fresh, empty database can use the full disk bandwidth for new writes. But as the database grows, compaction needs more of that bandwidth. If writes are heavy and compaction is not configured carefully, compaction can fall behind. Then unmerged segments pile up on disk until you run out of space, and reads slow down because they must check more files. SSTable-based engines typically do not throttle incoming writes when compaction cannot keep up. So you need explicit monitoring to notice this.

B-trees have one advantage here. Each key exists in exactly one place in the index. A log-structured engine may keep several copies of the same key in different segments. This makes B-trees attractive for databases that want strong transactional guarantees. In many relational databases, transaction isolation is done with locks on ranges of keys, and in a B-tree those locks can attach directly to the tree. Chapter 7 returns to this point.

B-trees are deeply built into database architecture and give consistently good performance for many workloads, so they are unlikely to disappear soon. Log-structured indexes are growing in popularity in newer datastores. There is no quick rule for picking one, so the book advises testing both empirically. The table below summarizes the trade-offs.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
LSM-trees (log-structured)Fast writes and high write throughput. Compact files with less fragmentation. Sequential disk writes.Slower reads, since several structures may be checked. Compaction can cause slow requests at high percentiles and can fall behind heavy writes. Write amplification.
B-trees (page-oriented)Fast reads and predictable response times. Each key lives in one place, so transaction locks attach easily to the tree.Each write touches at least two places (log and page), and whole pages are rewritten. Fragmentation wastes some space.

Other Indexing Structures

So far we have only discussed key-value indexes. These are like a primary key index in the relational model. A primary key uniquely identifies one row in a table, one document, or one vertex in a graph. Other records can refer to that row by its primary key, and the index is used to resolve those references.

Databases also commonly have secondary indexes. In a relational database, you can create several with the CREATE INDEX command, and they are often crucial for efficient joins. For example, in the Chapter 2 figure, you would most likely have a secondary index on the user_id columns, so you can find all the rows belonging to one user in each table.

A secondary index can be built from a key-value index. The difference is that keys are not unique. Many rows may share the same key. There are two ways to deal with that. One is to make each index value a list of matching row identifiers, like a postings list in a full-text index. The other is to make each key unique by appending a row identifier to it. Either way, both B-trees and log-structured indexes can serve as secondary indexes.

Storing values within the index

The key is what queries search for. The value can be one of two things. It can be the actual row, document, or vertex. Or it can be a reference to the row, which is stored somewhere else. In the second case, the place where rows are stored is called a heap file. A heap file keeps data in no particular order. It may be append-only, or it may track deleted rows so that their space can be reused.

The heap file approach avoids copying data when there are several secondary indexes. Each index just points to a location in the heap, and the row is stored in one place. When an update does not change the key, the heap file works well. If the new value is no larger than the old one, the record is overwritten in place. If it is larger, it has to move to a place with more room. Then either every index must be updated to point to the new location, or a forwarding pointer is left at the old location.

Sometimes the extra hop from the index to the heap is too slow for reads. Then you can store the indexed row directly inside the index. This is a clustered index. In MySQL’s InnoDB engine, a table’s primary key is always a clustered index, and secondary indexes point to the primary key rather than to a heap location. SQL Server lets you have one clustered index per table.

There is a middle option. A covering index, or an index with included columns, stores some of a table’s columns inside the index, but not all of them. If a query only needs the columns stored in the index, the index alone can answer it. The index is then said to cover the query.

As with any duplicated data, clustered and covering indexes speed up reads but need extra storage and slow down writes. The database also has to work harder to enforce transaction guarantees, since applications must never see inconsistencies caused by the duplication.

Multi-column indexes

Indexes so far map a single key to a value. That is not enough when you need to search several columns (or several fields in a document) at once.

The most common multi-column index is a concatenated index. It joins several fields into one key by appending one column after another, in an order set by the index definition. An old paper phone book works this way. It indexes last name and first name together, and gives you a phone number. Because of the sort order, you can find everyone with a given last name, or everyone with a given last name and first name pair. But the book notes that the index is useless for finding everyone with a particular first name alone.

Multi-dimensional indexes search several columns at once in a more general way. They matter most for geographic data. Suppose a restaurant-search website stores the latitude and longitude of each restaurant. When a user views a map, the site must find every restaurant inside the rectangle the user can see. That is a two-dimensional range query.

Example

The query below asks for restaurants inside one rectangle on the user’s map. The rectangle is set by a range of latitudes and a range of longitudes:

SELECT * FROM restaurants WHERE latitude > 51.4946 AND latitude < 51.5079
AND longitude > -0.1162 AND longitude < -0.1004;

A standard B-tree or LSM-tree cannot answer this efficiently. It can give you all restaurants in a band of latitudes, at any longitude, or all restaurants in a band of longitudes, at any latitude. It cannot do both at once. The rectangle needs both conditions to be applied together.

One option is to turn a two-dimensional location into a single number using a space-filling curve, which is a path that visits every cell of a grid. Then a normal B-tree index can be used. More commonly, specialized spatial indexes called R-trees are used. PostGIS, a geographic extension of PostgreSQL, implements its spatial indexes as R-trees. The book does not describe R-trees in detail.

Multi-dimensional indexes are not only for maps. An online shop could index products on three dimensions, red, green, and blue, to find items in a range of colors. A database of weather observations could index on date and temperature together. Then a query for all observations in 2013 where the temperature was between 25 and 30 degrees Celsius could be answered directly. With a one-dimensional index you would have to scan every record from 2013 and then filter by temperature, or do it the other way round. A two-dimensional index can narrow both at the same time. The HyperDex system uses this technique.

Full-text search and fuzzy indexes

All the indexes so far assume exact data. They support exact lookups, and ranges of a key with a sort order. They cannot find similar keys, such as misspelled words. That needs different techniques.

Full-text search engines can expand a search word to include its synonyms, ignore grammatical variations such as plurals and tenses, and find words that appear near each other in a document. They also support other features that depend on analyzing the language. To cope with typos, Lucene can search for words within a certain edit distance. An edit distance of 1 means one letter has been added, removed, or replaced.

Lucene’s term dictionary is SSTable-like, as described earlier. Queries need a small in-memory index that tells them where in the sorted file to look for a key. In LevelDB, that index is a sparse set of keys. In Lucene, it is a finite state automaton over the characters of the keys, similar to a trie (a tree that branches on characters). That automaton can be converted into a Levenshtein automaton, which searches efficiently for words within a given edit distance.

Other fuzzy search methods move toward document classification and machine learning. The book suggests an information retrieval textbook for more.

Keeping everything in memory

The structures so far all solve the limits of disks. Disks are awkward. Whether magnetic or SSD, data on disk must be laid out carefully for good read and write speed. We put up with this because disks have two big advantages. They are durable, meaning their contents survive a power cut. And they cost less per gigabyte than RAM (main memory).

As RAM gets cheaper, the cost argument weakens. Many datasets are not that big, so they can fit entirely in memory, perhaps spread across several machines. That has led to in-memory databases.
