Some in-memory key-value stores, such as Memcached, are for caching only. It is fine for their data to be lost when a machine restarts. Other in-memory databases aim for durability. They can get it from special hardware, such as battery-backed RAM. Or they can write a log of changes to disk, write periodic snapshots to disk, or copy the in-memory state to other machines. When such a database restarts, it reloads its state from disk, or over the network from a replica (a second copy of the data on another machine), unless special hardware is used.

Writing to disk is still a real part of an in-memory database. Here the disk is used only as an append-only log for durability, and reads are served entirely from memory. Disk files also have operational advantages. They can be backed up easily, and inspected and analyzed by outside tools.

Products such as VoltDB, MemSQL, and Oracle TimesTen are in-memory relational databases. Their vendors claim large speed gains from dropping all the overhead of managing data structures for disk. RAMCloud is an open source in-memory key-value store that stays durable, using a log-structured approach both in memory and on disk. Redis and Couchbase give weaker durability, because they write to disk asynchronously (in the background, after the write is acknowledged).

The book makes a surprising point. The speed advantage of in-memory databases does not come from avoiding disk reads. A disk-based engine may never read from disk either, if there is enough memory, because the operating system caches recently used disk blocks. The real advantage is that in-memory databases skip the cost of encoding in-memory structures into a form that can be written to disk.

In-memory databases can also offer data models that are hard to build on disk. Redis, for example, gives a database-like interface to data structures such as priority queues and sets. Because everything is in memory, its implementation is relatively simple.

Recent research suggests an in-memory design could handle data bigger than memory. The anti-caching approach evicts the least recently used data from memory to disk when memory runs short. When that data is needed again, it is loaded back. This is like what operating systems do with virtual memory and swap files. The database can do it better, because it works on individual records instead of whole memory pages. The indexes, however, still have to fit in memory, like the Bitcask example at the start of the chapter.

Future storage engines may also need changes if non-volatile memory (NVM) becomes common. That is still a new research area, but worth watching.

Transaction Processing or Analytics?

In the early days of business data processing, a database write usually matched a commercial transaction: a sale, an order placed with a supplier, a salary paid. As databases spread to areas without money changing hands, the word transaction stayed. It now means a group of reads and writes that form one logical unit. A transaction does not have to have the full ACID properties (atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability), which Chapter 7 covers. In this context, transaction processing just means letting clients make low-latency reads and writes, as opposed to batch jobs that run periodically, such as once a day. Batch processing is covered in Chapter 10.

Databases were used for many kinds of data, such as blog comments, game actions, and address book contacts. But the access pattern stayed similar. An application looks up a small number of records by some key, using an index. It inserts or updates records based on user input. Because these apps are interactive, this pattern is called online transaction processing, or OLTP.

Databases were also increasingly used for data analytics, which has very different access patterns. An analytic query typically scans a huge number of records, reads only a few columns of each, and computes aggregate statistics such as count, sum, or average. It does not return raw records. For a table of sales transactions, typical analytic questions would be:

  • What was the total revenue of each store in January?
  • How many more bananas than usual did we sell during the latest promotion?
  • Which brand of baby food is most often bought together with brand X diapers?

These queries are often written by business analysts and feed reports that help management make decisions. This is called business intelligence. To tell this pattern apart from transaction processing, it is called online analytic processing, or OLAP. (The book notes that the word “online” is unclear here. It probably means analysts use the system interactively, running exploratory queries rather than only fixed reports.)

Trade-offs

The difference between OLTP and OLAP is not always sharp, but the book’s table gives the typical characteristics.

PropertyTransaction processing (OLTP)Analytic systems (OLAP)
Main read patternSmall number of records per query, fetched by keyAggregate over a large number of records
Main write patternRandom-access, low-latency writes from user inputBulk import (ETL) or event stream
Primarily used byEnd users and customers, through a web applicationInternal analysts, for decision support
What the data representsThe latest state of the data at this momentA history of events that happened over time
Dataset sizeGigabytes to terabytesTerabytes to petabytes

Data Warehousing

A large company may have dozens of transaction systems. There is one for the customer website, one for the checkout systems in physical stores, one for warehouse inventory, one for vehicle routes, one for suppliers, and one for employees. Each is complex and needs its own team, so they run mostly independently of each other.

These OLTP systems are usually expected to be highly available and fast, because the business depends on them. Database administrators guard them closely. They are reluctant to let analysts run ad hoc analytic queries on them, because such queries can be expensive. A query that scans large parts of the dataset can slow down the transactions running at the same time.

The answer is a data warehouse: a separate database that analysts can query freely without affecting OLTP systems. It holds a read-only copy of data from all the company’s OLTP systems. Data is extracted from the OLTP databases, either by periodic dumps or by a continuous stream of changes. It is transformed into a schema that suits analysis, cleaned up, and loaded into the warehouse. This process is called Extract–Transform–Load, or ETL.

Data warehouses are now found in almost every large enterprise, but they are rare in small companies. Small companies tend to have fewer OLTP systems and much less data. That data can be queried in an ordinary SQL database, or even in a spreadsheet. In a large company, a lot of heavy lifting is needed to do something that is simple in a small one.

A big advantage of a separate warehouse is that it can be optimized for analytic access patterns. The indexing algorithms earlier in this chapter work well for OLTP, but they are not very good at analytic queries.

The divergence between OLTP databases and data warehouses

A data warehouse is most often relational, because SQL suits analytic queries well. Many graphical tools generate SQL, draw the results, and let analysts explore the data through operations such as drill-down (going into more detail) and slicing and dicing (filtering along different dimensions).

On the surface, a warehouse and an OLTP database look alike, since both have a SQL interface. Internally they can be very different, because they are tuned for very different queries. Many vendors now focus on one workload or the other, not both.

Some products, such as Microsoft SQL Server and SAP HANA, support both transaction processing and warehousing. But they are increasingly becoming two separate storage and query engines that share a common SQL interface.

Data warehouse vendors such as Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA, and ParAccel usually sell expensive commercial licenses. Amazon Redshift is a hosted version of ParAccel. More recently, many open-source SQL-on-Hadoop projects have appeared. They are young, but they aim to compete with commercial warehouses. Examples include Apache Hive, Spark SQL, Cloudera Impala, Facebook Presto, Apache Tajo, and Apache Drill. Some are based on Google’s Dremel paper.

Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics

Transaction processing uses many data models, chosen for each application. Analytics uses far fewer. Many warehouses follow a formulaic layout called a star schema, also known as dimensional modeling.

At the center of a star schema is a fact table. Each row of the fact table records an event at a particular time. In a grocery store, each row might be one customer buying one product. For website traffic, each row might be a page view or a click. Usually facts are kept as individual events, because that allows the most flexibility later. The downside is that fact tables grow extremely large. The book notes that a big enterprise may have tens of petabytes of transaction history in its warehouse, most of it in fact tables.

Some columns in a fact table are plain values, such as the price a product sold for and the cost of buying it, so the profit margin can be calculated. Other columns are foreign keys, which are references to dimension tables. Each row in a fact table is an event, and its dimensions describe the who, what, where, when, how, and why of that event.

A worked example from the book is a grocery retailer. Its fact table is called fact_sales. One of its dimensions is the product sold. Each row of dim_product is one kind of product on sale, with its stock-keeping unit (SKU, a unique product code), description, brand, category, fat content, package size, and so on. A row in fact_sales uses a foreign key to say which product was sold. If a customer buys several products at once, each product becomes a separate row in the fact table.

Dates and times are often dimension tables too. This lets the warehouse record extra facts about a date, such as whether it was a public holiday, so queries can compare sales on holidays and ordinary days.

The name comes from the picture. Draw the table relationships and the fact table sits in the middle, surrounded by its dimension tables, like the rays of a star.

A snowflake schema is a variant where dimensions are broken into further subdimensions. For example, brands and product categories could each get their own table, and dim_product would hold foreign keys to them instead of storing them as text. Snowflake schemas are more normalized (split into more tables with less repetition). Star schemas are often preferred because analysts find them simpler to work with.

Warehouse tables are often very wide. Fact tables often have over 100 columns, and sometimes several hundred. Dimension tables are wide too, because they hold every detail that might matter for analysis. A store dimension might record which services the store offers, whether it has an in-store bakery, its floor area, when it opened, when it was last remodeled, and how far it is from the nearest highway.

Column-Oriented Storage

If you have trillions of rows and petabytes of facts, storing and querying them efficiently is hard. Dimension tables are much smaller, often millions of rows. So the book focuses on how facts are stored.

A fact table may be over 100 columns wide, but a typical warehouse query uses only four or five of them at a time. Queries rarely need SELECT *. Here is the example from the book, which asks whether people buy more fresh fruit or candy on different days of the week.

Example

The query below looks at every sale of fresh fruit or candy during 2013, and counts how much was sold for each weekday and category. It touches a huge number of rows, but only three columns of fact_sales: date_key, product_sk, and quantity. All other columns are ignored.

SELECT
  dim_date.weekday, dim_product.category,
  SUM(fact_sales.quantity) AS quantity_sold
FROM fact_sales
JOIN dim_date ON fact_sales.date_key = dim_date.date_key
JOIN dim_product ON fact_sales.product_sk = dim_product.product_sk
WHERE dim_date.year = 2013 AND
  dim_product.category IN ('Fresh fruit', 'Candy')
GROUP BY dim_date.weekday, dim_product.category;

How can this run efficiently? In most OLTP databases, storage is row-oriented. All the values from one row are stored next to each other. Document databases work similarly, storing a whole document as one contiguous run of bytes, like the CSV log at the start of the chapter.

You might add indexes on fact_sales.date_key or fact_sales.product_sk, so the engine can find all sales on one date or for one product. But a row-oriented engine still has to load every matching row from disk, with all its 100-plus columns, parse each one, and then filter out the ones that do not match. That takes a long time.

The idea behind column-oriented storage is simple. Do not store the values of one row together. Store all the values of each column together. If each column is kept in its own file, the query reads and parses only the columns it uses. The rest are never touched. The book illustrates this in its Figure 3-10, shown below.

Column layout depends on each column file holding the rows in the same order. So to rebuild a whole row, take the 23rd entry from each column file and put them together. That gives the 23rd row of the table.

Column storage is easiest to explain with relational tables, but the idea works for other data models too. Parquet is a columnar format that supports a document model, and it is based on Google’s Dremel system.

Column Compression

Reading fewer columns cuts the load on the disk. The load can be cut further by compressing the data. Column storage often compresses very well. Look at the sequences of values in one column. They tend to be repetitive, which is a good sign for compression. Different columns suit different techniques. One technique that works especially well in warehouses is bitmap encoding.

Often a column has few distinct values compared with its number of rows. A retailer may have billions of sales transactions but only 100,000 distinct products. Bitmap encoding takes a column with n distinct values and turns it into n separate bitmaps, one for each value. Each bitmap has one bit per row. The bit is 1 if that row has the value, and 0 if it does not.

If n is small, like a country column with about 200 values, each bitmap can be stored with one bit per row. If n is large, most bits in most bitmaps are zero. Such bitmaps are called sparse. A sparse bitmap can also be run-length encoded, which means storing the length of each run of equal bits rather than every bit. This can make a column remarkably compact.

Bitmap indexes suit common warehouse queries very well. Consider these two examples.

Example

A list of products. The query WHERE product_sk IN (30, 68, 69) needs the rows for any of three products. The engine loads three bitmaps, one for product 30, one for 68, and one for 69. It then computes the bitwise OR of the three, which means a row is included if any bitmap has a 1 in that position. That is very efficient.

Two conditions at once. The query WHERE product_sk = 31 AND store_sk = 3 needs rows that match both conditions. The engine loads the bitmap for product 31 and the bitmap for store 3, and computes the bitwise AND. This works because the columns store rows in the same order. So the kth bit in one bitmap refers to the same row as the kth bit in the other.

There are other compression schemes for other kinds of data. The book points to an overview for those.

Watch out

Cassandra and HBase have “column families,” a concept inherited from Bigtable. Despite the name, they are not really column-oriented. Within each column family they store all the columns of a row together, along with a row key, and they do not use column compression. So the Bigtable model is still mostly row-oriented.

Memory bandwidth and vectorized processing

For warehouse queries that scan millions of rows, a big bottleneck is the bandwidth for moving data from disk into memory. But it is not the only one. Developers of analytic databases also work on the bandwidth from main memory into the CPU cache (a small, very fast memory close to the processor). They also try to avoid branch mispredictions (where the CPU guesses wrong about which path a program will take) and stalls in the instruction pipeline. They use SIMD instructions (single instructions that process several data items at once) on modern CPUs.

Column layout helps the CPU as well as the disk. The query engine can take a chunk of compressed column data that fits in the L1 cache (the smallest and fastest cache) and loop through it tightly, with no function calls. A CPU runs such a loop far faster than code that makes many function calls and checks for each record. Compression lets more rows fit into the same cache space. Operators like the bitwise AND and OR can work on these compressed chunks directly. This is called vectorized processing.

Sort Order in Column Storage

In a column store, the order of rows does not have to matter. The simplest choice is to store rows in the order they were inserted, because then a new row just appends one value to each column file. But you can also impose an order, as with the SSTables earlier, and use it as an indexing method.

You cannot sort each column on its own. Then the values would no longer line up by row. A row can only be rebuilt because the kth value in each column belongs to the same row. So the rows must be sorted as whole rows, even though they are stored by column. The database administrator chooses the sort columns based on the common queries.

Example

Suppose queries often target date ranges, such as the last month. Then date_key can be the first sort key. The query optimizer then scans only the rows from the last month, which is much faster than scanning every row.

A second sort key decides the order of rows that share the same first-key value. If date_key is first, product_sk might be second. Then all sales of the same product on the same day sit together, which helps queries that group or filter by product within a date range.

Sorting also helps compression. If the first sort column has few distinct values, then after sorting it contains long runs of the same value. Simple run-length encoding can squeeze that column down to a few kilobytes, even if the table has billions of rows. This effect is strongest on the first sort key. The second and third keys are more jumbled, so their runs are shorter. Columns further down the sort order look random and compress poorly. But sorting the first few columns is still a net win.

Several different sort orders

A clever extension came from C-Store, and was adopted by the commercial warehouse Vertica. Different queries benefit from different sort orders. So why not store the same data sorted in several different ways? Data has to be copied to several machines anyway, so that losing one machine does not lose data. You might as well store those copies sorted in different ways. Then each query can use the copy that suits it best.

This is somewhat like having several secondary indexes in a row-oriented store. But there is a big difference. A row-oriented store keeps each row in one place, in the heap file or a clustered index, and secondary indexes only hold pointers to it. A column store normally has no pointers to data elsewhere. It has only columns of values.

Writing to Column-Oriented Storage

These optimizations suit warehouses, where most of the load is large read-only queries from analysts. But compression, sorting, and column layout make writes harder. B-tree-style update in place is not possible with compressed columns. Inserting a row into the middle of a sorted table could mean rewriting all the column files, because rows are identified by their position in each column. The insert has to update every column consistently.

The earlier solution works here too: LSM-trees. All writes first go to an in-memory store, where they are added to a sorted structure and prepared for disk. This store can be row-oriented or column-oriented, it does not matter. When enough writes have built up, they are merged with the column files on disk and written out in bulk to new files. The book says this is essentially what Vertica does.

Queries must look at both the column data on disk and the recent writes in memory, and combine them. But the query optimizer hides this split. From an analyst’s point of view, inserts, updates, and deletes show up in later queries right away.

Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views

Not every warehouse is a column store. Traditional row-oriented databases and some other designs are also used. But columnar storage can be much faster for ad hoc analytic queries, so it is quickly gaining popularity.

Warehouse queries often use aggregate functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, or MAX. If many queries use the same aggregates, it is wasteful to crunch the raw data every time. Why not cache the counts or sums that queries use most?

One way is a materialized view. A normal (virtual) view is a table-like object whose contents come from a query. The view itself stores nothing. Reading it means running the query. A materialized view is an actual copy of the query results, written to disk. When you read a virtual view, the SQL engine expands it into its underlying query on the fly. When you read a materialized view, you read the stored results.

When the underlying data changes, a materialized view must be updated, because it is a denormalized copy (a copy that repeats information already stored elsewhere). The database can do this automatically, but it makes writes more expensive. That is why materialized views are rarely used in OLTP databases. In read-heavy warehouses, they can make more sense, though whether they actually speed up reads depends on the case.

A common special case is the data cube, also called an OLAP cube. It is a grid of aggregates, grouped by different dimensions.

Imagine for now that each fact has foreign keys to only two dimension tables, date and product. Draw a two-dimensional table with dates along one axis and products along the other. Each cell holds the aggregate, such as SUM, of an attribute such as net price, for all facts with that date and product. Then you can apply the same aggregate along a row or a column. That gives a summary reduced by one dimension: sales by product regardless of date, or sales by date regardless of product.

Facts often have more than two dimensions. The grocery example has five: date, product, store, promotion, and customer. Each cell then holds sales for one combination of all five. It is hard to picture a five-dimensional cube, but the idea is the same. Each cell can be summarized along any of the dimensions.

Example

A cube built on date and store can answer “total sales per store yesterday” by reading the totals for yesterday along the store dimension. There is no need to scan millions of rows. Certain queries become very fast, because their answers were computed in advance.

The downside is less flexibility. A cube only answers questions about its dimensions. For example, a cube with no price dimension cannot tell you what share of sales came from items costing more than $100. The raw data can, so most warehouses keep as much raw data as they can, and use cubes and aggregates only as a speed boost for certain queries.

Summary

Summary
  • Two kinds of workload. Storage engines fall into two broad groups: those optimized for transaction processing (OLTP), and those optimized for analytics (OLAP). OLTP systems are user-facing and touch few records per query, found through a key and an index. Disk seek time is often the bottleneck. Analytic systems handle fewer queries, but each one scans millions of records. Disk bandwidth is often the bottleneck, and column storage is an increasingly popular answer.
  • The log-structured school. This family only appends to files and deletes obsolete ones. It never changes a file once written. Bitcask, SSTables, LSM-trees, LevelDB, Cassandra, HBase, and Lucene belong here. Its key idea is turning random writes into sequential writes, which gives higher write throughput on hard drives and SSDs. These engines are a comparatively recent development.
  • The update-in-place school. This family treats disk as fixed-size pages that can be overwritten. B-trees are the biggest example. They are used in all major relational databases, and in many nonrelational ones.
  • Other structures. Secondary indexes, clustered and covering indexes, multi-column and multi-dimensional indexes, and fuzzy full-text indexes all extend the basic idea. In-memory databases keep all data in RAM, and use logs or snapshots for durability.
  • Warehouses and column storage. A data warehouse is a separate database for analysts, filled by ETL from OLTP systems. Star schemas organize it around fact tables and dimension tables. Column-oriented storage, with compression and sort orders, reads only the columns each query needs. Materialized views and data cubes precompute common aggregates.
  • Know your engine. Knowing these internals lets an application developer choose the right tool, and predict what a tuning parameter will change. It also helps you read the documentation for whichever database you use.

The chapter ends with 64 references to papers, documentation, and articles behind its claims. This retelling does not reproduce that list.

Check yourself

  1. A hash index keeps every key in memory. Why does that limit the approach, and what does the book say about keeping the values in memory too?

    Show answer

    The whole hash map must fit in RAM, so a very large number of keys breaks the design. Values do not need to fit in memory, because each one can be read from disk with a single seek.

  2. A B-tree update that splits a page writes several pages. Why do most B-tree implementations also keep a write-ahead log?

    Show answer

    If the database crashes after only some of those pages are written, the tree can be corrupted, for example by an orphan page that no parent points to. The log records each change before it is applied, so the tree can be restored to a consistent state after a crash.

  3. An LSM-tree gets heavy writes, but compaction cannot keep up. What goes wrong, and why does the book say you need monitoring?

    Show answer

    Unmerged segments pile up on disk until space runs out, and reads slow down because they must check more files. SSTable engines typically do not throttle incoming writes, so the problem can grow silently unless you watch for it.

  4. A fact table has over 100 columns, and a query reads only three. How does column storage reduce the work, and how is a whole row rebuilt from the column files?

    Show answer

    Only the three column files are loaded and parsed, so far less data is read from disk. Each column file keeps rows in the same order, so a row is rebuilt by taking the same position (for example the 23rd entry) from each column file.

Part I · Chapter 4

Encoding and Evolution

The big idea: programs change over time, and the data they write can outlive them by years. So the way data is encoded must let old and new code read each other’s data, both while a deployment is half finished and long after.

Applications change all the time. New features ship, business rules shift, and teams learn what users really need. Most feature changes also change the data the application stores. You may need to capture a new field, or show existing data in a new way. Chapter 1 called this ability to adapt evolvability.

Databases handle change in different ways. A relational database normally assumes one schema (the agreed structure of the data, such as its tables and columns) at a time. You can change that schema with a migration, which is an ALTER statement that rewrites the structure, but at any moment exactly one schema is in force. A schema-on-read database, also called schemaless, does not enforce a schema. It can hold a mix of old and new formats written at different times. Chapter 2 covers both approaches.

Changing the code is harder than changing the schema, because the code does not change everywhere at once. Server-side applications often use a rolling upgrade, also known as a staged rollout. The new version goes to a few nodes (machines or processes in a cluster) first. The team checks that it runs smoothly, then works through the remaining nodes one group at a time. This means a new version can go out without downtime, which encourages more frequent releases. Client-side applications are harder. The user decides when to install an update, so an old version may keep running for months.

So old and new versions of the code, and old and new data formats, may all coexist in the same system. To keep things running smoothly, the system needs compatibility in both directions:

  • Backward compatibility: newer code can read data that was written by older code.
  • Forward compatibility: older code can read data that was written by newer code.
Key idea

Backward compatibility lets new code read old data, and forward compatibility lets old code read new data. You need both during a rolling upgrade, because both versions are live at the same time.

Backward compatibility is usually not hard. You wrote the new code, so you know the format of the old data. You can handle it explicitly, even if that means keeping the old code around to read the old records. Forward compatibility is trickier. Old code has to ignore additions that a newer version made, without breaking.

This chapter looks at several formats for encoding data: JSON, XML, Protocol Buffers, Thrift, and Avro. It asks how each one handles schema changes, and how well it supports old and new data and code living side by side. It then looks at where these formats are used: for storing data in databases, for communication in web services and remote procedure calls (RPC, where one program calls a function on another machine as if it were local), and for message passing through queues and actor systems.

Formats for Encoding Data

Programs usually work with data in two forms. In memory, data lives in objects, structs, lists, arrays, hash tables, and trees. These structures are built for fast access by the CPU, and they often use pointers (memory addresses) to link parts together. When you want to write data to a file or send it over a network, you must turn it into a self-contained sequence of bytes, such as a JSON document. A pointer means nothing to another process, so the byte form looks quite different from the in-memory form.

The translation from the in-memory form to bytes is called encoding, also known as serialization or marshalling. The reverse translation is decoding, also known as parsing, deserialization, or unmarshalling.

Watch out

The word serialization is also used in the context of transactions, where it means something completely different. To avoid mixing the two, the book sticks with encoding. Encoding also has nothing to do with encryption, which the book does not cover.

Because this problem is so common, there are many libraries and formats to choose from. The book goes through them in roughly this order.

Language-Specific Formats

Many programming languages have built-in support for encoding objects in memory into bytes. Java has java.io.Serializable, Ruby has Marshal, and Python has pickle. Third-party libraries exist too, such as Kryo for Java. These built-in tools are convenient, because objects can be saved and restored with very little extra code. The book, however, points to several deep problems:

  • The format is tied to one language. Reading the data from another language is very hard. If you store data this way, you are committed to your current language for a long time, and you make it hard to share data with other organizations that use different languages.
  • Security. To restore an object, the decoder must be able to create instances of arbitrary classes. If an attacker can make your application decode a byte sequence of their choosing, they can create arbitrary classes. That is a common route to remote code execution, meaning running their own code on your machine.
  • Versioning is an afterthought. These libraries are built for quick and easy encoding, so they often ignore the awkward problems of forward and backward compatibility.
  • Efficiency is an afterthought too. That covers both the CPU time to encode or decode and the size of the result. Java’s built-in serialization, for example, is known for poor performance and a bloated encoding.

For these reasons, the book says it is generally a bad idea to use a language’s built-in encoding for anything except very short-lived purposes.

JSON, XML, and Binary Variants

Standardized encodings that many languages can write and read are the obvious next choice. JSON and XML are the main contenders. They are widely known and widely supported, and almost as widely disliked. XML is often criticized as too verbose and unnecessarily complicated. JSON became popular mainly because web browsers support it natively (it is a subset of JavaScript) and because it is simpler than XML. CSV, a plain table of comma-separated values, is another popular format, though it is less powerful.

JSON, XML, and CSV are textual, so people can read them to a degree, although their syntax is a favorite topic of debate. Beyond the surface details, they have some subtle problems:

  • Numbers are ambiguous. In XML and CSV you cannot tell a number from a string of digits without an external schema. JSON separates strings from numbers, but it does not distinguish integers from floating-point numbers (numbers with a decimal part, stored approximately), and it does not specify a precision. This matters for large integers. Any integer above 253 cannot be stored exactly in an IEEE 754 double-precision float, which is the standard number format used in many languages, including JavaScript. The numbers then become inaccurate after parsing. Twitter uses 64-bit numbers to identify each tweet, so its API returns each tweet ID twice: once as a JSON number and once as a decimal string. That workaround lets JavaScript applications get the right value.
  • Binary strings are not supported. JSON and XML handle Unicode text well, but they cannot hold a plain sequence of bytes with no character encoding. People work around this by encoding the bytes as text with Base64, and the schema says to decode that text as bytes. It works, but it is hacky, and it makes the data about 33 percent bigger.
  • Schema support is optional. Both XML and JSON have optional schema languages. These are powerful and complicated to learn and implement. XML schemas are fairly common, but many JSON-based tools skip schemas altogether. Because the right meaning of numbers and binary strings depends on the schema, applications without one must hardcode the decoding logic instead.
  • CSV has no schema at all. The application must define what each row and column means. If a change adds a row or column, you must handle it by hand. CSV is also vague. What happens if a value contains a comma or a newline? Its escaping rules have been formally written down, but not every parser implements them correctly.

Despite these flaws, JSON, XML, and CSV are good enough for many uses, and they will probably stay popular. They work especially well as data interchange formats, for sending data from one organization to another. In that setting, the hard part is getting both sides to agree on the format. Once they agree, it matters much less how pretty or efficient the format is.

Binary encoding

Data used only inside your own organization has less pressure to use a lowest-common-denominator format. You can pick one that is more compact or faster to parse. For a small dataset the gain is negligible. Once you reach terabytes, the choice of format can make a big difference.

JSON is less verbose than XML, but both use far more space than binary formats. That observation led to a large family of binary encodings for JSON, including MessagePack, BSON, BJSON, UBJSON, BISON, and Smile, and for XML, including WBXML and Fast Infoset. These formats have found niches, but none is as widely adopted as the textual versions. Some of them add datatypes, such as telling integers apart from floating-point numbers or adding binary strings. Otherwise they keep the JSON or XML data model unchanged. Since they do not use a schema, they must include every object field name inside the encoded data.

The book uses this record to compare the formats in the rest of the chapter:

{
  "userName": "Martin",
  "favoriteNumber": 1337,
  "interests": ["daydreaming", "hacking"]
}
Example

The book encodes this record with MessagePack, a binary encoding for JSON. The first few bytes work like this:

  1. The first byte, 0x83, says that an object follows (the top four bits are 0x80) with three fields (the bottom four bits are 0x03). If an object had more than 15 fields, a different type marker would be used, and the field count would take two or four bytes.
  2. The second byte, 0xa8, says a string follows (the top four bits are 0xa0) that is eight bytes long (the bottom four bits are 0x08).
  3. The next eight bytes are the field name userName in ASCII. The length was already given, so no end marker or escaping is needed.
  4. The next seven bytes hold the six-letter value Martin, with a prefix byte of 0xa6, and so on for the rest of the record.

The whole binary encoding is 66 bytes. The textual JSON, with whitespace removed, is 81 bytes. The saving is small, and the book asks whether a saving that size is worth losing human readability. All binary JSON encodings behave much the same way. The book then shows how the same record can be encoded in 32 bytes.

Thrift and Protocol Buffers

Apache Thrift and Protocol Buffers (usually shortened to protobuf) are binary encoding libraries built on the same principle. Protocol Buffers was first developed at Google, and Thrift at Facebook. Both were made open source in 2007 and 2008.

Both require a schema for any data they encode. You describe the schema in a small language called an interface definition language (IDL), which is a way to write down the shape of data so that tools can read it. In Thrift’s IDL, the example record looks like this:

struct Person {
  1: required string userName,
  2: optional i64 favoriteNumber,
  3: optional list<string> interests
}

The Protocol Buffers schema looks very similar:

message Person {
  required string user_name = 1;
  optional int64 favorite_number = 2;
  repeated string interests = 3;
}

Both tools come with a code generator. It takes a schema like these and produces classes in your chosen language that implement it. Application code calls the generated classes to encode or decode records.

Thrift actually has more than one binary format. Its two main ones are called BinaryProtocol and CompactProtocol. The book notes that a third, DenseProtocol, exists only in the C++ version, so it does not count as cross-language. BinaryProtocol encodes the example record in 59 bytes. Each field gets a type annotation, and a length where one is needed, such as the length of a string or the number of items in a list. The strings, such as “Martin”, are stored as UTF-8. The big difference from JSON is that there are no field names. Instead, each field carries a field tag, a number from the schema (1, 2, and 3 here). A field tag works like a short alias for a field name.

Example

Thrift’s CompactProtocol holds the same information in 34 bytes. It packs the field type and the tag number into a single byte, and it uses variable-length integers. Instead of a full eight bytes for the number 1337, it uses two bytes. The top bit of each byte says whether more bytes follow. Numbers from –64 to 63 fit in one byte, numbers from –8192 to 8191 fit in two, and bigger numbers take more bytes.

Protocol Buffers has only one binary format. It packs bits slightly differently from CompactProtocol, but it is otherwise very similar, and it fits the same record in 33 bytes.

There is one detail to note. Both schemas mark fields as required or optional, but that marker does not change the encoded bytes. Nothing in the binary data says whether a field was required. The only difference is that required adds a runtime check that fails if the field is not set. That check can help catch bugs.

Field tags and schema evolution

Schemas inevitably change over time. The book calls this schema evolution. How do Thrift and Protocol Buffers handle changes while keeping both backward and forward compatibility?

An encoded record is just the concatenation of its encoded fields. Each field is identified by its tag number and annotated with its datatype, such as string or integer. A field that is not set is simply left out of the record. This makes field tags critical to the meaning of the data. You can rename a field in the schema, because the encoded data never uses field names. But you cannot change a field’s tag, because that would make all the existing encoded data invalid.

Adding a field is safe if the new field gets a new tag number. Suppose old code, which does not know the new tag, reads data that new code wrote. It sees a tag it does not recognize, and it can skip that field. The datatype annotation tells the parser how many bytes to skip. That keeps forward compatibility: old code can read records written by new code.

Backward compatibility works too. As long as every field has a unique tag, new code can always read old data, because the tags still mean the same thing. There is one catch. A newly added field cannot be required. If it were, new code reading old data would fail the check, because the old code never wrote that field. So every field added after the schema’s first deployment must be optional or have a default value.

Removing a field is the same change with the compatibility concerns reversed. You can remove only an optional field, because a required field can never be removed. You must also never reuse a tag number. Old data may still contain the old tag somewhere, and new code must ignore that field rather than mistake it for something new.

Try it

Suppose a new version of a Protocol Buffers service adds a required field, and it is rolled out with a rolling upgrade. Which code would fail its required-field check first, and on which data? Think about which records were written before the new field existed.

Datatypes and schema evolution

What about changing the datatype of a field? That may be possible, but the documentation for each tool has the details. There is a risk that values lose precision or get truncated. Take the case of changing a 32-bit integer into a 64-bit integer. New code can read data written by old code, because the parser can fill the missing bits with zeros. But if old code reads data written by new code, the old code still stores the value in a 32-bit variable. If the decoded value does not fit in 32 bits, it gets truncated.

Protocol Buffers has no list or array datatype. Instead, a field can be marked repeated, which is a third option alongside required and optional. A repeated field is encoded as the same tag appearing several times in the record. That makes it safe to change an optional, single-valued field into a repeated, multi-valued one. New code reading old data sees a list with zero or one elements, depending on whether the field was present. Old code reading new data sees only the last element of the list.

Thrift has a dedicated list datatype, which is parameterized by the element type. That does not allow the same change from single value to many values that Protocol Buffers allows. In exchange, Thrift supports nested lists.

Avro

Apache Avro is another binary encoding format, and it works quite differently from Protocol Buffers and Thrift. It began in 2009 as a subproject of Hadoop, the big data framework, because Thrift was not a good fit for Hadoop’s use cases.

Avro also uses a schema to describe the data it encodes. It has two schema languages. One, Avro IDL, is meant for people to edit. The other is based on JSON and is easier for machines to read. In Avro IDL, the example record looks like this:

record Person {
  string userName;
  union { null, long } favoriteNumber = null;
  array<string> interests;
}

The same schema in its JSON form is:

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "Person",
  "fields": [
    {"name": "userName", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "favoriteNumber", "type": ["null", "long"], "default": null},
    {"name": "interests", "type": {"type": "array", "items": "string"}}
  ]
}

Notice that the Avro schema has no tag numbers at all. Encoding the example record with this schema produces 32 bytes, the smallest of all the encodings the chapter has seen. The breakdown is shown in a figure in the book, which this retelling does not reproduce.

Example

Here is what the 32 bytes contain. Nothing in the bytes says which field is which, or what type each value has. The encoding is just the values, one after another. A string is a length followed by its UTF-8 bytes. Nothing in the data says that it is a string. The same bytes could just as well be an integer or something else entirely. Integers use a variable-length encoding, the same one Thrift’s CompactProtocol uses.

To parse the data, you go through the fields in the order they appear in the schema, and the schema tells you the type of each one. That has a consequence. The data can be decoded correctly only by code that uses the exact same schema as the code that wrote it. A mismatch means the data is decoded wrongly, with no error to warn you.

So how does Avro support schema evolution, if both sides must agree on the schema?

The writer’s schema and the reader’s schema

When an application encodes data, to write it to a file or database or send it over a network, it uses the version of the schema it knows about. For example, that schema may be compiled into the application. This is the writer’s schema.

When an application decodes data, it expects the data to match some schema. This is the reader’s schema. It is the schema the application code relies on, and the code may have been generated from it during the build.

The key idea in Avro is that the writer’s schema and the reader’s schema do not have to be the same. They only need to be compatible. When data is decoded, the Avro library looks at the writer’s schema and the reader’s schema side by side, and it translates the data from the writer’s form into the reader’s form. The Avro specification defines exactly how this resolution works.

Fields are matched by name, so the two schemas can list their fields in a different order. If the reader meets a field that the writer’s schema has but the reader’s schema does not, it ignores that field. If the reader expects a field that the writer’s schema does not contain, the reader fills in the default value declared in its own schema.

Schema evolution rules

With Avro, forward compatibility means you can have a new version of the schema as the writer and an old version as the reader. Backward compatibility means you can have a new version as the reader and an old version as the writer.

To stay compatible, you may add or remove only a field that has a default value. The field favoriteNumber in the example schema has a default of null. Suppose you add a field with a default. The new field exists in the new schema but not the old one. When a reader using the new schema reads a record written with the old schema, the default fills in the missing field.

If you add a field with no default, new readers cannot read data from old writers, so backward compatibility breaks. If you remove a field with no default, old readers cannot read data from new writers, so forward compatibility breaks.

Avro handles nulls differently from many languages. In Avro, null is not an acceptable default for every variable. If a field may be null, you must say so with a union type, which means the field can hold one of several listed types. For example, union { null, long, string } field; means the field can be a number, a string, or null. You can use null as a default only if null is one of the branches of the union. (The book adds that the default must match the type of the union’s first branch. That is a specific limitation of Avro, not a general rule for unions.) This is a little more verbose than making everything nullable, but it prevents bugs by being explicit about what can be null. As a result, Avro has no optional and required markers like Protocol Buffers and Thrift. It uses union types and default values instead.

Changing a field’s datatype is possible as long as Avro can convert the old type to the new one. Renaming a field is possible, but a little tricky. The reader’s schema can list aliases, which are older names for a field. That lets it match an old writer’s field name against an alias. So a rename is backward compatible but not forward compatible. Adding a branch to a union type is also backward compatible but not forward compatible.

But what is the writer’s schema?

There is an important question so far left unanswered. How does the reader know which writer’s schema was used for a particular piece of data? You cannot include the whole schema with every record. The schema would often be much bigger than the encoded data, and that would cancel out the savings of the binary format. The answer depends on the context. The book gives four examples.

  • A large file of many records. A common use for Avro, especially with Hadoop, is a large file holding millions of records that all share one schema. The writer includes the schema once, at the start of the file. Avro defines a file format, called object container files, to do exactly this.
  • A database with records written at different times. Records may be written at different points in time, using different writer’s schemas, so you cannot assume that all records share one schema. The simplest approach is to put a version number at the start of every encoded record and keep a list of schema versions in the database. A reader fetches a record, reads its version number, looks up the matching writer’s schema, and then decodes the rest of the record. The book says LinkedIn’s Espresso works this way. The version number can be a simple incrementing integer or a hash of the schema.
  • Records sent over a network connection. When two processes talk over a two-way connection, they can agree on the schema version when the connection is set up, then use that schema for as long as the connection lasts. The Avro RPC protocol works like this.
  • A schema version database in general. Keeping the list of schema versions is useful in any case. It acts as documentation, and it gives you a chance to check whether the schemas are compatible with each other.

Dynamically generated schemas

Avro has one advantage over Protocol Buffers and Thrift: its schema has no tag numbers. Why does that matter? Keeping a few numbers in the schema might seem harmless.

The difference shows up with dynamically generated schemas. Imagine you want to dump the contents of a relational database to a file. A binary format avoids the problems of textual formats such as JSON, CSV, or SQL. With Avro, you can generate an Avro schema from the relational schema, in the JSON form shown earlier, and encode the contents with it into an Avro object container file. Each database table becomes a record schema. Each column becomes a field, and the column name becomes the field name.

Example

Now suppose the database schema changes. A table gains one column and loses another. You generate a new Avro schema from the updated database schema, and you export the data using it. The export process does not need to pay attention to the change. It converts the schema every time it runs. Anyone who reads the new files sees that the record’s fields have changed. Because fields are identified by name, the new writer’s schema can still be matched with the old reader’s schema.

With Thrift or Protocol Buffers, the field tags would usually have to be assigned by hand. Each time the database schema changed, an administrator would have to update the mapping from column names to field tags. That could be automated, but the generator would have to be very careful never to reuse a tag that was used before. Dynamically generated schemas were never a design goal of Thrift or Protocol Buffers. They were a design goal of Avro.

Code generation and dynamically typed languages

Thrift and Protocol Buffers depend on code generation. After you define a schema, you generate code in your language that implements it. This is useful in statically typed languages such as Java, C++, or C#. It lets decoded data use efficient in-memory structures. It also lets the compiler check types, and it lets the editor offer autocompletion when you write code that uses the data.

In dynamically typed languages such as JavaScript, Ruby, or Python, generating code gains little, because there is no compile-time type checker to satisfy. Code generation is often frowned on in these languages, since they otherwise avoid an explicit compilation step. For a dynamically generated schema, such as one made from a database table, code generation is an unnecessary obstacle between you and the data.

Avro offers code generation as an option for statically typed languages, but it works just as well without it. An object container file embeds the writer’s schema, so you can open it with the Avro library and look at the data much as you would look at a JSON file. The file describes itself. This is especially useful with dynamically typed data processing tools such as Apache Pig. In Pig, you can open some Avro files, start analyzing them, and write derived datasets back out in Avro format without thinking about schemas at all.

Here is how the four encodings compare on the same example record. The Avro bytes are the smallest, because the schema carries the field names and the types, and the data carries only values.

The Merits of Schemas

Protocol Buffers, Thrift, and Avro all use a schema to describe a binary encoding. Their schema languages are much simpler than XML Schema or JSON Schema. Those two support detailed validation rules, such as “this string must match this regular expression” or “this integer must be between 0 and 100.” Because Protocol Buffers, Thrift, and Avro are simpler to implement and to use, they have grown to support a fairly wide range of programming languages.

These ideas are not new. They have much in common with ASN.1, a schema language first standardized in 1984. ASN.1 was used to define various network protocols, and its binary encoding, DER, is still used to encode SSL certificates (X.509). ASN.1 supports schema evolution using tag numbers, much like Protocol Buffers and Thrift. However, it is also very complex and badly documented, so the book thinks it is probably not a good choice for new applications.

Many data systems also have a proprietary binary encoding of their own. Most relational databases have a network protocol for sending queries and getting responses back. These protocols are usually specific to one database. The vendor supplies a driver, such as one built on the ODBC or JDBC interfaces, that decodes the responses into in-memory data structures.

So, although textual formats such as JSON, XML, and CSV are widespread, schema-based binary encodings are also a viable option. They have several good properties:

  • They can be much more compact than the binary JSON variants, because they can leave field names out of the encoded data.
  • The schema is valuable documentation. Because decoding requires the schema, you can be sure it is up to date. Manually maintained documentation can easily drift away from reality.
  • Keeping a database of schemas lets you check forward and backward compatibility of a change before anything is deployed.
  • For statically typed languages, generating code from the schema allows type checking at compile time.

In summary, schema evolution gives the same kind of flexibility as schemaless JSON databases, while also giving you stronger guarantees about your data and better tools.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
Language-specific encodings (Java serialization, Ruby Marshal, Python pickle)Saving and restoring objects with very little codeTied to one language. Risky to decode untrusted bytes. Versioning and size are afterthoughts.
JSON, XML, CSVReadable, widely supported, and easy to share between organizationsAmbiguous numbers, no binary strings without Base64, optional schemas, and larger sizes.
Binary JSON variants (MessagePack and others)Somewhat smaller and faster to parse than JSONA small saving in the book’s example (66 bytes against 81). Field names stay in the data, and the data is no longer readable by eye.
Thrift and Protocol BuffersCompact. Clear compatibility rules based on field tags. Code generation for static languages.Schemas must be kept, and tags must be managed by hand. Data must be decoded before it can be read.
AvroThe smallest encoding in the example (32 bytes). Schema changes are matched by field name, which suits generated schemas.The reader must know the writer’s schema, so it must be stored or negotiated. Nullable fields need union types.

Modes of Dataflow

At the beginning of this chapter, we said that whenever you send data to a process that does not share your memory, you must encode it into bytes. That happens when you send data over a network or write it to a file. We then looked at many encodings and at how to keep them compatible. Compatibility is a relationship between the process that encodes the data and the process that decodes it.

That idea is abstract, and data can flow between processes in many ways. Who encodes the data, and who decodes it? The book looks at three common modes: data passed through databases, data passed through service calls, and data passed by asynchronous message passing.

Dataflow Through Databases

In a database, the process that writes encodes the data, and the process that reads decodes it. There may be just one process using the database. In that case, the reader is simply a later version of the same process. Storing something in the database is then a bit like sending a message to your future self. Backward compatibility is clearly needed here. Otherwise your future self could not decode what you wrote earlier.

In general, several processes often use a database at once. They might be different applications or services, or several copies of the same service running in parallel for scalability or fault tolerance. In a changing system, some of those processes will run newer code and some will run older code. For example, a new version may be part way through a rolling upgrade. So a value written by newer code may later be read by an older version that is still running. That means forward compatibility is also often needed for databases.

There is an additional snag. Suppose you add a field to a record schema, and the newer code writes a value for that field. Later, an older version of the code, which does not know about the field, reads the record, updates it, and writes it back. The desirable behavior here is for the old code to keep the new field intact, even though it cannot interpret it.

Example

The book walks through the snag in three steps, shown in the figure below.

  1. The newer app writes a record that includes the new field. The database now holds that field.
  2. The older app reads the same record. It does not know the new field, so it has no meaning for it.
  3. The older app saves its model object back to the database. If that object was built without the new field, the field is dropped, and the newer app’s data is lost.

The formats discussed earlier do support keeping unknown fields. But sometimes you have to take care at the application level. If you decode a database value into model objects in your application, and later re-encode those objects, the unknown field can be lost in that translation. This is not a hard problem to solve. You just need to be aware of it.

Different values written at different times

A database generally allows any value to be updated at any time. So within one database you may have some values written five milliseconds ago and others written five years ago. When you deploy a new version of a server-side application, you may replace the old version with the new one within a few minutes. The same is not true of the database contents. Five-year-old data will still be there in its original encoding, unless someone has explicitly rewritten it since. The book sums this up as: data outlives code.

Rewriting, or migrating, data into a new schema is possible, but it is expensive on a large dataset, so most databases avoid it where they can. Most relational databases allow simple schema changes, such as adding a new column with a null default, without rewriting the existing data. When an old row is read, the database fills in nulls for any columns that are missing from the encoded data on disk. LinkedIn’s document database Espresso uses Avro for storage, so it can use Avro’s schema evolution rules. MySQL is the exception the book points to: it often rewrites an entire table even when that is not strictly necessary, as the chapter on schema flexibility in the document model also noted.

The result is that schema evolution lets the whole database appear as if it were encoded with a single schema. The underlying storage may still hold records encoded with several historical versions of the schema.

Archival storage

You might take a snapshot of your database from time to time, for backup or to load into a data warehouse. In that case, the dump is usually encoded with the latest schema. The source database may hold a mixture of schema versions from different eras, but since you are copying the data anyway, you might as well encode the copy consistently.

A dump is written in one go and does not change afterward, so a format such as Avro object container files fits well. You could also encode the data in an analytics-friendly, column-oriented format such as Parquet, which the book covered in its discussion of column compression in Chapter 3. Chapter 10 says more about using data in archival storage.

Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC

When processes need to communicate over a network, there are a few ways to arrange it. The most common arrangement has two roles: clients and servers. A server exposes an API over the network, and clients connect to it to make requests. The API that a server exposes is known as a service.

The web works this way. Clients, which are web browsers, make GET requests to download HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and images. They make POST requests to submit data to the server. The API here is a standard set of protocols and formats: HTTP, URLs, SSL/TLS, and HTML. Because browsers, web servers, and website authors largely agree on these standards, any browser can open any website, at least in theory.

Browsers are not the only kind of client. A native app on a phone or desktop can also make network requests to a server. A JavaScript application running inside a browser can use XMLHttpRequest to make HTTP requests itself, a technique known as Ajax. In that case the server’s response is usually not HTML for a person to look at. It is data, often JSON, for the client-side code to process. HTTP may be the transport, but the API built on top of it is specific to each application, so client and server must agree on its details.

A server can also be a client of another service. A typical web application server acts as a client to a database. This approach is often used to split a large application into smaller services, organized by area of functionality. When one service needs something from another, it makes a request. This style has traditionally been called a service-oriented architecture (SOA). It has more recently been refined and rebranded as microservices.

Services are in some ways similar to databases. Both let clients submit and query data. But a database accepts arbitrary queries in the query languages discussed in Chapter 2. A service exposes an application-specific API that accepts only the inputs and outputs that the service’s business logic has predetermined. That restriction gives a degree of encapsulation. The service can place fine-grained limits on what clients can and cannot do.

A key goal of a service-oriented or microservices architecture is to make the application easier to change and maintain, by making each service independently deployable and evolvable. Each service should be owned by one team, and that team should be able to release new versions often without coordinating with other teams. So you should expect old and new versions of servers and clients to be running at the same time. The data encoding used by servers and clients must therefore be compatible across versions of the service’s API. That is exactly what this chapter has been about.

Web services

When HTTP is the protocol used to talk to a service, the service is called a web service. That name is a slight misnomer, because web services are used in more than just the web. The book lists three common contexts:

  1. A client application on a user’s device, such as a native phone app or a JavaScript web app using Ajax, makes requests to a service over HTTP. These requests usually travel over the public internet.
  2. One service makes requests to another service owned by the same organization, often within the same datacenter, as part of a service-oriented or microservices architecture. Software built to support this use is sometimes called middleware.
  3. One service makes requests to a service owned by a different organization, usually over the internet. This is how the backend systems of different organizations exchange data. It includes public APIs from online services, such as credit card processing, and OAuth, which allows shared access to user data.

There are two popular approaches to web services: REST and SOAP. The book says they are almost opposed in philosophy, and their supporters often argue about them heatedly.

REST is not a protocol. It is a design philosophy that builds on the principles of HTTP. It favors simple data formats, uses URLs to identify resources, and uses HTTP features for cache control, authentication, and negotiating the content type. REST has been gaining popularity over SOAP, at least for connecting services across organizations, and it is often associated with microservices. An API designed on these principles is called RESTful.

SOAP is an XML-based protocol for making network API requests. It is most commonly used over HTTP, but it aims to be independent of HTTP and avoids most of its features. Instead, it comes with a large and complicated set of related standards, called WS-*, which add various features. The API of a SOAP service is described in an XML-based language called the Web Services Description Language, or WSDL. WSDL enables code generation, so a client can call a remote service through local classes and method calls, which the framework encodes into XML messages and decodes again. That is useful in statically typed languages, and less so in dynamically typed ones.

WSDL is not designed to be read by people, and SOAP messages are often too complex to build by hand. So SOAP users rely heavily on tool support, code generation, and IDEs. If a programming language is not supported by the SOAP vendors, integrating with SOAP services is hard. Even though SOAP and its extensions are formally standardized, the implementations from different vendors often fail to interoperate. For these reasons, SOAP is still used in many large enterprises, but it has fallen out of favor in most smaller companies.

RESTful APIs tend to favor simpler approaches, with less code generation and automated tooling. A definition format such as OpenAPI, also known as Swagger, can describe a RESTful API and produce documentation from it. The book adds two notes. SOAP is not a requirement for SOA, because SOA is a general approach while SOAP is one specific technology. And even within each camp there are plenty of arguments, for example about HATEOAS, the idea of hypermedia as the engine of application state.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
RESTSimple formats, HTTP features, easy to try with a browser or curl, wide tool support, popular for cross-organization APIsLess generated code and less formal typing. Responses usually have no formally specified schema, so compatibility depends on discipline.
SOAPStrict, machine-readable WSDL contracts and generated client code, which suit statically typed languagesA large and complex standards stack. Hard to use without tools. Vendors often fail to interoperate, and it is hard to integrate from unsupported languages.

The problems with remote procedure calls (RPCs)

Web services are the latest version of a long line of technologies for making API requests over a network. Many of the earlier ones were heavily hyped but had serious problems. Enterprise JavaBeans (EJB) and Java’s Remote Method Invocation (RMI) work only in Java. The Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM) works only on Microsoft platforms. The Common Object Request Broker Architecture (CORBA) is excessively complex and does not provide backward or forward compatibility.

All of these rest on the idea of a remote procedure call, or RPC, which dates back to the 1970s. The RPC model tries to make a request to a remote service look the same as calling a function or method in your programming language, within the same process. This abstraction is called location transparency. It sounds convenient, but the book says the approach is fundamentally flawed. A network request is very different from a local function call:

  • Outcomes are unpredictable. A local function call is predictable. It succeeds or fails based only on parameters you control. A network request can be lost, or the remote machine can be slow or unavailable, and those problems are outside your control. Network problems are common, so you must plan for them, for example by retrying a failed request.
  • There is a third outcome: no answer. A local call returns a result, throws an exception, or never returns because it loops forever or the process crashes. A network request can also return with no result because of a timeout. Then you simply do not know what happened. You cannot tell whether the request got through. Chapter 8 discusses this in more detail.
  • Retries can repeat the action. If the requests are getting through and only the responses are lost, a retry performs the action again. Unless the protocol has a way to deduplicate (make repeated requests harmless, which is called idempotence), the action happens twice. Local function calls do not have this problem. Chapter 11 covers idempotence in more detail.
  • Speed varies wildly. A local function call takes about the same time each time you run it. A network request is much slower, and its time varies a lot. At a good moment it may finish in under a millisecond, but on a congested network or with an overloaded service the same request may take many seconds.
  • Parameters must be encoded. With a local call, you can pass a reference to an object in memory. With a network request, every parameter has to be encoded into bytes and sent. That is fine for numbers and strings, but it becomes a problem with larger objects.
  • Languages do not share types. The client and the service may be written in different languages, so the RPC framework must translate types from one language to another. This can be ugly, because not all languages have the same types. Recall the JavaScript problem with integers above 253. A single process written in a single language has no such problem.

Together, these mean there is no point in making a remote service look too much like a local object in your programming language. It is fundamentally a different thing. Part of the appeal of REST is that it does not pretend the service is local. It is openly a network protocol. Still, people keep building RPC libraries on top of REST.

Current directions for RPC

Despite these problems, RPC is not going away. Several RPC frameworks have been built on the encodings in this chapter. Thrift and Avro include RPC support. gRPC is an RPC implementation that uses Protocol Buffers. Finagle uses Thrift. Rest.li uses JSON over HTTP.

The newer generation of RPC frameworks is more explicit that a remote request is not a local function call. Finagle and Rest.li use futures, also called promises, which are objects that stand in for an asynchronous action that may fail. Futures also make it easier to send requests to several services in parallel and combine their results. gRPC supports streams, where a single call consists of a series of requests and responses over time, rather than just one of each.

Some of these frameworks also provide service discovery. That lets a client find out which IP address and port number a particular service is at. The book returns to this topic later, under request routing.

A custom RPC protocol with a binary encoding can perform better than something generic such as JSON over REST. A RESTful API has other strong advantages, though. It is easy to experiment with and debug, because you can call it from a web browser or the curl command-line tool without any code generation or installed software. It is supported by all mainstream programming languages and platforms. And there is a large ecosystem of tools for it, including servers, caches, load balancers, proxies, firewalls, monitoring, debugging, and testing tools.

For these reasons, REST seems to be the predominant style for public APIs. The main focus of RPC frameworks is requests between services owned by the same organization, usually within the same datacenter.

Data encoding and evolution for RPC

For evolvability, RPC clients and servers must be able to change and deploy independently. Compared with data flowing through databases, the book makes a simplifying assumption for services. It is reasonable to expect that all the servers will be updated first, and all the clients second. So you need backward compatibility on requests, meaning new servers must read requests from old clients. You also need forward compatibility on responses, meaning old clients must read responses from new servers.

The compatibility of an RPC scheme is inherited from the encoding it uses:

  • Thrift, gRPC (which uses Protocol Buffers), and Avro RPC evolve according to the compatibility rules of their encoding formats.
  • In SOAP, requests and responses are specified with XML schemas. These can be evolved, but there are some subtle pitfalls.
  • RESTful APIs most commonly use JSON for responses, with no formally specified schema. Requests use JSON, or URI-encoded or form-encoded parameters. Adding optional request parameters, and adding new fields to response objects, are usually considered compatible changes.

Compatibility is harder because RPC is often used across organizational boundaries. The provider of a service often cannot control its clients, so it cannot force them to upgrade. Compatibility must then be kept up for a long time, perhaps indefinitely. If a change that breaks compatibility is unavoidable, the provider often has to keep several versions of the service API running side by side.

There is no agreement on how API versioning should work, meaning how a client says which version of the API it wants. For RESTful APIs, the common approaches are a version number in the URL or in the HTTP Accept header. For services that use API keys to identify each client, another option is to store the version each client requested on the server. That choice can then be changed through a separate administrative interface. The book cites Stripe as an example of this approach.

Message-Passing Dataflow

So far we have looked at two patterns. In REST and RPC, one process sends a request and expects a response as quickly as possible. In databases, one process writes encoded data and another reads it at some later time. This final section looks at asynchronous message-passing systems, which sit somewhere between the two.

Like RPC, a message is delivered to another process with low latency, which means with little delay. Like a database, the message does not travel over a direct network connection. It goes through an intermediary called a message broker, also known as a message queue or message-oriented middleware. The broker stores the message for a while.

A broker has several advantages over direct RPC:

  • It can act as a buffer if the recipient is unavailable or overloaded, which improves reliability.
  • It can redeliver messages to a process that has crashed, so messages are not lost.
  • The sender does not need to know the IP address and port number of the recipient. This matters in the cloud, where virtual machines often come and go.
  • One message can be sent to several recipients.
  • It decouples the sender from the recipient. The sender just publishes messages and does not care who consumes them.

There is one difference from RPC. Message passing is usually one-way. The sender does not normally expect a reply. A process can send a response, but it would usually do so on a separate channel. This pattern is asynchronous. The sender does not wait for the message to be delivered. It sends the message and moves on.

Message brokers

In the past, the message broker market was dominated by commercial enterprise software from companies such as TIBCO, IBM WebSphere, and webMethods. More recently, open-source brokers such as RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, NATS, and Apache Kafka have become popular. Chapter 11 compares them in more detail.

The exact delivery rules depend on the implementation and its settings. In general, one process sends a message to a named queue or topic, and the broker makes sure the message is delivered to one or more consumers, which are processes that read messages, or to subscribers of that topic. Many producers, which are the processes that send messages, can write to the same topic, and many consumers can read from it.

A topic provides one-way dataflow. A consumer can also publish messages to another topic, so you can chain topics together, as Chapter 11 shows. Or a consumer can publish to a reply queue that the original sender reads. That gives a request and response flow, similar to RPC.

Message brokers usually do not enforce any particular data model. A message is just a sequence of bytes with some metadata, so you can use any encoding format. If the encoding is both backward and forward compatible, you have the most freedom. You can change publishers and consumers independently, and deploy them in any order.

If a consumer republishes messages to another topic, be careful to preserve any fields it does not understand. Otherwise you get the problem described earlier for databases, in which an old process drops a new field.

Distributed actor frameworks

The actor model is a programming model for concurrency inside a single process. Instead of working directly with threads, which brings problems such as race conditions, locking, and deadlock, the logic is placed inside actors.
