Each actor typically represents one client or one entity. It may hold some local state, which no other actor shares. Actors communicate by sending and receiving asynchronous messages. Delivery is not guaranteed. In some error scenarios, messages are lost. Each actor processes only one message at a time, so it does not need to worry about threads, and the framework can schedule each actor independently.

A distributed actor framework uses this model to scale an application across several nodes. The same message mechanism is used whether the sender and recipient are on the same node or on different nodes. If they are on different nodes, the message is transparently encoded into bytes, sent over the network, and decoded on the other side.

Location transparency works better in the actor model than in RPC. The reason is that the actor model already assumes messages can be lost, even inside one process. Network latency is still higher than inside one process. But there is less of a basic mismatch between local and remote communication.

A distributed actor framework is essentially a message broker and the actor model combined into one framework. Rolling upgrades still need care, though. Messages may be sent from a node running the new version to a node running the old version, and the other way around. So forward and backward compatibility still matter. The book describes three popular frameworks and how they encode messages:

  • Akka uses Java’s built-in serialization by default, which provides neither forward nor backward compatibility. You can replace it with something like Protocol Buffers, which gives you the ability to do rolling upgrades.
  • Orleans uses a custom encoding by default, which does not support rolling upgrades. To deploy a new version, you set up a new cluster, move traffic from the old cluster to the new one, and shut down the old one. As with Akka, custom serialization plug-ins can be used.
  • Erlang OTP makes it surprisingly hard to change record schemas, even though the system has many features designed for high availability. Rolling upgrades are possible, but they need careful planning. An experimental new maps datatype, introduced in Erlang R17 in 2014, may make this easier in the future. Maps are a JSON-like structure.

Summary

Summary
  • Rolling upgrades. Many services need rolling upgrades, where a new version is gradually deployed to a few nodes at a time, rather than to all nodes at once. This allows releases without downtime, so teams can ship small releases often. It also makes deployments less risky, because a faulty release can be spotted and rolled back before it affects many users. All of this helps evolvability, the ease of changing an application.
  • Compatibility in both directions. During a rolling upgrade, or for other reasons, different nodes run different versions of the code. So all data flowing through the system must be encoded to allow backward compatibility (new code reads old data) and forward compatibility (old code reads new data).
  • Language-specific encodings are tied to one language and often provide neither forward nor backward compatibility.
  • Textual formats such as JSON, XML, and CSV are widespread. Their compatibility depends on how you use them. Their optional schema languages can help or get in the way. They are vague about datatypes, so you must take care with numbers and binary strings.
  • Binary schema-driven formats such as Thrift, Protocol Buffers, and Avro allow compact, efficient encoding, with clearly defined forward and backward compatibility rules. Their schemas are useful as documentation and for code generation in statically typed languages. The downside is that data must be decoded before a person can read it.
  • Modes of dataflow. Databases, where the writer encodes and the reader decodes. RPC and REST, where the client encodes a request, the server decodes it and encodes a response, and the client decodes that. And asynchronous messaging through brokers or actors, where the sender encodes and the recipient decodes.
  • The conclusion. With a bit of care, backward and forward compatibility and rolling upgrades are quite achievable. The book ends on a hopeful note: rapid evolution and frequent deployments.

The chapter ends with a long list of references to papers, documentation, and blog posts that support its claims. This retelling does not reproduce that list.

Check yourself

  1. A newer version of an app adds a field and saves it to a record. An older version reads that record, changes an unrelated field, and saves it again. What must the older version do to avoid losing the new field?

    Show answer

    It must keep the unknown field intact when it writes the record back. The formats can preserve unknown fields, but if the app decodes the record into model objects and re-encodes them, the field can be dropped, so the app has to take care.

  2. Why must every field added to a Thrift or Protocol Buffers schema after its first deployment be optional or have a default value?

    Show answer

    New code will read old data, which was written before the field existed. A required-field check would fail on that data. Making the field optional or giving it a default keeps backward compatibility.

  3. A network request can end in a timeout, but a local function call cannot. Why does that matter when you decide to retry?

    Show answer

    After a timeout you do not know whether the request got through. If it did and only the response was lost, a retry performs the action a second time, unless the protocol deduplicates the requests (makes repeats harmless, which is called idempotence).

  4. Why is Avro friendlier than Thrift or Protocol Buffers when the schema is generated from a database table?

    Show answer

    Avro matches fields by name and its schema has no tag numbers. A regenerated schema can be used directly. Thrift and Protocol Buffers would need someone to assign and maintain field tags by hand, and never reuse one.

Part II

Distributed Data

Part II covers what changes when data lives on several machines, through copies of data (replication), splits of data (partitioning), transactions, and the limits of distributed systems.

A paraphrase of Richard Feynman’s remark in the Rogers Commission Report (1986): what is true must come before public relations, because reality cannot be fooled.

Part II · Chapter 5

Replication

The big idea: replication keeps the same data on several machines, so a system can survive failures and serve more readers. The hard part is that the copies can disagree for a while, and every replication method trades consistency, speed, and availability against one another.

Most people first meet databases on a single machine. Once a system grows, one machine is rarely enough. Part II of the book asks what changes when a database spans several machines that talk over a network. This chapter starts with replication, which means keeping copies of the same data on more than one machine. It is about how those copies stay in step, and what goes wrong when they do not.

Why Distribute Data?

A database on one machine has a clear limit. Once the data, the read load, or the write load grows past what one machine can handle, you can spread the work across several machines. The book gives three main reasons to distribute a database:

  • Scalability. If the volume of data or the load grows beyond one machine, the work can be spread across many.
  • Fault tolerance and high availability. If the application must keep working when one machine, several machines, the network, or a whole datacenter (a building full of servers) goes down, extra machines give redundancy. When one fails, another can take over.
  • Latency. Users around the world can be served by servers near them, so they do not wait for network packets to travel halfway around the planet.

Scaling to Higher Load

The simplest way to handle more load is to buy a more powerful machine. This is called vertical scaling, or scaling up. Many CPUs (processor chips), many RAM chips (memory), and many disks can be joined under one operating system. A fast internal link lets any CPU reach any part of the memory or disk. The whole thing is treated as one machine. This is called a shared-memory architecture.

It has three limits. First, cost grows faster than capacity. A machine with twice the CPUs, RAM, and disk usually costs much more than twice as much. Second, bottlenecks mean a machine twice the size cannot always handle twice the load. Third, fault tolerance is limited. High-end machines can swap out disks, memory modules, and even CPUs while running, but the whole machine still sits in one place, so it covers only one geographic location.

The book adds a footnote about very large machines. Some memory banks sit closer to one CPU than to others. This is called nonuniform memory access, or NUMA. To use such a machine well, the work still has to be split up so that each CPU mostly uses nearby memory. In other words, partitioning is needed even on a single machine.

A second option is the shared-disk architecture. Several machines, each with its own CPU and RAM, share one array of disks that they all reach over a fast network. The shared disks are attached through network attached storage (NAS) or a storage area network (SAN). This suits some data warehousing workloads, which are large systems used for reporting and analysis. But contention (machines waiting on each other) and the overhead of locking limit how far this design can scale.

Shared-Nothing Architectures

The other approach is the shared-nothing architecture, which has become very popular. Here each machine, or virtual machine, that runs the database software is called a node. Each node uses its own CPUs, RAM, and disks. Nodes coordinate only in software, over an ordinary network. This approach is also called scaling out or horizontal scaling, because you add more machines side by side rather than making one machine bigger.

The advantages are real. No special hardware is needed, so you can buy whatever machines give the best price for performance. Data can be spread across several geographic regions. That reduces latency for users, and it lets the system survive the loss of an entire datacenter. Cloud platforms make this affordable. Even a small company can now run a multi-region system without operating at the scale of a large internet company.

The book focuses on shared-nothing systems. It does so not because they suit every case, but because they demand the most care from the application developer. Once data lives on several nodes, the constraints and trade-offs of distributed systems apply, and the database cannot completely hide them from you. Shared-nothing designs also add complexity, and they sometimes limit which data models you can use. The book notes that in some cases a simple single-threaded program can perform significantly better than a cluster with over 100 CPU cores. Even so, shared-nothing systems can be very powerful. The next few chapters look at the issues that arise when data is distributed.

Replication Versus Partitioning

There are two common ways to spread data across nodes. They are separate mechanisms, but they often work together.

  • Replication keeps a copy of the same data on several nodes, possibly in different locations. Copies give redundancy. If some nodes are unavailable, the data can still be served from the others. Replication can also improve performance. This is the subject of Chapter 5.
  • Partitioning, also called sharding, splits a big database into smaller subsets called partitions. Different partitions can be assigned to different nodes. This is the subject of Chapter 6.

The two are often combined. The book’s Figure II-1 shows a database split into two partitions, with two replicas for each partition. Each partition has its own copies on its own machines. Later chapters cover transactions (Chapter 7), the many things that can go wrong in a data system (Chapter 8), and the fundamental limits of distributed systems (Chapter 9).

This chapter is about replication. Replication means keeping a copy of the same data on multiple machines connected by a network. The book gives three reasons to replicate:

  • To keep data geographically close to users, which reduces latency.
  • To let the system keep working when some of its parts fail, which increases availability.
  • To scale out the number of machines that can serve read queries, which increases read throughput (how many reads per second the system can answer).

For now, assume the dataset is small enough that every machine can hold a full copy. Chapter 6 drops that assumption and covers datasets too big for one machine.

If the data never changed, replication would be easy. You would copy it to every node once and stop. All the difficulty comes from changes. This chapter covers three popular algorithms for copying changes between nodes: single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication. Almost all distributed databases use one of these three approaches, and each has its own pros and cons.

There are other trade-offs too, such as whether copying happens synchronously or asynchronously, and how to handle a replica that has failed. These are often configuration options in a database. The details vary from one database to another, but the general principles are similar. Replication has been studied since the 1970s, and its principles have not changed much, because the basic constraints of networks have stayed the same. For a long time, though, many developers assumed a database ran on a single node. Mainstream use of distributed databases is more recent, which is why many developers have misunderstood ideas such as eventual consistency. The chapter explains those ideas as it goes.

Leaders and Followers

Each node that stores a copy of the database is called a replica. With several replicas, one question comes up immediately: how do we make sure all the data ends up on all the replicas? Every write has to be processed by every replica. Otherwise the replicas would stop holding the same data.

The most common solution is leader-based replication. It is also called active/passive, or master-slave replication. It works like this:

  1. One replica is designated the leader, also known as the master or primary. When clients want to write, they must send the write to the leader. The leader first writes the new data to its own storage.
  2. The other replicas are called followers. They are also known as read replicas, slaves, secondaries, or hot standbys. Whenever the leader writes new data, it also sends the change to all its followers, as part of a replication log or change stream. A replication log is an ordered record of changes. Each follower reads the log and applies the same writes in the same order that the leader did.
  3. When a client wants to read, it can query the leader or any follower. But writes are accepted only on the leader. From the client’s point of view, the followers are read-only.

The book notes that people define “hot,” “warm,” and “cold” standby differently. In PostgreSQL, a hot standby accepts reads from clients, while a warm standby applies changes but serves no queries. For the book’s purposes, the difference does not matter.

This mode of replication is a built-in feature of many relational databases, such as PostgreSQL (since version 9.0), MySQL, Oracle Data Guard, and SQL Server’s AlwaysOn Availability Groups. Some nonrelational databases use it too, including MongoDB, RethinkDB, and Espresso. It is not limited to databases. Distributed message brokers such as Kafka and RabbitMQ highly available queues also use leader-based replication. Some network filesystems and replicated block devices, such as DRBD, work the same way.

Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Replication

An important detail is whether replication happens synchronously or asynchronously. In a relational database this is often a setting you can change. Other systems are fixed to one or the other.

Example

Picture a website user who updates their profile image. The book follows the update through Figure 5-2, which has four parts: the user’s client, the leader, and two followers. Here is the sequence, step by step:

  1. The client sends the update request to the leader.
  2. The leader receives the request and writes the new image to its own storage.
  3. The leader forwards the change to follower 1 and waits for that follower to confirm it has the data. This is synchronous replication.
  4. In parallel, the leader forwards the change to follower 2 but does not wait for a reply. This is asynchronous replication.
  5. Only after follower 1 confirms does the leader tell the client the update succeeded. It also makes the write visible to other clients at that point.
  6. Meanwhile follower 2 gets the message only after a substantial delay.

Replication is usually quite fast. Most database systems apply changes to followers in less than a second. But nothing guarantees how long it takes. A follower can fall behind the leader by several minutes or more. That happens if the follower is recovering from a failure, if the system runs close to its maximum capacity, or if the network between the nodes has problems.

Synchronous replication has one clear advantage. The synchronous follower is guaranteed to have an up-to-date copy that matches the leader. If the leader suddenly fails, the data is still available on the follower. Its disadvantage is that if the synchronous follower stops responding, because it crashed or because of a network fault, the write cannot be processed. The leader must block all writes and wait until the synchronous replica is available again.

For that reason, making every follower synchronous is impractical. One node outage would halt the whole system. In practice, if you turn on synchronous replication, usually one follower is synchronous and the others are asynchronous. If the synchronous follower becomes unavailable or slow, one of the asynchronous followers is promoted to synchronous. This guarantees that an up-to-date copy exists on at least two nodes, the leader and one synchronous follower. The book notes that this setup is sometimes called semi-synchronous.

Leader-based replication is often configured to be fully asynchronous. Then, if the leader fails and cannot be recovered, any writes that were not yet copied to followers are lost. A write is therefore not guaranteed to be durable (kept safely for good), even after the client has been told it succeeded. The benefit is that the leader can keep processing writes even when all its followers have fallen behind. Weakening durability may sound like a bad trade, but asynchronous replication is widely used, especially when there are many followers or they are spread across the world. The chapter returns to this issue in its section on replication lag.

Research on Replication

Losing data when an asynchronous leader fails is a serious problem. Researchers have therefore kept looking for methods that lose no data but still perform well and stay available. One example is chain replication. It is a variant of synchronous replication, and it has been used successfully in a few systems, including Microsoft Azure Storage. There is also a strong link between replication consistency and consensus, which means getting several nodes to agree on a value. Chapter 9 explores that theory. This chapter sticks to the simpler forms of replication that are most common in practice.

Setting Up New Followers

From time to time you need a new follower, to add capacity or to replace a failed node. How do you make sure the new follower has an accurate copy of the leader’s data?

Copying the data files from one machine to another is not enough. Clients keep writing, so the data is always changing. A plain file copy would see different parts of the database at different moments, and the result might not make sense. You could lock the database so nothing changes during the copy, but that would stop writes, which goes against the goal of high availability. Fortunately, a follower can usually be set up with no downtime. Conceptually, the process has four steps:

  1. Take a consistent snapshot of the leader’s database at one point in time. If possible, do this without locking the whole database. Most databases support this, because backups need it too. Some systems need third-party tools for it, such as innobackupex for MySQL.
  2. Copy the snapshot to the new follower node.
  3. The follower connects to the leader and asks for all the data changes that happened since the snapshot. This works only if the snapshot is tied to an exact position in the leader’s replication log. That position has different names in different databases. PostgreSQL calls it the log sequence number, and MySQL calls it the binlog coordinates.
  4. When the follower has processed the backlog, it has caught up. From then on, it keeps processing changes as they happen.

The practical steps vary a lot from one database to another. In some systems the process is fully automated. In others it is a multi-step workflow that an administrator must carry out by hand.

Handling Node Outages

Any node can go down. It might fail unexpectedly, or it might be taken down on purpose, for example to reboot a machine and install a kernel security patch. Being able to reboot individual nodes without downtime is a big advantage for operations. So the goal is to keep the system as a whole running despite individual node failures, and to keep the impact of each outage as small as possible. How do you achieve that with leader-based replication?

Follower failure: catch-up recovery. Each follower keeps a log of the data changes it has received from the leader, stored on its own local disk. If a follower crashes and restarts, or if the network between it and the leader is interrupted for a while, recovery is fairly easy. From its log, the follower knows the last transaction it processed before the fault. It connects to the leader and asks for every change that happened while it was away. Once it has applied those changes, it has caught up and can go back to receiving the live stream.

Leader failure: failover. A failed leader is harder to handle. One of the followers must be promoted to be the new leader. Clients must be reconfigured to send their writes to the new leader. The other followers must start consuming changes from the new leader. This process is called failover.

Failover can be manual, where an administrator is notified and carries out the steps, or automatic. An automatic failover usually goes through three steps:

  1. Detect that the leader has failed. Many things could go wrong: a crash, a power outage, a network problem, and more. There is no foolproof way to tell which one it is. So most systems use a timeout. Nodes send messages to each other all the time, and if a node does not respond for some period, for example 30 seconds, it is assumed to be dead. A leader taken down on purpose for planned maintenance does not need this detection.
  2. Choose a new leader. This can be done by an election, in which a majority of the remaining replicas picks the leader. Or a previously elected controller node can appoint one. The best candidate is usually the replica with the most up-to-date changes from the old leader, because that minimizes data loss. Getting all the nodes to agree on the new leader is a consensus problem, which Chapter 9 discusses in detail.
  3. Reconfigure the system to use the new leader. Clients now send their writes to the new leader. The book covers this under request routing. There is a catch: if the old leader comes back, it may still believe it is the leader. It may not realize the other replicas have forced it to step down. The system must make sure the old leader becomes a follower and accepts the new leader.

Failover is full of things that can go wrong:

  • Lost writes. With asynchronous replication, the new leader may not have received all the writes from the old leader before it failed. If the old leader rejoins the cluster, what should happen to those writes? The new leader may have accepted conflicting writes in the meantime. The most common solution is to discard the old leader’s unreplicated writes. That can violate clients’ expectations about durability.
  • Discarding is dangerous when other systems depend on the database. Some data also lives in storage systems outside the database, and those must be kept consistent with it. The story below shows what happened in one real incident.
  • Split brain. In some faults, two nodes both believe they are the leader. This is called split brain. If both accept writes, and there is no process for resolving the conflicts, data is likely to be lost or corrupted. As a safety catch, some systems shut down one node when two leaders are detected. The book notes that this approach is known as fencing, or more bluntly, Shoot The Other Node In The Head (STONITH). If the mechanism is not designed carefully, both nodes can end up shut down.
  • Choosing the timeout. A longer timeout means a longer wait before recovery when the leader really has failed. A shorter timeout risks needless failovers. A temporary load spike or a delayed network packet can make a healthy leader look dead. If the system is already struggling, a needless failover is likely to make things worse.
Example

The book describes an incident at GitHub, step by step, to show how a failover can cause data problems:

  1. An out-of-date MySQL follower was promoted to be the leader.
  2. The database assigned primary keys (unique row IDs) with an autoincrementing counter. The new leader’s counter lagged behind the old leader’s counter.
  3. As a result, the new leader handed out some primary keys that the old leader had already assigned.
  4. Those same keys were also used in a Redis store, which was not part of the database.
  5. The two systems ended up inconsistent with each other, and some private data was shown to the wrong users.

There are no easy solutions to these problems. For this reason, some operations teams prefer to perform failovers manually, even when their software supports automatic failover. The issues in this section are not special to databases. Node failures, unreliable networks, and the trade-offs between consistency, durability, availability, and latency are fundamental problems in distributed systems. Chapters 8 and 9 discuss them in more depth.

Implementation of Replication Logs

How does leader-based replication work under the hood? Several methods are used in practice, and the book looks briefly at each.

Statement-based replication. In the simplest case, the leader logs every write request, or statement, that it executes, and sends that statement log to its followers. For a relational database, this means every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement is forwarded. Each follower parses and runs the SQL, as if the statement had come from a client. This sounds reasonable, but it can break in several ways:

  • A statement that calls a nondeterministic function, such as NOW() for the current time or RAND() for a random number, will probably produce a different value on each replica.
  • Statements that use an autoincrementing column, or that depend on existing data (such as UPDATE with a WHERE condition), must run in exactly the same order on every replica. Otherwise they may have different effects. This is limiting when many transactions run at once.
  • Statements with side effects, such as triggers, stored procedures, and user-defined functions, may cause different side effects on each replica, unless those side effects are completely deterministic.

These problems can be worked around. For example, the leader can replace a nondeterministic call with a fixed value when it logs the statement, so every follower gets the same value. But there are so many edge cases that other methods are generally preferred. MySQL used statement-based replication before version 5.1. It is still sometimes used because it is compact. By default, though, MySQL now switches to row-based replication (below) whenever a statement is nondeterministic. VoltDB uses statement-based replication and makes it safe by requiring transactions to be deterministic.

Write-ahead log (WAL) shipping. Chapter 3 explained that storage engines usually append every write to a log. In a log-structured storage engine, the log is the main storage, and its segments are compacted in the background. In a B-tree, which overwrites disk blocks in place, each change is first written to a write-ahead log, so the index can be restored to a consistent state after a crash. Either way, the log is an append-only sequence of bytes that contains every write. The same log can build a replica. Besides writing it to disk, the leader sends it across the network to its followers. The follower processes the log and builds an exact copy of the same data structures that the leader has.

This method is used in PostgreSQL and Oracle, among others. Its main disadvantage is that the log describes data at a very low level. It records which bytes changed in which disk blocks. That ties replication closely to the storage engine. If the database changes its storage format between versions, it is usually impossible to run different versions on the leader and the followers. That can matter a lot in operations. If the protocol allows a follower to run a newer software version than the leader, you can upgrade with zero downtime. First upgrade the followers, then fail over to one of the upgraded nodes as the new leader. With WAL shipping, that version mismatch is usually not allowed, so upgrades require downtime.

Logical (row-based) log replication. An alternative is to use one log format for replication and a different one for the storage engine. The replication log is then decoupled from the storage engine’s internals. This kind of log is called a logical log, to distinguish it from the physical storage format. For a relational database, a logical log is usually a sequence of records that describe writes to tables, one row at a time:

  • For an inserted row, the log contains the new values of all columns.
  • For a deleted row, the log contains enough to identify the row. Usually that is the primary key. If the table has no primary key, the old values of all columns must be logged.
  • For an updated row, the log contains enough to identify the row, plus the new values of all columns, or at least of the columns that changed.

A transaction that changes several rows produces several such records, followed by a record saying the transaction committed. MySQL’s binlog, when set to row-based replication, works this way. Because a logical log is separate from the storage engine, it is easier to keep backward compatible. Leader and follower can then run different software versions, or even different storage engines. A logical log is also easier for outside programs to read. That helps when you want to send a database’s contents to a data warehouse for offline analysis, or to build custom indexes and caches. This technique is called change data capture, which Chapter 11 covers.

Trigger-based replication. The methods so far are built into the database and need no application code. That is often what you want. But sometimes more flexibility is needed. You might want to replicate only a subset of the data, copy from one kind of database to another, or apply custom conflict-resolution logic (see the section on write conflicts below). In those cases, replication may have to move up into the application layer.

Some tools, such as Oracle GoldenGate, read the database’s log and make the changes available to an application. Another option uses features many relational databases offer: triggers and stored procedures. A trigger is custom code that the database runs automatically when a data change (a write transaction) happens. The trigger can record the change in a separate table. An external process reads that table, applies any needed application logic, and replicates the change to another system. Databus for Oracle and Bucardo for Postgres work this way. Trigger-based replication has greater overhead than the built-in methods, and it is more prone to bugs and limitations. But its flexibility can make it worth the cost.

Problems with Replication Lag

Surviving node failures is only one reason to replicate. The introduction listed others: scalability, meaning handling more requests than one machine can, and latency, meaning placing replicas near users.

Leader-based replication sends all writes through a single node. But read-only queries can go to any replica. Many web workloads consist mostly of reads with a small share of writes. For those, there is an attractive option: create many followers and spread the read requests across them. This takes load off the leader and lets nearby replicas answer reads. The total capacity for reads grows simply by adding followers. This read-scaling design only realistically works with asynchronous replication. If you tried to copy synchronously to every follower, one node failure or one network outage would make the entire system unavailable for writes. The more nodes you have, the more likely one of them is to be down, so a fully synchronous setup would be very unreliable.

The catch is that an application reading from an asynchronous follower may see outdated information if that follower has fallen behind. Two queries run at the same moment, one on the leader and one on a follower, can return different results. The follower simply has not yet received some writes. This inconsistency is temporary. If writes stop and you wait, the followers catch up and match the leader. Because the copies eventually agree, this behavior is called eventual consistency. The term was coined by Douglas Terry and colleagues, popularized by Werner Vogels, and became a rallying cry for many NoSQL projects. The book points out that it is not only NoSQL databases that behave this way. Followers in an asynchronously replicated relational database have the same characteristics.

The word “eventually” is deliberately vague. In general there is no limit to how far a replica can fall behind. Normally the delay between a write on the leader and its appearance on a follower, called the replication lag, may be a fraction of a second and not noticeable. But if the system runs near capacity, or if the network has a problem, the lag can grow to several seconds or even minutes. Once the lag is that large, the inconsistencies stop being a theory and become a real problem for applications. The rest of this section looks at three examples and some ways to solve them.

Reading Your Own Writes

Many applications let a user submit some data and then view what they submitted. It might be a record in a customer database or a comment on a discussion thread. New data must be sent to the leader. But when the user views it, the read can come from a follower. This pattern suits data that is viewed often but written only occasionally.

Example

Here is the problem with asynchronous replication, step by step:

  1. A user saves a change to their profile. The save goes to the leader.
  2. The leader accepts it, but the follower the user reads from has not received the change yet.
  3. The user reloads the page right away. The read goes to that follower.
  4. The page shows the old data. To the user it looks as though the save was lost, so they are understandably unhappy.

The fix is a guarantee called read-after-write consistency, also known as read-your-writes consistency. It promises that if a user reloads the page, they will always see the updates they made themselves. It makes no promise about other users. Their updates may not be visible yet. But it reassures each user that their own input has been saved.

How can a system with leader-based replication provide this? There are several techniques:

  • Read from the leader when the data may have been changed by the user. This needs a way to know, without querying, whether something might have been modified. For example, a user’s profile on a social network is normally editable only by its owner. A simple rule is to read your own profile from the leader and everyone else’s from a follower.
  • Use other criteria when most things are editable. If nearly everything can be edited by the user, reading everything from the leader would cancel the benefit of read scaling. Instead you could track the time of the last update and, for one minute after it, read from the leader. You could also monitor the replication lag on followers and avoid any follower that is more than a minute behind the leader.
  • Remember the timestamp of the last write. The client keeps the timestamp of its most recent write. The system then ensures that the replica serving the user’s reads reflects updates at least up to that timestamp. If the replica is not current enough, the read can go to another replica, or it can wait until the replica catches up. The timestamp can be a logical one, such as the log position, or the system clock. If it is the clock, clock synchronization becomes critical. Chapter 8 covers unreliable clocks.
  • Route leader-only requests to the right datacenter. If replicas are spread across datacenters, for proximity or availability, any request that must be served by the leader has to reach the datacenter that holds the leader.

Things get harder when the same user accesses the service from several devices, such as a desktop browser and a phone app. Then you may want cross-device read-after-write consistency. If someone enters information on one device, they should see it on another. This brings extra issues. The timestamp approach becomes harder, because code running on one device does not know what updates happened on the other. That metadata must be kept in one central place. There is also no guarantee that connections from different devices reach the same datacenter. A desktop on home broadband and a phone on cellular data may take completely different network routes. If the approach requires reading from the leader, you may first need to route all of a user’s devices to the same datacenter.

Try it

Think of a site where users edit their own profile and also read comments from other people. Which reads would you send to the leader, and which to followers? For each choice, say which guarantee the user keeps and which one they might lose.

Monotonic Reads

The second anomaly is that a user can see things moving backward in time. This happens when a user makes several reads, and each one goes to a different replica.

Example

Figure 5-4 in the book shows user 2345 making the same query twice:

  1. The first query goes to a follower with little lag. It returns a comment that user 1234 added recently.
  2. The user refreshes the page, and the second query goes to a follower with more lag. That follower has not yet received user 1234’s comment, so the comment is missing.

This is very confusing for user 2345. The comment appears and then disappears again. In effect, the second read observes the system at an earlier point in time than the first. The problem is worst when each page refresh is routed to a random server.

If the first query had returned nothing, the user would not have known that a comment was missing. The confusion comes from seeing newer data and then older data.

Monotonic reads is the guarantee that prevents this anomaly. It is weaker than strong consistency, but stronger than eventual consistency. A read can still return an old value. What monotonic reads promises is that if one user makes several reads in sequence, they will never read older data after having read newer data. Time never appears to go backward for that user. Different users may still read from different replicas.

One way to achieve monotonic reads is to make sure each user always reads from the same replica. The replica can be chosen by a hash of the user ID, rather than picked at random. If that replica fails, the user’s queries must be rerouted to another replica.

Consistent Prefix Reads

The third anomaly concerns causality, which means cause and effect. Consider a short dialog. Mr. Poons asks Mrs. Cake how far into the future she can see. Mrs. Cake answers that it is usually about ten seconds.

Example

There is a causal link between those two sentences: Mrs. Cake heard the question and answered it. Now imagine a third person listening to the conversation through followers. Mrs. Cake’s words pass through a follower with little lag. Mr. Poons’s words pass through a follower with longer lag, as Figure 5-5 illustrates. The listener hears the answer first and the question second. To the listener, Mrs. Cake seems to answer the question before it has been asked. The book calls such psychic powers impressive but very confusing.

Preventing this kind of anomaly requires another guarantee, called consistent prefix reads. It says that if a sequence of writes happens in a certain order, then anyone reading those writes will see them appear in that same order.

This problem is especially common in partitioned (sharded) databases, which Chapter 6 covers. If the database applies all writes in the same order everywhere, reads always see a consistent prefix, so the anomaly cannot happen. But in many distributed databases, different partitions operate independently. There is no global order of writes across them. A user reading the database may see some parts in an older state and other parts in a newer state.

There are two ways to address this. One is to make sure that writes which are causally related always go to the same partition. But in some applications that cannot be done efficiently. The other is to use algorithms that explicitly track causal dependencies. The chapter returns to that topic in the section on the happens-before relationship.

Solutions for Replication Lag

When you work with an eventually consistent system, think about how the application behaves if replication lag grows to several minutes or even hours. If the answer is “no problem,” that is fine. But if users would have a bad experience, design the system to provide a stronger guarantee, such as read-after-write consistency. Pretending that replication is synchronous when it is in fact asynchronous leads to problems later.

As discussed above, an application can provide a stronger guarantee than the database does, for example by reading certain data from the leader. But handling these issues in application code is complex and easy to get wrong. It would be better if application developers did not have to think about subtle replication issues, and could trust the database to do the right thing. This is why transactions exist. A transaction is a way for a database to provide stronger guarantees, so that the application can be simpler.

Single-node transactions have existed for a long time. But in the move to distributed databases, which are both replicated and partitioned, many systems abandoned them. Their argument was that transactions are too expensive in performance and availability, and that eventual consistency is unavoidable in a scalable system. There is some truth in that, but the claim is overly simple. The book develops a more nuanced view over the rest of the book. Chapters 7 and 9 return to transactions, and Part III discusses some alternative mechanisms.

Key idea

Choose the consistency guarantee your users need before you choose the replication setup. If a stale read would confuse users, use read-after-write consistency for their own changes, rather than assuming the copies agree.

Multi-Leader Replication

So far this chapter has considered only replication with a single leader. That is a common approach, but there are other options. The main downside of a single leader is that all writes must go through it. If you cannot reach the leader for any reason, such as a network interruption between you and the leader, you cannot write to the database at all.

A natural extension is to let more than one node accept writes. Replication still works the same way. Each node that processes a write forwards that data change to all the other nodes. This is called a multi-leader configuration. It is also known as master-master or active/active replication. Each leader acts as a follower to the other leaders at the same time.

Use Cases for Multi-Leader Replication

It rarely makes sense to use multi-leader replication inside a single datacenter, because the benefits seldom outweigh the extra complexity. There are some situations where it is reasonable, though. The book describes three.

Multi-datacenter operation. Imagine a database with replicas in several datacenters. You might want this so that the system can tolerate the failure of a whole datacenter, or so that it is closer to users. With normal single-leader replication, the leader must be in one datacenter, and all writes must go through it, even when the user is in another part of the world.

With multi-leader replication, each datacenter can have its own leader. Within each datacenter, regular leader and follower replication is used. Between datacenters, each datacenter’s leader replicates its changes to the leaders in the other datacenters. Figure 5-6 in the book shows this architecture. The two approaches compare as follows:

  • Performance. In single-leader replication, every write must cross the internet to the datacenter with the leader. That adds significant latency to writes, and it can defeat the purpose of having several datacenters. In multi-leader replication, each write is processed in the local datacenter and then replicated asynchronously to the others. The delay between datacenters is hidden from users, so the performance they perceive may be better.
  • Tolerance of datacenter outages. If the datacenter holding the leader fails, single-leader replication can promote a follower in another datacenter. In multi-leader replication, each datacenter keeps operating independently. When the failed datacenter comes back, replication catches up.
  • Tolerance of network problems. Traffic between datacenters usually crosses the public internet, which is less reliable than the local network. Single-leader replication is very sensitive to problems on this link, because its writes are made synchronously over it. Multi-leader replication with asynchronous copying can usually tolerate network trouble better, because a short interruption does not stop writes from being processed.
Trade-offs
ConcernSingle leader across datacentersMulti-leader across datacenters
Write speed for remote usersEvery write travels to the leader’s datacenterWrites are handled locally and copied asynchronously
Whole datacenter failsA follower elsewhere is promoted to leaderEach datacenter carries on, and replication catches up later
Link between datacenters is unreliableSensitive, because writes wait on this linkUsually tolerant, because writes do not wait on it
Conflicting writesCannot happen, because all writes go through one leaderMust be detected and resolved

Some databases support multi-leader configurations by default. Otherwise it is often set up with external tools, such as Tungsten Replicator for MySQL, BDR for PostgreSQL, and GoldenGate for Oracle.

Multi-leader replication has a big downside. The same data may be modified concurrently in two datacenters, and those write conflicts must be resolved. The section on handling write conflicts covers this. Also, because multi-leader replication was often added to databases after they were built, it can have subtle configuration pitfalls and surprising interactions with other features. Autoincrementing keys, triggers, and integrity constraints can all be problematic. For this reason, the book says multi-leader replication is often considered dangerous territory that should be avoided if possible.

Clients with offline operation. Multi-leader replication also fits apps that must keep working while disconnected from the internet. Consider the calendar apps on a phone, a laptop, and other devices. You need to see your meetings and add new ones at any time, whether or not the device is online. Any changes made offline must be synced with a server and your other devices when the device next connects.

In this case, every device has a local database that acts as a leader, because it accepts writes. An asynchronous multi-leader process syncs the calendar replicas across all your devices. The replication lag can be hours or even days, depending on when internet access is available. Architecturally, this is the same as multi-leader replication between datacenters, taken to the extreme. Each device is a “datacenter,” and the network between them is extremely unreliable. The book notes that the history of broken calendar sync implementations shows how tricky multi-leader replication is to get right. Some tools aim to make it easier. CouchDB, for example, is designed for this mode of operation.

Collaborative editing. Real-time editing tools let several people change one document at the same time. Etherpad and Google Docs are examples. The book notes that we do not usually think of collaborative editing as a replication problem. But it has much in common with offline editing. When one user edits, the change is applied at once to their local replica, which is the state of the document in their browser or app. It is then replicated asynchronously to the server and to anyone else editing the same document.

To guarantee there are no editing conflicts, the application can lock the document. A user must get the lock before editing. If another user wants to edit, they must wait until the first user commits their changes and releases the lock. This model is equivalent to single-leader replication with transactions on the leader. For faster collaboration, you can make the unit of change very small, such as a single keystroke, and skip locking. That lets several people edit at once. But it also brings all the challenges of multi-leader replication, including the need for conflict resolution.

Handling Write Conflicts

The biggest problem with multi-leader replication is that write conflicts can happen, so conflict resolution is required.

Example

Consider a wiki page that two users edit at the same moment (Figure 5-7 in the book). The title of the page is currently A.

  1. User 1 changes the title from A to B. The change is applied successfully on leader 1.
  2. At the same moment, user 2 changes the title from A to C. The change is applied successfully on leader 2.
  3. Later, the two leaders replicate their changes to each other, asynchronously.
  4. When the changes arrive, the system detects a conflict: two writes changed the same field in different ways.

This problem does not occur in a single-leader database, because there a second write to the same field is either made to wait or rejected.

Synchronous versus asynchronous conflict detection. In a single-leader database, the second writer either waits for the first write to finish or has its transaction aborted, which forces the user to retry. In a multi-leader setup, both writes succeed. The conflict is found only later, asynchronously, and by then it may be too late to ask the user to resolve it. You could make detection synchronous, waiting until the write has reached every replica before telling the user it succeeded. But then you lose the main advantage of multi-leader replication, which is that each replica accepts writes independently. If you want synchronous conflict detection, the book points out, you might as well use single-leader replication.

Conflict avoidance. The simplest strategy is to avoid conflicts. If the application ensures that all writes for a particular record go through the same leader, conflicts cannot occur. Many multi-leader implementations handle conflicts poorly, so avoiding them is often recommended. For example, in an application where users edit their own data, requests from a particular user can always be routed to the same datacenter, and that datacenter’s leader handles both reads and writes. Different users may have different home datacenters, perhaps chosen by geographic closeness. From any one user’s point of view, the setup is essentially single-leader. But sometimes the designated leader for a record must change. One datacenter may have failed, so traffic is rerouted, or a user may have moved closer to a different datacenter. In that situation, conflict avoidance breaks down, and you must handle the possibility of concurrent writes on different leaders.

Converging toward a consistent state. A single-leader database applies writes in a sequential order. If several updates touch the same field, the last one determines the final value. A multi-leader setup has no defined order of writes, so the final value is unclear. In Figure 5-7, leader 1 first sets the title to B and then to C. Leader 2 first sets it to C and then to B. Neither order is more correct than the other.

If each replica simply applied writes in the order it saw them, the database would end up inconsistent. Leader 1 would hold C and leader 2 would hold B. That is not acceptable. Every replication scheme must ensure that the data is eventually the same on all replicas. So the database must resolve the conflict in a convergent way, meaning all replicas arrive at the same final value once all changes have been replicated. There are several ways to do that:

  • Give each write a unique ID, such as a timestamp, a long random number, a UUID (a universally unique identifier), or a hash of the key and value. Pick the write with the highest ID as the winner, and throw away the others. If the ID is a timestamp, this is called last write wins (LWW). It is popular, but the book warns that it is dangerously prone to data loss. The chapter returns to LWW at the end.
  • Give each replica a unique ID, and let writes from a higher-numbered replica always win over writes from a lower-numbered one. This also loses data.
  • Merge the values somehow. For example, sort them alphabetically and join them together. In Figure 5-7 the merged title might be something like “B/C.”
  • Record the conflict in an explicit data structure that keeps all the information, and write application code that resolves it later, perhaps by asking the user.

Custom conflict resolution logic. The right way to resolve a conflict often depends on the application. So most multi-leader tools let you write resolution logic in application code. That code can run at write time or at read time:

  • On write. As soon as the database detects a conflict in the replicated changes, it calls a conflict handler. This handler usually cannot prompt a user, because it runs in a background process and must finish quickly. Bucardo, for example, lets you write a snippet of Perl for this purpose.
  • On read. When a conflict is detected, all the conflicting writes are stored. The next time the data is read, the multiple versions are returned to the application. The application may prompt the user or resolve the conflict automatically, then write the result back to the database. CouchDB works this way.
Watch out

Conflict resolution usually applies to one row or document at a time, not to a whole transaction. If a transaction writes several rows atomically, each of those writes is still considered separately when resolving conflicts.

Automatic Conflict Resolution

Conflict resolution rules can quickly become complicated, and custom code can be error-prone. Amazon is an often-cited example of surprising effects from a conflict handler. For some time, the handler for the shopping cart kept items that were added to the cart, but not items that were removed. Customers would sometimes see items reappear in their carts after they had removed them.

Researchers have looked into resolving concurrent changes automatically. The book mentions three lines of work:

  • Conflict-free replicated datatypes (CRDTs) are a family of data structures for sets, maps, ordered lists, counters, and similar things. They can be edited concurrently by several users, and they resolve conflicts automatically in sensible ways. Some CRDTs have been implemented in Riak 2.0.
  • Mergeable persistent data structures track history explicitly, a bit like the Git version control system. They use a three-way merge function, while CRDTs use a two-way merge.
  • Operational transformation is the conflict-resolution algorithm behind collaborative editors such as Etherpad and Google Docs. It was designed for concurrent editing of an ordered list of items, such as the characters that make up a text document.

Implementations of these algorithms in databases are still young. The book expects they will be built into more replicated systems over time. Automatic conflict resolution could make multi-leader data synchronization much simpler for applications.

What Is a Conflict?

Some conflicts are obvious. In the wiki example, two writes changed the same field in the same record, setting it to two different values. There is little doubt that this is a conflict.

Other conflicts are harder to spot. Consider a meeting room booking system that tracks which group has booked which room at which time. The application must ensure that a room is booked by only one group at a time, so no two bookings may overlap.

Example
  1. Two different groups try to book the same room for the same time.
  2. If both requests reach the same leader, the application can check availability and reject one of them.
  3. But if the two bookings are made on two different leaders, each leader may see the room as free. Each accepts its booking.
  4. When the leaders replicate, the system has two overlapping bookings for one room. That is a conflict, even though no single write looked wrong.

Checking availability before accepting a booking does not prevent this, because the two checks happen on different leaders. The book says there is no quick, ready-made answer. Later chapters trace a path toward understanding this kind of problem. Chapter 7 gives more examples of conflicts, and Chapter 12 discusses scalable ways to detect and resolve conflicts in replicated systems.

Multi-Leader Replication Topologies

A replication topology describes the communication paths along which writes travel from one node to another. With two leaders there is only one sensible topology: each leader sends all its writes to the other. With three or more leaders, several topologies are possible. Figure 5-8 in the book shows three.

The most general topology is all-to-all, where every leader sends its writes to every other leader. More restricted topologies are also used. MySQL, by default, supports only a circular topology. Each node receives writes from one node and forwards them, along with its own writes, to one other node. Another popular shape is the star, in which one designated root node forwards writes to all the others. A star can be generalized to a tree. (The book notes that this star is not the same as a star schema, which describes the structure of a data model rather than how nodes communicate.)

In circular and star topologies, a write may have to pass through several nodes before it reaches every replica. So nodes must forward the changes they receive from other nodes. To prevent infinite loops, each node is given a unique identifier. In the replication log, each write is tagged with the identifiers of all the nodes it has passed through. When a node receives a change tagged with its own identifier, it ignores the change, because it already processed it.

A weakness of circular and star topologies is that if a single node fails, it can interrupt the flow of replication messages between other nodes. They may be unable to communicate until the failed node is fixed. The topology could be reconfigured to work around the failed node, but in most deployments that reconfiguration has to be done by hand. A more densely connected topology, such as all-to-all, tolerates failures better, because messages can travel along different paths.

All-to-all has its own issue. Some network links are faster than others, for example because of congestion. As a result, some replication messages can overtake others.

Example

Figure 5-9 in the book shows how writes can arrive in the wrong order at a replica:

  1. Client A inserts a row into a table on leader 1.
  2. Client B then updates that same row on leader 3. B’s update depends on A’s insert.
  3. Leader 2 may receive the two writes in the wrong order. It first gets the update, which from its point of view is an update to a row that does not exist yet.
  4. Only later does it receive the insert, which should have come first.

This is a causality problem, similar to the consistent prefix reads problem above. The update depends on the earlier insert, so every node must process the insert first. Attaching a timestamp to every write is not enough, because clocks cannot be trusted to be synchronized well enough to order these events at leader 2. The book says a technique called version vectors can order them correctly, and the section on detecting concurrent writes explains it.

Many multi-leader systems implement conflict detection poorly. At the time the book was written, PostgreSQL BDR did not provide causal ordering of writes. Tungsten Replicator for MySQL did not even try to detect conflicts. If you use a multi-leader system, the book advises reading the documentation carefully and testing thoroughly to confirm it really provides the guarantees you believe it does.

Leaderless Replication

The approaches so far, single-leader and multi-leader, rely on the same idea. A client sends a write to one node, which is the leader, and the database copies it to the other replicas. The leader decides the order in which writes are processed, and followers apply the leader’s writes in that order.

Some data systems take a different approach. They drop the concept of a leader and let any replica accept writes directly from clients. Some of the earliest replicated data systems were leaderless, but the idea was mostly forgotten during the era when relational databases dominated. It became fashionable again after Amazon used it for its in-house Dynamo system. (The book notes that Dynamo is not available outside Amazon. AWS’s DynamoDB is a different product, built on single-leader replication.) Riak, Cassandra, and Voldemort are open source datastores with leaderless models inspired by Dynamo, so this kind of database is also called Dynamo-style.

In some leaderless systems the client sends each write directly to several replicas. In others, a coordinator node does this on the client’s behalf. Unlike a leader, though, the coordinator does not enforce any particular order of writes. The book says this difference has profound consequences for how the database is used.

Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down

Imagine a database with three replicas, and one of them is unavailable, perhaps because it is rebooting to install an update. With leader-based replication, if you want to keep accepting writes, you may need to fail over. With a leaderless design, there is no failover to perform.

Example

Figure 5-10 in the book shows what happens. The user with ID 1234 writes to a three-replica store, and one replica is down:

  1. The client sends the write to all three replicas at once.
  2. Replicas 1 and 2 are available. They store the write and reply “ok.”
  3. Replica 3 is down, so it misses the write.
  4. The client needs only two “ok” replies for the write to count as successful. It has two, so it accepts the write. It simply ignores the fact that one replica missed it.

Now suppose the unavailable node comes back online and clients start reading from it. Any writes made while it was down are missing from it, so reads from it may return stale, outdated values. To solve this, when a client reads, it does not send the request to just one replica. It sends read requests to several nodes in parallel. The client may get different answers from different nodes. The up-to-date value from one node may differ from a stale value on another. Version numbers tell the client which value is newer. The chapter explains version numbers later.

Read Repair and Anti-Entropy

The replication scheme should ensure that, eventually, all the data is copied to every replica. After a node comes back online, how does it catch up on the writes it missed? Dynamo-style datastores often use two mechanisms.

Read repair. When a client reads from several nodes in parallel, it can spot stale responses. In Figure 5-10, user 2345 receives a version 6 value from replica 3, and a version 7 value from replicas 1 and 2. The client can see that replica 3 is stale, so it writes the newer version 7 value back to replica 3. This works well for values that are read often.

Anti-entropy process. Some datastores also run a background process. It constantly looks for differences in the data between replicas, and copies any missing data from one replica to another. Unlike the replication log in leader-based replication, this process does not copy writes in any particular order. There may also be a significant delay before the data is copied.

Not all systems implement both. Voldemort, for example, currently has no anti-entropy process. Without one, values that are rarely read may be missing from some replicas, which reduces durability. Read repair only happens when a value is read by the application, so a value nobody reads may stay missing for a long time.

Quorums for Reading and Writing

In the example above, the write counted as successful even though only two of three replicas processed it. What if only one of the three accepted it? How far can this be pushed?

Suppose every successful write is guaranteed to be on at least two of the three replicas. Then at most one replica can be stale. If you read from at least two replicas, at least one of them must be up to date. If the third replica is down or slow, reads can still return an up-to-date value.

More generally, suppose there are n replicas. Every write must be confirmed by w nodes to count as successful. Every read must query at least r nodes. In the example, n = 3, w = 2, and r = 2. As long as w + r > n, we expect to read an up-to-date value. The reason is that at least one of the r nodes we read from must also be one of the w nodes that took the latest write. Reads and writes that follow these rules are called quorum reads and writes. You can think of w and r as the minimum number of votes needed for a read or write to be valid.

n = 3 replicas, w = 2 write confirmations, r = 2 read replies
w + r = 2 + 2 = 4, which is greater than n = 3
so every read set overlaps every write set in at least one node

In Dynamo-style databases, n, w, and r are typically configurable. A common choice is to make n an odd number, typically 3 or 5, and to set w = r = (n + 1) / 2, rounded up. But you can vary the numbers as you see fit. For example, a workload with few writes and many reads may benefit from w = n and r = 1. Reads become faster, but there is a disadvantage: a single failed node then makes every write fail.

There may be more than n nodes in the cluster. However, any given value is stored on only n of them. This allows the dataset to be partitioned, which supports datasets larger than one node can hold. Chapter 6 returns to partitioning.

The quorum condition, w + r > n, lets the system tolerate unavailable nodes in these ways:

  • If w is less than n, writes can still be processed while one node is unavailable.
  • If r is less than n, reads can still be processed while one node is unavailable.
  • With n = 3, w = 2, and r = 2, one unavailable node can be tolerated.
  • With n = 5, w = 3, and r = 3, two unavailable nodes can be tolerated.

Normally, reads and writes are sent to all n replicas in parallel. The values w and r decide how many of the n nodes must reply before the operation counts as successful. If fewer than the required w or r nodes are available, the write or read returns an error. A node can be unavailable for many reasons. It may be down, it may fail while running the operation (for example because its disk is full), or a network interruption may cut it off from the client. The system does not need to tell these apart. It only cares whether the node returned a successful response.

Example

Consider five replicas, with n = 5, w = 3, and r = 3. The book uses this case to show two unavailable nodes being tolerated:

  1. A write is successful once any 3 of the 5 replicas confirm it.
  2. A read asks 3 of the 5 replicas for their values.
  3. Because 3 + 3 is greater than 5, any 3 replicas you read must share at least one node with any 3 replicas that took the write. That shared node holds the latest value.
  4. If two replicas are down, the remaining three can still confirm a write and answer a read, so the system keeps working.
Try it

The book suggests w = n and r = 1 for workloads with few writes and many reads. Imagine you choose it for a 5-node cluster. Which operations get faster, and what happens to writes when one node is down? Compare your answer with the case n = 5, w = 3, r = 3.

Limitations of Quorum Consistency

If you have n replicas, and you choose w and r so that w + r > n, you can generally expect every read to return the most recent value written for a key. The set of nodes written to and the set of nodes read from must overlap. Among the nodes you read, at least one has the latest value (Figure 5-11 in the book illustrates this).

Often r and w are chosen to be a majority, meaning more than n/2 nodes. That ensures w + r > n while still tolerating up to n/2 node failures. But quorums do not have to be majorities. All that matters is that the sets of nodes used by reads and writes overlap in at least one node. Other quorum assignments are possible, which gives designers some flexibility in distributed algorithms.

You may also set w and r to smaller numbers, so that w + r ≤ n. Reads and writes are still sent to n nodes, but fewer successful responses are needed. This makes stale values more likely, because a read is more likely to miss the node with the latest value. The upside is lower latency and higher availability. If a network interruption cuts off many replicas, there is a better chance that reads and writes can still be processed. The database stops accepting writes or reads only when the number of reachable replicas falls below w or r.

Even with w + r > n, stale values can still be returned in several edge cases. The exact list depends on the implementation, but the book names these:

  • Sloppy quorums. If a sloppy quorum is used (explained below), the w writes may land on different nodes than the r reads. Then there is no guaranteed overlap.
  • Concurrent writes. If two writes happen at the same time, it is not clear which happened first. The only safe answer is to merge the concurrent writes. If a winner is picked by timestamp (last write wins), writes can be lost because of clock skew, meaning clocks that disagree with each other.
  • A write during a read. If a write happens at the same time as a read, the write may appear on only some replicas. It is then undetermined whether the read returns the old or the new value.
  • A failed write that was partly applied. A write may succeed on some replicas but fail on others, for example because the disks on some nodes are full. If it succeeds on fewer than w replicas overall, it is not rolled back where it did succeed. Subsequent reads may or may not return the value from that write, even though the client was told it failed.
  • Restoring from an old replica. If a node holding a new value fails, and its data is restored from a replica holding an old value, the number of replicas storing the new value may drop below w. The quorum condition then breaks.
  • Bad timing. Even when everything works correctly, timing can be unlucky in ways that break the guarantee. Chapter 9 discusses linearizability and quorums.

So although quorums appear to guarantee that a read returns the latest written value, in practice it is not so simple. Dynamo-style databases are generally optimized for use cases that can tolerate eventual consistency. The values w and r let you adjust the probability of reading stale values, but you should not treat them as absolute guarantees.

Rule of thumb

With w + r > n you get a good chance of reading the latest value, not a promise. Treat a quorum as a way to lower the odds of stale reads, not as a way to remove them.

In particular, you usually do not get the guarantees discussed earlier in the chapter, namely read-your-writes, monotonic reads, or consistent prefix reads. The anomalies described in that section can therefore happen in these applications. Stronger guarantees generally need transactions or consensus. Chapters 7 and 9 return to these topics.

Monitoring Staleness

From an operations point of view, it matters whether your databases return up-to-date results. Even if your application can tolerate stale reads, you need to know how healthy your replication is. If replication falls far behind, the system should alert you, so you can find the cause, such as a network problem or an overloaded node.

With leader-based replication, the database usually exposes metrics for replication lag, which you can feed into a monitoring system. This is possible because writes are applied to the leader and to followers in the same order, and each node has a position in the replication log, meaning the number of writes it has applied locally. Subtract a follower’s position from the leader’s position, and you have the replication lag.

With leaderless replication, monitoring is harder, because there is no fixed order in which writes are applied. If the database uses only read repair and has no anti-entropy process, there is no limit to how old a value might be. A value that is rarely read can be on a stale replica for a very long time, and the value returned could be ancient.

Some research has looked at measuring replica staleness in leaderless databases, and at predicting the expected percentage of stale reads from the parameters n, w, and r. This is not yet common practice. The book argues it would be good to include staleness measurements in the standard set of database metrics. Eventual consistency is a deliberately vague guarantee. For operations, it matters to be able to measure what “eventual” means in practice.

Sloppy Quorums and Hinted Handoff

A database with well-configured quorums can tolerate the failure of individual nodes without failover. It can also tolerate slow nodes, because a request does not have to wait for all n nodes. It can return as soon as w or r nodes have responded. These traits make leaderless databases attractive for use cases that need high availability and low latency, and that can accept occasional stale reads.

However, quorums as described so far are not as fault-tolerant as they could be. A network interruption can easily cut a client off from a large number of database nodes. Those nodes may be alive, and other clients may reach them. But to this client, cut off from them, they might as well be dead. In that situation, fewer than w or r reachable nodes may remain, so the client can no longer reach a quorum.

In a large cluster, with significantly more than n nodes, the client can probably still reach some database nodes during the interruption. Just not the particular nodes it needs to assemble a quorum for a given value. Here the designers face a trade-off:

  • Should they return errors to all requests that cannot reach a quorum of w or r nodes?
  • Or should they accept the writes anyway, and store them on reachable nodes that are not among the n nodes where that value normally lives?

The second option is called a sloppy quorum. Writes and reads still need w and r successful responses. But those responses may come from nodes outside the designated n “home” nodes for the value. The book compares it to being locked out of your house. You knock on the neighbor’s door and ask whether you can wait on their couch for a while.

Once the network interruption is fixed, any writes that one node temporarily accepted on behalf of another are sent to the proper “home” nodes. This is called hinted handoff. Back to the analogy: once you find your house keys, your neighbor politely asks you to get off the couch and go home.

Sloppy quorums are particularly useful for write availability. As long as any w nodes are available, the database can accept writes. But this means that even when w + r > n, you cannot be sure to read the latest value for a key. The latest value may have been temporarily written to nodes outside the n home nodes. So a sloppy quorum is not a quorum in the traditional sense. It gives only an assurance of durability: the data is stored on w nodes somewhere. There is no guarantee that a read of r nodes will see it until hinted handoff has completed.

Sloppy quorums are optional in all the common Dynamo implementations. In Riak they are enabled by default. In Cassandra and Voldemort they are disabled by default.

Multi-Datacenter Operation

Earlier, the chapter discussed cross-datacenter replication as a use case for multi-leader replication. Leaderless replication also suits multi-datacenter operation, because it is designed to tolerate conflicting concurrent writes, network interruptions, and latency spikes.

Cassandra and Voldemort build multi-datacenter support into the normal leaderless model. The number of replicas n includes nodes in all datacenters, and the configuration says how many of the n replicas should be in each datacenter. Each write from a client is sent to all replicas, wherever they are. But the client usually waits only for a quorum of nodes within its local datacenter. That way it is unaffected by delays and interruptions on the link between datacenters. Writes to the other datacenters are often configured to happen asynchronously, although the configuration offers some flexibility.

Riak takes a different route. It keeps all communication between clients and database nodes inside one datacenter, so n describes the number of replicas within a single datacenter. Replication between database clusters in different datacenters happens asynchronously, in the background. That is similar to multi-leader replication.

Detecting Concurrent Writes

Dynamo-style databases allow several clients to write to the same key at the same time. So conflicts will occur, even when strict quorums are used. The situation is similar to multi-leader replication, although in Dynamo-style databases conflicts can also arise during read repair or hinted handoff.

The core problem is that events may arrive in a different order at different nodes. Network delays vary, and failures are partial. The book gives an example.

Example

Figure 5-12 in the book shows two clients, A and B, writing to the same key X in a three-node datastore:

  1. Node 1 receives the write from A, but never receives the write from B because of a transient outage.
  2. Node 2 first receives the write from A, and then the write from B.
  3. Node 3 first receives the write from B, and then the write from A.

If each node simply overwrote the value for a key whenever a write arrived, the nodes would stay inconsistent forever. In the book’s final read, node 2 believes X is B, while the other nodes believe it is A.
