To become eventually consistent, the replicas must converge on the same value. How do they do that? Replicated databases could in principle handle this automatically, but most implementations are quite poor at it. If you want to avoid losing data, you need to know a lot about your database’s internals for conflict handling. The chapter explores the issue in more detail now.

Last Write Wins (Discarding Concurrent Writes)

One way to reach eventual convergence is to say that each replica needs to store only the most recent value. Older values can be overwritten and discarded. If you have a way to decide unambiguously which write is more recent, and every write is eventually copied to every replica, the replicas will converge.

But “recent” is a misleading word here. In the example above, neither client knew about the other when it sent its write. So it is not clear which write happened first. In fact, it does not really make sense to say either one happened first. The two writes are concurrent, which means their order is undefined.

Even so, you can force an arbitrary order. Attach a timestamp to each write, treat the biggest timestamp as the most recent, and discard any write with an earlier timestamp. This algorithm is called last write wins, or LWW. It is the only conflict resolution method supported in Cassandra, and an optional feature in Riak.

LWW achieves convergence, but at the cost of durability. If several concurrent writes hit the same key, all of them may have been reported as successful to the client, because each was written to w replicas. Yet only one of them survives. The others are silently discarded. LWW may even drop writes that were not concurrent at all, as the book discusses in its section on timestamps for ordering events.

Lost writes may be acceptable in some situations, such as caching. If losing data is not acceptable, LWW is a poor choice. The only safe way to use a database with LWW is to make sure each key is written only once and is then treated as immutable (never changed). That avoids any concurrent updates to the same key. For example, the book recommends using a UUID as the key in Cassandra, so that every write operation gets a unique key.

The Happens-Before Relationship and Concurrency

How do we decide whether two operations are concurrent or not? The book builds intuition with examples. In Figure 5-9, the two writes are not concurrent. A’s insert happens before B’s increment, because the value B increments is the value A inserted. B’s operation builds on A’s, so B must have happened later. We say that B is causally dependent on A. In contrast, the two writes in Figure 5-12 are concurrent. When each client started its operation, it did not know that another client was doing an operation on the same key. Neither depends on the other.

The book defines the terms this way. An operation A happens before another operation B if B knows about A, depends on A, or builds on A in some way. Whether one operation happens before another is the key to defining concurrency. Two operations are concurrent if neither happens before the other. Put simply, neither knows about the other. So for any two operations A and B, there are three possibilities. Either A happened before B, or B happened before A, or they are concurrent. If one operation happened before another, the later one should overwrite the earlier one. If they are concurrent, there is a conflict to resolve.

Concurrency, time, and relativity. You might think two operations are concurrent only if they happen “at the same time.” But it does not matter whether they literally overlap in time. Clocks in distributed systems are unreliable, so it is hard to tell whether two things truly happened at the same moment. Chapter 8 covers that. For defining concurrency, exact timing does not matter. Two operations are concurrent if both are unaware of each other, whatever their physical times. This idea has a loose link to the special theory of relativity, which says information cannot travel faster than light. Two events too far apart to affect each other cannot influence each other in the time between them. In computer systems the situation is similar. If the network was slow or interrupted, two operations can happen some time apart and still be concurrent, because the network problem stopped one from knowing about the other.

Capturing the Happens-Before Relationship

Next is an algorithm that decides whether two operations are concurrent or whether one happened before the other. To keep things simple, start with a database that has only one replica. Then generalize to a leaderless database with several replicas.

Figure 5-13 in the book shows two clients concurrently adding items to the same shopping cart. (If that seems too trivial, picture two air traffic controllers adding aircraft to the sector they track.) The cart starts empty. Between them, the clients make five writes:

Example
  1. Client 1 adds milk to the cart. This is the first write to that key, so the server stores it and assigns it version 1. The server echoes the value and version number back to the client.
  2. Client 2 adds eggs. It does not know that client 1 has just added milk, so it thinks its eggs are the only item. The server assigns this write version 2. It cannot tell that the eggs replace the milk, so it stores eggs and milk as two separate values. It returns both values to client 2 with version 2.
  3. Client 1 has not seen client 2’s write. It wants to add flour, so it thinks the cart holds milk and sends [milk, flour] with version 1. The server can tell that this write supersedes the earlier [milk] value, but it is concurrent with [eggs]. So the server assigns version 3 to [milk, flour], overwrites the version 1 value, keeps the version 2 value [eggs], and returns both remaining values.
  4. Client 2 wants to add ham, and it does not know about the flour. It received [milk] and [eggs] in its last response, so it merges them with ham to form [eggs, milk, ham]. It sends that with version 2. The server sees that version 2 overwrites [eggs] but is concurrent with [milk, flour]. So the two remaining values are [milk, flour] at version 3 and [eggs, milk, ham] at version 4.
  5. Client 1 wants to add bacon. It last received [milk, flour] and [eggs] at version 3, so it merges them and adds bacon, giving [milk, flour, eggs, bacon]. It sends that with version 3. This overwrites [milk, flour], and [eggs] was already overwritten earlier. But the new value is concurrent with [eggs, milk, ham], so the server keeps both.

The book draws the dataflow between these operations as a graph, where arrows show which operation happened before which other operation. The later operation knew about or depended on the earlier one. The clients are never fully up to date with the server, because there is always another operation going on concurrently. But old versions of the value do get overwritten eventually, and no writes are lost.

The server can determine whether two operations are concurrent by looking at version numbers. It does not need to interpret the value itself, so the value could be any data structure. The algorithm works like this:

  • The server keeps a version number for every key. It increments the version number each time the key is written, and stores the new version number with the value.
  • When a client reads a key, the server returns all values that have not been overwritten, along with the latest version number. A client must read a key before it writes to it.
  • When a client writes a key, it must include the version number from its prior read. It must also merge all the values it received in that read. The response to a write can look like a read, returning all current values, which allows several writes to be chained together, as in the shopping cart example.
  • When the server receives a write with a particular version number, it can overwrite all values with that version number or below, because they have been merged into the new value. But it must keep all values with a higher version number, because those are concurrent with the incoming write.

A write that includes the version number from a prior read tells the server which earlier state the write is based on. If you write without a version number, the write is treated as concurrent with all other writes. So it overwrites nothing. It is simply returned as one of the values on later reads.

Merging Concurrently Written Values

This algorithm makes sure no data is silently dropped. But it asks clients to do extra work. When several operations happen concurrently, clients must clean up afterward by merging the concurrent values. Riak calls these concurrent values siblings.

Merging siblings is essentially the same problem as conflict resolution in multi-leader replication. One simple approach is to pick one value, based on version number or timestamp, which is last write wins. But that loses data. So you may need something more intelligent in application code.

For a shopping cart, a reasonable way to merge siblings is to take the union of their items. In the example, the two final siblings are [milk, flour, eggs, bacon] and [eggs, milk, ham]. Notice that milk and eggs appear in both, even though each was written only once. The merged cart might be [milk, flour, eggs, bacon, ham], without duplicates.

But if people can also remove items from their carts, a plain union can give the wrong answer. Suppose an item was removed in only one of two sibling carts. The union would bring the removed item back, because the other sibling still contains it. To prevent this, the system cannot simply delete an item from the database when it is removed. Instead it must leave a marker with a suitable version number, showing that the item was removed. Such a deletion marker is called a tombstone. The book recalls that tombstones appeared earlier, in the context of log compaction in hash indexes.

Merging siblings in application code is complex and error-prone. So some efforts aim to design data structures that merge automatically, as discussed in the section on automatic conflict resolution. For example, Riak’s datatype support uses CRDTs that can merge siblings sensibly, including preserving deletions.

Version Vectors

The example above used only one replica. How does the algorithm change when there are several replicas and no leader?

A single version number per key is not enough when several replicas accept writes at the same time. Instead, each key needs a version number for each replica, as well as the per-key number. Each replica increments its own version number when it processes a write. It also keeps track of the version numbers it has seen from each of the other replicas. Together, this information tells the system which values to overwrite and which to keep as siblings. The collection of version numbers from all the replicas is called a version vector.

A few variants of the idea are in use. The most interesting is probably the dotted version vector, used in Riak 2.0. The book does not go into the details, but it works in much the same way as the shopping cart example.

Like the version numbers in the single-replica example, version vectors are sent from the database replicas to clients when values are read. They must be sent back to the database when the value is written later. Riak encodes the version vector as a string it calls the causal context. The version vector lets the database tell overwrites apart from concurrent writes.

As before, the application may still need to merge siblings. The version vector structure makes it safe to read from one replica and then write back to another. Doing so may create siblings, but no data is lost, as long as the siblings are merged correctly.

Version vectors and vector clocks. A version vector is sometimes also called a vector clock, although the two are not quite the same. The difference is subtle, and the book points to references for details. In brief, when comparing the state of replicas, version vectors are the right data structure to use.

Trade-offs
ApproachGood atCosts
Single-leaderEasy to understand, with no conflict resolution. All writes are ordered by one node.All writes go through one node. Followers can serve stale reads. Failover is risky, and asynchronous copies can lose recent writes.
Multi-leaderWrites accepted in several places, including across datacenters and on devices that are offline. Robust against faulty nodes and network trouble.Write conflicts must be detected and resolved. Configuration is subtle, and many systems detect conflicts poorly.
LeaderlessNo failover needed. Keeps working when nodes are down or slow, and can tolerate latency spikes.Reads can be stale. Conflicts happen, and the application may have to merge siblings. Guarantees are weak unless transactions or consensus are added.

Summary

Summary

This chapter looked at replication, which keeps copies of the same data on several machines. The book gives three reasons for replicating: to keep data close to users, to keep the system working when parts fail, and to scale out the reads a system can serve.

  • Three approaches. In single-leader replication, clients send all writes to one leader, which streams changes to followers. Reads can go to any replica, but reads from followers may be stale. In multi-leader replication, clients send each write to one of several leaders, which exchange changes with each other and with followers. In leaderless replication, clients send each write to several nodes and read from several nodes in parallel, to detect and fix stale copies.
  • Synchronous or asynchronous. Asynchronous replication is fast when the system runs smoothly. But when replication lag grows and servers fail, promoting an asynchronously updated follower to leader can lose recently committed data. Failover also brings split brain and other risks, so it needs care.
  • Lag and guarantees. Replication lag can cause strange effects. Three guarantees help applications behave sensibly: read-after-write consistency, so users see their own submitted data; monotonic reads, so users never see time go backward; and consistent prefix reads, so users see causally ordered data, such as a question and its reply in the right order.
  • Concurrency. Multi-leader and leaderless replication allow concurrent writes, so conflicts can occur. The happens-before relationship tells you whether two operations were concurrent. Version numbers and version vectors let a database detect concurrency. Merging the concurrent values, with tombstones for deletions, keeps data from being silently lost.

Replication is a simple goal, keeping a copy of the same data on several machines. Yet it turns out to be a tricky problem. It requires careful thought about concurrency and about all the things that can go wrong. At a minimum, you must deal with unavailable nodes and network interruptions. Subtler faults, such as silent data corruption caused by software bugs, are harder still. The next chapter continues with data that is distributed across multiple machines, through the counterpart of replication: splitting a large dataset into partitions. The book’s reference list for this chapter has 61 entries. This retelling does not reproduce them.

Check yourself

  1. An asynchronous leader fails, and an asynchronous follower is promoted to be the new leader. What can happen to writes that clients were told had succeeded?

    Show answer

    Writes that had not yet been copied to that follower can be lost. Asynchronous replication does not guarantee durability, so the new leader may never see them, and the most common fix is to discard the old leader’s unreplicated writes when it rejoins.

  2. A user saves a profile change, then reloads the page and sees the old data, because the read was served by a follower that was still behind. Which guarantee is missing, and how could the application provide it?

    Show answer

    The missing guarantee is read-after-write consistency, also called read-your-writes. One fix is to read the user’s own profile from the leader and everyone else’s from followers. Another is to remember the timestamp of the last write and make sure the replica used for reads is at least that current.

  3. A database has n = 5 replicas, with w = 3 and r = 3. How many nodes can be unavailable while reads and writes still succeed, and why does a read see the latest write?

    Show answer

    Two nodes can be unavailable. Since w + r = 6 is greater than n = 5, any set of 3 nodes used for a read must share at least one node with any set of 3 nodes that accepted the latest write. That shared node holds the latest value.

  4. Two leaders in a multi-leader system concurrently set a wiki page title to B and to C. Why does last write wins lose data here, and what are two alternatives that keep more information?

    Show answer

    Last write wins keeps only the write with the highest timestamp and silently discards the other. Both writes were reported as successful, so one user’s change disappears. Two alternatives are to merge the values, for example into “B/C,” or to keep both as conflicting values and let application code or a user resolve them later.

Part II · Chapter 6

Partitioning

The big idea: when a dataset or its traffic is too big for one machine, split it into partitions and spread them across nodes. The hard parts are choosing how to split the data, keeping the load even, and sending each request to the right node.

Chapter 5 covered replication, which means keeping several copies of the same data on different nodes. A node is simply one machine in a cluster. Replication alone is not enough when a dataset is very large or when queries arrive at a very high rate. For those cases, the data has to be broken into partitions, which are also called shards. Each partition is one slice of the whole dataset.

The chapter opens with a 1962 line from the computing pioneer Grace Murray Hopper, “We must state relationships, not procedures.” It is an epigraph, a short quote set before the chapter text.

Watch out

Different products use different names for the same idea. The book lists them: a shard in MongoDB, Elasticsearch and SolrCloud, a region in HBase, a tablet in Bigtable, a vnode (virtual node) in Cassandra and Riak, and a vBucket in Couchbase. The book keeps the word partitioning, because it is the most established term. Also, partitioning here has nothing to do with a network partition, which is a fault where nodes cannot reach each other. Chapter 8 covers those faults.

Partitioning and Replication

Why split data at all? The main reason is scalability. Different partitions can live on different nodes in a shared-nothing cluster, which is a design where each machine has its own memory and disks and does not share them with other machines. A large dataset can then be spread across many disks, and the query load across many processors. A query that touches only one partition can run on that partition’s node alone. So adding nodes adds query throughput. Large, complex queries that touch many partitions can be run in parallel as well, although that is much harder to get right.

Partitioned databases are not new. Products such as Teradata and Tandem NonStop SQL pioneered the idea in the 1980s. NoSQL databases and Hadoop-based data warehouses brought it back later. Some systems are built for transactional workloads (many small reads and writes), and others for analytics (large scans and reports). The workload changes how a system is tuned, but the basics of partitioning apply to both.

The chapter first looks at ways to partition large datasets and at how indexes interact with partitioning. Then it covers rebalancing, which is moving data when nodes are added or removed. Last, it gives an overview of how a database routes each request to the right partition and runs queries.

Partitioning is usually combined with replication, so that each partition has copies on several nodes. This is for fault tolerance, so that one dead machine does not lose data. Each record still belongs to exactly one partition, but that partition may be stored on several nodes.

A single node may hold more than one partition. Under leader–follower replication, one copy of each partition is the leader, which takes the writes, and the other copies are followers, which copy the leader’s changes. The leader of each partition sits on one node, and its followers sit on other nodes. Each node can lead some partitions and follow others. The book’s Figure 6-1 shows this layout.

Everything from Chapter 5 about replication applies equally to partitions. The choice of partitioning scheme is mostly independent of the choice of replication scheme. So the chapter leaves replication aside from here on.

Partitioning of Key-Value Data

Say you have a large amount of data and want to partition it. How do you decide which records go on which node?

The goal is to spread both the data and the query load evenly. If every node takes a fair share, then in theory 10 nodes can handle 10 times the data and 10 times the read and write throughput of one node. This assumes replication is ignored for now.

If the split is unfair, so that some partitions hold more data or receive more queries than others, the partitioning is called skewed. Skew makes partitioning much less effective. In the extreme case, all the load lands on one partition. Then nine of the ten nodes sit idle, and the one busy node is the bottleneck. A partition with disproportionately high load is called a hot spot.

The simplest way to avoid hot spots would be to assign each record to a node at random. That spreads the data quite evenly. But it has a big disadvantage. When you want to read one particular item, you have no way of knowing which node holds it, so you must query all nodes in parallel.

We can do better. Assume for now a simple key-value model, where every record is found by its primary key, which is the field that uniquely identifies it. An old paper encyclopedia works this way. You look up an entry by its title, and because the entries are in alphabetical order, you can find the right one quickly.

Partitioning by Key Range

One approach is to give each partition a continuous range of keys, from some minimum to some maximum. This is like the volumes of a paper encyclopedia, shown in the book’s Figure 6-2. If you know where the boundaries between ranges are, you can tell which partition holds a given key. If you also know which node holds which partition, you can send the request straight to that node. With the encyclopedia, you pick the correct volume off the shelf.

The key ranges do not have to be evenly spaced, because the data itself may not be evenly spread. In the encyclopedia, volume 1 holds words starting with A and B, but volume 12 holds words starting with T, U, V, X, Y and Z. Giving each volume two letters would leave some volumes much bigger than others. To spread the data evenly, the boundaries must adapt to the data. An administrator can choose the boundaries by hand, or the database can choose them automatically. The book returns to this in its section on rebalancing. Bigtable and its open-source equivalent HBase use key range partitioning, as do RethinkDB and MongoDB before version 2.4.

Inside each partition, keys can be kept in sorted order. This makes range scans easy, which means reading all the keys between two values. You can also treat the key as a concatenated index, which combines several fields into one key, sorted by the first field and then the next. That lets you fetch several related records in one query.

Take an application that stores readings from a network of sensors, where the key is the timestamp of each measurement in the form year-month-day-hour-minute-second. Range scans are very useful here. They let you fetch, say, all the readings from one month in one go.

Example

Sensors and a timestamp key. Here is what goes wrong, step by step:

  1. Partitions are time ranges, one partition per day.
  2. Sensors write their readings to the database as the measurements happen.
  3. Every new reading has a timestamp from today, so it belongs to today’s range.
  4. All of today’s writes therefore go to the same partition, while the older partitions sit idle.

The partition for today can be overloaded with writes, while the rest of the cluster does nothing. The book’s fix is to put something other than the timestamp first in the key. For example, prefix each timestamp with the sensor name. The partitioning is then first by sensor name and then by time. If many sensors are active at once, the write load spreads across the partitions. The cost is that to read the values of several sensors over a time range, you need a separate range query for each sensor name.

Hot:    2026-10-19 08:00:01
Better: sensor-17 | 2026-10-19 08:00:01
        sensor-42 | 2026-10-19 08:00:01
Key idea

Sorted keys make range scans easy. But a key that grows over time, such as a timestamp, can send all new writes to one partition. Check the access pattern before you pick the key.

Partitioning by Hash of Key

Because of the risk of skew and hot spots, many distributed datastores use a hash function to decide which partition a key belongs to. A hash function is a formula that turns any input into a number. A good one spreads skewed input evenly across its output range.

Take a 32-bit hash function that works on strings. Each new string produces a seemingly random number between 0 and 232 − 1. Even when two input strings are very similar, their hashes land all over that range. For partitioning, the hash function does not need to be strong enough for security. Cassandra and MongoDB use MD5, and Voldemort uses the Fowler–Noll–Vo function. Many programming languages have built-in hash functions for their hash tables, but the book warns that these are often unsuitable here. In Java’s Object.hashCode() and Ruby’s Object#hash, the same key can produce different hash values in different processes.

Once you have a suitable hash function, you give each partition a range of hash values rather than a range of keys. Every key whose hash falls inside a partition’s range is stored in that partition. This is shown in the book’s Figure 6-3. The partition boundaries can be evenly spaced, or they can be picked pseudorandomly. The second option is the approach known as consistent hashing, which the book covers in a short section below.

This technique is good at spreading keys fairly across partitions. But it has a cost. Using the hash of the key for partitioning loses a useful property of key range partitioning, which is efficient range queries. Keys that were once next to each other are now scattered over all the partitions, so their sort order is gone. In MongoDB, if you turn on hash-based sharding, any range query has to be sent to all partitions. Riak, Couchbase and Voldemort do not support range queries on the primary key at all.

Hash partitioning gives up range queries, but Cassandra offers a compromise between the two strategies. A table in Cassandra can have a compound primary key made of several columns. Only the first column is hashed to choose the partition. The other columns are used as a concatenated index that sorts the data within the partition on disk.

So a query cannot search over a range of values in the first column. But if the query fixes a single value for the first column, it can run an efficient range scan over the other columns.

Example

Updates from a social media user. Suppose the primary key for an update is (user_id, update_timestamp). Here is what the design gives you:

  1. The first part, user_id, is hashed to pick the partition. Different users may land on different partitions.
  2. All the updates from one user are stored together, on one partition.
  3. Within that partition, the updates are sorted by timestamp.
  4. So you can fetch all updates by one user within a time interval, already in timestamp order, with one efficient query.

The book notes that this makes a neat data model for one-to-many relationships, where one user posts many updates.

Consistent Hashing

The term consistent hashing comes from Karger and colleagues. It describes a way of spreading load evenly across a large internet-wide system of caches, such as a content delivery network (CDN, a network of servers that keep copies of content close to users). It uses randomly chosen partition boundaries, so there is no need for central control or for distributed consensus (nodes agreeing on a shared decision).

The word “consistent” here has nothing to do with replica consistency, which is covered in Chapter 5, or with ACID consistency, which is covered in Chapter 7. It describes a particular approach to rebalancing. The book says this approach does not work very well for databases, so it is rarely used in practice. Some database documentation still mentions consistent hashing, but the book says that documentation is often inaccurate. Its advice is to avoid the confusing term and just call the technique hash partitioning. The book itself later uses the term for one approach that it calls the closest match to the original definition, so you will still meet it in its own text.

Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots

Hashing a key to choose its partition helps reduce hot spots. But it cannot remove them completely. In the extreme case, where all reads and writes are for the same key, every request still goes to the same partition. The hash of two identical keys is the same.

This kind of workload is unusual, but it does happen. On a social media site, a celebrity with millions of followers may cause a storm of activity when they post something. That can mean a large volume of writes to the same key. The key might be the celebrity’s user ID, or the ID of the post that everyone is commenting on. Hashing the key does not help, because identical IDs still hash to the same place.

Today most data systems cannot compensate for a workload this skewed by themselves. So it is the application’s job to reduce the skew. If one key is known to be very hot, a simple technique is to add a random number to the beginning or end of the key. A two-digit decimal random number, from 00 to 99, splits the writes across 100 different keys. Those keys can then be placed on different partitions.

Example

Splitting one hot key into 100. Here is the technique step by step:

  1. Identify the key that is receiving a flood of writes.
  2. On each write, append a random two-digit number, so the same key becomes one of 100 keys.
  3. The writes now spread across 100 keys, which can sit on 100 different places in the cluster.
  4. A read now has to fetch all 100 keys and combine the results.
  5. Keep a record of which keys are split, so the reads know where to look.

The split has a price. Reads now do extra work, because they must read the data from all 100 keys and combine it. The technique is also only worth using for the small number of hot keys. For the vast majority of keys, with low write throughput, the random number would be wasted effort. So you also need some way to track which keys are split.

Perhaps in the future, data systems will detect and compensate for skewed workloads automatically. For now, the book says, you need to think through these trade-offs for your own application.

Try it

The book’s fix for the sensor timestamp hot spot puts the sensor name first in the key. What does a query for all sensors during a single hour cost after that change? Compare it with the cost before the change.

Partitioning and Secondary Indexes

Everything so far relies on a key-value model. If records are only ever accessed by primary key, the partition can be worked out from that key. Reads and writes can then be routed to the partition responsible for it.

Things get more complicated when secondary indexes are involved. A secondary index is an index on some other field, not the primary key. It usually does not identify one record uniquely. Instead, it lets you search for records that have a particular value. Examples are: find all actions by user 123, find all articles containing the word “hogwash,” or find all cars whose color is red.

Secondary indexes are the bread and butter of relational databases, and they are common in document databases too. Some key-value stores, such as HBase and Voldemort, have avoided them because they add implementation complexity. Others, such as Riak, have started adding them because they are so useful for modeling data. Secondary indexes are also the reason search servers such as Solr and Elasticsearch exist.

The problem is that secondary indexes do not map neatly onto partitions. The book describes two main ways to partition a database that has them: document-based partitioning and term-based partitioning.

Watch out

If your database supports only a key-value model, you might be tempted to build a secondary index yourself in application code, as a mapping from values to primary keys. That is possible, but you must take great care to keep the index consistent with the data. Race conditions, which happen when two operations interleave in an unlucky order, and intermittent write failures, where some changes are saved and others are not, can easily leave the two out of step. The book points to its discussion of multi-object transactions in Chapter 7 for the deeper reason.

Partitioning Secondary Indexes by Document

Imagine you run a website for selling used cars. Each listing has a unique ID, called the document ID. You partition the database by document ID. For example, IDs 0 to 499 go in partition 0, IDs 500 to 999 go in partition 1, and so on. This is shown in the book’s Figure 6-4.

You want users to search for cars by color and by make, so you need a secondary index on color and on make. In a document database these would be fields, and in a relational database they would be columns. If you declare the index, the database can maintain it automatically. For example, whenever a red car is added, the partition that holds it adds that car’s ID to the list for the index entry color:red.

In this design, each partition is completely separate. Each partition keeps its own secondary indexes, and those cover only the documents in that partition. It does not care what is stored in the other partitions. Whenever you write to the database, to add, remove or update a document, you deal only with the partition that holds that document’s ID. Because of this, a document-partitioned index is also called a local index, as opposed to the global index described in the next section.

Reading from a document-partitioned index needs care, though. Unless you did something special with the document IDs, there is no reason why all the red cars would be in the same partition. In the book’s example, red cars appear in both partition 0 and partition 1. So to search for red cars, you must send the query to every partition and combine all the results. This pattern is called scatter/gather. It can make reads on secondary indexes quite expensive. Even when the partitions are queried in parallel, scatter/gather is prone to the tail latency amplification described in Chapter 1, where the slowest partition sets the response time.

Even so, the approach is widely used. MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud and VoltDB all use document-partitioned secondary indexes. Most database vendors recommend structuring the partitioning so that a secondary index query can be served from a single partition. But that is not always possible, especially when a query uses several secondary indexes at once, such as filtering cars by color and make together.

Example

Searching for red cars in a used-car site. Here is what happens, step by step:

  1. The client sends “color is red” to every partition, because any partition may hold red cars.
  2. Each partition looks up color:red in its own local index and returns the IDs it found.
  3. The results from all partitions are combined into one list.

Writing is cheaper. When one new red car is added, only the partition that holds its ID needs to change.

Partitioning Secondary Indexes by Term

Instead of giving each partition its own index, you can build a global index that covers the data in all partitions. But you cannot store that index on one node, because it would likely become a bottleneck and defeat the purpose of partitioning. So the global index must be partitioned too. It can be partitioned differently from the primary key index.

The book’s Figure 6-5 shows the idea. Red cars from all partitions appear under color:red in the index. The index is partitioned so that colors starting with the letters a to r are in partition 0, and colors starting with s to z are in partition 1. The index on make is partitioned in a similar way, with the boundary between f and h.

This is called a term-partitioned index, because the term you are looking for decides which partition holds the index entry. Here a term would be color:red. The word “term” comes from full-text indexes, a special kind of secondary index, where the terms are all the words that appear in a document.

As before, you can partition the index by the term itself, or by a hash of the term. Partitioning by the term itself is useful for range scans, for example on a numeric property such as the asking price of a car. Partitioning on a hash of the term gives a more even spread of load.

The advantage of a global, term-partitioned index over a document-partitioned one is that reads can be more efficient. Instead of scatter/gather over all partitions, a client needs to contact only the partition that holds the term it wants.

The downside is that writes are slower and more complicated. A write to a single document may affect several partitions of the index, because every term in that document might sit on a different partition, on a different node.

In an ideal world, the index would always be up to date, so that every document written would appear in the index straight away. In a term-partitioned index, that would need a distributed transaction across all the partitions affected by the write. A distributed transaction is one atomic change spread over several machines. Not every database supports one. The book covers transactions in Chapters 7 and 9.

In practice, updates to global secondary indexes are often asynchronous. That means the index is updated after the write returns, not as part of it. So if you read the index shortly after a write, the change you just made may not be visible yet. Amazon DynamoDB, for example, says its global secondary indexes are normally updated within a fraction of a second, but may see longer delays when the infrastructure has faults. Riak’s search feature also uses global term-partitioned indexes, and so does the Oracle data warehouse, where you can choose between local and global indexing. Chapter 12 returns to how term-partitioned indexes are implemented.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
Document-partitioned (local) indexWrites touch one partition. Simple to keep correct.Reads scatter to all partitions and gather the results, which is slow and prone to tail latency amplification.
Term-partitioned (global) indexReads go to one partition, so they are fast and cheap.Writes touch several index partitions and are slower and harder. Index updates are often asynchronous, so a read may be briefly stale.

Rebalancing Partitions

Over time, things change in a database. The query throughput grows, so you want more CPUs to handle the load. The dataset grows, so you want more disks and more RAM to store it. A machine fails, so other machines must take over its work. Each of these changes calls for data and requests to move from one node to another. Moving load from one node in the cluster to another is called rebalancing.

Whatever partitioning scheme is used, rebalancing is usually expected to meet a few minimum requirements:

  • After rebalancing, the load (data stored, reads and writes) should be shared fairly among the nodes.
  • While rebalancing is happening, the database should keep accepting reads and writes.
  • No more data than necessary should move between nodes, so that rebalancing is fast and does not overload the network or disks.

Strategies for Rebalancing

There are several ways to assign partitions to nodes. The book walks through them in turn.

How not to do it: hash mod N. Earlier, the book said it is best to split the range of possible hashes into ranges and give each range to a partition. For example, a key goes to partition 0 if its hash is below a boundary b0, to partition 1 if its hash is between b0 and b1, and so on. You might wonder why we don’t just use mod, the remainder operator. For example, hash(key) mod 10 returns a number from 0 to 9. With 10 nodes numbered 0 to 9, that looks like an easy way to assign each key to a node.

The problem is that if the number of nodes N changes, most of the keys have to move from one node to another. Take a key whose hash is 123456. With 10 nodes, it starts on node 6, because 123456 mod 10 is 6. When you grow to 11 nodes, it must move to node 3, because 123456 mod 11 is 3. When you grow to 12 nodes, it must move to node 0. Such frequent moves make rebalancing excessively expensive. We need an approach that does not move data more than necessary.

Example

One key, three cluster sizes. The key’s hash is 123456 throughout:

  1. With 10 nodes, the key goes to node 6 (123456 mod 10 is 6).
  2. Grow to 11 nodes, and the key must move to node 3 (123456 mod 11 is 3).
  3. Grow to 12 nodes, and it must move again, to node 0 (123456 mod 12 is 0).

The key moved on every change, and most other keys do too.

Fixed number of partitions. The fix is fairly simple. Create many more partitions than there are nodes, and assign several partitions to each node. For example, a database on a cluster of 10 nodes might be split into 1,000 partitions from the start, so that about 100 partitions are assigned to each node.

Now, when a node is added to the cluster, the new node can take a few partitions from every existing node, until the partitions are fairly distributed again. If a node is removed, the same thing happens in reverse. Figure 6-6 in the book shows a new node being added this way.

Only entire partitions move between nodes. The number of partitions does not change, and neither does the assignment of keys to partitions. Only the assignment of partitions to nodes changes. That change is not immediate, because it takes time to transfer a large amount of data over the network. So while the transfer is in progress, the old assignment is still used for any reads and writes.

In principle, you can also account for mismatched hardware. By giving more partitions to the more powerful nodes, you can make those nodes take a larger share of the load. This approach is used by Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase and Voldemort.

In this setup, the number of partitions is usually fixed when the database is first set up and not changed afterward. The book notes that partitions could be split and merged, but a fixed number is operationally simpler, so many fixed-partition databases skip splitting altogether. This means the number of partitions chosen at the start is the maximum number of nodes you can ever have. So you must choose it high enough to allow for future growth. But each partition carries management overhead, so choosing too high a number is also a mistake.

Choosing the right number is hard when the total size of the dataset is hard to predict. A dataset may start small and grow much larger. Each partition holds a fixed fraction of the total data, so each partition grows as the cluster’s data grows. If partitions become very large, rebalancing and recovery from node failures get expensive. If they are too small, the overhead adds up. The best performance comes when partitions are “just right,” neither too big nor too small. That is hard to achieve when the number of partitions is fixed but the dataset size varies.

Dynamic partitioning. A fixed number of partitions with fixed boundaries would be very inconvenient for key range partitioning. If you got the boundaries wrong, all the data could end up in one partition while the others stayed empty. Reconfiguring the boundaries by hand would be tedious. So key range databases such as HBase and RethinkDB create partitions dynamically.

When a partition grows beyond a configured size, it is split into two partitions, so that roughly half of the data goes to each side. On HBase, the default size is 10 GB. Conversely, if a lot of data is deleted and a partition shrinks below a threshold, it can be merged with an adjacent partition. The process is similar to what happens at the top level of a B-tree, a common on-disk index structure covered in Chapter 3.

As with fixed partitions, each partition is assigned to one node, and each node can handle several partitions. After a large partition has been split, one of its two halves can be moved to another node to balance the load. On HBase, the partition files are transferred through HDFS, the underlying distributed filesystem.

Example

A partition that keeps growing. Here is the life of one partition under dynamic partitioning:

  1. The partition starts small and stays on one node.
  2. Writes keep arriving, and the partition grows past the configured size, which is 10 GB by default on HBase.
  3. The partition is split into two, with about half the data in each.
  4. One of the two halves is transferred to another node, so the load is shared.
  5. If later deletes shrink a partition below a threshold, it is merged with a neighbor.

An advantage of dynamic partitioning is that the number of partitions adapts to the total data volume. If there is only a small amount of data, a small number of partitions is enough, so the overhead stays low. If there is a huge amount of data, the size of each partition is limited to a configured maximum.

There is a caveat, though. An empty database starts with a single partition, because there is no information yet about where to draw the boundaries. While the dataset is small, until it reaches the point where the first partition is split, all writes go through a single node while the other nodes sit idle. To ease this, HBase and MongoDB let you configure an initial set of partitions on an empty database. This is called pre-splitting. With key range partitioning, pre-splitting requires that you already know what the key distribution is going to look like.

Dynamic partitioning is not limited to key range partitioning. It works equally well with hash-partitioned data. MongoDB, since version 2.4, supports both key range and hash partitioning, and it splits partitions dynamically in either case.

Partitioning proportionally to nodes. With dynamic partitioning, the number of partitions is proportional to the size of the dataset, because splitting and merging keep each partition’s size between a fixed minimum and maximum. With a fixed number of partitions, the size of each partition is proportional to the dataset. In both cases, the number of partitions does not depend on the number of nodes.

A third option, used by Cassandra and Ketama, is to make the number of partitions proportional to the number of nodes. In other words, each node holds a fixed number of partitions. Now the size of each partition grows with the dataset while the number of nodes stays the same. But when you add nodes, the partitions become smaller again. A larger data volume generally needs more nodes to store it, so this approach keeps the size of each partition fairly stable.

When a new node joins the cluster, it randomly picks a fixed number of existing partitions to split. For each one, it takes ownership of one half and leaves the other half where it is. The random choice can produce unfair splits. But when you average over many partitions, the new node ends up with a fair share of the load. In Cassandra, the default is 256 partitions per node. Cassandra 3.0 introduced an alternative rebalancing algorithm that avoids unfair splits.

Choosing partition boundaries at random requires hash-based partitioning, because the boundaries are picked from the range of numbers that the hash function produces. This approach is the one that corresponds most closely to the original definition of consistent hashing. Newer hash functions can achieve a similar effect with less metadata overhead.

Trade-offs
StrategyGood atCosts
Hash mod NVery simple to write.When the number of nodes changes, most keys move.
Fixed number of partitionsOnly whole partitions move. Operationally simple.The partition count is fixed at setup. Partition sizes swing with the dataset, and too many partitions add overhead.
Dynamic partitioningThe number of partitions adapts to the data. Fits key range partitioning.An empty database starts with one partition, so early writes hit one node. Pre-splitting needs advance knowledge of the keys.
Partitions proportional to nodesPartition size stays fairly stable as the cluster grows.Random splits can be unfair for any single join, and the approach requires hash partitioning.

Operations: Automatic or Manual Rebalancing

One important question about rebalancing is whether it happens automatically or manually. There is a gradient between two extremes. At one end, rebalancing is fully automatic: the system decides on its own when to move partitions from one node to another, with no administrator involved. At the other end, it is fully manual: an administrator explicitly configures which node holds which partition, and the assignment changes only when the administrator changes it. Couchbase, Riak and Voldemort sit in between. They generate a suggested partition assignment automatically, but an administrator must approve it before it takes effect.

Fully automatic rebalancing is convenient, because there is less routine work. But it can be unpredictable. Rebalancing is an expensive operation. It means rerouting requests and moving a large amount of data between nodes. If it is not done carefully, it can overload the network or the nodes, and it can slow down other requests while it runs.

Example

Automatic rebalancing makes a bad situation worse. The book describes how automation can combine badly with automatic failure detection:

  1. One node becomes overloaded and is slow to respond to requests.
  2. The other nodes decide that the slow node is dead.
  3. They automatically rebalance the cluster to move load away from it.
  4. That moves extra load onto the already overloaded node, the other nodes and the network.
  5. The situation gets worse, and it can turn into a cascading failure, where one failure triggers the next.
Key idea

Rebalancing is expensive and can surprise you. For that reason, it can be a good idea to keep a human in the loop. The process is slower than a fully automatic one, but it helps prevent operational surprises.

Request Routing

The dataset is now partitioned across many nodes on many machines. One question remains. When a client wants to make a request, how does it know which node to connect to? As partitions are rebalanced, the assignment of partitions to nodes changes. Someone has to keep track of those changes so that the answer to the question is always right. If I want to read or write the key “foo,” which IP address and port number should I connect to?

This is an instance of a more general problem called service discovery, which is not limited to databases. Any software that is reachable over a network has this problem, especially if it runs in a redundant setup on several machines for high availability. Many companies have written their own service discovery tools, and many of these have been released as open source.

At a high level there are three approaches, shown in the book’s Figure 6-7:

  1. Any node. Clients may contact any node, for example through a round-robin load balancer, which hands each request to the next server in turn. If that node happens to own the right partition, it handles the request directly. If not, it forwards the request to the right node, receives the reply, and passes it back to the client.
  2. A routing tier. All requests go first to a routing tier. This tier works out which node should handle each request and forwards it. It does not handle any requests itself. It is simply a partition-aware load balancer.
  3. Client awareness. The client knows how the data is partitioned and which node holds which partition. It connects directly to the right node, with no intermediary.

In every case, the central problem is this: how does the component making the routing decision, whether that is a node, the routing tier or the client, learn about changes in the assignment of partitions to nodes?

This is hard, because all the participants must agree. If they disagree, requests get sent to the wrong nodes and are not handled correctly. There are protocols for reaching agreement in a distributed system, but they are difficult to implement correctly. Chapter 9 covers them.

Many distributed data systems use a separate coordination service, such as ZooKeeper, to keep track of this cluster metadata (information about the cluster’s layout). Each node registers itself in ZooKeeper. ZooKeeper keeps the authoritative mapping of partitions to nodes. Other actors, such as the routing tier or a partition-aware client, subscribe to this information. Whenever a partition changes owner, or a node is added or removed, ZooKeeper notifies the routing tier so it can update its routing information. The book shows this as Figure 6-8.

LinkedIn’s Espresso uses Helix for cluster management, and Helix in turn relies on ZooKeeper. Espresso implements a routing tier on top of that. HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka also use ZooKeeper to track partition assignment. MongoDB has a similar architecture, but it uses its own config server implementation, with mongos daemons as the routing tier.

Cassandra and Riak take a different approach. They use a gossip protocol, in which nodes pass cluster-state information among themselves, to spread any changes. A request can be sent to any node, and that node forwards it to the right node for the requested partition. This is the first approach in the list above. It puts more complexity in the database nodes, but it avoids depending on an external coordination service such as ZooKeeper.

Couchbase does not rebalance automatically, which simplifies its design. It is normally set up with a routing tier called moxi, which learns about routing changes from the cluster nodes.

Clients still need the IP addresses to connect to, whether they use a routing tier or send requests to a random node. Those addresses change far less often than the assignment of partitions to nodes. So it is usually enough to use DNS, the domain name system, to look them up.

Trade-offs
Routing approachGood atCosts
Any node, with forwardingClients stay simple, and any node can be contacted.Extra network hop when the node does not own the partition. More logic inside every database node.
Routing tierClients stay simple, and routing logic is kept in one place.Another component to run. It adds a hop, and it must learn about every change.
Client-aware routingNo intermediary, so the fewest hops.Every client must track partition changes, which makes clients more complex.

While a partition is being moved, routing has to follow the rule from the rebalancing section. Requests keep going to the old owner until the transfer is finished. Only then does the routing information change. Figure 6-7 shows the routing options; the diagram below shows how a rebalance moves partitions while the routing rule stays in force.

Parallel Query Execution

So far the chapter has focused on simple queries that read or write a single key, plus scatter/gather queries for document-partitioned secondary indexes. That is about the level of access that most NoSQL distributed datastores support.

Massively parallel processing (MPP) relational databases, which are often used for analytics, are much more sophisticated about the queries they support. A typical data warehouse query contains several joins (combining rows from several tables), filters, groupings and aggregations (such as totals or averages). The MPP query optimizer, the part that plans how a query runs, breaks such a query into stages and partitions. Many of these can run in parallel on different nodes of the cluster. Queries that scan large parts of the dataset benefit especially from this kind of parallel execution.

Fast parallel execution of data warehouse queries is a specialized topic, and because analytics matters so much to businesses, it attracts a lot of commercial interest. The book discusses some techniques for parallel query execution in Chapter 10. For a more detailed overview of parallel databases, it points to its references.

Summary

Summary
  • Why partition. Partitioning is needed when there is so much data that storing and processing it on one machine is no longer feasible. The goal is to spread data and query load evenly across machines and avoid hot spots, which are nodes with disproportionately high load. That takes a partitioning scheme that suits your data, plus rebalancing when nodes join or leave.
  • Key range partitioning. Keys are sorted, and a partition owns all the keys from some minimum up to some maximum. Sorting allows efficient range queries. The risk is hot spots if the application often reads or writes keys that are close together in the sorted order. These partitions are usually rebalanced dynamically, by splitting a range in two when a partition gets too big.
  • Hash partitioning. A hash function is applied to each key, and a partition owns a range of hash values. This destroys the ordering of keys, so range queries become inefficient, but load may be spread more evenly. When hashing, it is common to create a fixed number of partitions up front, assign several to each node, and move whole partitions when nodes come and go. Dynamic partitioning also works.
  • Hybrid. A compound key can combine the two, using one part of the key to pick the partition and another part for sort order.
  • Document-partitioned (local) secondary indexes. Each index is stored in the same partition as the primary key and value it describes. A write updates only one partition, but a read of the index needs scatter/gather across all partitions.
  • Term-partitioned (global) secondary indexes. The index is partitioned by the indexed values. One index entry may point to records from all partitions of the primary key. A write may update several index partitions, but a read can be served from a single partition.
  • Request routing. Ways to route a query to the right partition range from simple partition-aware load balancing to sophisticated parallel query engines. Clients, routing tiers and nodes all need current knowledge of which node owns which partition, often supplied by a coordination service such as ZooKeeper or by a gossip protocol.
  • Independence and its limits. Each partition operates mostly independently, and that is what lets a partitioned database scale across machines. But operations that must write to several partitions are harder to reason about. For example, what happens if the write to one partition succeeds and the write to another fails? The following chapters address that question.

The chapter ends with a numbered list of 33 references to papers, books and online articles, which this retelling does not repeat.

Check yourself

  1. A sensor database uses timestamps as keys with range partitioning by day. Why do writes pile up on one partition, and what change does the book suggest?

    Show answer

    Every new reading has today’s timestamp, so all writes go to today’s partition while the others sit idle. The book suggests putting the sensor name before the timestamp, which spreads writes across sensors. The cost is a separate range query for each sensor when you read several of them.

  2. Hashing spreads keys evenly, yet a celebrity’s post still overloads one partition. Why does hashing not help, and what can the application do?

    Show answer

    All writes to the same key produce the same hash, so they still land on one partition. The application can append a random number, such as two digits for 100 keys, to split the writes. Reads must then fetch all 100 keys and combine them, and the app must track which keys are split.

  3. A site mostly reads “all red cars” and can accept slower writes. Should its secondary index be document-partitioned or term-partitioned, and why?

    Show answer

    Term-partitioned. A term-partitioned index lets a read go to one partition, so it is cheap. Its writes are slower and touch several index partitions, and updates are often asynchronous. A document-partitioned index would need scatter/gather across all partitions for every red-car search.

  4. With hash mod N, what goes wrong when a cluster grows from 10 to 11 nodes, and what does a fixed number of partitions change?

    Show answer

    When N changes, most keys move to a different node. The book’s example key moves from node 6 to node 3. With a fixed number of partitions, keys always map to the same partition. Only whole partitions move between nodes, and the key-to-partition mapping never changes.

Part II · Chapter 7

Transactions

The big idea: a transaction groups several reads and writes into one all-or-nothing unit. Its isolation level decides how much of other clients’ activity you have to handle yourself. Stronger isolation costs performance, and weaker isolation leaves some race conditions for the application to solve.

The chapter opens with a 2012 paper from Google about its Spanner database. Some people have argued that full two-phase commit (a protocol that makes several machines commit together, covered in Chapter 9) is too expensive to support. The Spanner authors took the other side. It is better, they argued, to let programmers deal with slowdowns caused by heavy transaction use as they appear, “rather than always coding around the lack of transactions.”

Data systems can go wrong in many ways:

  • The database software or hardware can fail at any time, including in the middle of a write.
  • The application can crash at any time, including halfway through a series of operations.
  • The network can cut the application off from the database, or one database node off from another.
  • Several clients can write at the same time and overwrite each other’s changes.
  • A client can read data that does not make sense because it was only partly updated.
  • Race conditions between clients, where the result depends on the exact timing of their steps, can cause surprising bugs.

A reliable system has to handle these faults so that they do not bring the whole system down. But fault handling is a lot of work. You have to think through everything that can go wrong, and then test that your solution really works.

For decades, transactions have been the main way to simplify this. A transaction lets an application group several reads and writes into one logical unit. Conceptually, all of them run as one operation. Either the whole transaction succeeds, which is called a commit, or it fails, which is called an abort (or a rollback), and none of its writes are kept. If a transaction aborts, the application can safely try again. Error handling also gets much simpler, because the application does not have to deal with partial failure. That is the case where some operations succeed and others fail.

Transactions are not a law of nature. People created them to simplify the programming model. Because the database takes care of certain errors and concurrency problems, the application is free to ignore them. The book calls these promises safety guarantees.

Not every application needs transactions. Sometimes it is worth weakening the guarantees, or dropping them, for higher performance or availability. Some safety properties can also be achieved without transactions. So the real question is which guarantees you need, and what each one costs. To answer it, you need to know exactly what transactions promise, even in bad circumstances.

This chapter looks at many things that can go wrong, and at the algorithms databases use to guard against them. It goes deep into concurrency control, which is how a database handles several clients using the same data at the same time. It covers race conditions such as dirty reads, lost updates, write skew, and phantoms, and it explains isolation levels such as read committed, snapshot isolation, and serializability. The material applies to single-node and distributed databases alike. Chapter 8 covers the extra problems that only distributed systems have.

The Slippery Concept of a Transaction

Almost all relational databases today support transactions, and so do some nonrelational ones. Most follow a style introduced in 1975 by IBM System R, the first SQL database. Some details have changed since then, but the basic idea has stayed almost the same for forty years. The transaction support in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server is strikingly similar to System R’s.

In the late 2000s, nonrelational databases, often called NoSQL, became popular. They offered new data models (see Chapter 2), and they included replication (keeping copies of data on several machines) and partitioning (splitting data across machines) by default. Transactions were the main casualty. Many of these new databases dropped transactions entirely, or redefined the word to mean a much weaker set of guarantees.

A popular belief grew up with these systems. Transactions were seen as the opposite of scalability, and it was assumed that any large system must give them up to get good performance and high availability. Database vendors, on the other side, often presented transactions as an essential feature for serious applications that hold valuable data. The book says both views are exaggerated. Transactions have advantages and limits, like any design choice, and the rest of the chapter explains both.

The Meaning of ACID

The safety guarantees that transactions provide are described by the acronym ACID. It stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter coined the term in 1983, trying to create precise words for fault-tolerance mechanisms in databases.

In practice, each database implements ACID in its own way, so two “ACID” systems can behave differently. Isolation in particular is full of ambiguity. The high-level idea is sound, but the details matter. When a vendor says its system is ACID compliant, it is unclear what you can actually expect. The book says ACID has mostly become a marketing term.

Systems that are not ACID are sometimes called BASE, which stands for Basically Available, Soft state, and Eventual consistency. The book points out that BASE is even vaguer than ACID. The only sensible definition of BASE is that it means not ACID, which can mean almost anything.

Let’s look at each letter in turn, because that will sharpen the idea of a transaction.

Atomicity. In everyday computing, “atomic” means something that cannot be broken into smaller parts. In multi-threaded programming, an atomic operation means that no other thread can see it half finished. In ACID, atomicity means something different. It is not about concurrency. It describes what happens when a fault strikes partway through a set of writes. A process may crash, a network connection may drop, a disk may fill up, or a constraint may be violated. If the writes were grouped into an atomic transaction, and the transaction cannot commit, then the database aborts it and undoes every write it had already made.

Without atomicity, an error in the middle of several changes leaves you guessing which changes took effect. Retrying might make the same change twice and create duplicate or wrong data. With atomicity, an aborted transaction changed nothing, so the application can retry it safely. Being able to abort a transaction and discard all its writes is the defining feature of ACID atomicity. The book admits that abortability would have been a more accurate name, but atomicity is the word everyone uses. The multi-threaded sense of atomic is covered by isolation, which is the next letter.

Consistency. The word consistency is badly overloaded. The book lists four meanings. Chapter 5 uses it for replicas that agree, and for eventual consistency when copies update asynchronously. Chapter 6 uses consistent hashing, a partitioning method for rebalancing. The CAP theorem (Chapter 9) uses consistency to mean linearizability, a strict rule about how recent a read must be. In ACID, consistency means something else: the database is in a good state according to rules the application defines.

Those rules are called invariants, which are statements about the data that must always be true. In an accounting system, for example, the credits and debits across all accounts must balance. If a transaction starts with a database that obeys the invariants, and every write in the transaction keeps it valid, the invariants still hold at the end. However, the database cannot know your invariants. It can check some of them, such as foreign key or uniqueness constraints, but otherwise it stores whatever the application writes. The application has to define its transactions correctly.

So the book makes a sharp point. Atomicity, isolation, and durability are properties of the database. Consistency in the ACID sense is a property of the application, which relies on the database’s atomicity and isolation to achieve it. That is why the book says the letter C does not really belong in ACID. Joe Hellerstein has remarked that the C was added to make the acronym work, and it was not considered important at the time.

Isolation. Most databases are used by several clients at once. That is no problem when they read and write different parts of the database. It becomes a problem when they touch the same records, because then you can get race conditions. Here is a simple one.

Example

Two clients increment a counter that is stored in the database. The database has no built-in increment, so each client must read the current value, add 1, and write the new value back. The counter starts at 42, and two increments should bring it to 44. Here is what can happen, step by step:

  1. Client 1 reads the counter and gets 42.
  2. Client 2 reads the counter before client 1 has written anything, and it also gets 42.
  3. Client 1 adds 1 and writes 43.
  4. Client 2 adds 1 to its copy of 42, which gives 43, and writes 43. Its write replaces client 1’s write.

Two increments happened, but the counter reads 43 instead of 44. The book’s Figure 7-1 shows this race, and a simplified version appears below.

Isolation, in the ACID sense, means that concurrently running transactions cannot step on each other’s toes. The classic database textbooks formalize isolation as serializability. Each transaction behaves as if it were the only transaction running on the database. When the transactions have committed, the result is the same as if they had run one after another, even though in reality they may have overlapped.

In practice, serializable isolation is rarely used, because it has a performance cost. Some popular databases, such as Oracle 11g, do not implement it at all. Oracle does have an isolation level named “serializable,” but what it actually provides is snapshot isolation, a weaker guarantee. The book explores snapshot isolation and other weaker levels later in the chapter.

Durability. A database is supposed to be a safe place to keep data. Durability is the promise that once a transaction has committed, its data will not be forgotten, even after a hardware fault or a crash.

On a single node, durability usually means the data has been written to nonvolatile storage, such as a hard drive or SSD (storage that keeps data when power is off). It also usually involves a write-ahead log, which is a log of changes written before the main data structures are changed. The log allows recovery if the data on disk is corrupted. In a replicated database, durability may mean that the data has been copied to some number of nodes. The database must wait until those writes or copies finish before it reports the transaction as committed.

The book reminds us that perfect durability does not exist. If all your hard disks and all your backups were destroyed at the same time, nothing the database could do would save your data.

Replication and durability. Historically, durability meant writing to an archive tape. Later it meant writing to a disk or SSD, and more recently it has come to mean replication. Which is best? The book says nothing is perfect:

  • If you write to a disk and the machine dies, the data is safe but unreachable until you fix the machine or move the disk to another one. A replicated system can stay available.
  • A correlated fault, such as a power outage or a bug that crashes every node on the same input, can knock out all replicas at once. Anything that exists only in memory is lost. So writing to disk still matters for in-memory databases.
  • In an asynchronously replicated system, the most recent writes may be lost when the leader (the node that accepts writes) fails. Chapter 5 covers this.
  • SSDs have been shown to break their guarantees when power is cut suddenly. Even the fsync call, which asks the operating system to flush data to disk, is not always reliable. Disk firmware can have bugs too.
  • Subtle interactions between the storage engine and the filesystem can cause bugs that are hard to track down, and can corrupt files after a crash.
  • Data on disk can gradually become corrupted without anyone noticing. If so, replicas and recent backups may be corrupted as well, and you may have to restore from an older backup.
  • One study found that between 30 and 80 percent of SSDs develop at least one bad block during their first four years. Magnetic hard drives have fewer bad sectors but fail completely more often.
  • An SSD that is left unpowered can start losing data within a few weeks, depending on the temperature.

In practice, no single technique gives absolute guarantees. There are only risk-reduction techniques, including writing to disk, replicating to remote machines, and keeping backups. They should be used together. The book’s advice is to take any theoretical guarantee with a healthy grain of salt.

Single-Object and Multi-Object Operations

To recap, atomicity and isolation describe what the database should do when a client makes several writes in one transaction. Atomicity means that if an error happens halfway through, the transaction is aborted and the writes made so far are discarded. You do not have to worry about partial failure, because you get an all-or-nothing guarantee. Isolation means that concurrently running transactions should not interfere. If one transaction makes several writes, another transaction should see either all of them or none of them, never a subset.

These definitions assume you want to change several objects (rows, documents, or records) at once. Such multi-object transactions are often needed when several pieces of data must stay in sync. Here is an example from an email application.

Example

To show the number of unread messages for a user, you could count them with a query. But if the user has many emails, that query may be too slow. So you decide to store the unread count in a separate field, a kind of denormalization (storing the same information twice to make reads faster). Now every new message must also increment the counter, and every message marked as read must decrement it.

In the book’s Figure 7-2, user 2 sees a problem. The mailbox listing shows an unread message, but the counter still shows zero, because the counter update has not happened yet. Isolation would prevent this. User 2 would see either both the new email and the updated counter, or neither, never a halfway point. The book notes that a wrong counter is not a critical problem in an email app, but the same pattern with a customer’s account balance and a payment would matter a lot.

Figure 7-3 in the book shows why atomicity matters here. If an error occurs somewhere during the transaction, the mailbox and the unread counter can get out of sync. In an atomic transaction, if the counter update fails, the whole transaction is aborted, and the inserted email is rolled back.

Multi-object transactions need a way to decide which reads and writes belong together. In relational databases, this is usually done with the client’s TCP connection, the network link to the database server. On one connection, everything between a BEGIN TRANSACTION and a COMMIT counts as one transaction. The book says this is not ideal. If the connection is interrupted, the transaction must be aborted. If the interruption happens after the client asks for a commit but before the server confirms it, the client cannot know whether the transaction was committed. A transaction manager could instead group operations by a unique transaction identifier that is not tied to any one connection. The book returns to this idea later.

Many nonrelational databases have no way to group operations at all. Some offer a multi-put that updates several keys in one call. But that does not necessarily mean it is a transaction. The call may succeed for some keys and fail for others, leaving the database partly updated.

Single-object writes. Atomicity and isolation also matter when you change a single object. Imagine writing a 20 KB JSON document to a database. Several things could go wrong:

  • If the network drops after the first 10 KB, does the database store that unparseable fragment?
  • If power fails while the database is overwriting the old value on disk, do the old and new values end up spliced together?
  • If another client reads the document while the write is in progress, does it see a partly updated value?

These issues would be very confusing, so storage engines almost always aim to give atomicity and isolation for a single object, such as one key-value pair, on one node. Atomicity usually comes from a log used for crash recovery. Isolation usually comes from a lock on each object, which allows only one thread to access the object at a time.

Some databases also offer more complex single-object operations. An atomic increment removes the need for a read-modify-write cycle like the one in the counter example. A compare-and-set operation writes a new value only if the current value has not changed since you last read it. Both are useful for preventing lost updates, which we will return to shortly. However, they are not transactions in the usual sense. A transaction groups operations on multiple objects into one unit. Some vendors have used marketing labels for single-object operations, such as lightweight transactions, and the book considers that terminology misleading.

Strictly speaking, the word atomic in “atomic increment” uses the multi-threaded meaning. In the ACID sense, it should be called an isolated or serializable increment. The book admits this is a nitpick.

The need for multi-object transactions

Many distributed datastores have abandoned multi-object transactions. They are hard to build across partitions, and they can get in the way when very high availability or performance is needed. But nothing fundamentally prevents transactions in a distributed database, and Chapter 9 discusses how they can be built.
