Could an application work with only a key-value model and single-object operations? Some can. But in many cases, writes to several objects must be coordinated:

  • Relational data. A row in one table often holds a foreign key (a reference) to a row in another table. In a graph-like model, a vertex has edges to other vertices. Multi-object transactions keep these references valid. If you insert several records that refer to each other, the references must be correct, or the data becomes nonsense.
  • Document data. Fields that change together are often in the same document, and updating one document is a single-object write, so it needs no multi-object transaction. But document databases without joins encourage denormalization, which means the same information is copied into several documents. When that information changes, several documents must be updated together, and transactions stop the copies from going out of sync.
  • Secondary indexes. In a database with secondary indexes (an extra lookup structure built on a field other than the main key), almost every change must update the index too. From a transaction point of view, each index is a separate object. Without isolation, a record can appear in one index but not in another while the second update is still pending.

Applications like these can be built without transactions. But error handling becomes much harder without atomicity, and concurrency problems appear without isolation. The book discusses weak isolation next, and it looks at alternative approaches in Chapter 12.

Handling errors and aborts

A key feature of a transaction is that it can be aborted and safely retried after an error. ACID databases follow this philosophy. If the database is in danger of violating atomicity, isolation, or durability, it would rather abandon the transaction entirely than leave it half finished.

Not all systems follow that rule. Datastores with leaderless replication (Chapter 5) work on a best effort basis. The database will do as much as it can, and if it hits an error, it will not undo what it has already done. Recovering from errors is then the application’s job.

Many developers prefer to think only about the happy path, not the details of error handling. Popular object-relational mapping (ORM) frameworks, such as Rails’s ActiveRecord and Django, do not retry aborted transactions. An error usually becomes an exception that bubbles up the program, so the user’s input is thrown away and they see an error message. The book calls this a shame, because the whole point of aborts is to enable safe retries.

Retrying an aborted transaction is simple and effective, but it has limits:

  • If the transaction actually succeeded, but the network failed while the server was sending its confirmation, the client thinks it failed. Retrying then performs the transaction twice, unless you have an extra deduplication mechanism at the application level.
  • If the error was caused by overload, retrying adds more load and makes the problem worse. To avoid this feedback cycle, limit the number of retries, use exponential backoff (waiting longer after each failed attempt), and handle overload errors differently from other errors where you can.
  • Retry only after transient errors, such as a deadlock, an isolation violation, a temporary network problem, or a failover (switching to a backup node). After a permanent error, such as a constraint violation, a retry is pointless.
  • If the transaction also has side effects outside the database, those may happen even if the transaction aborts. For example, you would not want to send an email again on every retry. If several systems must commit or abort together, two-phase commit can help, and Chapter 9 discusses it.
  • If the client process crashes while retrying, any data it was trying to write is lost.

Weak Isolation Levels

If two transactions do not touch the same data, they can safely run in parallel, because neither depends on the other. Concurrency problems only arise when one transaction reads data that another is changing, or when two transactions try to change the same data at the same time.

Concurrency bugs are hard to find by testing. They only appear when timing goes wrong, which may happen rarely and be difficult to reproduce. Concurrency is also hard to reason about, especially in a large application where you may not know which other code touches the database. Even with only one user at a time, development is hard. With many users, any piece of data could change at any moment.

For that reason, databases have long tried to hide concurrency issues by providing transaction isolation. In theory, serializable isolation lets you pretend that no concurrency is happening. The database guarantees that transactions have the same effect as if they ran one at a time.

In practice, serializable isolation has a performance cost, and many databases do not want to pay it. So it is common for systems to use weaker levels of isolation. These protect against some concurrency problems but not all. They are much harder to understand, and they can lead to subtle bugs. Even so, they are widely used.

Concurrency bugs caused by weak isolation are not just theoretical. They have caused substantial loss of money, led to investigations by financial auditors, and corrupted customer data. A common reaction is to say that financial data should only be handled by an ACID database. The book says that misses the point. Many popular relational databases, which are usually called ACID, use weak isolation by default, so they would not necessarily have prevented these bugs. Instead of trusting a label, we need to understand the kinds of concurrency problems that exist and how to prevent them.

The rest of this section looks at several weak isolation levels used in practice. It discusses which race conditions each one allows and which it blocks, so you can choose the right level for your application. It explains serializability in detail after that. The discussion is informal and uses examples. Rigorous definitions are in the academic literature.

Read Committed

The most basic level of transaction isolation is read committed. It makes two guarantees:

  1. When you read from the database, you see only committed data. This means no dirty reads.
  2. When you write to the database, you overwrite only committed data. This means no dirty writes.

Some databases also support an even weaker level called read uncommitted. It prevents dirty writes but does not prevent dirty reads.

No dirty reads. Suppose a transaction has written some data but has not yet committed or aborted. If another transaction can see that uncommitted data, it is called a dirty read. Transactions at the read committed level must prevent dirty reads. Any writes a transaction makes become visible to others only when it commits, and then all of its writes become visible at once. The book’s Figure 7-4 shows this. User 1 has set x to 3, but user 2 still gets the old value, 2, because user 1 has not committed yet.

The book gives two reasons why preventing dirty reads is useful:

  • If a transaction updates several objects, a dirty read lets another transaction see some of the updates but not others. In Figure 7-2, the user sees the new unread email but not the updated counter. A partly updated database is confusing for users, and it can push other transactions into wrong decisions.
  • If a transaction aborts, its writes must be rolled back, as in Figure 7-3. If the database allowed dirty reads, another transaction might have read data that was later rolled back and never committed. Reasoning about the consequences quickly becomes mind-bending.

No dirty writes. What happens when two transactions try to update the same object at once? The order of the writes is not known, but normally the later write overwrites the earlier one. A dirty write is different. It happens when the later write overwrites a value written by a transaction that has not yet committed. Read committed prevents this, usually by delaying the second write until the first transaction commits or aborts.

Example

Think of a used car site where Alice and Bob try to buy the same car at the same moment. Buying the car takes two writes. The listing must be updated to show the buyer, and the sales invoice must be sent to the buyer. Dirty writes can mix up these two writes:

  1. Alice’s transaction writes her name to the listing. It has not committed yet.
  2. Bob’s transaction overwrites the listing with his name, before Alice’s transaction has finished. This is a dirty write.
  3. Bob’s transaction writes the sales invoice for Bob.
  4. Alice’s transaction writes the sales invoice for Alice, and it is the last invoice write.

The listing now shows Bob as the buyer, but the invoice goes to Alice. Each of the two writes was the winner of a different table.

The book’s Figure 7-5 shows this mix-up. Read committed prevents it, because the second write waits until the first transaction has committed or aborted.

Read committed does not prevent the counter race from earlier, though. In that case the second write happens after the first transaction has committed, so it is not a dirty write. It is still wrong, but for a different reason. The section on preventing lost updates covers how to make such counter increments safe.

Implementing read committed. Read committed is a very popular isolation level. It is the default in Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012, MemSQL, and many other databases. Most often, databases prevent dirty writes with row-level locks. A lock is a claim that stops others from using the same thing. When a transaction wants to modify a row or document, it must first acquire a lock on it, and hold the lock until it commits or aborts. Only one transaction can hold the lock at a time. If another transaction wants to write to the same object, it must wait. Databases do this automatically in read committed mode and stronger modes.

Preventing dirty reads could use the same kind of lock. A reader would briefly acquire the lock and release it right after reading. But the book says this approach does not work well in practice. One long-running write transaction could force many read-only transactions to wait until it finishes. That slows read-only work and makes the system harder to operate, because a slowdown in one part of an application can spread to another part through lock waiting.

So most databases prevent dirty reads in a different way. For each object being written, the database remembers two values: the old committed value and the new value set by the transaction that currently holds the write lock. While the transaction is ongoing, other transactions that read the object are simply given the old value. Only when the new value is committed do readers switch to it. The book says the only mainstream databases that still use locks for read committed are IBM DB2, and SQL Server with read_committed_snapshot switched off.

Snapshot Isolation and Repeatable Read

Read committed looks like it does everything a transaction needs. It allows aborts, which atomicity requires. It prevents reading the incomplete results of other transactions. It prevents concurrent writes from getting mixed together. Those are useful features, and much stronger than what you get from a system with no transactions at all.

But concurrency bugs can still happen at this level. Figure 7-6 in the book shows one of them, called read skew.

Example

Alice has $1,000 of savings at a bank, split across two accounts with $500 each. A transaction then moves $100 from one account to the other. If Alice looks at her balances at the same moment that transfer is running, she can see a mix of before and after. The book does not say which account is which, but the numbers only add up if she reads the receiving account first. Here is one way it can happen:

  1. Alice reads the receiving account. It shows $500, because the incoming payment has not arrived yet.
  2. The transfer commits. $100 moves out of the other account and into the receiving account.
  3. Alice reads the other account. It shows $400, because the outgoing transfer has been made.
  4. Alice has now seen $900 in total. It looks as though $100 has vanished into thin air.

If Alice read the receiving account again at the end of the transaction, she would see $600. That is why this anomaly is called a nonrepeatable read, or read skew. Each balance she saw had been committed at the time she read it, so read committed allows this. The book notes that the word skew is overloaded. Earlier in the book it means an unbalanced workload with hot spots, but here it means a timing anomaly.

For Alice, this is not a lasting problem. She will probably see consistent balances if she reloads the page a few seconds later. But some situations cannot tolerate even temporary inconsistency:

  • Backups. A backup copies the entire database, which may take hours on a large database. Writes keep arriving during the copy, so some parts of the backup hold older data and other parts hold newer data. If you restore from that backup, inconsistencies such as the disappearing money become permanent.
  • Analytic queries and integrity checks. Some queries scan large parts of the database, for analytics or for a periodic check that the data is not corrupted. If they see different parts of the database at different points in time, their results are likely to be nonsense.

Snapshot isolation is the most common solution to this problem. The idea is that each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database. The transaction sees all the data that was committed at the moment it started. Even if other transactions change the data afterward, this transaction keeps seeing the old data from that point in time. Snapshot isolation is a boon for long-running, read-only queries such as backups and analytics, because a query is much easier to reason about when the data it reads is frozen. Snapshot isolation is supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL with the InnoDB storage engine, Oracle, SQL Server, and others.

Implementing snapshot isolation. Like read committed, snapshot isolation usually uses write locks to prevent dirty writes. That means a transaction that writes can block another transaction that writes to the same object. Reads, however, need no locks at all. The key principle is that readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. A long-running read query can work on a consistent snapshot while normal writes continue, with no lock contention between them.

To make this work, the database must keep several committed versions of an object, because different in-progress transactions may need to see the state at different points in time. Because it keeps several versions side by side, this technique is called multi-version concurrency control, or MVCC. Storage engines that support snapshot isolation usually use MVCC for read committed as well. The difference is that read committed takes a fresh snapshot for each query, while snapshot isolation uses the same snapshot for the whole transaction.

The book walks through how PostgreSQL does this. When a transaction starts, it is given a unique, ever-increasing transaction ID, called a txid. Whenever a transaction writes anything, the data it writes is tagged with its own txid. (The book notes that txids are 32-bit numbers, so they wrap around after about four billion transactions. PostgreSQL’s vacuum process cleans up old data so the wrap-around does not cause errors.)

Each row in a table records two extra fields. The created_by field holds the txid of the transaction that inserted the row. The deleted_by field is empty at first. When a transaction deletes a row, the row is not removed right away. It is marked for deletion by setting deleted_by to the deleting transaction’s txid. Later, when no transaction can still access the old data, a garbage collection process removes such rows and frees their space.

An update is handled as a delete followed by a create. The book’s example is transaction 13, which deducts $100 from account 2, changing its balance from $500 to $400. After that, the accounts table contains two rows for account 2. One row holds $500 and is marked as deleted by transaction 13. The other holds $400 and was created by transaction 13. The figure below shows these two versions.

Visibility rules. When a transaction reads from the database, the transaction IDs decide which object versions it can see. Clear visibility rules let the database present a consistent snapshot to the application. The rules work like this:

  1. At the start of each transaction, the database makes a list of all other transactions that are still in progress, meaning not yet committed or aborted. Any writes those transactions have made are ignored, even if they commit later.
  2. Any writes made by aborted transactions are ignored.
  3. Any writes made by a transaction with a later transaction ID, which means one that started after the current transaction, are ignored, whether or not it has committed.
  4. All other writes are visible to the application’s queries.

These rules apply to both creating and deleting objects. Back to transaction 13: when transaction 12 reads account 2, it sees a balance of $500. The deletion of the $500 row was made by transaction 13, and by rule 3, transaction 12 cannot see that deletion. The $400 row was also created by 13, so it is invisible to 12 for the same reason.

Put another way, an object is visible to a reader if two things are true. First, the transaction that created the object had already committed when the reader’s transaction started. Second, the object is not marked for deletion, or if it is, the transaction that requested the deletion had not yet committed when the reader’s transaction started.

A long-running transaction can keep using its snapshot for a long time. It may keep reading values that other transactions overwrote or deleted long ago. Because the database never updates values in place, but creates a new version each time a value changes, it can provide these consistent snapshots at only a small extra cost.

Indexes and snapshot isolation. How do indexes work when there are several versions of each object? One option is for the index to point to all versions of an object. An index query then filters out any versions that are not visible to the current transaction. When garbage collection removes old versions that no transaction can see, the matching index entries can be removed too. Real systems have many optimizations here. For example, PostgreSQL avoids updating indexes when two versions of the same object fit on the same page.

Another approach is used in CouchDB, Datomic, and LMDB. These systems use B-trees (a common on-disk tree structure for indexes), but in an append-only, copy-on-write form. They never overwrite pages of the tree when they are updated. Instead, they create a new copy of each modified page. The parent pages, all the way up to the root, are copied and updated to point to the new child pages. Pages that a write does not touch are not copied, and they stay unchanged. Every write transaction, or batch of them, creates a new tree root, and each root is a consistent snapshot of the database at the moment it was created. This means there is no need to filter objects by transaction ID. The cost is a background process for compaction and garbage collection.

Repeatable read and naming confusion. Snapshot isolation is useful, especially for read-only transactions. But many databases that implement it give it different names. Oracle calls it serializable, while PostgreSQL and MySQL call it repeatable read. The reason is that the SQL standard does not have a concept of snapshot isolation. The standard is based on the 1975 definition of isolation levels in System R, and snapshot isolation was not invented until later. The standard defines a level called repeatable read, which looks superficially similar. PostgreSQL and MySQL call their snapshot isolation level repeatable read, because that lets them claim standards compliance.

The book says the standard’s definition of isolation levels is flawed. It is ambiguous and imprecise, and it is not as independent of implementation as a standard should be. Several databases implement repeatable read, but they differ widely in what they actually guarantee. A formal definition of repeatable read exists in the research literature, but most implementations do not satisfy it. To make matters worse, IBM DB2 uses the name repeatable read to mean serializability. As a result, the book says, nobody really knows what repeatable read means.

Key idea

Snapshot isolation gives each transaction a frozen view of the data, so readers and writers do not block each other. Check the documentation of your database for what its “repeatable read” or “serializable” level really guarantees.

Preventing Lost Updates

So far, the read committed and snapshot isolation levels have been about what a read-only transaction can see while other transactions write. We have mostly ignored what happens when two transactions write concurrently. We have covered dirty writes, which are one type of write-write conflict. There are other kinds of conflicts between writing transactions, and the best known is the lost update problem from the counter example.

A lost update can happen when an application reads a value, changes it in its own code, and writes the new value back. This is called a read-modify-write cycle. If two transactions do this at the same time, one of the changes can be lost, because the second write does not include the first change. The book says the later write clobbers the earlier one. This pattern appears in several scenarios:

  • Incrementing a counter or updating an account balance. You must read the current value, calculate the new one, and write it back.
  • Making a local change to a complex value, such as adding an element to a list inside a JSON document. You must parse the document, change it, and write back the whole thing.
  • Two users editing the same wiki page at once, where each user saves by sending the entire page to the server, overwriting whatever is there.

Because this is such a common problem, several solutions have been developed.

Atomic write operations. Many databases provide atomic update operations. These remove the need for a read-modify-write cycle in application code, and they are usually the best solution if your change can be expressed in terms of them. For example, this instruction is safe against concurrent changes in most relational databases:

UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 WHERE key = 'foo';

Document databases such as MongoDB provide atomic operations for changing part of a JSON document. Redis provides atomic operations on data structures such as priority queues. Not every write can be expressed this way. A wiki edit involves arbitrary text editing, so it does not fit. Where atomic operations do fit, though, they are usually the best choice.

Atomic operations are usually implemented by taking an exclusive lock on the object when it is read, so no other transaction can read it until the update has been applied. This technique is sometimes called cursor stability. Another option is to force all atomic operations onto a single thread. The book warns that object-relational mapping frameworks make it easy to accidentally write unsafe read-modify-write code, instead of using the database’s atomic operations. That is a potential source of subtle bugs that are hard to find by testing.

Explicit locking. If the database’s atomic operations do not provide what you need, the application can lock the objects it is about to update. The application reads, modifies, and writes, and if another transaction tries to read the same object at the same time, that transaction must wait for the first one to finish.

Consider a multiplayer game in which several players can move the same piece. An atomic operation may not be enough, because the application must also check that each move follows the game’s rules. That logic cannot sensibly be written as a database query. So you might use a lock to stop two players from moving the same piece at once, as in this example:

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM figures
WHERE name = 'robot' AND game_id = 222
FOR UPDATE;
-- Check whether move is valid, then update the position
-- of the piece that was returned by the previous SELECT.
UPDATE figures SET position = 'c4' WHERE id = 1234;
COMMIT;

The FOR UPDATE clause tells the database to take a lock on all the rows returned by the query. This works, but you have to think carefully about your application logic. It is easy to forget to add a necessary lock somewhere in the code, and that creates a race condition.

Automatically detecting lost updates. Atomic operations and locks prevent lost updates by forcing read-modify-write cycles to run one after another. There is another option. Let the cycles run in parallel, and have the transaction manager detect a lost update. If it does, it aborts the offending transaction, and the application retries its read-modify-write cycle.

This check is efficient when combined with snapshot isolation. PostgreSQL’s repeatable read, Oracle’s serializable level, and SQL Server’s snapshot isolation level all detect lost updates automatically and abort the offending transaction. MySQL with InnoDB, however, does not detect lost updates at its repeatable read level. Some authors argue that a database must prevent lost updates to count as providing snapshot isolation, so under that definition MySQL does not provide it. The advantage of automatic detection is that application code does not need any special database feature. You can forget a lock or an atomic operation and introduce a bug, but automatic detection happens anyway, so it is less error-prone.

Compare-and-set. In databases that do not provide full transactions, you will sometimes find an atomic compare-and-set operation. Its purpose is to avoid lost updates by allowing a change only if the value has not changed since you last read it. If the current value no longer matches what you read, the update has no effect, and the read-modify-write cycle must be retried.

For example, to stop two users from overwriting each other’s edits of a wiki page, you might write:

-- This may or may not be safe, depending on the database implementation
UPDATE wiki_pages SET content = 'new content'
WHERE id = 1234 AND content = 'old content';

If the content has changed, the update does nothing, so you must check whether it took effect and retry if needed. But if the database lets the WHERE clause read from an old snapshot, the statement may not prevent lost updates, because the condition can still be true while another write is happening. Check whether your database’s compare-and-set is safe before relying on it.

Conflict resolution and replication. In replicated databases, preventing lost updates has another dimension. Copies of the data sit on several nodes, and the same data can be changed on different nodes at the same time. Locks and compare-and-set assume there is a single up-to-date copy of the data. Multi-leader and leaderless databases usually allow several concurrent writes and replicate them asynchronously. They cannot guarantee a single up-to-date copy, so lock-based and compare-and-set techniques do not apply. (The book revisits this in its discussion of linearizability.)

Instead, as discussed in Chapter 5, a common approach is to allow concurrent writes to create several conflicting versions of a value, called siblings. Application code or special data structures then resolve and merge those versions afterward. Atomic operations can work well in a replicated setting, especially if they are commutative. That means you can apply them in a different order on different replicas and still get the same result. Incrementing a counter and adding an element to a set are both commutative. This is the idea behind the datatypes in Riak 2.0, which prevent lost updates across replicas by merging concurrent updates so that none are lost.

By contrast, the last write wins (LWW) conflict resolution method is prone to lost updates, as Chapter 5 discussed. LWW is the default in many replicated databases, which makes this a real trap.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
Atomic operations (such as value = value + 1)Simple and fast, with no application locks. Good for counters and changes to one value.Only works when your change fits the operation. ORMs can bypass it without anyone noticing.
Explicit locking (such as SELECT FOR UPDATE)Works for any logic, including game rules that cannot be written as queries.Easy to forget a lock. Transactions wait on each other, which slows things down.
Automatic lost update detectionNo special application code. Less error-prone, because the check runs for every update.Available only in some databases. Aborted work must be retried. MySQL’s repeatable read does not detect it.
Compare-and-setA lightweight check when the database has no full transactions.Only safe if the database’s check reads current data. Needs a retry loop.
Commutative merges in replicated databasesConcurrent updates on different replicas combine without losing any.Needs datatypes designed for merging, such as counters and sets. Last write wins loses data.

Write Skew and Phantoms

Dirty writes and lost updates are race conditions where concurrent transactions write to the same object. Several subtler race conditions also exist. The book introduces one with a hospital example.

Imagine you are writing an application for doctors to manage their on-call shifts. The hospital usually has several doctors on call at any time, but it must always have at least one. A doctor may give up a shift, for example because they are sick, but only if a colleague remains on call for that shift.

Example

Alice and Bob are the two doctors on call for a particular shift. Both feel unwell, and both click the button to go off call at about the same time. Here is what happens, step by step (the book’s Figure 7-8):

  1. Alice’s transaction checks whether at least two doctors are on call. The answer is yes, there are two, so it proceeds.
  2. Bob’s transaction runs the same check at the same time. It also sees two doctors, so it proceeds.
  3. Alice’s transaction updates her own record to take herself off call.
  4. Bob’s transaction updates his own record the same way.
  5. Both transactions commit. Now nobody is on call, which breaks the rule that at least one doctor must be on call.

The database uses snapshot isolation, so both checks read a snapshot that showed two doctors. Each transaction acted on that snapshot, and neither noticed the other.

Characterizing write skew. This anomaly is called write skew. It is neither a dirty write nor a lost update, because the two transactions update two different objects, Alice’s record and Bob’s record. The conflict is less obvious, but it is still a race condition. If the two transactions had run one after another, the second doctor would have been stopped. The anomaly was possible only because the transactions ran concurrently.

You can think of write skew as a generalization of the lost update problem. Write skew can happen when two transactions read the same objects, and then each updates some of them. Different transactions may update different objects. If they update the same object, you get a dirty write or a lost update instead, depending on the timing.

There are fewer ways to prevent write skew than lost updates. The book lists these options:

  • Atomic single-object operations do not help, because several objects are involved.
  • Automatic lost update detection does not help either. Write skew is not detected automatically in PostgreSQL’s repeatable read, MySQL’s InnoDB repeatable read, Oracle’s serializable level, or SQL Server’s snapshot isolation level. Preventing it automatically requires true serializable isolation.
  • Some databases let you configure constraints, such as uniqueness, foreign keys, or restrictions on a value, and then enforce them. The rule “at least one doctor on call” involves several objects, and most databases have no built-in constraint for that. You may be able to implement it with triggers or materialized views, depending on the database.
  • If you cannot use serializable isolation, the second-best option is probably to explicitly lock the rows the transaction depends on. For the doctors, you could write:
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM doctors
WHERE on_call = true
AND shift_id = 1234 FOR UPDATE;
UPDATE doctors
SET on_call = false
WHERE name = 'Alice'
AND shift_id = 1234;
COMMIT;

As before, FOR UPDATE tells the database to lock all the rows that the query returns.

Watch out

Snapshot isolation is not serializability. A transaction can read a consistent snapshot and still make a decision that a concurrent transaction has made false. Check each place where code reads data and then writes based on what it read.

More examples of write skew. Write skew may seem like an obscure issue at first, but once you know the pattern, you will notice it in more places. The book gives several examples.

Meeting room booking. Suppose you want to ensure that no meeting room is booked twice at the same time. When someone wants to book a room, you first check for overlapping bookings for that room. If there are none, you create the meeting. The code looks like this:

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
-- Check for any existing bookings that overlap with the period of noon-1pm
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM bookings
WHERE room_id = 123 AND
end_time > '2015-01-01 12:00' AND start_time < '2015-01-01 13:00';
-- If the previous query returned zero:
INSERT INTO bookings
(room_id, start_time, end_time, user_id)
VALUES (123, '2015-01-01 12:00', '2015-01-01 13:00', 666);
COMMIT;

Snapshot isolation does not prevent another user from concurrently inserting a conflicting meeting. To guarantee there are no scheduling conflicts, you once again need serializable isolation. (The book notes that PostgreSQL can do this more elegantly with range types, which are not widely supported elsewhere.)

Multiplayer game. The explicit lock in the earlier game example stops two players from moving the same piece at the same time. But it does not stop two players from moving two different pieces onto the same square, or from making some other move that breaks the game’s rules. Depending on the rule, a unique constraint might help. Otherwise, the game is open to write skew.

Claiming a username. On a site where every user needs a unique username, two people may try to register the same name at the same time. You could use a transaction to check whether the name is taken and, if not, create the account. But that is not safe under snapshot isolation, for the same reason as before. Here, a unique constraint is a simple fix. The second transaction that tries to register the name is aborted because it violates the constraint.

Preventing double-spending. A service that lets users spend money or points must check that a user does not spend more than they have. One way is to insert a tentative spending item into the user’s account, list all the items, and check that the total is still positive. If two spending items are inserted concurrently, they may together make the balance negative, while neither transaction notices the other.

Phantoms causing write skew. All of these examples follow a similar pattern:

  1. A SELECT query checks whether some requirement is met by searching for rows that match a condition. For example, there are at least two doctors on call, or there are no bookings for the room at that time, or the position on the board is empty, or the username is free, or there is enough money.
  2. Based on the result, the application decides how to continue. It may go ahead, or it may report an error and abort.
  3. If the application goes ahead, it makes a write (an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE) and commits.

The write changes the premise of the decision in step 2. If you repeated the SELECT after the write, you would get a different answer, because the write changed the set of rows matching the condition. The steps can also happen in a different order. For example, the write could come first, then the SELECT, and then the transaction could decide whether to commit or abort.

In the doctor example, the row changed in step 3 was one of the rows returned in step 1. So the transaction could be made safe by locking those rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE. The other examples are different. They check for the absence of rows that match a condition, and the write adds a new row that matches the same condition. If the query in step 1 returns no rows, SELECT FOR UPDATE has nothing to lock.

This effect is called a phantom. It happens when a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another transaction. Snapshot isolation avoids phantoms for read-only queries. But in read-write transactions like these, phantoms can lead to tricky write skew. The figure below shows how it happens with the meeting room.

Materializing conflicts. If the problem with phantoms is that there is no object to attach a lock to, perhaps you can create one. For the meeting room, you could make a table of rooms and time slots, with one row for each room and each 15-minute period. You would create these rows ahead of time, for example for the next six months. A booking transaction then locks the rows for the room and time it wants, using SELECT FOR UPDATE. After it has the locks, it can check for overlapping bookings and insert the new booking as before. The extra table does not store booking details. It is purely a set of locks.

This approach is called materializing conflicts, because it takes a phantom and turns it into a lock conflict on a concrete set of rows that exist in the database. But it is hard and error-prone to figure out how to materialize conflicts. It is also ugly to let a concurrency control mechanism leak into your application’s data model. For those reasons, the book says materializing conflicts should be a last resort. A serializable isolation level is much preferable in most cases.

The next figure puts the weak levels side by side. It shows which race conditions each level can still allow, using the examples from this section.

Serializability

This chapter has shown several transactions that are prone to race conditions. Some are prevented by read committed and snapshot isolation, but others are not, and write skew and phantoms are especially tricky. The book describes the situation as sad, for three reasons:

  • Isolation levels are hard to understand, and databases implement them inconsistently. The meaning of “repeatable read” varies a lot from one system to another.
  • If you look at your application code, it is hard to tell whether it is safe at a particular isolation level. This is especially true in a large application, where you may not know everything that runs concurrently.
  • There are no good tools for detecting race conditions. Static analysis might help in principle, but research techniques have not yet become practical. Testing for concurrency problems is hard, because they are nondeterministic and only appear when you get unlucky with timing.

This is not a new problem. It has existed since the 1970s, when weak isolation levels were first introduced. The answer from researchers has always been the same: use serializable isolation.

Serializable isolation is usually regarded as the strongest level. Even though transactions may run in parallel, the end result is the same as if they ran one at a time. If each transaction behaves correctly when run alone, it keeps behaving correctly when run alongside others. In other words, the database prevents all possible race conditions.

If serializable isolation is so much better, why is not everyone using it? To answer that, we need to look at how serializability is implemented and how each approach performs. Most databases that provide serializability today use one of three techniques:

  • Actual serial execution, which runs transactions one at a time in a fixed order.
  • Two-phase locking (2PL), which for several decades was the only viable option.
  • Optimistic concurrency control, in the form of serializable snapshot isolation (SSI).

For now, these techniques are discussed mainly for single-node databases. Chapter 9 looks at how they can be extended to transactions that span multiple nodes.

Actual Serial Execution

The simplest way to avoid concurrency problems is to remove the concurrency altogether. Execute only one transaction at a time, in serial order, on a single thread. This sidesteps the problem of detecting and preventing conflicts, because the resulting isolation is serializable by definition.

It is surprisingly recent that database designers decided this was feasible. Around 2007, they concluded that a single-threaded loop for running transactions could work. For the previous thirty years, multi-threaded concurrency had been considered essential for good performance. Two developments changed that view:

  • RAM became cheap enough that, for many use cases, the entire active dataset fits in memory. When every item a transaction needs is already in memory, transactions run much faster than when they wait for data to load from disk.
  • Designers realized that OLTP (online transaction processing, the many small reads and writes that make up a live application) transactions are usually short and touch only a few records. Long-running analytic queries are usually read-only, so they can run on a consistent snapshot using snapshot isolation, outside the serial execution loop.

Serial execution is used in VoltDB/H-Store, Redis, and Datomic. A system designed for single-threaded execution can sometimes outperform a system that supports concurrency, because it avoids the coordination overhead of locking. But its throughput is limited to that of a single CPU core. To make the most of that one thread, transactions need to be structured differently from the traditional form.

Encapsulating transactions in stored procedures. In the early days of databases, the intention was that one database transaction could cover an entire flow of user activity. Booking an airline ticket is a multi-stage process. You search for routes, fares, and seats. You decide on an itinerary. You book seats on each flight, enter passenger details, and make a payment. It seemed neat for all of that to be one transaction, committed atomically.

But humans are slow to make up their minds and to respond. If a transaction must wait for user input, the database has to support a potentially huge number of open transactions, most of them idle. Most databases cannot do that efficiently. So almost all OLTP applications keep transactions short, avoiding interactive waits inside a transaction. On the web, this means a transaction commits within the same HTTP request (a single request from browser to server). A new request starts a new transaction.

Even with the human removed from the critical path, transactions still usually run in an interactive, client-server style, one statement at a time. The application makes a query, reads the result, perhaps makes another query depending on that result, and so on. Queries and results travel back and forth between the application and the database server, which is often on another machine. A lot of time is spent on that network traffic. If the database handled only one transaction at a time, throughput would be dreadful, because the database would spend most of its time waiting for the application to send the next query. So systems with single-threaded serial execution do not allow interactive multi-statement transactions.

Instead, the application submits the whole transaction code to the database ahead of time, as a stored procedure. A stored procedure is a piece of code that lives inside the database and runs when called. If all the data a transaction needs is in memory, the stored procedure can execute very quickly, without waiting for any network or disk input or output. The figure shows the difference, using the on-call example.

Pros and cons of stored procedures. Stored procedures have existed in relational databases for a long time. They have been part of the SQL standard (SQL/PSM) since 1999. They have a somewhat bad reputation, for several reasons:

  • Each database vendor has its own language, such as PL/SQL for Oracle, T-SQL for SQL Server, and PL/pgSQL for PostgreSQL. These languages have not kept up with general-purpose programming languages. They look archaic, and they lack the library ecosystem that most programming languages have.
  • Code inside a database is harder to manage. Compared with an application server, it is harder to debug, awkward to keep in version control and deploy, trickier to test, and difficult to connect to a metrics system for monitoring.
  • A database is often more sensitive to performance than an application server, because one database instance is shared by many application servers. A badly written stored procedure that uses a lot of memory or CPU time can cause far more trouble than the same mistake in application code.

The book says these problems can be overcome. Modern implementations of stored procedures have abandoned PL/SQL and use general-purpose languages instead. VoltDB uses Java or Groovy, Datomic uses Java or Clojure, and Redis uses Lua. With stored procedures and in-memory data, running all transactions on a single thread becomes practical. Stored procedures avoid waiting for I/O, and they skip the overhead of other concurrency control methods, so they can reach good throughput on one thread.

VoltDB also uses stored procedures for replication. Instead of copying a transaction’s writes from one node to another, it runs the same stored procedure on each replica. This requires the procedures to be deterministic, meaning they produce the same result on every node. If a transaction needs the current date and time, it must get them through special deterministic APIs.

Rule of thumb

When transactions run one at a time, every transaction must be small and fast. One slow transaction stalls all the others, so keep each transaction short and keep its work inside memory.

Partitioning. Running all transactions serially makes concurrency control much simpler. But it limits the transaction throughput of the database to the speed of one CPU core on one machine. Read-only transactions can run elsewhere, using snapshot isolation. But for applications with high write throughput, the single transaction processor can become a serious bottleneck.

To scale across several CPU cores and several nodes, you can partition your data, as Chapter 6 described. VoltDB supports this. If you can find a way to split the dataset so that each transaction reads and writes only within one partition, then each partition can have its own transaction thread, running independently of the others. Each CPU core can get its own partition, so throughput can grow in a straight line with the number of cores.

Any transaction that needs to access several partitions is a different matter. The database must coordinate it across all the partitions it touches. The stored procedure has to run in lockstep across all those partitions, so that the whole system stays serializable. Cross-partition transactions carry extra coordination overhead, so they are much slower than single-partition ones. The book gives a figure for VoltDB: about 1,000 cross-partition writes per second. That is orders of magnitude below its single-partition throughput, and it cannot be raised by adding more machines.

Whether transactions can stay within one partition depends on the structure of the application’s data. Simple key-value data can often be partitioned easily. Data with several secondary indexes is likely to need a lot of cross-partition coordination (see Chapter 6 on partitioning and secondary indexes).

Summary of serial execution. Serial execution has become a practical way to get serializable isolation, within certain limits:

  • Every transaction must be small and fast, because one slow transaction can stall all transaction processing.
  • It works only where the active dataset fits in memory. Rarely used data could be moved to disk, but if a single-threaded transaction needed it, the system would become very slow. The book notes that the best solution in that case may be to abort the transaction, fetch the data into memory in the background while other transactions continue, and then restart the transaction. This is called anti-caching.
  • Write throughput must be low enough for a single CPU core. Otherwise, transactions must be partitioned in a way that avoids cross-partition coordination.
  • Cross-partition transactions are possible, but there is a hard limit on how much they can be used.

Two-Phase Locking (2PL)

2PL is not 2PC. Two-phase locking sounds similar to two-phase commit, but they are completely different things. Two-phase commit is covered in Chapter 9.

For around thirty years, there was only one widely used algorithm for serializability in databases: two-phase locking, or 2PL. (Sometimes it is called strong strict two-phase locking, SS2PL, to distinguish it from other variants.)

We saw earlier that locks are often used to prevent dirty writes. If two transactions try to write the same object, a lock makes the second writer wait until the first one has finished, whether it committed or aborted. Two-phase locking is similar, but its lock requirements are much stronger. Several transactions may read the same object at the same time, as long as nobody is writing it. But as soon as anyone wants to write, meaning modify or delete the object, that transaction needs exclusive access:

  • If transaction A has read an object and transaction B wants to write it, B must wait until A commits or aborts. This ensures that B cannot change the object behind A’s back.
  • If transaction A has written an object and transaction B wants to read it, B must wait until A commits or aborts. Reading an old version of the object, as the counter race did, is not acceptable under 2PL.

Under 2PL, writers block readers, and readers block writers. Snapshot isolation has the opposite mantra: readers never block writers, and writers never block readers. That is the key performance difference between the two. On the other hand, 2PL provides serializability, so it protects against all the race conditions in this chapter, including lost updates and write skew.

Implementation of two-phase locking. 2PL is used by the serializable isolation level in MySQL (InnoDB) and SQL Server, and by the repeatable read level in IBM DB2. Blocking readers and writers is implemented by a lock on each object in the database. A lock can be held in shared mode or in exclusive mode:

  • To read an object, a transaction must first acquire the lock in shared mode. Several transactions can hold a shared lock at once. If another transaction already holds an exclusive lock on the object, the reader must wait.
  • To write an object, a transaction must acquire the lock in exclusive mode. No other transaction may hold any lock on it, shared or exclusive, so if any lock exists, the writer must wait.
  • If a transaction first reads and then writes an object, it can upgrade its shared lock to an exclusive lock. The upgrade works the same way as getting an exclusive lock directly.
  • Once a transaction has acquired a lock, it must keep holding it until the end of the transaction, whether it commits or aborts. This is where the name comes from. In the first phase, while the transaction runs, it acquires locks. In the second phase, at the end, it releases them all.

With so many locks in use, it is easy for transaction A to get stuck waiting for transaction B to release a lock, while B is waiting for A. This situation is called a deadlock. The database detects deadlocks automatically and aborts one of the transactions so the others can make progress. The application must retry the aborted transaction. The figure below shows the basic rule in a timeline.

Performance of two-phase locking. The big downside of 2PL, and the reason many systems have not used it since the 1970s, is performance. Transaction throughput and query response times are much worse under 2PL than under weak isolation. This is partly because acquiring and releasing all those locks has overhead. More importantly, it is because concurrency is reduced. By design, if two transactions could do something that might cause a race condition, one of them has to wait for the other to finish.

Traditional relational databases do not limit how long a transaction can run, because they were designed for interactive applications that wait for human input. When one transaction has to wait for another, there is no limit on how long the wait can last. Even if you keep your own transactions short, a queue can form when several transactions want the same object. A transaction may have to wait for several others to finish before it can do anything. For this reason, databases running 2PL can have quite unstable latencies. They can be very slow at high percentiles (see Chapter 1) when there is contention. It may take just one slow transaction, or one that touches a lot of data and acquires many locks, to bring the rest of the system to a halt. That instability is a problem when robust operation is required.

Deadlocks can also happen with lock-based read committed. But under 2PL serializable isolation, they occur much more often, depending on the access patterns of your transactions. This is an extra performance problem. When a transaction is aborted because of a deadlock and then retried, it has to do all its work again. If deadlocks are frequent, the wasted effort can be significant.

Predicate locks. The lock description so far glossed over a subtle detail. Earlier, we discussed phantoms, where one transaction changes the results of another transaction’s search. A database with serializable isolation must prevent phantoms too.

In the meeting room example, if one transaction has searched for bookings of a room in a certain time window, no other transaction may concurrently insert or update a booking for that same room and time range. Inserting bookings for other rooms, or for the same room at a different time that does not affect the proposed booking, is fine.

How can this be implemented? Conceptually, we need a predicate lock. It works like the shared and exclusive locks described above. But instead of belonging to one particular object, such as a row, it belongs to every object that matches a search condition. For example, the lock would cover all bookings that match this query:

SELECT * FROM bookings
WHERE room_id = 123 AND
end_time > '2018-01-01 12:00' AND
start_time < '2018-01-01 13:00';

A predicate lock restricts access in two ways:

  • If transaction A wants to read objects matching a condition, as in that SELECT, it must acquire a shared predicate lock on the condition. If transaction B already holds an exclusive lock on any object matching the condition, A must wait until B releases it.
  • If transaction A wants to insert, update, or delete any object, it must first check whether the old or the new value matches any existing predicate lock. If transaction B holds a matching predicate lock, A must wait until B has committed or aborted.

The key idea is that a predicate lock applies even to objects that do not exist yet, but might be added later. These are the phantoms. If 2PL includes predicate locks, the database prevents all forms of write skew and other race conditions, so its isolation is truly serializable.

Index-range locks. Predicate locks do not perform well. If many transactions hold locks, checking whether a new write matches any of them takes a lot of time. For that reason, most databases that use 2PL implement index-range locks, also called next-key locking. This is a simplified approximation of predicate locking.

It is safe to simplify a predicate by making it match a larger set of objects. For example, a predicate lock on bookings for room 123 between noon and 1 p.m. can be approximated by locking bookings for room 123 at any time. Or it can be approximated by locking all rooms between noon and 1 p.m. This is safe, because any write that matches the original predicate will also match the approximation.

In the room booking database, you would probably have an index on the room_id column, and perhaps indexes on start_time and end_time. Without them, the query above would be very slow on a large database. Two cases follow:

  • If the index is on room_id, and the database uses it to find existing bookings for room 123, the database can attach a shared lock to that index entry. That marks the fact that a transaction has searched for bookings of room 123.
  • If the database instead uses a time-based index to find bookings, it can attach a shared lock to a range of values in that index. That marks the fact that a transaction has searched for bookings overlapping noon to 1 p.m. on January 1, 2018.

Either way, an approximation of the search condition is attached to one of the indexes. If another transaction wants to insert, update, or delete a booking for the same room or an overlapping time, it must update the same part of the index. It will meet the shared lock and have to wait until the lock is released. This gives effective protection against phantoms and write skew. Index-range locks are less precise than predicate locks, and they may lock a bigger range of objects than strictly necessary. But they have much lower overhead, so they are a good compromise.

If there is no suitable index where a range lock can be attached, the database can fall back to a shared lock on the entire table. This is a safe fallback, but it is not good for performance, because it stops all other transactions from writing to the table.

Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

This chapter has painted a bleak picture of concurrency control. Two-phase locking gives serializability but performs poorly. Serial execution gives serializability but does not scale well. Weak isolation levels perform well but allow race conditions such as lost updates, write skew, and phantoms. Are serializable isolation and good performance fundamentally at odds?

Perhaps not. An algorithm called serializable snapshot isolation (SSI) is very promising. It provides full serializability, but with only a small performance penalty compared with snapshot isolation. SSI is fairly new. It was first described in 2008, and it was the subject of Michael Cahill’s PhD thesis. Today, SSI is used in single-node databases, as the serializable level in PostgreSQL since version 9.1. It is also used in distributed databases, and FoundationDB uses a similar algorithm. Because SSI is young compared with other concurrency control methods, it is still proving itself in practice. But it may be fast enough to become the default one day.

Pessimistic versus optimistic concurrency control. Two-phase locking is a pessimistic concurrency control method. It assumes that if anything might go wrong, it is better to wait until the situation is safe. A lock held by another transaction is the sign that something might go wrong. This is like the mutual exclusion used to protect data structures in multi-threaded programming. Serial execution is pessimistic to an extreme. It is like giving each transaction an exclusive lock on the whole database, or on one partition, for the whole time it runs. The design compensates by making each transaction very fast, so the lock is held only briefly.

By contrast, serializable snapshot isolation is an optimistic concurrency control method. Instead of blocking when something potentially dangerous happens, transactions carry on, hoping everything will turn out all right. When a transaction wants to commit, the database checks whether anything bad happened, meaning whether isolation was violated. If so, the transaction is aborted and must be retried. Only transactions that executed serializably are allowed to commit.

Optimistic concurrency control is an old idea, and its advantages and disadvantages have been debated for a long time. It performs badly under high contention, where many transactions try to access the same objects, because a large share of them must abort. If the system is already close to its maximum throughput, the extra load from retried transactions can make performance worse. But if there is enough spare capacity, and contention is not too high, optimistic methods tend to perform better than pessimistic ones. Contention can also be reduced with commutative atomic operations. If several transactions want to increment a counter, the order of the increments does not matter, as long as the counter is not read in the same transaction. So the increments can all be applied without conflicting.

SSI is built on snapshot isolation. All reads within a transaction come from a consistent snapshot, as described earlier. This is the main difference from older optimistic techniques. On top of snapshot isolation, SSI adds an algorithm that detects serialization conflicts among writes, and it decides which transactions to abort.

Decisions based on an outdated premise. Earlier, we saw a recurring pattern under snapshot isolation. A transaction reads some data, examines the result, and decides to take an action, which is a write, based on what it saw. But under snapshot isolation, the result of the original query may no longer be up to date when the transaction commits, because the data may have changed in the meantime.

Put another way, the transaction is acting on a premise, which is a fact that was true when the transaction began. For example, “there are currently two doctors on call.” By the time the transaction commits, the premise may no longer be true. The database does not know how the application uses a query result. To be safe, it must assume that any change to the result means the transaction’s writes may be invalid. In other words, there may be a causal dependency between the queries and the writes. To provide serializable isolation, the database must detect when a transaction may have acted on an outdated premise, and then abort that transaction.

There are two cases to detect. The first is a read of a stale MVCC version, where an uncommitted write happened before the read. The second is a write that affects a prior read, where the write happens after the read.

Detecting stale MVCC reads. Recall that snapshot isolation is usually implemented with MVCC. When a transaction reads from a consistent snapshot, it ignores writes made by other transactions that had not yet committed when the snapshot was taken. The book’s Figure 7-10 shows how this can go wrong.

Example
  1. Transaction 42 changes Alice’s on-call status. The change is not yet committed.
  2. Transaction 43 starts and reads the list of doctors on call. Because 42 has not committed, 43 ignores that write. It sees Alice as still on call, with on_call = true.
  3. Transaction 42 commits.
  4. Transaction 43 now wants to commit. The write it ignored has now taken effect. Its premise, that Alice is on call, is no longer true, so it must not commit.

To prevent this, the database tracks when a transaction ignores another transaction’s writes because of MVCC visibility rules. When the transaction wants to commit, the database checks whether any of those ignored writes have since been committed. If they have, the transaction must be aborted.

Why wait until commit? Why not abort transaction 43 as soon as the stale read happens? If transaction 43 were read-only, it would not need aborting, because there would be no risk of write skew. When transaction 43 makes its read, the database does not yet know whether it will later write. Transaction 42 might also still abort, or still be uncommitted when 43 tries to commit, and then the read would not turn out to be stale after all. By avoiding unnecessary aborts, SSI keeps snapshot isolation’s support for long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.

Detecting writes that affect prior reads. The second case is when another transaction modifies data after it has been read. The book’s Figure 7-11 shows this. Transactions 42 and 43 both search for on-call doctors during shift 1234. Two-phase locking had index-range locks for this kind of search. SSI uses a similar technique, except that its locks do not block other transactions.

If there is an index on shift_id, the database can use the index entry for shift 1234 to record that transactions 42 and 43 read this data. If there is no index, the database can track the information at the table level. This information only needs to be kept for a while. After a transaction and all its concurrent transactions have finished, the database can forget what that transaction read.

When a transaction writes to the database, it looks in the indexes for other transactions that have recently read the affected data. This is like acquiring a write lock on the affected key range. But instead of blocking until the readers commit, the lock acts as a tripwire. It notifies the transactions that the data they read may no longer be up to date.

Example
  1. Transactions 42 and 43 both read the on-call doctors for shift 1234.
  2. Transaction 43 writes a change to that shift. The tripwire tells transaction 42 that its earlier read is outdated, and it tells 43 the same about 42’s write.
  3. Transaction 42 commits first, and it succeeds. Although 43’s write affected 42’s read, 43 has not committed, so its write has not yet taken effect.
  4. When transaction 43 tries to commit, the conflicting write from 42 has already been committed. So 43 must abort.

Performance of serializable snapshot isolation. As always, many engineering details affect how well an algorithm works in practice. One trade-off is the granularity at which the database tracks reads and writes. If it tracks each transaction’s activity in great detail, it can be precise about which transactions must abort. But that bookkeeping can become expensive. Coarser tracking is faster, but it may cause more aborts than strictly necessary.

Sometimes a transaction can safely read information that another transaction has overwritten. Depending on what else happened, it may be possible to prove that the result is still serializable. PostgreSQL uses this kind of reasoning to reduce unnecessary aborts.

Compared with two-phase locking, the big advantage of SSI is that no transaction needs to block while waiting for a lock held by another. As under snapshot isolation, writers do not block readers, and readers do not block writers. This makes query latency more predictable and less variable. Read-only queries can run on a consistent snapshot without any locks, which is very appealing for read-heavy workloads.

Compared with serial execution, SSI is not limited to the throughput of one CPU core. FoundationDB spreads the detection of serialization conflicts across several machines, so it can scale to very high throughput. Even when data is split across machines, transactions can read and write several partitions and still get serializable isolation.

The rate of aborts has a large effect on SSI’s overall performance. A transaction that reads and writes data over a long period is likely to run into conflicts and abort. So SSI requires read-write transactions to be fairly short, although long-running read-only transactions may be acceptable. However, SSI is probably less sensitive to slow transactions than two-phase locking or serial execution.

Trade-offs
ApproachGood atCosts
Actual serial executionSerializable by design, with no conflict detection needed. Fast when data fits in memory and transactions are short.Limited to one CPU core per partition. No interactive transactions. One slow transaction stalls everything. Cross-partition work is slow.
Two-phase locking (2PL)Strong guarantee against every race condition. Decades of experience behind it.Readers and writers block each other. Latency is unstable under contention. Deadlocks are more frequent, and retries waste work.
Serializable snapshot isolation (SSI)Readers never block. Latency is predictable. Read-only queries need no locks. Only a small penalty over snapshot isolation.Some transactions abort and must be retried. Read-write transactions must stay short. Extra bookkeeping to track reads and writes.
Key idea

Only serializable isolation protects against every race condition in this chapter. Weaker levels are faster, but each one leaves some race conditions to be handled by the application.

Summary

Summary
  • Transactions let an application treat a group of reads and writes as one unit. If the unit fails, it is aborted, and the application can retry. Many concurrency and fault problems reduce to a simple abort.
  • Atomicity means all-or-nothing: an aborted transaction’s writes are discarded. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other. Durability means committed data is not forgotten. Consistency is the application’s job, based on its own rules.
  • Dirty reads, where one client sees another client’s uncommitted writes, and dirty writes, where one client overwrites another’s uncommitted data, are prevented by read committed and stronger levels.
  • Read skew, where a client sees different parts of the database at different times, is usually prevented by snapshot isolation. It is usually built with MVCC.
  • Lost updates, where two read-modify-write cycles overwrite each other, are prevented by atomic operations, explicit locks, automatic detection in some systems, or compare-and-set. Replicated systems need merge-friendly approaches instead.
  • Write skew, where a decision is based on a premise that another transaction has made false, is prevented only by serializable isolation, or by careful explicit locking.
  • Phantom reads, where a write changes the result of another transaction’s search, are blocked by snapshot isolation for read-only queries. Phantoms that cause write skew need index-range locks, materialized conflicts, or serializable isolation.
  • The three ways to get serializability are actual serial execution, two-phase locking, and serializable snapshot isolation. Each makes a different trade-off between speed, scaling, and aborts.

Transactions are an abstraction layer. They let an application pretend that certain concurrency problems, and certain hardware and software faults, do not exist. A large class of errors is reduced to a simple transaction abort, and the application only needs to try again.

Not every application is affected by all of these problems. An application with very simple access patterns, such as reading and writing a single record, can probably manage without transactions. But for more complex access patterns, transactions greatly reduce the number of error cases you have to think about. Without transactions, errors such as process crashes, network interruptions, power outages, full disks, and unexpected concurrency can leave data inconsistent in many ways. Denormalized data can easily fall out of sync with its source. Without transactions, it becomes very hard to reason about the effects that several interacting accesses can have on the database.

In this chapter, the book went deep into concurrency control. It discussed several widely used isolation levels, particularly read committed, snapshot isolation (sometimes called repeatable read), and serializable. It described each one by the race conditions it allows and blocks, and it noted that the names used by different databases do not always match. Transactions in distributed databases bring a new set of hard challenges, which the next two chapters take up.

Check yourself

  1. Two clients each read a counter that holds 42, and then each writes 43. Why does the counter end at 43 instead of 44? Would read committed isolation alone prevent this?

    Show answer

    Both clients read before either wrote, so the second write replaced the first with the same value, and one increment was lost. Read committed does not prevent it, because the second write happens after the first transaction commits, so it is not a dirty write. Fixes include an atomic increment, an explicit lock, automatic lost update detection, or compare-and-set.

  2. Under snapshot isolation, transaction 12 starts before transaction 13 commits. Transaction 13 changes account 2 from $500 to $400. What balance does transaction 12 see, and why?

    Show answer

    It sees $500. Transaction 13 created the $400 version, which 12 cannot see. It also marked the $500 version as deleted, but that deletion is invisible to 12 because 13 had not committed when 12 started.

  3. A booking transaction runs a SELECT to find overlapping bookings for a room, finds none, and then inserts a booking. Why can SELECT FOR UPDATE not fix this race?

    Show answer

    The SELECT returns no rows, so there is nothing to lock. A concurrent insert by another transaction is a phantom, because it changes the result of the search. The fixes are to materialize conflicts into lock rows, use index-range locks, or use serializable isolation.

  4. Why does serializable snapshot isolation check for stale reads at commit time, rather than aborting as soon as a stale read happens?

    Show answer

    When the read happens, the database does not know whether the transaction will later write. A read-only transaction does not need aborting, because it cannot cause write skew. The writer that the read ignored might also still abort, which would make the read valid after all. Waiting until commit avoids unnecessary aborts.

Part II · Chapter 8

The Trouble with Distributed Systems

The big idea: when a program runs on many machines joined by a network, parts of it can fail while other parts keep working. Messages can be lost or delayed, clocks can be wrong, and a process can freeze for a long time without knowing it. Each machine has to act on guesses about the others, so the software must be built to stay correct even when those guesses are wrong.

Earlier chapters were, in a way, too kind. They discussed a replica taking over when a leader dies, replication lag, and isolation levels that handle concurrent writes. Each of those topics involves something going wrong. But the book says the last few chapters were still too optimistic. This chapter turns the pessimism up to the maximum and assumes that anything that can go wrong will go wrong. Experienced operators, the book adds, will tell you that is a reasonable assumption, and some of them have frightening stories from past battles.

Working with a distributed system, which is a set of separate computers connected by a network and working together, is fundamentally different from writing software for a single computer. The main difference is that there are many new ways for things to go wrong. This chapter gives a taste of the problems that come up in practice, and it shows what we can and cannot rely on.

One note on scope. The book assumes that faults are non-Byzantine, which means that machines do not deliberately lie. The section on Byzantine faults later in the chapter explains what that means and why the book sets it aside.

The job of an engineer is still to build systems that do their job, meaning they meet the guarantees that users expect, despite everything going wrong. Chapter 9 looks at algorithms that can provide such guarantees. This chapter first explains the challenges. It covers problems with networks, problems with clocks and timing, and how avoidable each one is. Then it asks how a node can think about the state of the whole system, and how it can reason about things that have already happened, when it cannot be sure what has happened.

Faults and Partial Failures

When you write a program on a single computer, it usually behaves in a predictable way. Either it works or it does not. Buggy software may make the computer seem to be having a bad day, and a reboot may fix it, but the cause is almost always bad software rather than the machine itself.

There is no basic reason why one computer should be flaky. When the hardware works, the same operation gives the same result every time. The book calls this deterministic. If the hardware breaks, for example from memory corruption or a loose connector, the usual result is a total failure: a kernel panic, a crash screen, or a machine that will not start. A single computer with good software is either working fully or broken. It is rarely something in between.

This is a deliberate design choice. If an internal fault happens, computers are built to crash completely rather than return a wrong answer, because wrong answers are hard and confusing to deal with. So a computer hides the messy physical reality under it and presents an idealized model that behaves with mathematical precision. A CPU instruction always does the same thing. Data written to memory or disk stays intact. The book notes that this goal of always-correct computation goes back to the very first digital computers.

A distributed system is different. Once software runs on several computers connected by a network, we no longer work in that idealized model. We have to face the messy physical world, where many things can go wrong. The book illustrates the range of failures with an anecdote from an operator named Coda Hale. In his limited experience, he had seen long-lasting network partitions inside one data center, failures of the power distribution units that feed racks, switch failures, racks accidentally power-cycled, whole-data-center network and power failures, and a driver who crashed his pickup truck into a data center’s air conditioning system. He said he was not even an ops person.

In a distributed system, some parts may be broken in unpredictable ways while other parts work fine. This is called a partial failure. The difficulty is that partial failures are nondeterministic, which means they do not happen the same way each time. If you do anything that involves several nodes and the network, it may sometimes work and sometimes fail in ways you cannot predict. You may not even know whether something succeeded, because the time a message takes to cross the network is also unpredictable. The book says this nondeterminism, and the possibility of partial failures, is what makes distributed systems hard to work with.

Cloud Computing and Supercomputing

People have built large computing systems in several different ways, and the philosophies lead to different ways of handling faults. The book describes a spectrum:

  • High-performance computing (HPC) sits at one end. Supercomputers with thousands of CPUs run heavy scientific jobs such as weather forecasting or molecular dynamics, which simulates how atoms and molecules move.
  • Cloud computing sits at the other end. The term is not very well defined, but it usually means multi-tenant data centers (many customers share the same facilities), commodity computers (ordinary, inexpensive machines) connected by an IP network, often Ethernet, resources allocated on demand, and metered billing.
  • Traditional enterprise data centers lie somewhere in between.

A supercomputer handles faults in a particular way. A job saves a checkpoint, a snapshot of its state, to durable storage (storage that survives a crash) from time to time.
