If one node fails, the common solution is to stop the whole cluster’s work. After the faulty node is repaired, the computation restarts from the last checkpoint. So a supercomputer behaves more like one computer than like a distributed system. Partial failure is allowed to escalate into total failure. If any part breaks, everything is stopped, much as a kernel panic stops a single machine.

The book focuses instead on systems for internet services, which look very different from supercomputers. The differences are these:

  • Many internet services are online. They must serve users with low latency (short delay) at any time. Stopping the whole cluster for repairs is not acceptable. Offline batch jobs, such as weather simulations, can be stopped and restarted with fairly low impact.
  • Supercomputers use specialized hardware, where each node is quite reliable. The nodes talk through shared memory and remote direct memory access (RDMA, a way for one machine to read another’s memory directly). Cloud nodes are commodity machines. They can give similar performance at lower cost thanks to economies of scale, but they fail more often.
  • Large datacenter networks are usually built on IP and Ethernet, arranged in Clos topologies, which are designs that give high bisection bandwidth (a lot of capacity between the two halves of the network). Supercomputers often use specialized layouts such as meshes and toruses, which suit the known communication patterns of their jobs.
  • The bigger a system gets, the more likely something in it is broken. Over time, broken things get fixed and new things break. With thousands of nodes, it is reasonable to assume that something is always broken. If the error strategy is simply to give up, a large system can spend much of its time recovering from faults rather than doing useful work.
  • If the system keeps working even when nodes fail, operations get easier. You can perform a rolling upgrade (Chapter 4), restarting one node at a time while the service keeps serving users. In a cloud, if one virtual machine is slow, you can kill it and ask for a new one, hoping the new one will be faster.
  • A geographically distributed deployment keeps data close to users to reduce latency. Communication then usually goes over the internet, which is slower and less reliable than a local network. Supercomputers assume their nodes are close together.

So if we want distributed systems to work, we must accept that partial failure can happen, and build fault tolerance into the software. In other words, we need to build a reliable system from unreliable parts. The book reminds us that there is no such thing as perfect reliability, so we need to understand the limits of what we can realistically promise.

Partial failure matters even in a small system with only a few nodes. In a small system, most parts are probably working correctly most of the time. But sooner or later some part will become faulty, and the software will have to handle it. The fault handling must be part of the software’s design. The people who operate the software also need to know what behavior to expect when a fault happens.

It would be unwise to assume that faults are rare and hope for the best. You should consider a wide range of possible faults, including fairly unlikely ones, and create those situations on purpose in your test environment to see what happens. The book sums up the attitude this way: in distributed systems, suspicion, pessimism, and paranoia pay off.

Building a Reliable System from Unreliable Components

You might think that a system can only be as reliable as its weakest part. That intuition is wrong. It is an old idea in computing to build a more reliable system out of less reliable parts. Two examples from the book:

  • Error-correcting codes let digital data cross a channel that sometimes gets bits wrong, such as a wireless network with radio interference. Extra bits sent with the data let the receiver fix small errors.
  • IP, the Internet Protocol, is unreliable. It may drop, delay, duplicate, or reorder packets (small chunks of data). TCP, the Transmission Control Protocol, runs on top of IP and provides a more reliable transport. It retransmits missing packets, removes duplicates, and reassembles packets in the order they were sent.

There is still a limit. Error-correcting codes can handle a few single-bit errors, but if interference swamps the signal, there is a hard limit on how much data can get through. TCP can hide packet loss, duplication, and reordering from the application, but it cannot remove delays from the network.

A more reliable higher layer is still useful, even though it is not perfect. It takes care of some tricky low-level faults, so the faults that remain are usually easier to reason about and handle. The book returns to this idea in its discussion of the end-to-end argument later in the book.

Unreliable Networks

The distributed systems this book focuses on are shared-nothing systems. That means a group of machines connected by a network. The network is the only way the machines can talk to each other. Each machine has its own memory and disk, and one machine cannot read another machine’s memory or disk. It can only ask for something by making a request over the network.

Shared-nothing is not the only way to build a system, but it has become the main approach for internet services. It is relatively cheap because it needs no special hardware. It can run on commodity cloud services. And it can reach high reliability by spreading copies across several geographically distributed data centers.

The internet, and most internal data center networks (often Ethernet), are asynchronous packet networks. One node can send a message, which is a packet, to another. But the network makes no promise about when the packet will arrive, or whether it will arrive at all. If you send a request and expect a response, many things can go wrong. The book lists six:

  1. Your request may have been lost. Perhaps someone unplugged a network cable.
  2. Your request may be waiting in a queue and will be delivered later. Perhaps the network or the recipient is overloaded.
  3. The remote node may have failed. Perhaps it crashed or was powered down.
  4. The remote node may have stopped responding for a while, for example during a long garbage collection pause (a moment when the language runtime stops the program to clean up memory). It will start responding again later.
  5. The remote node may have processed your request, but the response was lost on the network. Perhaps a switch was misconfigured.
  6. The remote node may have processed your request, but the response is delayed and will arrive later. Perhaps the network or your own machine is overloaded.

The book’s Figure 8-1 shows these possibilities. The key point is that you cannot tell them apart from the sending side. If there is no response, you cannot know whether the request was lost, the remote node is down, or the response was lost.

Example

Here is the situation the book describes, step by step. A client sends a request to a server. The server receives it and carries out the work, for example writing a record to its database. Then the server sends back a response, but the response is lost on the network. The client waits. No reply comes. The client’s timeout fires, and it gives up. Now the client has to decide what to do. It does not know whether the write happened. If it retries, the write may happen twice. If it does not retry, the write may never have happened at all. The client has no way to find out from the messages alone.

The sender cannot even tell whether its packet was delivered. The only way to find out is for the recipient to send a response, and that response can be lost or delayed too. In an asynchronous network, these cases look the same. All you know is that no response has arrived yet. If you send a request and get no reply, it is impossible to tell why.

The usual way to handle this is a timeout. You wait for a set time, then give up and assume the response will not come. But a timeout does not answer the question. You still do not know whether the remote node received your request. And if the request is still sitting in a queue somewhere, it may still reach the recipient later, even though you have given up on it.

Network Faults in Practice

People have built computer networks for decades, and you might hope they would be reliable by now. The book says we have not yet managed it. Systematic studies and plenty of anecdotes show that network problems are surprisingly common, even in a data center run by one company. One study of a medium-sized data center found about 12 network faults per month. Half of them disconnected a single machine, and half disconnected a whole rack. Another study measured failure rates for top-of-rack switches, aggregation switches, and load balancers. It found that adding redundant networking gear does not reduce faults as much as you might hope, because redundancy does not protect against human error, such as a misconfigured switch. Human error is a major cause of outages.

Public cloud services such as Amazon EC2 are known for frequent short network glitches. Well-run private data center networks can be more stable. But nobody is immune. In one case, a problem during a software upgrade of a switch triggered a network topology reconfiguration, and packets were delayed for more than a minute. Sharks have been reported to bite undersea cables. Another odd fault is a network interface that sometimes drops all incoming packets while still sending outgoing ones. A link that works in one direction does not guarantee the other direction works.

Watch out

A network partition, also called a netsplit, is when one part of the network is cut off from the rest. The book mostly uses the broader term network fault instead, to avoid confusion with partitions, meaning shards, of a storage system, which Chapter 6 covers.

Even if network faults are rare where you work, your software must handle them, because any communication over a network can fail. There is no way around it. If error handling for network faults is not defined and tested, almost anything can happen. The book gives two examples. A cluster can become deadlocked and stay unable to serve requests even after the network recovers. Or the system could even delete all of your data. If software ends up in a situation no one anticipated, it may do arbitrary things.

Handling network faults does not always mean tolerating them without a visible effect. If your network is normally reliable, a sensible choice may be to show an error message to users while the network has problems. But you still need to know how your software reacts to network trouble, and make sure it can recover. It can even make sense to trigger network problems on purpose and watch how the system responds. That is the idea behind Chaos Monkey, which the book mentioned in its discussion of reliability in Chapter 1.

Detecting Faults

Many systems need to detect faulty nodes automatically. A load balancer must stop sending requests to a dead node by taking it out of rotation. In a database with single-leader replication, if the leader fails, one of the followers must be promoted to be the new leader. But the uncertainty about the network makes it hard to tell whether a node is working. In a few specific cases, you may get explicit feedback that something is wrong:

  • If you can reach the machine where the node should run, but no process is listening on the port, the operating system will usually refuse the connection quickly. It replies with a TCP RST or FIN packet. But if the node crashed while it was handling your request, you still have no way of knowing how much of the work it finished.
  • If a node’s process crashed or was killed by an administrator, but the machine’s operating system still runs, a script can tell the other nodes about the crash. Then another node can take over without waiting for a timeout. The book says HBase does this.
  • If you can see the management interface of the network switches in your data center, you can ask them about link failures at the hardware level, such as a machine that has been powered down. This is not possible over the internet, in a shared data center where you cannot reach the switches, or when the management interface itself is unreachable because of a network problem.
  • If a router is sure the address you are trying to reach is unreachable, it may reply with an ICMP Destination Unreachable message. But the router does not have any magic way to detect failures either. It is subject to the same limits as everything else on the network.

Fast feedback about a remote node being down is useful, but you cannot count on it. TCP may acknowledge that a packet was delivered, but the application may have crashed before it handled that packet. If you need to be sure a request succeeded, you need a positive response from the application itself.

The reverse also holds. If something goes wrong, you might get an error response from some layer of the stack. But in general you have to assume you will get no response at all. You can retry a few times (TCP retries on its own, but you may also retry at the application level), wait for a timeout to elapse, and then declare the node dead if you still have not heard back.

Timeouts and Unbounded Delays

If a timeout is the only sure way to detect a fault, how long should it be? The book says there is no simple answer.

A long timeout means a long wait before a node is declared dead. During that time, users may wait or see error messages. A short timeout detects faults faster, but it carries a higher risk of wrongly declaring a node dead when it has only suffered a temporary slowdown, such as a load spike on the node or the network.

Declaring a node dead too early is a real problem. Suppose the node is actually alive and in the middle of an action, such as sending an email. Another node takes over, and then the first node finishes its work. The action may be performed twice. The book returns to this issue in its discussion of knowledge and truth later in the chapter, and in Chapters 9 and 11.

When a node is declared dead, its responsibilities move to other nodes. That adds load to the other nodes and to the network. If the system is already struggling under high load, declaring nodes dead too early can make things worse. A node that was not dead, only slow because of overload, may have its work moved to others, and that can overload them in turn. This is a cascading failure. In the extreme case, every node declares every other node dead, and everything stops working.

Example

The book imagines a made-up system that gives strong guarantees, to show what a good timeout would look like. Suppose the network guarantees a maximum delay, called d, for each packet. Every packet either arrives within time d, or it is lost, and delivery never takes longer than d. Suppose also that a node that has not failed always handles a request within some time r. Then you can guarantee that every successful request gets a response within time 2d + r. The request takes up to d to arrive, the handling takes up to r, and the reply takes up to d to come back. If no response arrives within 2d + r, you know that either the network or the remote node is not working. In that imaginary system, 2d + r would be a reasonable timeout.

Real systems have neither guarantee. Asynchronous networks have unbounded delays. They try to deliver packets as quickly as possible, but there is no upper limit on how long a packet may take. And most server software cannot promise to handle a request within some maximum time. For failure detection, it is not enough for a system to be fast most of the time. If your timeout is short, a single brief spike in round-trip times can throw the whole system off balance.

Network Congestion and Queueing

When you drive, travel times on a road network vary most because of traffic jams. On computer networks, the variation in packet delays is mostly caused by queueing, which means waiting in line. There are four main places where packets wait:

  • Network switches. If several nodes send packets to the same destination at the same time, the switch must queue them and feed them into the destination link one at a time. On a busy link, a packet may wait a while for its turn. This is called network congestion. If so much data arrives that the switch’s queue fills up, packets are dropped and must be sent again, even though the network itself is working fine.
  • The receiving machine. When a packet reaches the destination machine and all of its CPU cores are busy, the operating system queues the incoming request until the application is ready to handle it. Depending on the load, that wait can be of any length.
  • Virtual machines. In a virtualized environment, the running operating system may be paused for tens of milliseconds while another virtual machine uses the CPU core. During that time, the paused VM cannot read incoming data, so the virtual machine monitor buffers it. That adds yet more variation to network delays.
  • TCP flow control. TCP also limits how fast a node sends, to avoid overloading a network link or the receiver. This is also called congestion avoidance or backpressure. It means data can queue at the sender, before it even enters the network.

The book’s Figure 8-2 shows the switch case. Ports 1, 2, and 4 are all trying to send packets to port 3, so the switch queue for port 3 can fill up.

TCP also decides for itself when a packet is lost. If a packet is not acknowledged within a timeout, which TCP calculates from the round-trip times it has observed, the packet is treated as lost and sent again automatically. The application never sees the loss or the resend. It does see the delay, which includes waiting for the timeout and then waiting for the retransmitted packet to be acknowledged.

TCP Versus UDP

Some latency-sensitive applications, such as video calls and Voice over IP (VoIP), use UDP rather than TCP. UDP is a simpler protocol that sends packets without any of TCP’s guarantees. This is a trade-off between reliability and variability of delay. UDP does not do flow control and does not retransmit lost packets, so it avoids some causes of variable delay. It is still affected by switch queues and by scheduling delays on the machines.

UDP is a good choice when late data is worthless. In a VoIP call, there is usually no time to retransmit a lost packet before its audio is due to play. So the application fills the missing audio with silence, which causes a brief break in the sound, and moves on. The retry happens at the human layer, when the listener asks the speaker to say the sentence again.

The book adds a practical point about shared networks. In public clouds and multi-tenant data centers, network links, switches, and even each machine’s network card and CPUs (on virtual machines) are shared with other customers. Batch jobs such as MapReduce can easily saturate network links. You have no control over, and no view of, what other customers are using. If a noisy neighbor nearby uses a lot of resources, your network delays can vary widely.

In such environments, the only way to choose a timeout is by experiment. Measure the distribution of network round-trip times over a long period, and across many machines, to see how much they typically vary. Then, taking your application’s needs into account, pick a balance between slow failure detection and the risk of premature timeouts.

A better approach is to stop using a fixed timeout at all. A system can keep measuring response times and their variability (called jitter), and adjust its timeouts automatically to match what it observes. This can be done with a Phi Accrual failure detector, which the book says Akka and Cassandra use. TCP’s retransmission timeouts work in a similar way.

Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Networks

Distributed systems would be much simpler if the network delivered packets within some fixed maximum delay and never dropped them. Why can’t we fix this at the hardware level, so that software does not have to worry about it?

The book compares datacenter networks with the traditional fixed-line telephone network, which is extremely reliable. Delayed audio and dropped calls are very rare. A phone call needs a constantly low end-to-end delay, and enough bandwidth to carry your voice. Wouldn’t it be nice to have that kind of predictability in computer networks?

On a telephone network, a call sets up a circuit. A fixed, guaranteed amount of bandwidth is reserved for the call along the whole route between the two callers, and it stays in place until the call ends.

Example

The book uses an ISDN telephone network as an example. It runs at a fixed rate of 4,000 frames per second. When a call is set up, it gets 16 bits of space in every frame, in each direction. So for the length of the call, each side is guaranteed to send exactly 16 bits of audio every 250 microseconds. Because the space is reserved before the data moves, a frame does not wait in a queue at each router along the way. The maximum end-to-end delay is therefore fixed. The book calls this a bounded delay.

Why not do the same for computer networks? A circuit is very different from a TCP connection. A circuit reserves a fixed amount of bandwidth that nobody else can use while the call lasts. A TCP connection opportunistically uses whatever bandwidth is free. If you give TCP a block of data, such as an email or a web page, it tries to transfer it as fast as possible. While a TCP connection is idle, it uses no bandwidth. The book adds a footnote that TCP keepalive packets are the rare exception.

If datacenter networks and the internet were circuit-switched, you could set a guaranteed maximum round-trip time when a circuit was set up. But they are not. Ethernet and IP are packet-switched protocols, which means packets share links and can queue, so delays are not bounded. These protocols have no concept of a circuit.

Why do datacenters and the internet use packet switching? The answer is that they are optimized for bursty traffic, which arrives in sudden bursts with quiet gaps between. A circuit suits an audio or video call, which needs a fairly constant number of bits per second for the whole call. But requesting a web page, sending an email, or transferring a file has no particular bandwidth requirement. We just want it done as quickly as possible.

Imagine transferring a file over a circuit. You would have to guess a bandwidth to reserve. If you guess too low, the transfer is needlessly slow and network capacity sits unused. If you guess too high, the circuit cannot be set up, because the network cannot promise that much bandwidth. Using circuits for bursty transfers therefore wastes capacity and makes transfers slower. TCP, by contrast, adapts its rate to whatever capacity is available.

There have been attempts at hybrid networks that support both circuit and packet switching. The book mentions ATM, Asynchronous Transfer Mode, which competed with Ethernet in the 1980s. It did not gain much adoption outside the core switches of telephone networks. (It has nothing to do with cash machines, despite the shared acronym.) InfiniBand is somewhat similar. It does flow control at the link layer, which reduces queueing inside the network, but it can still suffer delays when links are congested. With careful use of quality of service (prioritizing and scheduling packets) and admission control (limiting how fast senders may send), it is possible to imitate circuit switching on a packet network, or to offer a statistically bounded delay.

Latency and Resource Utilization

More generally, you can think of variable delays as a consequence of dynamic resource partitioning, which means sharing a resource out on the fly rather than in fixed slices.

Say a wire between two telephone switches can carry up to 10,000 simultaneous calls. Each circuit uses one of those call slots. The wire is divided in a static way. Even if your call is the only one on the wire, and the other 9,999 slots are empty, your circuit still gets the same fixed bandwidth as when the wire is full.

The internet shares bandwidth dynamically. Senders push and jostle to get their packets across the wire as fast as possible, and the switches decide from one moment to the next which packet goes next. This has the downside of queueing. But it maximizes how much of the wire is used. The wire has a fixed cost, so if you use more of it, each byte you send is cheaper.

A similar trade-off appears with CPUs. If several threads share one CPU core dynamically, a thread sometimes has to wait in the operating system’s run queue while another thread runs. So its pauses vary in length. But this uses the hardware better than giving each thread a fixed share of CPU cycles. Better hardware use is also a big reason to run virtual machines.

Latency guarantees can be achieved if resources are statically partitioned, with dedicated hardware and exclusive bandwidth. But this costs utilization, so it is more expensive. Multi-tenancy with dynamic partitioning gives better utilization and is cheaper, but it brings variable delays. The book’s conclusion is that variable delays in networks are not a law of nature. They are simply the result of a cost and benefit trade-off.

ApproachGood atCosts
Circuits, or static partitioning with reserved bandwidthBounded, predictable delay and latency guaranteesReserved capacity can sit unused. Hardware use goes down and cost goes up.
Packet switching with dynamic sharing (IP, Ethernet)High utilization, so each byte is cheaper. Good for bursty traffic.Queueing causes variable, unbounded delays.

Quality of service is not currently enabled in multi-tenant datacenters, in public clouds, or over the internet. So today’s technology cannot guarantee network delays or reliability. We have to assume that congestion, queueing, and unbounded delays will happen. That means there is no single correct timeout value. Timeouts must be set by experiment.

Unreliable Clocks

Clocks and time matter a great deal. Applications use clocks to answer questions such as these:

  1. Has this request timed out yet?
  2. What is the 99th percentile response time of this service?
  3. How many queries per second did this service handle, on average, in the last five minutes?
  4. How long did the user spend on our site?
  5. When was this article published?
  6. At what date and time should the reminder email be sent?
  7. When does this cache entry expire?
  8. What is the timestamp on this error message in the log file?

The first four questions measure a duration, which is the time between two events. The last four describe a point in time, which is a particular date and time.

In a distributed system, time is tricky. Communication is not instant. A message takes time to cross the network. The time when a message is received is always later than the time when it was sent, but because the delays vary, we do not know by how much. This sometimes makes it hard to work out the order in which things happened when several machines are involved.

Each machine also has its own clock, which is a hardware device, usually a quartz crystal oscillator. These devices are not perfectly accurate, so each machine has its own sense of time, which may run slightly faster or slower than the others. Clocks can be synchronized to some degree. The most common method is the Network Time Protocol (NTP), which adjusts a computer’s clock according to the time reported by a group of servers. Those servers get their time from a more accurate source, such as a GPS receiver.

Monotonic Versus Time-of-Day Clocks

Modern computers have at least two kinds of clocks, and the two serve different purposes. Both measure time, but you need to know which one to use.

A time-of-day clock does what you would expect of a clock. It returns the current date and time according to a calendar, which is also called wall-clock time. For example, clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME) on Linux and System.currentTimeMillis() in Java return the number of seconds, or milliseconds, since the epoch. The epoch is midnight UTC on January 1, 1970, counted in the Gregorian calendar, and it does not count leap seconds. Some systems use other reference dates.

Time-of-day clocks are usually synchronized with NTP. So a timestamp from one machine should mean the same as a timestamp from another. But time-of-day clocks have oddities. If the local clock is too far ahead of the NTP server, it may be forcibly reset, and then it appears to jump back to an earlier time. These jumps, and the fact that clocks often ignore leap seconds, make time-of-day clocks unsuitable for measuring elapsed time. Older Windows systems also moved time forward in coarse steps of 10 milliseconds. Recent systems are much better, so this is less of a problem now.

A monotonic clock is suitable for measuring a duration, such as a timeout or a service’s response time. clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC) on Linux and System.nanoTime() in Java are examples. The name comes from the fact that a monotonic clock is guaranteed to always move forward, while a time-of-day clock may jump back.

You read a monotonic clock at one point, do something, and read it again later. The difference between the two readings is the elapsed time. The absolute value of a monotonic clock means nothing, though. It might count nanoseconds since the computer booted, or something else arbitrary. It makes no sense to compare monotonic values from two different computers, because they do not mean the same thing.

On a server with several CPU sockets, each CPU may have its own timer, and those timers are not necessarily synchronized. Operating systems try to hide this and present a monotonic view to application threads even when they run on different CPUs. The book advises taking that guarantee with a pinch of salt. NTP can also adjust the speed of the monotonic clock, which is called slewing, if it notices the local quartz runs faster or slower than the NTP server. By default, NTP can speed up or slow down the clock by up to 0.05 percent. But NTP cannot make a monotonic clock jump forward or back. Monotonic clocks are usually good to microseconds or better.

In a distributed system, a monotonic clock is usually fine for measuring elapsed time such as timeouts. It does not assume that the clocks of different nodes are synchronized, and it is not sensitive to small measurement inaccuracies.

ClockGood forCosts
Time-of-day (wall-clock)Dates and times that should match across machines, such as an article’s publish timeCan jump backward or forward. Not reliable for measuring how much time has passed.
MonotonicDurations, such as timeouts and response times, on one machineOnly meaningful on the same machine. Its absolute value means nothing.

Clock Synchronization and Accuracy

Monotonic clocks do not need synchronizing. Time-of-day clocks must be set according to an NTP server or another external time source, or they are not useful. But our methods for getting a clock to show the correct time are not as reliable or accurate as we might hope. Hardware clocks and NTP can be fickle. The book gives several examples:

  • Drift. A computer’s quartz clock is not very accurate. It drifts, meaning it runs faster or slower than it should, and the drift changes with temperature. Google assumes a drift of 200 ppm (parts per million) for its servers. That is 6 milliseconds of drift for a clock that is resynchronized with a server every 30 seconds. For a clock resynchronized only once a day, the drift grows to about 17 seconds. This drift limits the best accuracy you can get, even when everything works.
  • Forced resets. If a computer’s clock differs too much from an NTP server, it may refuse to synchronize, or its local clock may be forcibly reset. Any application that observes the time before and after the reset may see time go backward or suddenly jump forward.
  • Silent firewalls. If a node is accidentally blocked from reaching NTP servers, the mistake may go unnoticed for some time. The book says anecdotal evidence suggests this does happen.
  • Network delay. NTP cannot be more accurate than the network delay allows. On a congested network with variable delays, there is a limit to its accuracy. One experiment found a minimum error of 35 ms over the internet, and occasional spikes in delay caused errors of around a second. With large delays, the NTP client may give up entirely.
  • Wrong servers. Some NTP servers are wrong or misconfigured, and report times that are off by hours. NTP clients are fairly robust, because they query several servers and ignore outliers. Still, the book says it is somewhat worrying to bet the correctness of your systems on the time you were told by a stranger on the internet.
  • Leap seconds. A leap second makes a minute 59 or 61 seconds long. That breaks timing assumptions in systems not designed for it. Leap seconds have crashed many large systems, which shows how easily wrong assumptions about clocks can creep into a system. One possible fix is for NTP servers to lie a little. They spread the leap second adjustment gradually over a day, a method called smearing. But actual NTP server behavior varies in practice.
  • Virtual machines. In a VM, the hardware clock is itself virtualized. When a CPU core is shared between VMs, each VM is paused for tens of milliseconds while another runs. From the application’s point of view, the pause looks like the clock suddenly jumping forward.
  • Devices you do not control. On phones and embedded devices, you probably cannot trust the hardware clock at all. Some users set their clock to a wrong date on purpose, for example to get around timing limits in games. The clock may then show a time far in the past or future.

Very good clock accuracy is possible if you invest enough. The book gives an example from finance. A draft European regulation called MiFID II requires high-frequency trading firms to synchronize their clocks to within 100 microseconds of UTC. The aim is to help debug market anomalies, such as flash crashes, and to detect market manipulation. Such accuracy can be reached with GPS receivers, the Precision Time Protocol (PTP), and careful deployment and monitoring. But it takes significant effort and expertise, and there are many ways clock synchronization can go wrong. If your NTP daemon is misconfigured, or a firewall blocks NTP traffic, the clock error from drift can grow large quickly.

Relying on Synchronized Clocks

Clocks seem simple and easy to use, but they have a surprising number of pitfalls. A day does not always have exactly 86,400 seconds. Time-of-day clocks can move backward. And the time on one node may be quite different from the time on another.

Earlier, the chapter showed that networks can drop packets and delay them arbitrarily. Networks behave well most of the time, but software must still be designed for the occasional fault and handle it gracefully. The same goes for clocks. They work well most of the time, but robust software must be ready for clocks that are wrong.

Wrong clocks are easy to miss. If a machine’s CPU is defective or its network is misconfigured, the machine probably will not work at all, and someone will notice and fix it quickly. But if its quartz clock is defective or its NTP client is misconfigured, most things will seem to work fine. The clock quietly drifts further from reality. If software depends on an accurately synchronized clock, the result is more likely to be silent, subtle data loss than a dramatic crash.

So if you use software that needs synchronized clocks, you must also monitor the clock offsets between all your machines. Any node whose clock drifts too far from the others should be declared dead and removed from the cluster. This monitoring catches broken clocks before they do much damage.

Timestamps for Ordering Events

One situation shows how tempting, and how dangerous, it is to rely on clocks. The problem is ordering events across several nodes. If two clients write to a distributed database, which write happened first? Which one is more recent?

The book’s Figure 8-3 shows a dangerous use of time-of-day clocks in a database with multi-leader replication. (Multi-leader replication lets several nodes accept writes, and the example is similar to Figure 5-9 in Chapter 5.)

Example

Walk through the book’s example step by step. Client A writes x = 1 on node 1. The write is replicated to node 3. Client B reads that value and increments it on node 3, so now x = 2. Finally, both writes are replicated to node 2. Each write is tagged with a timestamp from the clock of the node where it started. Node 1 stamps its write at 42.004 seconds. Node 3 stamps client B’s later write at 42.003 seconds. The clocks are well synchronized here. The skew between node 1 and node 3 is under 3 ms, which the book says is probably better than you can expect in practice.

Even so, the timestamps order the events the wrong way. The write x = 1 has the larger timestamp, 42.004, while x = 2 has 42.003. Yet x = 2 clearly happened later. When node 2 receives both writes, it decides that x = 1 is the more recent value, and it throws away x = 2. Client B’s increment is lost.

The conflict resolution strategy used here is called last write wins (LWW). The write with the highest timestamp is kept and the others are discarded. LWW is widely used in multi-leader replication and in leaderless databases such as Cassandra and Riak. Some systems create timestamps on the client rather than the server, but that does not fix the basic problems with LWW:

  • Writes can disappear. A node with a slow clock cannot overwrite values written by a node with a fast clock until the clock skew between them has passed. This can silently drop arbitrary amounts of data, with no error reported to the application.
  • Sequential and concurrent writes look the same. LWW cannot tell apart writes that happened one after another in quick succession, like client B’s increment in the example, and writes that were truly concurrent, where neither writer knew about the other. Extra causality tracking, such as version vectors, is needed to avoid violating causality.
  • Ties. Two nodes can generate the same timestamp, especially when the clock has only millisecond resolution. You need a tiebreaker, which can be a large random number, but that approach can also violate causality.

So even though it is tempting to keep the most recent value and discard the rest, the definition of recent depends on a local time-of-day clock, which may well be wrong. Even with tightly synchronized clocks, a packet could be sent at 100 ms by the sender’s clock and arrive at 99 ms by the recipient’s clock. That would make it look as if the packet arrived before it was sent, which is impossible.

Could NTP be made accurate enough to rule out such wrong orderings? The book says probably not. NTP’s accuracy is limited by the network round-trip time, along with other errors such as quartz drift. For correct ordering, the clock would need to be far more accurate than the thing you are measuring, which is the network delay.

Logical clocks are a safer way to order events. They are based on counters that go up, rather than on an oscillating quartz crystal. A logical clock does not measure the time of day or seconds elapsed. It only records whether one event happened before or after another. Time-of-day and monotonic clocks, which measure real elapsed time, are also called physical clocks. Chapter 9 looks at ordering in more detail.

Clock Readings Have a Confidence Interval

You may be able to read a machine’s time-of-day clock with microsecond or even nanosecond resolution. But a fine-grained reading does not mean the value is accurate to that precision. In fact, it most likely is not. The drift of an imprecise quartz clock can easily be several milliseconds, even if you sync with an NTP server on the local network every minute. With an NTP server on the public internet, the best accuracy is probably tens of milliseconds, and the error can spike to over 100 ms when the network is congested.

So it does not make sense to think of a clock reading as a single point in time. It is better to think of it as a range with a confidence interval. For example, a system might be 95 percent confident that the time now is between 10.3 and 10.5 seconds past the minute, but it cannot know any more precisely than that. If you only know the time to within plus or minus 100 ms, the microsecond digits in a timestamp are essentially meaningless.

The size of the uncertainty depends on your time source. If you have a GPS receiver or an atomic clock attached directly to your computer, the manufacturer reports the expected error range. If you get the time from a server, the uncertainty is based on three things: the quartz drift expected since your last sync, the uncertainty of the NTP server, and the network round-trip time to the server. That is a first approximation, and it assumes you trust the server.

Unfortunately, most systems do not expose this uncertainty. When you call clock_gettime(), the return value does not say what the expected error is. You cannot tell whether the confidence interval is five milliseconds or five years.

Google’s TrueTime API in Spanner is an interesting exception. It explicitly reports the confidence interval of the local clock. When you ask it for the time, you get two values, [earliest, latest]. These are the earliest and latest possible times. Based on its uncertainty calculations, the clock knows the actual current time lies somewhere in that interval. How wide the interval is depends, among other things, on how long it has been since the local quartz clock was last synchronized with a more accurate source.

Key idea

A clock reading is not a point in time. It is a range, and the honest question is how wide that range is. Most clocks do not say, so you cannot trust a timestamp to be more precise than its error bound.

Synchronized Clocks for Global Snapshots

Chapter 7 discussed snapshot isolation, a feature that lets read-only transactions see the database in a consistent state at one point in time, without locking out read-write transactions. It is very useful for backups and analytics that run for a long time.

The most common way to implement snapshot isolation uses a transaction ID that always increases. A write with a higher transaction ID than the snapshot is invisible to that snapshot. On a single node, a simple counter is enough to generate these IDs.

But when a database is spread across many machines, possibly in several data centers, a single global counter is hard to build, because generating it requires coordination. The IDs also have to reflect causality. If transaction B reads a value written by transaction A, then B must have a higher ID than A. Otherwise the snapshot would not be consistent. With lots of small, fast transactions, generating IDs in a distributed system becomes an unbearable bottleneck. The book adds that distributed sequence generators, such as Twitter’s Snowflake, can produce roughly increasing unique IDs at scale, but they usually cannot guarantee an order that matches causality.

Could we use timestamps from synchronized time-of-day clocks as transaction IDs? If the synchronization were good enough, the IDs would have the right properties. Later transactions would have higher timestamps. The problem is the uncertainty about clock accuracy.

Spanner does exactly this across data centers, using the confidence interval from TrueTime. The key observation is simple. Take two confidence intervals, each with an earliest and a latest possible time. Call them A and B. If the two intervals do not overlap, so that A ends before B begins, then B definitely happened after A. There can be no doubt. Only when the intervals overlap are we unsure which came first.

Example

Work through the figure below. Interval A covers part of the time line, and interval B lies entirely after it, with a gap in between. Spanner can be sure B happened after A. Now look at intervals C and D. They overlap in the middle, so Spanner cannot say which one happened first.

To make transaction timestamps reflect causality, Spanner deliberately waits for the length of the confidence interval before it commits a read-write transaction. The wait ensures that any transaction that might later read the data has a sufficiently later time, so their confidence intervals do not overlap. To keep the wait short, the clock uncertainty must also be small. For this reason Google deploys a GPS receiver or an atomic clock in each data center, which keeps clocks synchronized to within about 7 ms.

The book says using synchronized clocks for distributed transaction semantics is an active research area. These ideas are interesting, but outside Google they have not yet made it into mainstream databases.

Process Pauses

Here is another example of dangerous clock use. Say you have a database with a single leader per partition, and only the leader may accept writes. How does a node know that it is still the leader, meaning the other nodes have not declared it dead, so that it can safely accept writes?

One option is for the leader to obtain a lease from the other nodes. A lease is similar to a lock with a timeout. Only one node can hold the lease at a time. When a node gets the lease, it knows it is the leader for a set amount of time, until the lease expires. To stay leader, the node must renew the lease periodically, before it expires. If the node fails, it stops renewing, and another node can take over when the lease runs out.

The book sketches the request-handling loop of such a leader like this:

while (true) {
  request = getIncomingRequest();
  // Ensure that the lease always has at least 10 seconds remaining
  if (lease.expiryTimeMillis - System.currentTimeMillis() < 10000) {
    lease = lease.renew();
  }
  if (lease.isValid()) {
    process(request);
  }
}

The book points out two problems with this code. Walk through them in order.

The first problem is that the code relies on synchronized clocks. The expiry time on the lease is set by a different machine. That machine might calculate it as the current time plus 30 seconds. But the expiry is compared with the local system clock. If the two clocks are out of sync by more than a few seconds, the code starts doing strange things.

The second problem remains even if we switch to a monotonic clock on the local machine. The code assumes that very little time passes between the moment it checks the lease and the moment it processes the request. Normally that is true, so the 10-second buffer is more than enough. But what if the program pauses unexpectedly? Imagine the thread stops for 15 seconds right around the lease.isValid() check, then carries on. By the time it processes the request, the lease has probably expired, and another node has already taken over as leader. Nothing tells the thread that it was paused for so long. The code will not notice the expired lease until the next loop iteration, by which time it may already have done something unsafe.

Example

Put the two problems together with numbers, as an illustration. Suppose the lease has 12 seconds left when the loop checks it. That is more than 10 seconds, so the code does not renew. The check of isValid() returns true. Then the thread is frozen for 15 seconds, perhaps by a garbage collection pause. When it wakes up, the lease expired 3 seconds ago. Another node is the leader now. But process(request) runs anyway, because the thread has no idea that time has passed.

Is it crazy to assume a thread might pause that long? Unfortunately, it is not. The book lists several ways it can happen:

  • Garbage collection. Many language runtimes, such as the Java Virtual Machine, have a garbage collector that sometimes has to stop all running threads. These stop-the-world pauses have been known to last several minutes. Even so-called concurrent collectors, such as the HotSpot JVM’s CMS, still have to stop the world from time to time. Pauses can often be reduced by changing allocation patterns or tuning settings, but if you want robust guarantees, you must assume the worst.
  • Virtual machine suspension. A virtual machine can be suspended, which pauses all its processes and saves its memory to disk, and later resumed. This can happen at any point and last any length of time. It is sometimes used for live migration of a VM from one host to another without a reboot. The length of the pause then depends on how fast the processes are writing to memory.
  • Laptops. On end-user devices, execution can be suspended and resumed at any time, for example when you close a laptop lid.
  • Context switches and steal time. When the operating system switches to another thread, or the hypervisor switches to another VM, the running thread can be paused at any point. The CPU time spent in other VMs is called steal time. On a heavily loaded machine with a long queue of threads, a paused thread may wait a long time to run again.
  • Disk access. If the application does synchronous disk access, a thread may pause while a slow disk operation completes. Disk access can also happen when the code does not seem to mention files. For example, the Java class loader loads class files lazily, the first time they are used. I/O pauses and GC pauses can even combine. If the disk is a network filesystem or a network block device, such as Amazon’s EBS, the I/O delay also varies with the network.
  • Paging. If the operating system allows swapping memory to disk, a simple memory access can cause a page fault, and the thread waits while a page is read from disk. Under high memory pressure, the system can spend most of its time swapping pages in and out and get little real work done. This is called thrashing. To avoid it, paging is often disabled on server machines, since it is better to kill a process than risk thrashing.
  • Signals. A Unix process can be paused by sending it the SIGSTOP signal, for example by pressing Ctrl-Z in a shell. It stops getting CPU time until it is resumed with SIGCONT, and then it carries on where it left off. Even if your environment does not normally use SIGSTOP, an operations engineer might send it by accident.

All of these can preempt a running thread at any point and resume it later, without the thread noticing. The problem is similar to making multi-threaded code on one machine thread-safe. You cannot assume anything about timing, because arbitrary context switches and parallel execution can happen.

On a single machine, we have good tools for thread safety, such as mutexes, semaphores, atomic counters, lock-free data structures, and blocking queues. These do not translate directly to distributed systems. A distributed system has no shared memory. It has only messages sent over an unreliable network.

So a node in a distributed system must assume its execution can pause for a significant time at any point, even in the middle of a function. During that pause, the rest of the world keeps moving, and may even declare the paused node dead. Eventually the node continues running, without noticing that it slept, until it checks the clock later.

Response Time Guarantees

In many programming languages and operating systems, threads and processes can pause for an unbounded amount of time. Those reasons for pausing can be eliminated if you try hard enough.

Some software runs where failing to respond within a specified time can cause serious damage. Computers that control aircraft, rockets, robots, and cars must respond quickly and predictably to sensor input. The software has a deadline, and missing it may cause the whole system to fail. These are called hard real-time systems.

Watch out

In embedded systems, real-time means a system is carefully designed and tested to meet timing guarantees in all circumstances. On the web, the word is used more loosely, for servers pushing data to clients, or for stream processing without hard response time limits. The book’s sense is the strict one.

Take a car’s airbag. If sensors detect a crash, you do not want the airbag release to be delayed by an inopportune garbage collection pause in the airbag software.

Providing real-time guarantees needs support from every level of the software stack. You need a real-time operating system that can schedule processes with a guaranteed share of CPU time at set intervals. Library functions must document their worst-case execution times. Dynamic memory allocation may be restricted or banned entirely. Real-time garbage collectors exist, but the application must still make sure it does not give the collector too much work. And a huge amount of testing and measurement is needed to confirm the guarantees hold.

All of this costs a lot more work, and it sharply limits which programming languages, libraries, and tools you can use, since most of them give no real-time guarantees. That is why real-time development is expensive, and why it is mostly used in safety-critical embedded devices. Real-time is also not the same as high performance. Real-time systems may have lower throughput, because they must put timely responses ahead of everything else. The book links back to the idea that resource sharing makes performance vary.

For most server-side data processing systems, real-time guarantees are neither economical nor suitable. So these systems have to live with the pauses and clock instability that come from running in a non-real-time environment.

Limiting the Impact of Garbage Collection

The bad effects of process pauses can be reduced without expensive real-time scheduling. Language runtimes have some freedom in when they schedule garbage collection. They can track how fast objects are allocated and how much free memory is left over time.

One emerging idea is to treat a GC pause like a brief, planned outage of a node. While one node collects its garbage, the other nodes handle the clients’ requests. If the runtime can warn the application that a GC pause is coming soon, the application can stop sending new requests to that node. It waits for the requests in progress to finish, and then runs the GC while no requests are active. This hides GC pauses from clients and reduces the high percentiles of response time. Some latency-sensitive financial trading systems use this approach.

A variant is to use the garbage collector only for short-lived objects, which are fast to collect. The process is restarted periodically, before it accumulates enough long-lived objects to need a full collection. One node is restarted at a time, and traffic is moved away from it before the planned restart, in the same way as a rolling upgrade from Chapter 4.

These measures cannot fully prevent garbage collection pauses. But they can usefully reduce their impact on the application.

Knowledge, Truth, and Lies

So far the chapter has covered how distributed systems differ from programs on a single computer. There is no shared memory. There is only message passing over an unreliable network with variable delays. And the systems suffer from partial failures, unreliable clocks, and process pauses.

The results are disorienting if you are not used to distributed systems. A node cannot know anything for sure. It can only make guesses from the messages it receives, or does not receive, over the network. A node can learn the state of another node, such as what data it has stored or whether it is working correctly, only by exchanging messages with it. If a remote node does not respond, there is no way to know its state. Problems in the network cannot reliably be told apart from problems at the node.

This leads to some philosophical questions. What do we know to be true or false in our system? How sure can we be of that knowledge, if our ways of sensing and measuring are unreliable? Should software obey the laws we expect of the physical world, such as cause and effect?

We do not need to solve the meaning of life to build a working system. In a distributed system, we can state the assumptions we make about behavior, which is called the system model, and design the system so that it meets those assumptions. Algorithms can be proved to work correctly within a given system model. So reliable behavior is achievable, even when the underlying model promises very little.

However, making software well behaved in an unreliable system model is not simple. The rest of this chapter explores knowledge and truth in distributed systems. That helps us think about which assumptions we can make and which guarantees we want to provide. Chapter 9 then looks at algorithms that give particular guarantees under particular assumptions.

The Truth Is Defined by the Majority

Imagine a network with an asymmetric fault. A node can receive every message sent to it, but the messages it sends out are dropped or delayed. The node is working perfectly well and receives requests from other nodes. But the other nodes never hear its responses. After some timeout, they declare it dead. The book describes this as a nightmare. The node is carried off to the graveyard, insisting that it is alive, and nobody can hear it, so the funeral goes on regardless.

Example

The book gives three scenarios, and each one shows a node that cannot trust its own view.

Scenario one: the silent node. The node receives messages but its replies vanish. The other nodes time out and declare it dead. The node insists it is fine, but no one can hear it.

Scenario two: the node that notices. In a less nightmarish version, the node sees that its own messages are not being acknowledged, so it realizes there must be a network fault. But the other nodes still declare it dead, and the node cannot do anything about it.

Scenario three: the long pause. A node hits a long stop-the-world garbage collection pause that lasts a full minute. All its threads are frozen, so it processes no requests and sends no responses. The other nodes wait, retry, grow impatient, and eventually declare the node dead. Then the garbage collection finishes, and the node carries on as if nothing happened. The other nodes are surprised to see the supposedly dead node rejoin, fully healthy and chatting cheerfully. The node does not even realize that a minute has gone by, because from its point of view hardly any time has passed.

The moral of these stories is that a node cannot necessarily trust its own judgment. A distributed system cannot rely on a single node, because any node may fail at any time, which could leave the system stuck and unable to recover.

Instead, many distributed algorithms rely on a quorum, which is a vote among the nodes. A decision needs a minimum number of votes from several nodes, so the system does not depend on any one node. The book covers quorums for reading and writing in Chapter 5.

That includes decisions to declare a node dead. If a quorum of nodes declares another node dead, the node must be considered dead, even if it still feels very much alive. The individual node must accept the quorum’s decision and step down.

Usually the quorum is an absolute majority, meaning more than half of the nodes, although other kinds of quorums are possible. A majority quorum lets the system keep working when some nodes fail. With three nodes, one failure can be tolerated. With five nodes, two failures can be tolerated. It is also safe. There can be only one majority in the system, so two majorities cannot reach conflicting decisions at the same time. The book says consensus algorithms that use quorums are covered in Chapter 9.

The Leader and the Lock

Many systems need exactly one of something. For example:

  • Only one node may be the leader for a database partition. Two leaders would cause split brain, where two nodes both accept conflicting writes.
  • Only one transaction or client may hold the lock on a resource or object. That prevents two writers from corrupting it.
  • Only one user may register a particular username, because a username must uniquely identify a user.

Doing this in a distributed system takes care. Even if a node believes it is the chosen one, whether that is the leader of the partition, the holder of the lock, or the handler of the user who grabbed the username, that does not mean a quorum agrees. A node may once have been the leader. But if the other nodes declared it dead in the meantime, because of a network interruption or a GC pause, it may have been demoted, and another leader may already have been elected.

If such a node keeps acting as the chosen one, it may cause trouble in a system that is not carefully designed. It can send messages to other nodes in its self-appointed role. If the other nodes believe it, the system as a whole may do something wrong.

The book gives an example of a data corruption bug caused by a wrong implementation of locking. HBase used to have this problem. Say you want to make sure a file in a storage service is accessed by only one client at a time, because if several clients wrote to it, it would be corrupted. You try to do this by requiring each client to obtain a lease from a lock service before it touches the file.

Example

Here is the failure in Figure 8-4, step by step. Client 1 obtains the lease on the file. Then client 1 is paused for too long, perhaps by a long GC pause. The lease expires. Client 2 obtains a lease on the same file and starts writing to it. Then client 1 comes back. It believes, incorrectly, that its lease is still valid, so it goes ahead and writes to the file too. The two clients’ writes clash, and the file is corrupted.

This is the process-pause problem from earlier in the chapter. The client that holds the lease can be paused for too long, and when it returns, it does not know that its lease has expired.

Fencing Tokens

When a lock or lease protects access to a resource, such as the file storage in Figure 8-4, we need to ensure that a node holding a false belief about being the chosen one cannot disrupt the rest of the system. A simple technique for this is called fencing.

Assume that every time the lock server grants a lock or lease, it also returns a fencing token. This is a number that increases every time a lock is granted. The lock service might increment it each time. Then every write sent to the storage service must include the client’s current fencing token.

Example

The book walks through Figure 8-5. Client 1 acquires the lease with a token of 33. Then it goes into a long pause, and the lease expires. Client 2 acquires the lease with a token of 34. The number always increases. Client 2 sends its write to the storage service, including the token 34. Later, client 1 wakes up and sends its write, including its old token 33. The storage server remembers that it has already processed a write with a higher token, 34. So it rejects the request with token 33. Client 1’s stale write is blocked.

The lock server does the numbering, and the storage server does the checking. Storage must actively check tokens by rejecting any write with an older token than one it has already processed. It is not enough for clients to check their own lock status, because a paused client does not know its lock has gone.

Some resources do not support fencing tokens directly. You may still be able to work around that. For a file storage service, for example, you could include the fencing token in the file name. But some kind of check is necessary, so that requests outside the lock’s protection are not processed.

ZooKeeper, a lock service, can supply this kind of number. Its transaction ID, called zxid, or its node version, called cversion, is guaranteed to increase monotonically, so either one can serve as a fencing token.

Checking tokens on the server may sound like extra burden. But the book argues it is a good thing. A service should not assume its clients will always behave well. Clients are often run by people whose priorities differ from the people who run the service. So any service should protect itself from accidentally abusive clients.

Try it

A client holds a lock and writes to a file storage service. Suppose the storage service has no fencing check at all. Describe the order of events that would let an old client overwrite a newer client’s write. Then describe what one extra check on the storage server, comparing tokens, would change.

Byzantine Faults

Fencing tokens can catch and block a node that is acting by mistake, for example because it has not yet found out its lease has expired. But if a node wanted to subvert the system deliberately, it could easily send messages with a fake fencing token.

In this book, the working assumption is that nodes are unreliable but honest. They may be slow or never respond, because of a fault. Their state may be outdated, because of a GC pause or network delay. But if a node does respond, it is telling the truth to the best of its knowledge. It is playing by the rules of the protocol.

Distributed systems problems become much harder if nodes may lie, meaning they send arbitrary faulty or corrupted responses. For example, a node might claim to have received a message when it did not. Such behavior is called a Byzantine fault. Reaching agreement in this untrusting environment is known as the Byzantine Generals Problem.

The Byzantine Generals Problem

The Byzantine Generals Problem generalizes the Two Generals Problem. In that puzzle, two army generals need to agree on a battle plan. They camp at two different sites and can only communicate by messenger, and the messengers may be delayed or lost, just like packets on a network. Chapter 9 discusses this problem of consensus in more detail.

In the Byzantine version, there are n generals who need to agree, and some of them are traitors. Most generals are loyal and send truthful messages. The traitors may try to deceive and confuse the others by sending fake messages, while staying hidden. Nobody knows in advance who the traitors are.

The name is a joke about history. Byzantium was an ancient Greek city that later became Constantinople, now Istanbul. There is no evidence that its generals were any more prone to conspiracy than others. The word Byzantine was used in politics for something excessively complicated, bureaucratic, and devious, long before computers. The author, Leslie Lamport, wanted a nationality that would not offend readers, and was advised that naming the problem after a real nationality would be a poor choice.

A system is Byzantine fault-tolerant if it keeps operating correctly even when some nodes malfunction and do not obey the protocol, or when malicious attackers interfere with the network. The book names two situations where this matters:

  • Aerospace. In a spacecraft or aircraft, radiation can corrupt data in a computer’s memory or CPU register. The computer may then respond to other nodes in unpredictable ways. Because a failure would be very expensive, such as an aircraft crashing or a rocket colliding with the International Space Station, flight control systems must tolerate Byzantine faults.
  • Organizations that do not trust each other. Where several organizations take part, some may try to cheat or defraud others. A node cannot simply trust messages from another party if they might be sent with bad intent. Peer-to-peer networks such as Bitcoin and other blockchains are one way to get mutually distrusting parties to agree on whether a transaction happened, without a central authority.

In the kinds of systems this book discusses, the book usually assumes there are no Byzantine faults. In your data center, all the nodes are controlled by your organization, so they can hopefully be trusted. Radiation levels are low enough that memory corruption is not a major problem. Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols are quite complicated, and fault-tolerant embedded systems rely on support from the hardware. For most server-side data systems, the cost of deploying Byzantine fault tolerance makes it impractical.

Web applications, however, must expect arbitrary and malicious behavior from clients under end-user control, such as web browsers. That is why input validation, sanitization, and output escaping matter so much, to prevent attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. But the book notes that we normally do not use Byzantine fault-tolerant protocols for this. Instead, the server is made the authority on what client behavior is allowed. In peer-to-peer networks, where there is no such central authority, Byzantine fault tolerance is more relevant.

Example

A software bug can also be seen as a Byzantine fault. But if you deploy the same software to every node, a Byzantine fault-tolerant algorithm cannot save you. These algorithms usually need a supermajority, meaning more than two-thirds of the nodes, to be working correctly. With four nodes, at most one may malfunction. To defend against a bug this way, you would need four independent implementations of the same software, and hope that the bug appears in only one of them.

Security is similar. You might hope a protocol could protect you from vulnerabilities, security breaches, and malicious attacks. The book says this is not realistic either. In most systems, if an attacker can compromise one node, they can probably compromise all of them, because they are running the same software. So traditional tools, including authentication, access control, encryption, and firewalls, remain the main protection against attackers.

Weak Forms of Lying

Although the book assumes nodes are generally honest, it can be worth adding mechanisms that guard against weak forms of lying. These include invalid messages caused by hardware problems, software bugs, and misconfiguration. Such protections do not amount to full Byzantine fault tolerance, since they would not stop a determined attacker. But they are simple, practical steps toward better reliability. The book gives three examples:

  • Corrupted packets. Packets sometimes get corrupted by hardware faults or by bugs in operating systems, drivers, and routers. Corrupted packets are usually caught by the checksums built into TCP and UDP, but sometimes they slip through. Simple checksums in your own application-level protocol are usually enough protection.
  • Input from outside. A public application must carefully check all user input. For example, it should confirm that a value is within a reasonable range, and limit the size of strings so that a large input cannot cause denial of service through huge memory allocations. An internal service behind a firewall may get away with less strict checks, but basic sanity checks, such as in protocol parsing, are a good idea.
  • Several time servers. An NTP client can be configured with several server addresses. When it synchronizes, it contacts all of them, estimates their errors, and checks that a majority of servers agree on a time range. As long as most servers are healthy, a misconfigured server that reports a wrong time is detected as an outlier and excluded. Using several servers makes NTP more robust than using just one.

System Model and Reality

Many algorithms have been designed to solve distributed systems problems. For example, Chapter 9 examines solutions to the consensus problem. To be useful, these algorithms must tolerate the faults of distributed systems described in this chapter. They also must not depend too heavily on the details of the hardware and software they run on.

That means we need to formalize the kinds of faults we expect. We do this by defining a system model. It is an abstraction that describes what an algorithm may assume. Timing assumptions fall into three system models that are in common use.

  • Synchronous model. This model assumes bounded network delay, bounded process pauses, and bounded clock error. It does not imply that clocks are exactly synchronized or that delay is zero. It only means that you know network delay, pauses, and clock drift will never exceed some fixed upper bound. The book says this is not a realistic model of most practical systems, because unbounded delays and pauses do occur.
  • Partially synchronous model. Here, a system behaves like a synchronous one most of the time, but sometimes it exceeds the bounds for network delay, process pauses, and clock drift. The book calls this a realistic model of many systems. Most of the time networks and processes behave well, otherwise nothing would ever get done. But any timing assumption may be shattered now and then. When that happens, delay, pauses, and clock error may become arbitrarily large.
  • Asynchronous model. The algorithm is not allowed to make any timing assumptions. It does not even have a clock, so it cannot use timeouts. Some algorithms can be designed for this model, but it is very restrictive.

Besides timing, we must consider node failures. The book lists three common models for nodes:

  • Crash-stop faults. A node can fail in only one way, by crashing. It may suddenly stop responding at any moment, and after that it is gone forever. It never comes back.
  • Crash-recovery faults. A node may crash at any moment and may start responding again after some unknown time. Its stable storage, meaning nonvolatile disk storage, survives the crash. But its in-memory state is assumed to be lost.
  • Byzantine (arbitrary) faults. A node may do absolutely anything, including trying to trick and deceive other nodes.

For modeling real systems, the partially synchronous model with crash-recovery faults is generally the most useful. The table below sums up the three timing models.

Timing modelWhat it assumesHow realistic
SynchronousKnown upper bounds on delay, pauses, and clock errorNot realistic. Unbounded delays and pauses do occur.
Partially synchronousBounds hold most of the time, and sometimes break badlyRealistic for many systems, and the usual choice for modeling.
AsynchronousNo timing assumptions, and no clock, so no timeoutsPossible to design for, but very restrictive.

Correctness of an Algorithm

To say an algorithm is correct, we can describe its properties. The book uses sorting as a simple example. A sorted output has the property that, for any two distinct elements, the element further to the left is smaller than the one further to the right. That is just a formal way of saying the list is sorted.

In the same way, we can write down the properties we want from a distributed algorithm. For example, if we are generating fencing tokens for a lock, we may require three properties:

  • Uniqueness. No two requests for a fencing token return the same value.
  • Monotonic sequence. If request x returned token tx, and request y returned token ty, and x completed before y began, then tx is less than ty.
  • Availability. A node that requests a fencing token and does not crash eventually receives a response.

An algorithm is correct in a system model if it always satisfies its properties in all the situations that the model says may occur. But this raises a question. If all nodes crash, or every network delay suddenly becomes infinitely long, then no algorithm can get anything done. The model has to allow for that.

Safety and Liveness

To make this clearer, the book separates two kinds of properties. In the fencing example, uniqueness and monotonic sequence are safety properties. Availability is a liveness property. A clue is that liveness properties often include the word eventually in their definition. And yes, the book notes, eventual consistency is a liveness property.

Safety is often described informally as nothing bad happening, and liveness as something good eventually happening. The book warns not to read too much into these phrases, because what counts as good or bad is subjective. The real definitions are precise and mathematical.

  • If a safety property is violated, you can point to a particular moment when it broke. For example, if uniqueness is violated, you can identify the exact operation that returned a duplicate token. Once a safety property is violated, the violation cannot be undone. The damage is done.
  • A liveness property works the other way round. It may not hold at some point in time. For example, a node may have sent a request but not yet received a response. But there is always hope that it will be satisfied in the future, by a response arriving.

This distinction helps us with difficult system models. For distributed algorithms, it is common to require that safety properties always hold, in every possible situation of the model. Even if all nodes crash, or the whole network fails, the algorithm must not return a wrong result. Liveness properties are allowed caveats. For example, we could say that a request needs a response only if a majority of nodes have not crashed, and only if the network eventually recovers from an outage. The partially synchronous model requires that the system eventually returns to a synchronous state. Any network interruption lasts only a finite time and is then repaired.

Mapping System Models to the Real World

Safety and liveness, along with system models, are very useful for reasoning about whether a distributed algorithm is correct. But when you implement an algorithm in practice, the messy facts of reality come back to bite. The system model turns out to be a simplified abstraction of reality.

For example, algorithms in the crash-recovery model usually assume that data in stable storage survives crashes. But what happens if data on disk is corrupted, or wiped out by a hardware error or a misconfiguration? What happens if a server has a firmware bug and fails to recognize its hard drives on reboot, even though the drives are attached correctly?

Quorum algorithms rely on each node remembering the data it claims to have stored. If a node suffers from amnesia and forgets data it stored earlier, the quorum condition breaks, and so does the algorithm’s correctness. The book suggests that a new system model might be needed, one in which stable storage mostly survives crashes but sometimes gets lost. But that model is harder to reason about.

A theoretical description can declare that certain things are simply assumed not to happen. In non-Byzantine systems, we do have to assume some faults cannot happen. But a real implementation may still need code for the case where something happens that was supposed to be impossible. The book notes that even this handling may boil down to printing a message and exiting, so that a human operator can clean up the mess. The book says this is arguably the difference between computer science and software engineering.

That does not make theoretical system models worthless. Quite the opposite. They help distill the complexity of real systems into a manageable set of faults that we can reason about. That lets us understand a problem and attack it systematically. We can prove an algorithm correct by showing its properties always hold in some system model.

A proof does not guarantee that the implementation will always behave correctly on a real system. But it is a very good first step. Theoretical analysis can uncover problems in an algorithm that might stay hidden for a long time in a real system, and only bite when a timing assumption is broken by unusual circumstances. The book concludes that theoretical analysis and empirical testing are equally important.

Summary

Summary
