  • Packets. A packet sent over the network may be lost or arbitrarily delayed. The reply may be lost or delayed too. So if you get no reply, you have no idea whether the message got through.
  • Clocks. A node’s clock may be far out of sync with other nodes, even with NTP. It may suddenly jump forward or back in time. Relying on it is dangerous, because you most likely do not have a good measure of its error interval.
  • Processes. A process may pause for a long time at any point, for example during a stop-the-world garbage collector run. Other nodes may declare it dead, and then it may come back to life without realizing that it was paused.
  • Partial failure. These partial failures are the defining feature of distributed systems. Whenever software does anything that involves other nodes, it may fail, go slow at random, or not respond at all, and eventually time out. We try to build software that tolerates partial failure, so the whole system keeps working even when some parts are broken.
  • Detection is hard. The first step in tolerating faults is detecting them, and even that is hard. Most systems have no accurate way to tell whether a node has failed. So algorithms rely on timeouts. But timeouts cannot tell network failures from node failures, and variable delays can make a healthy node look like it has crashed. Nodes can also be degraded, or limping, which is harder to handle than a clean failure. The book gives the example of a gigabit network card that drops to 1 Kb/s because of a driver bug.
  • Tolerating faults is hard too. There is no global variable, no shared memory, and no common knowledge between machines. Nodes cannot even agree on what time it is. Information flows only by sending it over the unreliable network. No single node can safely make a major decision alone. We need protocols that enlist the help of other nodes and try to reach a quorum agreement.
  • Keep it on one machine if you can. A single computer can do a great deal these days, and distributed systems engineers often regard a problem as trivial if it can be solved on one computer. Avoid opening that box if you can. But scalability is not the only reason to distribute. Fault tolerance and low latency, by placing data near users, cannot be achieved with a single node.
  • Not a law of nature. The book explored whether unreliable networks, clocks, and processes are unavoidable. They are not. Hard real-time guarantees and bounded delays are possible, but they are very expensive and leave hardware less utilized. Most non-safety-critical systems choose cheap and unreliable over expensive and reliable.
  • Supercomputers and services. A supercomputer assumes reliable parts, so when one component fails, the whole job stops and restarts. A distributed system can, in theory, run forever without interruption at the service level, because faults and maintenance can be handled node by node. In practice, a bad configuration change rolled out to all nodes can still bring a distributed system to its knees.
  • Next steps. This chapter has been about problems and has been pessimistic on purpose. The next chapter moves on to solutions, with algorithms designed to cope with these problems.

Check yourself

  1. A client sends a write to a server and its request times out. Why can’t the client tell whether the server processed the write?

    Show answer

    The request might have been lost, the server might be down or slow, or the server might have processed the request and only the reply was lost or delayed. In an asynchronous network these cases look the same from the sender’s side. All the client knows is that no response has arrived yet.

  2. In the book’s clock example, node 3 writes x = 2 with timestamp 42.003, after node 1 wrote x = 1 with timestamp 42.004. Why does last write wins drop the later write?

    Show answer

    Last write wins keeps the write with the highest timestamp. Node 1’s timestamp is larger, so x = 1 looks more recent, even though x = 2 really happened later. The clocks were nearly synchronized, but a skew of a few milliseconds was enough to reverse the order, and client B’s increment was lost.

  3. A lease holder checks that its lease is still valid, and then pauses for 15 seconds before processing the request. What goes wrong, and how do fencing tokens prevent the damage?

    Show answer

    The lease may expire during the pause, and another node may become leader and write. The paused node does not notice until its next loop, so it may already have processed a stale request. With fencing tokens, the storage server remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects any write carrying an older token, so the stale write is blocked, even though the paused client believes it still holds the lease.

  4. Spanner waits for the length of a clock confidence interval before it commits a read-write transaction. Why is that wait needed?

    Show answer

    The wait makes sure that any later transaction has a timestamp interval that does not overlap with the earlier one. Non-overlapping intervals prove the order of the two transactions, so the timestamps reflect causality. The wait is kept short by keeping clock uncertainty small, using GPS receivers or atomic clocks in each data center.

Part II · Chapter 9

Consistency and Consensus

The big idea: a distributed system can promise stronger behavior, such as acting as if there were only one copy of the data. Those promises cost speed and availability. Getting several machines to agree on one answer, which is called consensus, is the foundation for many of these promises, and it is much harder than it looks.

In a distributed system, many things can go wrong, as Chapter 8 showed. The simplest response to a failure is to let the whole service fail and show the user an error message. If that is not acceptable, the system has to tolerate faults. That means it keeps working correctly even when some internal part is broken.

This chapter looks at algorithms and protocols for building fault-tolerant distributed systems. It assumes that every problem from Chapter 8 can happen. Packets can be lost, reordered, duplicated, or delayed for an arbitrary time. Clocks are approximate at best. Nodes (the individual machines in the system) can pause, for example during garbage collection, or crash at any moment.

The best way to build a fault-tolerant system is to find general-purpose abstractions with useful guarantees, implement them once, and let applications rely on them. Chapter 7 used this idea for transactions. Inside a transaction, the application can pretend that crashes do not happen (atomicity), that nobody else is touching the data at the same time (isolation), and that the disks never fail (durability). The crashes and disk failures still happen, but the transaction hides them.

The rest of this chapter looks for abstractions like that for distributed systems. One of the most important is consensus, which means getting all the nodes to agree on something. Reaching consensus, even when the network drops messages and processes fail, is a surprisingly tricky problem.

Once you have a working consensus implementation, applications can use it for many purposes. Take a database with single-leader replication, where one node accepts all the writes and the others copy them. If the leader dies, the database must fail over to another node. The remaining nodes can use consensus to elect a new leader. It is important that there is only one leader, and that all nodes agree who it is. If two nodes both believe they are the leader, that is called split brain, and it often leads to data loss. Correct consensus implementations help avoid this.

Later in the chapter, under “Distributed Transactions and Consensus,” the book looks at algorithms that solve consensus and related problems. First, though, it explores the range of guarantees and abstractions that a distributed system can offer. Some things can be done in the presence of faults, and some cannot. The limits have been studied in depth, both in theory and in practice. This chapter gives an overview of those limits.

Researchers have studied these topics for decades, so there is a lot of material and this chapter can only scratch the surface. The book does not go into the formal models and proofs. It sticks to informal intuition, and its references point to more depth for readers who want it.

Consistency Guarantees

Chapter 5 looked at timing issues in a replicated database, called replication lag. If you look at two database nodes at the same moment, you will often see different data on each. Write requests arrive at different nodes at different times. This happens no matter which replication method is used: single-leader, multi-leader, or leaderless.

Most replicated databases offer at least eventual consistency. This means that if you stop writing and wait long enough, all reads will eventually return the same value. The inconsistency is temporary, and it fixes itself, as long as network faults are also eventually repaired. The book notes that “convergence” would be a better name, because all the replicas converge to the same value.

However, eventual consistency is a very weak promise. It does not say when the replicas will converge. Until they do, reads could return almost anything, or nothing at all. For example, if you write a value and then read it right away, you may not see the value you just wrote. The read might be routed to a different replica that has not received the write yet. Chapter 5 called this the problem of reading your own writes.

Eventual consistency is hard for application developers because it behaves very differently from a variable in a normal single-threaded program. If you assign a value to a variable and read it a moment later, you expect the new value. You do not expect the old value, or an error. A database looks a bit like a variable that you can read and write, but its behavior is much more complicated.

When a database provides only weak guarantees, you have to stay constantly aware of its limits, or you will assume too much by accident. Bugs can be subtle and hard to find by testing, because the application works well most of the time. The edge cases of eventual consistency usually appear only when there is a fault, such as a network interruption, or when many requests arrive at once.

This chapter explores stronger consistency models that a data system can choose to provide. Stronger guarantees are not free. A system with stronger guarantees may be slower, or less fault-tolerant, than one with weaker guarantees. Still, strong guarantees are appealing because they are easier to use correctly. Once you have seen a few consistency models, you will be better placed to choose the one that fits your needs.

There is some similarity between distributed consistency models and the transaction isolation levels from Chapter 7. But they are mostly separate concerns. Transaction isolation is mainly about avoiding race conditions between transactions that run at the same time. Distributed consistency is mainly about keeping replicas in step with each other, in spite of delays and faults.

The chapter covers three linked areas. It starts with linearizability, one of the strongest consistency models in common use, and examines its pros and cons. Next it looks at how events are ordered in a distributed system, especially causality and total ordering. Last, it looks at how to commit a distributed transaction atomically. That final topic leads to the consensus problem.

Linearizability

In an eventually consistent database, if you ask two replicas the same question at the same time, you may get two different answers. That is confusing. It would be much simpler if the database gave the illusion that there is only one replica, meaning only one copy of the data. Then every client would see the same data, and nobody would have to worry about replication lag.

This idea is called linearizability. It is also known as atomic consistency, strong consistency, immediate consistency, or external consistency. The exact definition is subtle, and the rest of this section works through it. The basic idea is to make the system look as if there is only one copy of the data, and as if every operation on that copy is atomic (it happens all at once, with no partial state visible).

In a linearizable system, as soon as one client successfully finishes a write, every client that reads afterwards must see the value that was just written. The value read must be the most recent one. It cannot come from a stale cache or a lagging replica. In other words, linearizability is a recency guarantee. Here is an example of a system that is not linearizable.

Example

The book describes a sports website that was not linearizable. Alice and Bob are sitting in the same room, both checking their phones for the result of the 2014 FIFA World Cup final. Here is what happens, step by step:

  1. The final score is announced.
  2. Alice refreshes her page, sees the winner, and tells Bob excitedly.
  3. Bob hits reload on his own phone. His request goes to a database replica that is lagging behind.
  4. His phone still shows the game as in progress.

If Alice and Bob had reloaded at exactly the same moment, two different results would not be surprising, because neither could know exactly when the server handled each request. But Bob started his request after he heard Alice shout the score. So he expects his result to be at least as fresh as hers. His stale result breaks linearizability.

What Makes a System Linearizable?

The basic idea is simple: the system should look like a single copy of the data. But pinning down exactly what that means takes some care. The book uses a few more examples to make it precise.

Consider three clients reading and writing the same key x. In the research literature, a single value like this is called a register. In practice, it could be one key in a key-value store, one row in a relational database, or one document in a document database. The book’s picture shows only what the clients see, not the inside of the database. Each bar is one client request. The left end of the bar is when the request was sent, and the right end is when the reply arrived. Because network delays vary, a client never knows exactly when the database handled its request. It only knows that the handling happened somewhere between sending and receiving.

The register supports two kinds of operations:

  • read(x) ⇒ v means the client asked to read register x, and the database returned the value v.
  • write(x, v) ⇒ r means the client asked to set register x to the value v, and the database replied r, which is either ok or an error.

Now take a register x that starts at 0. Client C writes the value 1. While that happens, clients A and B keep polling the database to read the latest value. What can A and B see?

  • A read that finishes before the write begins must return the old value, 0.
  • A read that starts after the write has finished must return the new value, 1, if the database is linearizable. The write was handled at some point between its start and end. A read that starts after the write ended must be handled after the write, so it must see the new value.
  • Reads that overlap the write in time may return either 0 or 1. We cannot tell whether the write has already taken effect when the read is handled. These reads are called concurrent with the write.

That is still not enough. If reads that overlap a write can return either the old or the new value, readers could see the value flip back and forth between 0 and 1 several times while the write is in progress. That is not what we expect from a system that imitates a single copy of the data. (A register that behaves this way, where overlapping reads may return old or new, is known as a regular register. It is weaker than linearizable.)

To fix this, linearizability adds one more rule. Once any read has returned the new value, every later read, from the same client or any other, must also return the new value. Imagine that at some moment between the start and end of the write, the value of x flips atomically from 0 to 1. Once a read has seen the 1, all reads after that point must see the 1, even if the write has not formally finished.

Here is how that plays out. Client A is the first to read the new value 1. Just after A’s read returns, client B starts a new read. Because B’s read starts after A’s read has finished, B must also return 1, even though C’s write is still in progress. This is the same situation as Alice and Bob. Once Alice has seen the new result, Bob must see it too.

Key idea

Linearizability means once any client has read a new value, every later read must return that value or something newer. The system must look as if there is only one copy of the data.

The next picture shows exactly where each operation takes effect. The timeline below is the same idea in a simpler form. One client writes, and two others read. A read that starts after another read has already seen the new value must also return the new value. The highlighted bar is the bad outcome.

The book then shows a more complex case, in which a third kind of operation is added: a compare-and-set, written cas(x, vold, vnew) ⇒ r. A compare-and-set is an atomic operation. If the current value of x equals v_old, the database sets it to v_new. If x is not equal to v_old, the register is left alone and the operation returns an error. Here r is the database’s reply, ok or error.

In this more detailed picture, each operation has a marker at the moment it seems to have taken effect. If you join the markers in order, the result must be a valid sequence for a register. Each read must return the value set by the most recent write before it. Linearizability also requires that the joined line always moves forward in time, never backward. That is what guarantees recency: once a new value has been written or read, every later read sees that value until it is overwritten.

The book points out several details in that picture:

  • Client B sent its read first. Then client D sent a request to set x to 0, and then client A sent a request to set x to 1. Yet B’s read returns 1, the value A wrote. This is acceptable. It means the database handled D’s write first, then A’s write, then B’s read. The requests were concurrent, so this order is allowed. Perhaps B’s request was delayed in the network and only reached the database after both writes.
  • B’s read returned 1 before A received the database’s ok for its write. Again this is fine. It does not mean the value was read before it was written. The ok reply to A was just delayed on the way back.
  • This model does not assume any transaction isolation. Other clients can change the value at any time. For example, C first reads 1 and then reads 2, because B changed the value between C’s two reads. A compare-and-set can check that a value has not changed underneath you. B’s and C’s compare-and-set requests succeed. D’s fails, because by the time the database handled it, x was no longer 0.
  • The last read by B, shown in a shaded bar, is not linearizable. It overlaps with C’s compare-and-set, which changes x from 2 to 4. If there were no other requests, it would be fine for B’s read to return 2. However, client A has already read the new value 4 before B’s read began. So B is not allowed to return an older value than A saw. This is the same situation as Alice and Bob again.

That is the intuition behind linearizability, and the formal definition makes it more precise. It is possible, though expensive, to test whether a real system behaves linearizably. You record the timing of every request and reply, then check whether they can be arranged into a valid sequential order.

Linearizability Versus Serializability

Linearizability is easy to confuse with serializability, from Chapter 7. Both words seem to mean something like “the operations can be arranged in one sequential order.” But they are two different guarantees, and the difference matters.

Serializability is an isolation property of transactions. A transaction may read and write several objects, such as rows, documents, or records. Serializability guarantees that transactions behave as if they ran one after another, each running to completion before the next starts. The serial order may differ from the order in which the transactions actually ran.

Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of one register, which is a single object. It does not group operations into transactions. So it does not prevent problems like write skew, which Chapter 7 described, unless you take extra steps such as materializing conflicts.

A database can provide both properties, and the combination is called strict serializability or strong one-copy serializability (strong-1SR). Implementations of serializability based on two-phase locking, or on actual serial execution, are typically linearizable. Serializable snapshot isolation is not. It reads from a consistent snapshot to avoid lock contention between readers and writers. The whole point of a snapshot is that it does not include writes that are newer than the snapshot. So reads from the snapshot are not linearizable.

Trade-offs
PropertySerializabilityLinearizability
What it applies toTransactions that touch many objectsReads and writes of one register (one object)
GuaranteeResults match some one-at-a-time order of the transactions. That order may differ from the real order.Each operation takes effect at one point in time, in real time order, so reads see the latest write
Prevents write skew by itselfYes, when implemented as true serializabilityNo, because it does not group operations into transactions
Typical implementationsTwo-phase locking and actual serial execution are usually linearizable. Serializable snapshot isolation is not.Consensus-based coordination services and single-leader reads from the leader

Relying on Linearizability

When is linearizability actually needed? Checking the final score of a sports match is a light example. A result that is a few seconds out of date is unlikely to cause harm. But there are areas where linearizability is required for the system to work correctly.

Locking and leader election. A system with single-leader replication must make sure there is really only one leader, not several. One way to elect a leader is to use a lock. Every node that starts up tries to acquire the lock, and the one that succeeds becomes the leader. However the lock is implemented, it must be linearizable. All nodes must agree which node owns the lock, or the lock is useless. Coordination services such as Apache ZooKeeper and etcd are often used for distributed locks and leader election. They use consensus algorithms to offer linearizable operations in a fault-tolerant way. Consensus is covered later in this chapter. Implementing locks and leader election correctly still has many subtle details, such as the fencing issue described in Chapter 8. Libraries such as Apache Curator provide higher-level recipes on top of ZooKeeper. Still, a linearizable storage service is the basic foundation for these tasks.

Locks are also used at a much finer level in some distributed databases. Oracle Real Application Clusters (RAC) uses a lock per disk page, with several nodes sharing the same disk storage. Because these linearizable locks sit on the critical path of every transaction, RAC deployments usually have a dedicated network between the database nodes.

Constraints and uniqueness guarantees. Uniqueness constraints are common in databases. A username or email address must identify exactly one user. In a file storage service, two files cannot have the same path and name. If you want to enforce this as the data is written, so that when two people concurrently create a user or file with the same name, one of them gets an error, you need linearizability. This is similar to a lock. When someone registers a username, it is like acquiring a lock on that name. It is also similar to an atomic compare-and-set: set the username to this user’s ID, provided it is not already taken.

The same issue appears in other rules. A bank account balance must never go negative. You must not sell more items than the warehouse has in stock. Two people must not both book the same seat on a flight or in a theater. Each of these rules needs a single, up-to-date value, such as the account balance, the stock level, or the seat occupancy, that all nodes agree on.

In real applications, these rules are sometimes handled loosely. If a flight is overbooked, the airline can move customers to another flight and offer compensation. In that case linearizability may not be needed. The book returns to such loosely enforced rules in its discussion of timeliness and integrity. But a hard uniqueness constraint, like the one a relational database enforces, does require linearizability. Other constraints, such as foreign key references or simple attribute checks, can be implemented without linearizability.

Cross-channel timing dependencies. Look again at the football example. Bob only knew that his result was stale because there was a second channel of communication: Alice’s voice. If Alice had said nothing, Bob would have refreshed again and eventually seen the final score. The violation was noticed only because a second channel existed.

Computer systems have the same pattern. Imagine a website where users upload photos, and a background process resizes the photos to smaller thumbnails so they download faster. The web server instructs the image resizer through a message queue (Chapter 11 covers queues). The web server does not put the whole photo on the queue, because most message brokers are built for small messages, and a photo can be several megabytes. Instead, the photo is first written to a file storage service. Once that write completes, the instruction to resize it goes onto the queue.

If the file storage service is linearizable, the system works fine. If it is not, there is a race. The message queue, steps 3 and 4, might be faster than the internal replication inside the storage service. When the resizer fetches the image in step 5, it might see an old version of the photo, or no photo at all. If it resizes the old version, the full-size image and the thumbnail in storage are permanently inconsistent.

This problem happens because there are two communication channels: the file storage and the message queue. Without linearizability’s recency guarantee, the two channels can race. This is the same kind of race as in the Alice and Bob example, where the database replication and Alice’s voice were two channels.

Linearizability is not the only fix, but it is the simplest to understand. If you control the extra channel, as with the message queue but not with Alice’s voice, you can use other approaches. These are similar to the ideas for reading your own writes from Chapter 5, but they add complexity.

Implementing Linearizable Systems

Now that we have seen where linearizability helps, how might we build a system that offers it? The simplest answer, since linearizability means “behave as if there is one copy of the data,” is to really use only one copy. But a single copy cannot tolerate faults. If the node holding it fails, the data is lost, or at least unavailable until the node comes back.

The usual way to make a system fault-tolerant is replication, where copies of the data live on several nodes. The book compares the replication methods from Chapter 5 to see which can be made linearizable.

Single-leader replication: potentially linearizable. In a single-leader system, the leader holds the primary copy used for writes, and the followers keep backup copies. If you read from the leader, or from followers that are updated synchronously, reads have the potential to be linearizable. However, not every single-leader database is linearizable. Some are not by design, for example because they use snapshot isolation. Others fail because of concurrency bugs. Reading from the leader also assumes you know for sure who the leader is. A node can think it is the leader when it is not. If that deluded leader keeps serving requests, it is likely to break linearizability. With asynchronous replication, a failover can even lose committed writes, which breaks both durability and linearizability.

Consensus algorithms: linearizable. Some consensus algorithms, covered later in this chapter, look a lot like single-leader replication. But consensus protocols include measures against split brain and stale replicas. Because of these details, consensus algorithms can implement linearizable storage safely. ZooKeeper and etcd work this way.

Multi-leader replication: not linearizable. Systems with multiple leaders process writes concurrently on several nodes and replicate them asynchronously. That can produce conflicting writes that need to be resolved. Those conflicts exist only because there is no single copy of the data, so the system is not linearizable.

Leaderless replication: probably not linearizable. In Dynamo-style leaderless systems, some people claim “strong consistency” is possible by requiring quorum reads and writes, where w + r is greater than n. (Here n is the number of replicas, w is how many must confirm a write, and r is how many must answer a read.) Depending on the exact quorum setup, and on how you define strong consistency, this claim is not quite true. Last-write-wins conflict resolution based on time-of-day clocks, as in Cassandra, is almost certainly not linearizable, because clock timestamps cannot be guaranteed to match the real order of events. Sloppy quorums also rule out linearizability. Even strict quorums can be non-linearizable, as the next example shows.

Linearizability and Quorums

Intuitively, strict quorum reads and writes in a Dynamo-style system should be linearizable. But when network delays vary, race conditions can appear. The book’s example has these steps:

  1. The register x starts at 0. A writer client is setting x to 1 by sending the write to all three replicas (n = 3, w = 3).
  2. At the same time, client A reads from a quorum of two nodes (r = 2). It sees the new value 1 on one of those nodes.
  3. Also at the same time, client B reads from a different quorum of two nodes. It gets the old value 0 from both.

The quorum condition is met, since w + r is greater than n. Even so, this execution is not linearizable. B’s request begins after A’s request has finished, yet B returns the old value while A returned the new one. This is Alice and Bob once more.

It is possible to make Dynamo-style quorums linearizable, but at a cost in speed. A reader must perform read repair (a fix-up that writes the newest value back to stale replicas) synchronously, before it returns the result. A writer must read the latest state from a quorum of nodes before it sends its write. But Riak does not perform synchronous read repair, because of the performance penalty. Cassandra does wait for read repair to finish on quorum reads. However, it still loses linearizability when several writes to the same key happen concurrently, because it uses last-write-wins conflict resolution.

Also, only linearizable reads and writes can be built this way. A linearizable compare-and-set cannot, because it requires a consensus algorithm. So the safest assumption is that a leaderless system with Dynamo-style replication does not provide linearizability.

The Cost of Linearizability

Some replication methods can give linearizability and others cannot. It is worth looking at the costs of linearizability more closely. Chapter 5 described multi-leader replication as a good choice for multi-datacenter setups, where each datacenter has its own copy of the data. The following example shows what happens to linearizability when the links between datacenters fail.

Consider what happens if the network between the two datacenters is interrupted. Assume the network inside each datacenter still works, and clients can reach their local datacenter, but the two datacenters cannot connect to each other.

With a multi-leader database, each datacenter can keep working normally. Writes from one datacenter are replicated to the other asynchronously, so they simply queue up and are exchanged when the connection is restored.

With single-leader replication, the leader must be in one of the datacenters. All writes, and all linearizable reads, must go to that leader. So a client connected to the follower datacenter must send its requests synchronously across the network to the leader’s datacenter. When the network between datacenters is cut, clients near the follower cannot reach the leader. They cannot write, and they cannot do linearizable reads. They can still read from their local follower, but that data might be stale, which means it is not linearizable. If the application needs linearizable reads and writes, it becomes unavailable in the follower datacenter until the link is repaired. Clients that can reach the leader’s datacenter are not affected.

The CAP Theorem

This issue is not only a feature of single-leader and multi-leader replication. Any linearizable database has it, no matter how it is built. It is not specific to multi-datacenter setups either. It can happen on any unreliable network, even inside one datacenter. The trade-off looks like this:

Trade-offs
When the network splits replicasApplication needs linearizabilityApplication does not need linearizability
What a cut-off replica doesIt must wait for the network to be fixed, or return an error. Either way, it is unavailable.Each replica keeps processing requests on its own, for example in a multi-leader setup.
What the client getsCorrect, up-to-date answers, or no answerAn answer that is available now, but not linearizable

In short, applications that do not require linearizability can be more tolerant of network problems. This insight is popularly known as the CAP theorem. It is named after Eric Brewer, who introduced it in 2000, although designers of distributed databases had known the trade-off since the 1970s. Some people label the two choices CP (consistent but not available during a partition) and AP (available but not consistent during a partition). The book says that labeling scheme has several flaws, so it is best avoided.

CAP was first proposed as a rule of thumb, without precise definitions, to start a discussion about trade-offs in databases. At the time, many distributed databases tried to offer linearizable behavior on a cluster that shared storage. CAP encouraged database engineers to explore a wider design space of shared-nothing systems, where each node has its own storage. Those systems were better suited to large web services. The book credits CAP with this change in culture, which can be seen in the explosion of new database technologies since the mid-2000s, known as NoSQL.

The Unhelpful CAP Theorem

CAP is often summarized as three properties, consistency, availability, and partition tolerance, of which you can pick two. The book says this phrasing is misleading. A network partition is a kind of fault. So it is not something you can choose to avoid. Partitions will happen whether you like it or not.

When the network is working correctly, a system can provide both consistency (linearizability) and full availability. When a network fault occurs, you have to choose between linearizability and full availability. A better way to phrase CAP is: a system must be either consistent or available when partitioned. A more reliable network means you make this choice less often, but at some point the choice cannot be avoided.

The book also points out that “availability” has several contradictory definitions in the CAP discussion. The formal theorem does not match the usual meaning of the word. Many systems that call themselves “highly available” do not meet CAP’s particular definition. So there is a lot of misunderstanding around CAP. The book concludes that it does not help us understand systems better, and it is best avoided.

The formal CAP theorem is very narrow. It considers only one consistency model, linearizability, and one kind of fault, network partitions. A partition here means nodes that are alive but disconnected from each other. (The book uses the word “partitioning” elsewhere to mean splitting a dataset into smaller pieces, which is sharding in Chapter 6. A network partition is a different thing, but the P in CAP is the same word.) The formal theorem says nothing about network delays, dead nodes, or other trade-offs. So although CAP was historically influential, it has little practical value for designing systems. There are many more impossibility results in distributed systems, and CAP has since been replaced by more precise results. It is now mostly of historical interest.

Linearizability and Network Delays

Linearizability is useful, but surprisingly few systems actually provide it. Even the RAM in a modern multi-core CPU is not linearizable. If a thread on one core writes to a memory address, and a thread on another core reads that address shortly afterward, it is not guaranteed to see the value just written, unless a memory barrier (also called a fence) is used.

The reason is that each CPU core has its own cache and store buffer. A memory access goes to the cache first, and changes are written out to main memory asynchronously. Reading from the cache is much faster than reading main memory, so this design is essential for good performance. But now there are several copies of the data, and they are updated asynchronously, so linearizability is lost.

Why accept that trade-off? It makes no sense to justify the multi-core memory model with the CAP theorem. Inside one computer we usually assume reliable communication. We do not expect one CPU core to keep working normally if it is cut off from the rest of the computer. The reason for dropping linearizability is performance, not fault tolerance. The same is true of many distributed databases that do not provide linearizable guarantees. They do so mainly to be faster, not mainly for fault tolerance. Linearizability is slow, and it is slow all the time, not just during network faults.

Can we find a faster way to build linearizable storage? The answer appears to be no. Attiya and Welch proved that if you want linearizability, the response time of reads and writes is at least proportional to the uncertainty of network delays. In a network with highly variable delays, like most computer networks, the response time of linearizable reads and writes will inevitably be high. No faster linearizable algorithm exists. Weaker consistency models can be much faster, so this trade-off matters a lot for latency-sensitive systems. Chapter 12 discusses ways of avoiding linearizability without giving up correctness.

Ordering Guarantees

A linearizable register behaves as if there is only one copy of the data, and every operation appears to take effect atomically at one point in time. That definition implies that operations run in some well-defined order. Figure 9-4 in the book showed this by joining the operations up in the order in which they seem to have run.

Ordering has been a recurring theme in this book, which suggests it may be a fundamental idea. Here are some other places where ordering has come up:

  • In Chapter 5, the main job of the leader in single-leader replication is to decide the order of writes in the replication log. That is the order in which followers apply them. Without a single leader, concurrent operations can conflict.
  • Serializability, from Chapter 7, means transactions behave as if they ran in some sequential order. That can be achieved by literally running them one after another, or by letting them run concurrently while preventing conflicts with locks or aborts.
  • Chapter 8 used timestamps and clocks to bring order to a disorderly world, for example to decide which of two writes happened later.

There are deep connections between ordering, linearizability, and consensus. The topic is more theoretical than the rest of the book, but it helps clarify what systems can and cannot do.

Ordering and Causality

One reason ordering keeps coming up is that it helps preserve causality. Causality is the link between cause and effect: one thing happens because of another. The book has seen several examples of why causality matters:

  • Answers before questions. In Chapter 5 (Figure 5-5), an observer saw the answer to a question before the question itself. That is confusing, because the person answering must have seen the question first. There is a causal dependency between the question and the answer.
  • Updates before creation. In Figure 5-9, writes in a system with three leaders overtook one another because of network delays. One replica saw an update to a row that did not exist yet. Causality here means a row must be created before it can be updated.
  • Concurrent writes. Chapter 5 observed that for any two operations A and B, there are three possibilities. Either A happened before B, or B happened before A, or A and B are concurrent. The “happened before” relationship is another way of expressing causality. If A happened before B, then B might have known about A, built on A, or depended on A. If A and B are concurrent, there is no causal link between them. Neither knew about the other.
  • Consistent snapshots. Chapter 7 said that a transaction reads from a consistent snapshot. Consistent means consistent with causality. If the snapshot contains an answer, it must also contain the question being answered. Observing the whole database at one point in time gives this property: the effects of everything that causally happened before that point are visible, and nothing that happened causally after it is visible. Read skew, the non-repeatable reads from Figure 7-6, means reading data in a state that breaks causality.
  • Write skew. In Figure 7-8, Alice was allowed to go off call because her transaction saw that Bob was still on call, and the same happened the other way round. Going off call causally depends on the observation of who is on call. Serializable snapshot isolation detects write skew by tracking these causal dependencies between transactions.
  • The football example. In Figure 9-1, Bob got a stale result after hearing Alice shout the score. That is a causality violation. Alice’s exclamation depends on the announcement of the score, so Bob should see the score too. The image resizer example had the same pattern.

Causality imposes an order on events. A cause comes before its effect. A message is sent before it is received. A question comes before its answer. And like real life, one thing leads to another. One node reads some data and writes something as a result. A second node reads what was written and writes something else in turn. These chains of dependent operations define the causal order of a system, which is the record of what happened before what.

If a system obeys the ordering imposed by causality, we say it is causally consistent. For example, snapshot isolation provides causal consistency. When you read from the database and see some piece of data, you must also be able to see any data that causally came before it, unless that earlier data has been deleted in the meantime.

The Causal Order Is Not a Total Order

A total order lets you compare any two elements. If you are given two natural numbers, such as 5 and 13, you can always say which is greater. Mathematical sets are different. Is the set {a, b} greater than {b, c}? You cannot compare them, because neither is a subset of the other. They are incomparable. So sets are only partially ordered. In some cases one set is greater than another, and in other cases the two cannot be compared.

The difference between total and partial orders shows up in the database consistency models:

  • Linearizability gives a total order of operations. If the system behaves as if there is one copy of the data, and every operation is atomic, then for any two operations you can say which one happened first. The timeline in the earlier figure shows this.
  • Causality gives a partial order. Two operations are concurrent if neither happened before the other. Two events are ordered if they are causally related, meaning one happened before the other. They are incomparable if they are concurrent. Some operations are ordered with respect to each other, and some are not.

So, under this definition, a linearizable datastore has no concurrent operations. It has one timeline along which all operations are totally ordered. Requests may wait in line to be handled, but the store handles each one atomically at a single point in time, acting on a single copy of the data. Concurrency would mean the timeline branches and then merges again. Operations on different branches are incomparable. Chapter 5’s jumble of concurrent operations (Figure 5-14) is like this, with arrows showing the causal dependencies. That is a partial order, not a straight line.

Distributed version control systems such as Git work the same way. Often one commit comes after another in a straight line. Sometimes there are branches, when several people work on a project at once. Merges are created when those concurrent commits are combined. The version history is a graph of causal dependencies.

Linearizability Is Stronger Than Causal Consistency

What is the relationship between causal order and linearizability? The answer is that linearizability implies causality. Any linearizable system preserves causality correctly. In particular, if a system has several communication channels, such as the message queue and the file storage service in the photo example, linearizability keeps causality intact automatically. The components do not have to pass timestamps around to each other to make it work.

That is what makes linearizable systems simple to understand and appealing. However, as discussed earlier, making a system linearizable can hurt its performance and availability, especially when network delays are large, as they are in geographically distributed systems. For this reason, some distributed data systems have given up linearizability. That gives them better performance, but it can make them harder to work with.

The good news is that there is a middle ground. Linearizability is not the only way to preserve causality. A system can be causally consistent without paying the performance cost of linearizability. In that case the CAP theorem does not apply. In fact, causal consistency is the strongest consistency model that does not slow down because of network delays and that stays available when the network fails.

In many cases, systems that appear to need linearizability really need only causal consistency, which is cheaper to provide. Based on this observation, researchers are exploring new kinds of databases that preserve causality, with performance and availability close to those of eventually consistent systems. This research is recent, and not much of it has reached production yet. There are still challenges to solve. But it is a promising direction for future systems.

Capturing Causal Dependencies

The book does not go into all the detail of how a non-linearizable system can maintain causal consistency. It explores a few key ideas.

To maintain causality, you need to know which operation happened before which other operation. That is a partial order. Concurrent operations may be processed in any order, but if one operation happened before another, every replica must process them in that order. So when a replica processes an operation, it must first make sure that all operations causally before it have already been processed. If one of those earlier operations is missing, the later one must wait until it arrives.

To find causal dependencies, you need a way to describe what a node “knows.” If a node had already seen the value X when it issued the write Y, then X and Y may be causally related. The analysis resembles a fraud investigation: did the CEO know about X at the time the CEO made decision Y?

The techniques for finding which operation happened before which are similar to those in Chapter 5, under detecting concurrent writes. That section was about a leaderless store, where you must detect concurrent writes to the same key to avoid lost updates. Causal consistency goes further. It must track causal dependencies across the whole database, not just for one key. Version vectors can be generalized to do this.

To work out the causal ordering, the database needs to know which version of the data the application read. That is why, in Chapter 5’s Figure 5-13, the version number from the earlier operation is passed back to the database with a write. A similar idea appears in the conflict detection of serializable snapshot isolation. When a transaction wants to commit, the database checks whether the version of the data it read is still up to date. To do this, it keeps track of which data has been read by which transaction.

Sequence Number Ordering

Causality is an important idea, but actually tracking every causal dependency can become impractical. In many applications, clients read a lot of data before they write something. It is then unclear whether the write depends on all of that data or only some of it. Tracking every read would be a large overhead.

There is a better way: use sequence numbers or timestamps to order events. A timestamp does not have to come from a time-of-day clock. Chapter 8 showed that physical clocks have many problems. A timestamp can instead come from a logical clock. A logical clock is an algorithm that produces a sequence of numbers to identify operations, usually by incrementing a counter for each operation.

Such sequence numbers are compact, often only a few bytes. They also give a total order. Every operation gets a unique number, and you can always compare two numbers to see which operation happened later.

We can even create sequence numbers in a total order that is consistent with causality. The promise is this: if operation A causally happened before B, then A has a lower sequence number than B. Concurrent operations may be ordered arbitrarily. Such a total order captures all the causality information, but it also imposes more order than causality strictly requires.

In a database with single-leader replication, the replication log already defines a total order of writes that is consistent with causality. The leader increments a counter for each operation, so each entry in the log gets a sequence number that goes up. If a follower applies the writes in the order they appear in the log, its state is always causally consistent, even if it lags behind the leader.

Noncausal Sequence Number Generators

If there is not a single leader, because you use multi-leader or leaderless replication, or because the database is partitioned, it is less clear how to generate sequence numbers. The book lists several methods used in practice:

  • Separate sets per node. For example, with two nodes, one node generates only odd numbers and the other only even numbers. In general, you can reserve some bits of each number to hold a unique node ID, so two nodes never produce the same number.
  • Time-of-day timestamps. You can attach a timestamp from a physical clock to each operation. Such timestamps are not sequential, but if they have high enough resolution, they might be enough to order operations totally. The last-write-wins conflict resolution method uses this.
  • Preallocated blocks. For example, node A might claim the block of numbers from 1 to 1,000, and node B might claim 1,001 to 2,000. Each node then assigns numbers from its own block, and claims a new block when its supply runs low.

All three options perform better and scale better than sending every operation through one leader that increments a counter. They produce a unique, roughly increasing number for each operation. But all three have a problem. Their sequence numbers are not consistent with causality, because they do not capture the order of operations across different nodes:

  • Each node may handle a different number of operations per second. If one node generates even numbers and the other odd numbers, the even counter may fall behind the odd one, or the other way round. Given an odd-numbered and an even-numbered operation, you cannot tell accurately which one causally happened first.
  • Physical clock timestamps suffer from clock skew, which can make them inconsistent with causality. Figure 8-3 showed a case where an operation that causally happened later was given a lower timestamp. (It is possible to make physical timestamps consistent with causality. Google’s Spanner estimates the expected clock skew and waits out the uncertainty interval before committing a write, so a causally later transaction always gets a greater timestamp. But most clocks cannot provide the uncertainty figure that this method needs.)
  • With the block allocator, one operation may get a number in the range 1,001 to 2,000, while a causally later operation gets a number from 1 to 1,000. Again the numbers contradict causality.

The book also notes that a total order that ignores causality is easy to create but not very useful. For example, you could give each operation a random UUID and sort by UUID. That is a valid total order, but the UUIDs say nothing about which operation really happened first, or whether two operations were concurrent.

Lamport Timestamps

There is a simple method for generating sequence numbers that is consistent with causality. It is called a Lamport timestamp. Leslie Lamport proposed it in 1978, in what is now one of the most cited papers in distributed systems.

Each node has a unique identifier, and each node keeps a counter of how many operations it has processed. The Lamport timestamp is a pair of (counter, node ID). Two nodes may sometimes have the same counter value, but including the node ID makes every timestamp unique.

A Lamport timestamp has no relation to a time-of-day clock, but it does give a total order. If you have two timestamps, the one with the greater counter is the greater timestamp. If the counters are equal, the one with the greater node ID is greater.

So far this is essentially the same as the even and odd counters described above. The key idea that makes Lamport timestamps consistent with causality is this: every node and every client keeps track of the maximum counter value it has seen so far, and includes that maximum on every request. When a node receives a request or response with a maximum counter greater than its own counter, it immediately moves its own counter up to that maximum.

Figure 9-8 shows this. Client A receives a counter value of 5 from node 2. Then it sends that maximum of 5 on to node 1. At that moment, node 1’s counter is only 1. But it is immediately moved forward to 5. So the next operation on node 1 gets an incremented counter of 6.

As long as the maximum counter value travels with every operation, this scheme keeps the Lamport ordering consistent with causality. Every causal dependency leads to an increased timestamp.

Lamport timestamps are sometimes confused with version vectors, which were covered in Chapter 5. They have some similarities, but different purposes. Version vectors can tell whether two operations are concurrent or whether one causally depends on the other. Lamport timestamps always enforce a total order. From the total order of Lamport timestamps, you cannot tell whether two operations are concurrent or causally dependent. The advantage of Lamport timestamps over version vectors is that they are more compact.

Timestamp Ordering Is Not Sufficient

Lamport timestamps define a total order that is consistent with causality. But they are not quite enough to solve many common problems in distributed systems.

Take a system that must make sure a username identifies exactly one user account. If two users try to create an account with the same username at the same time, one should succeed and the other should fail. Chapter 8 touched on this problem in the section about the leader and the lock.

At first glance, a total order such as Lamport timestamps seems enough. If two accounts with the same username are created, pick the one with the lower timestamp as the winner, since it grabbed the name first. Let the one with the greater timestamp fail. Because timestamps are totally ordered, the comparison is always valid.

That works for deciding the winner after the fact. Once you have collected all the username-creation operations in the system, you can compare their timestamps. But it does not work when a node has just received a request to create a username and must decide right now whether it succeeds. At that moment the node does not know whether another node is concurrently creating an account with the same name, or what timestamp that other node will assign.

To be sure that no other node is creating the same username with a lower timestamp, you would have to check with every other node to see what it is doing. If one of those nodes has failed, or cannot be reached because of a network problem, the system would grind to a halt. That is not the kind of fault-tolerant system we need.

The root problem is that a total order of operations only emerges after you have collected all of them. If another node has generated operations you have not seen yet, you cannot build the final order. Those unknown operations may need to be inserted at various positions in the total order.

The conclusion is this. To enforce something like a username uniqueness constraint, a total order is not enough. You also need to know when the order is final. If you have an operation to create a username, and you are sure no other node can slip a claim for the same name in ahead of your operation, then you can safely declare your operation successful. The idea of knowing when a total order is final is captured in the topic of total order broadcast.

Try it

Two nodes each receive a request to register the same username at about the same time. Node 1 stamps its request with the Lamport timestamp (4, node 1), and node 2 stamps its request with (4, node 2). Which request has the lower timestamp? Then ask yourself what node 1 still does not know before it can safely declare its request the winner.

Total Order Broadcast

If your program runs on a single CPU core, it is easy to define a total order of operations. It is simply the order in which the CPU ran them. In a distributed system, getting all the nodes to agree on one total order is tricky. Earlier in this section we looked at ordering by timestamps and sequence numbers, and found that it is weaker than single-leader replication. If you use timestamp ordering to enforce a uniqueness constraint, you cannot tolerate any faults.

Single-leader replication decides the total order of operations by picking one node as the leader, and running all operations in sequence on that leader’s CPU. The challenge is twofold. First, how to scale the system if the load is more than one leader can handle. Second, how to fail over if the leader fails (Chapter 5 covered handling node outages). In the research literature, this problem is called total order broadcast, or atomic broadcast.

Watch out

Scope of the ordering guarantee. Partitioned databases with one leader per partition usually keep order only within each partition. So they cannot offer guarantees that span partitions, such as consistent snapshots or foreign key references across partitions. A total order across all partitions is possible, but it needs extra coordination.

Total order broadcast is usually described as a protocol for passing messages between nodes. Informally, it must satisfy two safety properties at all times:

  • Reliable delivery. No messages are lost. If a message is delivered to one node, it is delivered to all nodes.
  • Totally ordered delivery. Messages are delivered to every node in the same order.

A correct algorithm must keep both properties true even if a node or the network is faulty. Messages will not be delivered while the network is cut. But an algorithm can keep retrying, so that the messages get through once the network is repaired, and they must still arrive in the correct order.

Using Total Order Broadcast

The consensus services ZooKeeper and etcd actually implement total order broadcast. That is a hint of a strong connection between total order broadcast and consensus, which the chapter explores later.

Total order broadcast is exactly what database replication needs. If every message is a write to the database, and every replica processes the same writes in the same order, the replicas stay consistent with each other, apart from temporary replication lag. This principle is called state machine replication. Chapter 11 returns to it.

It can also implement serializable transactions. Chapter 7 described actual serial execution. If every message is a deterministic transaction, meaning one that runs as a stored procedure with a predictable result, and every node processes the messages in the same order, then the partitions and replicas of the database stay consistent with each other.

An important property of total order broadcast is that the order is fixed at delivery time. A node is not allowed to insert a message retroactively into an earlier position, if later messages have already been delivered. This is what makes total order broadcast stronger than timestamp ordering.

Another way to see total order broadcast is as a way of building a log, such as a replication log, a transaction log, or a write-ahead log. Delivering a message is like appending to the log. Since all nodes deliver the same messages in the same order, they can all read the log and see the same sequence of messages.

Total order broadcast is also useful for a lock service that hands out fencing tokens (Chapter 8 explained them). Every request to acquire the lock is appended to the log as a message. All messages are numbered in the order they appear in the log. That sequence number can serve as a fencing token, because it always increases. ZooKeeper calls this sequence number the zxid.

Implementing Linearizable Storage Using Total Order Broadcast

Figure 9-4 showed that a linearizable system has a total order of operations. Does that mean linearizability is the same as total order broadcast? Not quite, but the two are closely linked.

Total order broadcast is asynchronous. Messages are reliably delivered in a fixed order, but there is no guarantee about when a given message will arrive. One recipient may lag behind the others. Linearizability, by contrast, is a recency guarantee: a read must see the latest value written.

Still, if you have total order broadcast, you can build linearizable storage on top of it. For example, you can make sure usernames uniquely identify accounts. Imagine that for every possible username there is a linearizable register that supports an atomic compare-and-set. Every register starts with the value null, which means the name is free. To claim a username, you run a compare-and-set on that name’s register, setting it to the user’s account ID, on the condition that the current value is null. If several users try to grab the same name at once, only one compare-and-set will succeed. The others will see a value other than null, because of linearizability.

The book shows how to implement such a linearizable compare-and-set using total order broadcast as an append-only log:

  1. Append a message to the log, tentatively saying which username you want to claim.
  2. Read the log, and wait for the message you appended to be delivered back to you.
  3. Check for any messages in the log that claim the same username. If the first such message is your own, you have succeeded. You can commit the claim, perhaps by appending another message, and tell the client. If the first message for that username is from another user, abort the operation.

Because log entries are delivered to all nodes in the same order, if several writes are concurrent, all nodes agree which one came first. The first conflicting write wins and later ones are aborted. So all nodes agree on whether each write was committed or aborted. A similar approach can implement serializable multi-object transactions on top of a log.

This procedure ensures linearizable writes. It does not guarantee linearizable reads. If you read from a store that is updated asynchronously from the log, the value may be stale. To be precise, the procedure gives sequential consistency, also called timeline consistency, which is slightly weaker than linearizability. To make reads linearizable, there are three options:

  • Sequence the reads through the log. Append a message, read the log, and perform the actual read when your message is delivered back to you. The message’s position in the log defines the point in time at which the read happens. Quorum reads in etcd work somewhat like this.
  • If the log lets you fetch the position of its latest message in a linearizable way, query that position, wait until all entries up to that position have been delivered to you, and then do the read. This is the idea behind ZooKeeper’s sync() operation.
  • Read from a replica that is updated synchronously on writes, and so is sure to be up to date. This technique is used in chain replication.

Implementing Total Order Broadcast Using Linearizable Storage

The previous section showed how to build a linearizable compare-and-set from total order broadcast. The book also shows the reverse. If you assume linearizable storage exists, you can build total order broadcast from it.

The easiest way is to assume a linearizable register that stores an integer and supports an atomic increment-and-get operation. An atomic compare-and-set would also do the job.

The algorithm is simple. For every message you want to send with total order broadcast, you run increment-and-get on the linearizable integer. You attach the value you got back to the message as a sequence number. Then you send the message to all nodes, resending any that are lost. Recipients deliver the messages in order of their sequence numbers.

Note the key difference from Lamport timestamps. The numbers from incrementing a linearizable register form a sequence with no gaps. So if a node has delivered message 4 and then receives message 6, it knows it must wait for message 5 before it can deliver message 6. With Lamport timestamps, that is not the case. This is the key difference between total order broadcast and timestamp ordering.

How hard can it be to build a linearizable integer with an atomic increment-and-get? If nothing ever failed, it would be easy: keep the integer in a variable on one node. The problem is handling the case where the network connection to that node is interrupted, and restoring the value if the node fails. The book makes the point that if you think hard enough about linearizable sequence number generators, you inevitably end up with a consensus algorithm.

This is no coincidence. It can be proved that a linearizable compare-and-set register (or increment-and-get register) and total order broadcast are both equivalent to consensus. If you can solve one of these problems, you can transform that solution into one for the others. The book calls this quite a profound and surprising insight.

It is now time to tackle the consensus problem directly.

Distributed Transactions and Consensus

Consensus is one of the most important and fundamental problems in distributed computing. On the surface it seems simple. Informally, the goal is to get several nodes to agree on something. You might think that cannot be too hard. Yet many broken systems have been built on the mistaken belief that the problem is easy.

Consensus appears late in the book because the topic is subtle, and understanding it needs background knowledge. Even among researchers, the understanding of consensus took decades to become clear, and many misunderstandings came along the way. Now that the book has covered replication (Chapter 5), transactions (Chapter 7), system models of failure (Chapter 8), linearizability, and total order broadcast, it is ready to tackle consensus.

There are several situations where nodes must agree. Two of them are important here:

  • Leader election. In a database with single-leader replication, all nodes need to agree which node is the leader. The leadership can become contested if some nodes cannot talk to others because of a network fault. Consensus is needed to avoid a bad failover that leads to split brain. If there were two leaders, both would accept writes, their data would diverge, and the result would be inconsistency and data loss.
  • Atomic commit. In a database that supports transactions spanning several nodes or partitions, a transaction may fail on some nodes while succeeding on others. To keep the atomicity of ACID transactions, all nodes must agree on the outcome. Either they all abort, if anything went wrong, or they all commit, if nothing did. This instance of consensus is called the atomic commit problem. Atomic commit is formalized slightly differently from consensus. An atomic commit can succeed only if every participant votes to commit, while consensus may decide on any value that one of the participants proposed. But the two problems can be reduced to each other. Non-blocking atomic commit is harder than consensus, and the book discusses it later under three-phase commit.

The Impossibility of Consensus

You may have heard of the FLP result, named after its authors Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson. It proves that there is no algorithm that always reaches consensus if there is a risk that a node may crash. In a distributed system, we must assume nodes may crash. So reliable consensus looks impossible. Yet the book has been discussing algorithms that achieve consensus. What is going on?

The answer is that the FLP result is proved in the asynchronous system model. That is a very restrictive model. It assumes a deterministic algorithm that cannot use any clocks or timeouts. If an algorithm is allowed to use timeouts, or some other way of identifying nodes it suspects have crashed (even if the suspicion is sometimes wrong), then consensus becomes solvable. Even allowing the algorithm to use random numbers is enough to get around the impossibility result.

So although the FLP result is of great theoretical importance, distributed systems can usually achieve consensus in practice.

The plan for the rest of the section is as follows. The book first examines atomic commit in more detail. In particular, it discusses the two-phase commit (2PC) algorithm, which is the most common way of solving atomic commit. It is built into various databases, messaging systems, and application servers. It turns out that 2PC is a kind of consensus algorithm, but not a very good one. By learning from 2PC, the book works toward better consensus algorithms, such as those used in ZooKeeper (called Zab) and etcd (called Raft).

Atomic Commit and Two-Phase Commit (2PC)

Chapter 7 explained that the purpose of transaction atomicity is to give simple semantics when something goes wrong in the middle of several writes. A transaction ends in one of two ways. It either commits, which makes all of its writes permanent, or it aborts, which rolls back all of its writes, undoing or discarding them.

Atomicity stops failed transactions from leaving the database full of half-finished results and half-updated state. This matters most for multi-object transactions, and for databases that maintain secondary indexes. A secondary index is a separate structure from the main data. So if you change some data, the matching change must also be made in the index. Atomicity keeps the index consistent with the main data. An index that disagrees with the data would not be very useful.

From Single-Node to Distributed Atomic Commit

For a transaction that runs on a single database node, the storage engine usually provides atomicity. When the client asks the node to commit, the database makes the transaction’s writes durable, typically in a write-ahead log, and then appends a commit record to the log on disk. If the database crashes during this, the transaction is recovered from the log when the node restarts. If the commit record was successfully written to disk before the crash, the transaction counts as committed. If not, its writes are rolled back.

So on a single node, whether a transaction commits depends crucially on the order in which data reaches the disk: first the data, then the commit record. The key moment is when the disk finishes writing the commit record. Before that moment, the transaction can still be aborted by a crash. After it, the transaction is committed, even if the database crashes. The important point is that a single device, the controller of one disk attached to one node, makes the commit atomic.

But what if several nodes are involved in one transaction? For example, you might have a multi-object transaction in a partitioned database, or a term-partitioned secondary index, where the index entry lives on a different node from the primary data. Most NoSQL distributed datastores do not support such distributed transactions. Some clustered relational systems do, and the book discusses them later.

In these cases, it is not enough to send a commit request to every node and commit independently on each one. The commit could easily succeed on some nodes and fail on others, which would break atomicity. Here are three ways that can happen:

  • Some nodes may detect a constraint violation or a conflict, so they must abort, while other nodes can commit successfully.
  • Some commit requests may be lost in the network, and eventually abort because of a timeout, while other commit requests get through.
  • Some nodes may crash before the commit record is fully written. They roll back when they recover, while other nodes commit successfully.

If some nodes commit and others abort, the nodes become inconsistent with each other, just like the inconsistent replicas in Chapter 7. And once a transaction has committed on one node, it cannot be taken back later, if it turns out to have aborted on another node. So a node must commit only when it is certain that all the other nodes in the transaction will also commit.

Key idea

A commit must be irrevocable. Once committed, it cannot be retracted. Other clients may already be relying on the committed data, and a node should commit only when every other node in the transaction is certain to commit.

The reason for this rule is that once data is committed, it becomes visible to other transactions, and other clients may start relying on it. This is the basis of the read committed isolation level from Chapter 7. If a transaction could abort after committing, any transaction that had read its data would be based on data that was retroactively declared never to have existed. Those transactions would have to be reverted too.

It is possible for the effects of a committed transaction to be undone later by another, compensating transaction. But from the database’s point of view, that is a separate transaction. So any correctness rules that span transactions become the application’s problem.

Introduction to Two-Phase Commit

Two-phase commit is an algorithm for atomic transaction commit across several nodes. It guarantees that either all nodes commit or all nodes abort. It is a classic algorithm in distributed databases. It is used internally in some databases, and it is available to applications through XA transactions, which the Java Transaction API supports, or through WS-AtomicTransaction for SOAP web services.

Instead of a single commit request, as in a single-node transaction, the commit or abort process in 2PC is split into two phases. That is where the name comes from. Figure 9-9 in the book shows a successful run. The picture below is a simplified version of it.

Watch out

Do not confuse 2PC and 2PL. Two-phase commit (2PC) and two-phase locking (2PL, from Chapter 7) are two very different things. 2PC provides atomic commit across nodes in a distributed database. 2PL provides serializable isolation. It is best to treat them as entirely separate ideas and ignore the unfortunate similarity in their names.

2PC uses a component that does not normally appear in single-node transactions: a coordinator, which is also called a transaction manager. The coordinator is often a library inside the same application process that requests the transaction, for example embedded in a Java EE container. It can also be a separate process or service. The book lists Narayana, JOTM, BTM, and MSDTC as examples of coordinators.

A 2PC transaction begins with the application reading and writing data on several database nodes, as normal. These nodes are called participants. When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator starts phase 1. It sends a prepare request to each participant, asking whether it is able to commit. The coordinator then tracks the answers:

  • If every participant replies yes, meaning it is ready to commit, the coordinator sends a commit request in phase 2, and the commit takes place.
  • If any participant replies no, the coordinator sends an abort request to all nodes in phase 2.
Example

The book compares this to a traditional wedding ceremony. The minister asks the bride and the groom, one at a time, whether each wants to marry the other. Typically both say yes. Once the minister has both answers, the minister pronounces them married. The marriage is now committed, and the news is announced to everyone present. If either the bride or the groom does not say yes, the ceremony is called off.

A System of Promises

From this short description, it may not be clear why two-phase commit ensures atomicity while one-phase commit across several nodes does not. The prepare and commit requests can be lost just as easily in the two-phase case. What makes 2PC different? To see why it works, we need to look at the process in more detail:

  1. When the application wants to begin a distributed transaction, it asks the coordinator for a transaction ID. This ID is globally unique.
  2. The application starts a single-node transaction on each participant, and attaches the global transaction ID to it. All reads and writes happen in these single-node transactions. If anything goes wrong at this stage, such as a node crashing or a request timing out, the coordinator or any participant can abort.
  3. When the application is ready to commit, the coordinator sends a prepare request to every participant, tagged with the global transaction ID. If any of these requests fails or times out, the coordinator sends an abort request for that transaction ID to all participants.
  4. When a participant receives a prepare request, it must make sure it can definitely commit the transaction under all circumstances. That includes writing all the transaction’s data to disk, so that a crash, a power failure, or running out of disk space is not an acceptable excuse for refusing to commit later. It also includes checking for conflicts and constraint violations. If it replies yes, it promises to commit the transaction without error if asked. In other words, the participant gives up its right to abort, but it has not yet committed.
  5. When the coordinator has all the answers to its prepare requests, it makes a definitive decision. It commits only if every participant voted yes.
