The coordinator must write that decision to its own transaction log on disk, so that it knows the outcome if it crashes later. This write is called the commit point.
  6. Once the decision is on disk, the commit or abort request is sent to all participants. If that request fails or times out, the coordinator must retry forever until it succeeds. There is no going back. If the decision was to commit, it must be carried out, however many retries it takes. If a participant crashed in the meantime, the transaction will be committed when that participant recovers. Since it voted yes, it cannot refuse to commit when it comes back.

The protocol contains two crucial points of no return. When a participant votes yes, it promises it will definitely be able to commit later, although the coordinator may still choose to abort. And once the coordinator decides, the decision is irrevocable. Those two promises are what guarantee the atomicity of 2PC. A single-node atomic commit combines both of these events into one: writing the commit record to the transaction log.

The marriage analogy fits here too. Before saying yes, each person is free to abort the wedding by saying no. After saying yes, nobody can retract it. If you faint right after saying yes, and do not hear the minister make the pronouncement, the marriage still happened. When you wake, you can find out whether you are married by asking the minister for the status of your global transaction ID. Or you can wait for the minister to retry the commit request, since the retries continued while you were unconscious.

Coordinator Failure

The book has explained what happens if a participant or the network fails during 2PC. If any prepare request fails or times out, the coordinator aborts the transaction. If any commit or abort request fails, the coordinator retries it indefinitely. It is less clear what happens if the coordinator itself crashes.

If the coordinator fails before it sends the prepare requests, a participant can safely abort the transaction. But once a participant has received a prepare request and voted yes, it can no longer abort on its own. It must wait to hear from the coordinator whether the transaction committed or aborted. If the coordinator crashes, or the network fails at this point, the participant can do nothing but wait. A participant in this state is called in doubt, or uncertain.

The next picture shows this case. The coordinator decided to commit, and database 2 received the commit request. But the coordinator crashed before it could send the commit request to database 1. So database 1 does not know whether to commit or abort. A timeout does not help. If database 1 aborts on its own after a timeout, it will end up inconsistent with database 2, which has committed. Similarly, it is not safe for database 1 to commit on its own, because another participant may have aborted.

Without hearing from the coordinator, the participant has no way of knowing whether to commit or abort. In principle, the participants could talk among themselves to find out how each one voted, and reach an agreement. But that is not part of the 2PC protocol.

So the only way 2PC can complete is by waiting for the coordinator to recover. This is why the coordinator must write its commit or abort decision to its transaction log on disk before it sends commit or abort requests. When the coordinator recovers, it reads its log to find the status of every in-doubt transaction. Any transaction without a commit record in the coordinator’s log is aborted. So the commit point of 2PC comes down to a regular single-node atomic commit on the coordinator.

Try it

Compare two moments in two-phase commit. In the first, the coordinator crashes before it sends any prepare request. In the second, a participant has already replied yes, and then the coordinator crashes. In which case can the participant abort on its own, and why does the answer change?

Three-Phase Commit

Two-phase commit is called a blocking atomic commit protocol, because 2PC can get stuck waiting for the coordinator to recover. In theory it is possible to make an atomic commit protocol non-blocking, so that it does not get stuck when a node fails. In practice, making that work is not straightforward.

An alternative called three-phase commit (3PC) has been proposed. However, 3PC assumes a network with bounded delay and nodes with bounded response times. Most practical systems have unbounded network delay and process pauses, as Chapter 8 showed, so 3PC cannot guarantee atomicity in them.

In general, a non-blocking atomic commit needs a perfect failure detector, meaning a reliable way of telling whether a node has crashed. In a network with unbounded delay, a timeout is not a reliable failure detector, because a request can time out because of a network problem even when no node has crashed. For this reason, 2PC continues to be used, despite the known problem with coordinator failure.

Distributed Transactions in Practice

Distributed transactions, especially those built on two-phase commit, have a mixed reputation. On one hand, they are seen as providing an important safety guarantee that would be hard to achieve otherwise. On the other hand, they are criticized for causing operational problems, hurting performance, and promising more than they can deliver. Many cloud services choose not to implement distributed transactions, because of the operational problems they cause.

Some implementations carry a heavy performance penalty. For example, distributed transactions in MySQL have been reported to be over 10 times slower than single-node transactions. So it is not surprising that people advise against using them. Much of the performance cost of 2PC comes from the extra disk flushes (fsync) needed for crash recovery, and from the extra network round trips.

However, the book says we should not dismiss distributed transactions outright. They hold important lessons. To begin, it is important to be precise about what “distributed transaction” means. Two quite different types are often confused:

  • Database-internal distributed transactions. Some distributed databases, which use replication and partitioning in their standard setup, support transactions among their own nodes. VoltDB and the NDB storage engine of MySQL Cluster are examples. Here, all the nodes in the transaction run the same database software.
  • Heterogeneous distributed transactions. Here the participants are two or more different technologies. They might be two databases from different vendors, or even a non-database system such as a message broker. A distributed transaction across these systems must still ensure atomic commit, even though the systems are entirely different inside.

Database-internal transactions do not have to be compatible with any other system. So they can use any protocol and apply optimizations specific to that one technology, and they often work quite well. Heterogeneous transactions are much more challenging.

Exactly-Once Message Processing

Heterogeneous distributed transactions allow different systems to be combined in powerful ways. For example, a message from a message queue can be acknowledged as processed if and only if the database transaction that processes it was successfully committed. This is done by committing the message acknowledgment and the database writes together, in one atomic transaction. With distributed transaction support, this is possible even when the message broker and the database are unrelated technologies running on different machines.

If either the message delivery or the database transaction fails, both are aborted. So the message broker can safely redeliver the message later. By committing the message and the side effects of processing it atomically, the message is effectively processed exactly once, even if it took a few retries before it succeeded. The abort discards any side effects of the partly completed attempt.

Example

Suppose that processing a message includes sending an email, and the email server does not support two-phase commit. If the processing fails and is retried, the email could be sent two or three times. But if all the side effects of processing a message are rolled back when the transaction aborts, the processing step can be retried safely, as if nothing had happened. The catch is that every system affected by the transaction must be able to use the same atomic commit protocol.

The book returns to exactly-once message processing in Chapter 11. First, it looks at the atomic commit protocol that allows such heterogeneous distributed transactions.

XA Transactions

X/Open XA (short for eXtended Architecture) is a standard for implementing two-phase commit across heterogeneous technologies. It was introduced in 1991 and has been widely implemented. Many traditional relational databases support XA, including PostgreSQL, MySQL, DB2, SQL Server, and Oracle. Message brokers that support it include ActiveMQ, HornetQ, MSMQ, and IBM MQ.

XA is not a network protocol. It is a C API for interfacing with a transaction coordinator. Bindings exist for other languages too. In the Java EE world, XA transactions are provided through the Java Transaction API (JTA). JTA is supported by drivers for databases that use Java Database Connectivity (JDBC), and by drivers for message brokers that use the Java Message Service (JMS).

XA assumes your application uses a network driver or client library to talk to the participant databases or messaging services. If the driver supports XA, it calls the XA API to find out whether an operation should be part of a distributed transaction. If so, it sends the necessary information to the database server. The driver also exposes callbacks through which the coordinator can ask the participant to prepare, commit, or abort.

The transaction coordinator implements the XA API. The standard does not say how it must be implemented. In practice, the coordinator is often just a library loaded into the same process as the application that issues the transaction. It is not a separate service. It keeps track of the participants in a transaction. It collects their responses after asking them to prepare, through a callback into the driver. And it uses a log on the local disk to record the commit or abort decision for each transaction.

If the application process crashes, or the machine it runs on dies, the coordinator goes with it. Any participants with prepared but uncommitted transactions are then stuck in doubt. Because the coordinator’s log is on the application server’s local disk, that server must be restarted. The coordinator library must read the log to recover the outcome of each transaction. Only then can it use the driver’s XA callbacks to ask the participants to commit or abort. The database server cannot contact the coordinator directly, because all communication has to go through its client library.

Holding Locks While in Doubt

Why do we care so much about a transaction being stuck in doubt? Can’t the rest of the system just carry on, and ignore the in-doubt transaction, which will be cleaned up eventually?

The problem is locking. Chapter 7 explained that database transactions usually take an exclusive lock on any row they modify, to prevent dirty writes. If you want serializable isolation, a database using two-phase locking must also take a shared lock on any row the transaction reads.

The database cannot release those locks until the transaction commits or aborts. In the book’s Figure 9-9, this is the shaded area. So with two-phase commit, a transaction must hold its locks for as long as it is in doubt. If the coordinator crashes and takes 20 minutes to start up again, those locks are held for 20 minutes. If the coordinator’s log is lost entirely, the locks may be held forever, or at least until an administrator resolves the situation by hand.

While the locks are held, no other transaction can modify those rows. Depending on the database, other transactions may even be blocked from reading them. So other transactions cannot simply carry on with their work. If they need the same data, they are blocked. This can make large parts of an application unavailable until the in-doubt transaction is resolved.

Recovering From Coordinator Failure

In theory, if the coordinator crashes and restarts, it should recover cleanly from its log and resolve any in-doubt transactions. In practice, orphaned in-doubt transactions do happen. These are transactions for which the coordinator cannot decide the outcome for some reason, for example because the transaction log was lost or corrupted by a software bug. These transactions cannot be resolved automatically. They sit in the database forever, holding locks and blocking other transactions.

Even rebooting the database servers does not fix this. A correct implementation of 2PC must keep the locks of an in-doubt transaction even across restarts. Otherwise it would risk breaking atomicity. It is a sticky situation.

The only way out is for an administrator to decide, by hand, whether to commit or roll back each such transaction. The administrator must check the participants of each in-doubt transaction, see whether any participant has already committed or aborted, and then apply the same outcome to all the others. This can require a lot of manual effort. It usually happens under high stress and time pressure during a serious production outage. Otherwise, why would the coordinator be in such a bad state?

Many XA implementations have an emergency escape hatch called heuristic decisions. These let a participant unilaterally decide to commit or abort an in-doubt transaction without a decision from the coordinator. The word “heuristic” here is a polite way of saying the decision will probably break atomicity, because it goes against the promises of two-phase commit. Heuristic decisions are meant only for getting out of catastrophic situations, not for regular use.

Limitations of Distributed Transactions

XA transactions solve a real and important problem: keeping several participant data systems consistent with each other. But as the book has shown, they also bring major operational problems. The key realization is that the transaction coordinator is itself a kind of database, because it stores transaction outcomes. So it needs the same care as any other important database. Several problems follow from this:

  • Single point of failure. If the coordinator is not replicated, and runs on only one machine, it is a single point of failure for the whole system. Its failure causes other application servers to block on the locks held by in-doubt transactions. Surprisingly, many coordinator implementations are not highly available by default, or have only basic replication support.
  • Application servers stop being stateless. Many server-side applications follow a stateless model, favored by HTTP. All their durable state is in a database, so application servers can be added and removed at will. But when the coordinator runs inside the application server, the nature of the deployment changes. The coordinator’s logs become a crucial part of the durable state, as important as the databases themselves, because they are needed to recover in-doubt transactions after a crash. Such application servers are no longer stateless.
  • Lowest common denominator. XA has to work with a wide range of data systems, so it can only offer what they all share. For example, it cannot detect deadlocks across different systems, because that would need a standard protocol for systems to exchange information about the locks each transaction is waiting for. It also does not work with serializable snapshot isolation, because that would need a protocol for identifying conflicts across different systems.
  • Database-internal transactions are less limited. For transactions inside a single distributed database, the limits are not as severe. For example, a distributed version of serializable snapshot isolation is possible. But there is still a basic problem. For 2PC to commit a transaction, every participant must respond. So if any part of the system is broken, the transaction fails too. Distributed transactions tend to amplify failures. That runs against the goal of building fault-tolerant systems.

Do these facts mean we should give up on keeping several systems consistent with each other? Not quite. There are other methods that achieve the same thing without the pain of heterogeneous distributed transactions. The book returns to them in Chapters 11 and 12. But first it wraps up the topic of consensus.

Fault-Tolerant Consensus

Informally, consensus means getting several nodes to agree on something. For example, several people might try to book the last seat on an airplane or in a theater at the same time, or try to register the same username. A consensus algorithm can decide which one of these mutually incompatible operations should win.

The problem is normally formalized like this. One or more nodes may propose values, and the algorithm decides on one of them. In the seat-booking example, each node handling a customer’s request may propose the ID of the customer it is serving. The decision then says which customer got the seat.

In this formal version, a consensus algorithm must satisfy four properties:

  • Uniform agreement. No two nodes decide differently.
  • Integrity. No node decides twice.
  • Validity. If a node decides value v, then v was proposed by some node.
  • Termination. Every node that does not crash eventually decides some value.

The book notes that this version is called uniform consensus, and that it is equivalent to ordinary consensus in asynchronous systems with unreliable failure detectors. It also uses the word “nodes” where academic papers say “processes.”

The first two properties, agreement and integrity, are the core of consensus. Everyone decides on the same outcome, and once a decision is made, nobody can change their mind. The validity property exists mainly to rule out trivial solutions. For example, an algorithm that always decides null, no matter what was proposed, would satisfy agreement and integrity. But it would not satisfy validity.

If you do not care about fault tolerance, the first three properties are easy. You can hardcode one node as a dictator, and let that node make all the decisions. But if that one node fails, the system can no longer make any decisions. This is exactly what happened with two-phase commit. If the coordinator fails, in-doubt participants cannot decide whether to commit or abort.

The termination property is what formalizes fault tolerance. It says that a consensus algorithm cannot just sit around doing nothing forever. It must make progress, and even if some nodes fail, the other nodes must still reach a decision. In the terms used in the book, termination is a liveness property: something good eventually happens. The other three are safety properties: something bad never happens. (The book discusses safety and liveness in its chapter on system models.)

The system model of consensus assumes that when a node crashes, it suddenly disappears and never comes back. The book suggests imagining an earthquake that destroys the datacenter holding your node, so that the node is buried under 30 feet of mud and is never coming back online. In this model, any algorithm that has to wait for a node to recover cannot satisfy termination. In particular, two-phase commit does not meet the requirements for termination.

Of course, if every node crashes and none is running, no algorithm can decide anything. There is a limit to how many failures an algorithm can tolerate. It can be proved that any consensus algorithm needs at least a majority of nodes to be working correctly in order to guarantee termination. That majority can safely form a quorum, which was described in Chapter 5.

So the termination property holds only under the assumption that fewer than half of the nodes are crashed or unreachable. Most consensus implementations, however, keep the safety properties (agreement, integrity, and validity) even when a majority of nodes fail or there is a severe network problem. A large outage can stop the system from processing requests. But it cannot corrupt the consensus system into making invalid decisions.

Most consensus algorithms also assume there are no Byzantine faults. A Byzantine fault is one where a node does not follow the protocol correctly, for example by sending contradictory messages to different nodes. If that happens, it can break the safety properties. It is possible to make consensus robust against Byzantine faults, as long as fewer than one-third of the nodes are Byzantine-faulty. But the book does not have room to discuss those algorithms in detail.

Consensus Algorithms and Total Order Broadcast

The best-known fault-tolerant consensus algorithms are Viewstamped Replication (VSR), Paxos, Raft, and Zab. They have many similarities, but they are not the same. The book does not go into the full details of each one. It is enough to know the high-level ideas they share, unless you are implementing a consensus system yourself. The book advises against doing that, because it is very hard.

Most of these algorithms do not use the formal model directly. That model proposes and decides on a single value, while satisfying the four properties. Instead, they decide on a sequence of values. That makes them total order broadcast algorithms, which were covered earlier in this chapter.

Total order broadcast requires that messages are delivered exactly once, in the same order, to all nodes. This is equivalent to running several rounds of consensus. In each round, the nodes propose the message they want to send next, and then decide on the next message to be delivered in the total order. So total order broadcast is equivalent to repeated rounds of consensus, with each consensus decision corresponding to one message delivery. The properties carry over:

  • Because of consensus agreement, all nodes deliver the same messages in the same order.
  • Because of integrity, messages are not duplicated.
  • Because of validity, messages are not corrupted or made up out of thin air.
  • Because of termination, messages are not lost.

Viewstamped Replication, Raft, and Zab implement total order broadcast directly. That is more efficient than running a separate round of consensus for each value. In the case of Paxos, this optimization is called Multi-Paxos.

Single-Leader Replication and Consensus

Chapter 5 described single-leader replication. It sends all writes to the leader and applies them to the followers in the same order, which keeps the replicas up to date. Isn’t that essentially total order broadcast? If so, how did we get away without worrying about consensus in Chapter 5?

The answer comes down to how the leader is chosen. If the leader is chosen manually, by people in the operations team who configure it, then you have a consensus algorithm of the dictatorial kind. Only one node is allowed to accept writes, and so it decides the order of writes in the replication log. If that node goes down, the system cannot accept writes until the operators manually configure a different leader. This can work well in practice. But it does not satisfy the termination property of consensus, because it needs a human to intervene before progress can be made.

Some databases perform automatic leader election and failover. They promote a follower to be the new leader if the old one fails, as discussed in Chapter 5. That brings us closer to fault-tolerant total order broadcast, and so to solving consensus.

However, there is a problem. Earlier we discussed split brain, and said that all nodes need to agree who the leader is. Otherwise two nodes could each believe they are the leader and push the database into an inconsistent state. So we need consensus in order to elect a leader. But the consensus algorithms described above are total order broadcast algorithms. Total order broadcast is like single-leader replication, and single-leader replication requires a leader. So we seem to be stuck. To elect a leader, we first need a leader. To solve consensus, we first need to solve consensus.

How do we break out of this loop? The answer is epoch numbering, described next.

Epoch Numbering and Quorums

All of the consensus protocols discussed so far use a leader in some form, but they do not guarantee the leader is unique at all times. Instead they make a weaker guarantee. The protocols define an epoch number, which is called the ballot number in Paxos, the view number in Viewstamped Replication, and the term number in Raft. Within each epoch, the protocol guarantees that there is only one leader.

Every time the current leader is thought to be dead, a vote is started among the nodes to elect a new leader. That election is given a new, larger epoch number. So epoch numbers are totally ordered and always increase. If two different leaders in two different epochs conflict, perhaps because the earlier leader was not actually dead, the leader with the higher epoch number wins.

Before a leader is allowed to decide anything, it must check that no other leader with a higher epoch number might be about to make a conflicting decision. How can a leader know it has not been ousted by another node? Chapter 8 introduced the idea that the truth is defined by the majority. A node cannot fully trust its own judgment. Just because a node thinks it is the leader does not mean the other nodes accept it as leader.

So the leader must collect votes from a quorum of nodes. For every decision a leader wants to make, it sends the proposed value to the other nodes and waits for a quorum to respond in favor. The quorum is usually, but not always, a majority of the nodes. A node votes in favor of a proposal only if it is not aware of any other leader with a higher epoch.

That gives two rounds of voting. One vote chooses the leader. A second vote approves the leader’s proposal. The key insight is that the quorums in these two votes must overlap. If a vote on a proposal succeeds, at least one of the nodes that voted for it must also have taken part in the most recent leader election. So if the vote on a proposal does not reveal any higher epoch number, the current leader can conclude that no leader election with a higher epoch has happened. It can be sure it still holds the leadership, and then safely decide the proposed value.

The picture below is a simplified view of this rule, with three nodes. Epoch 1 has node A as leader. Node A stops being the leader when the others start an election in epoch 2. Node B starts the election, node C votes for B, and B becomes leader. A stale message from A that still carries epoch 1 is refused by nodes that have already seen epoch 2.

This voting process looks similar to two-phase commit. But there are big differences. In 2PC the coordinator is not elected. Fault-tolerant consensus algorithms need votes from only a majority of nodes, whereas 2PC needs a yes vote from every participant. The table below summarizes the comparison. Consensus algorithms also define a recovery process, by which nodes reach a consistent state after a new leader is elected. This ensures the safety properties are always met. These differences are the key to the correctness and fault tolerance of consensus.

Trade-offs
AspectTwo-phase commitFault-tolerant consensus
Who decidesA coordinator that is fixed in advance, not electedA leader chosen by a vote, identified by an epoch number
Votes neededA yes from every participantA majority of nodes
Recovery after a failureNot defined by the protocol. Participants wait for the coordinator, and may hold locks for a long time.Defined by the protocol. A new leader brings nodes into a consistent state, and progress continues while a majority is working.

Limitations of Consensus

Consensus algorithms are a major breakthrough for distributed systems. They bring concrete safety properties (agreement, integrity, and validity) to systems where everything else is uncertain. And they remain fault-tolerant, meaning they can keep making progress as long as a majority of nodes are working and reachable. They provide total order broadcast, so they can also implement linearizable atomic operations in a fault-tolerant way.

Even so, they are not used everywhere, because their benefits come at a cost:

  • Synchronous replication. The voting that nodes do before a proposal is decided is a kind of synchronous replication. Databases are often configured for asynchronous replication instead. With asynchronous replication, some committed data can be lost on failover. But many people accept that risk for better performance.
  • Strict majority. Consensus systems always need a strict majority to operate. You need at least three nodes to tolerate one failure, because the remaining two out of three form a majority. You need at least five nodes to tolerate two failures, because the remaining three out of five form a majority. If a network failure cuts some nodes off from the rest, only the majority part can make progress. The rest is blocked.
  • Fixed membership. Most consensus algorithms assume a fixed set of nodes that vote. You cannot simply add or remove nodes. Extensions that allow membership to change over time exist, but they are much less well understood.
  • Reliance on timeouts. Consensus systems usually rely on timeouts to detect failed nodes. In environments with highly variable network delays, especially geographically distributed ones, a node may wrongly believe the leader has failed because of a temporary network issue. That does not harm safety. But frequent leader elections lead to terrible performance, because the system spends more time choosing a leader than doing useful work.
  • Sensitivity to bad links. Some consensus algorithms are very sensitive to network problems. The book cites Raft as having unpleasant edge cases. If the whole network works correctly except for one link that is consistently unreliable, leadership can keep bouncing between two nodes, or the current leader can be forced to resign again and again. Then the system effectively never makes progress. Other consensus algorithms have similar problems, and designing algorithms that handle unreliable networks better is still an open research problem.

Membership and Coordination Services

Projects like ZooKeeper or etcd are often described as “distributed key-value stores” or “coordination and configuration services.” Their API looks much like a database’s. You can read and write the value for a given key, and iterate over keys. So if they are basically databases, why do they go to the effort of implementing a consensus algorithm? What makes them different from other databases?

To understand this, it helps to see how a service like ZooKeeper is used. As an application developer, you will rarely use ZooKeeper directly, because it is not well suited as a general-purpose database. It is more likely that you will rely on it indirectly, through another project. HBase, Hadoop YARN, OpenStack Nova, and Kafka all depend on ZooKeeper running in the background. So what do those projects get from it?

ZooKeeper and etcd are designed to hold small amounts of data that fit entirely in memory, although they still write to disk for durability. You would not want to store all of your application’s data there. That small amount of data is replicated across all the nodes using a fault-tolerant total order broadcast algorithm. As discussed earlier, total order broadcast is just what database replication needs. If each message is a write, applying the same writes in the same order keeps the replicas consistent.

ZooKeeper is modeled after Google’s Chubby lock service. It implements total order broadcast, and therefore consensus. It also offers several other features that turn out to be very useful when building distributed systems:

  • Linearizable atomic operations. Using an atomic compare-and-set, you can implement a lock. If several nodes try the same operation at once, only one succeeds. The consensus protocol guarantees the operation is atomic and linearizable, even if a node fails or the network is interrupted at any point. A distributed lock is usually implemented as a lease, which has an expiry time, so that it is eventually released if the client fails. Chapter 8 covers process pauses, which is why leases matter.
  • Total ordering of operations. As Chapter 8 discussed, when a resource is protected by a lock or lease, you need a fencing token to stop clients from conflicting with each other after a process pause. The fencing token is a number that increases every time the lock is acquired. ZooKeeper provides this by totally ordering all operations. Each operation gets a monotonically increasing transaction ID (zxid) and a version number (cversion).
  • Failure detection. Clients keep a long-lived session on the ZooKeeper servers. The client and server exchange heartbeats to check that the other is still alive. If the connection is briefly interrupted, or one ZooKeeper node fails, the session remains active. But if the heartbeats stop for longer than the session timeout, ZooKeeper declares the session dead. Any locks held by that session can be set to release automatically when the session times out. ZooKeeper calls these ephemeral nodes.
  • Change notifications. One client can read locks and values created by another client, and it can also watch them for changes. So a client can find out when another client joins the cluster, because that client wrote a value. It can also find out when another client fails, because its session times out and its ephemeral nodes disappear. By subscribing to notifications, a client avoids polling repeatedly to check for changes.

Of these features, only the linearizable atomic operations really require consensus. But it is the combination of all of them that makes systems like ZooKeeper so useful for distributed coordination.

Allocating Work to Nodes

The ZooKeeper and Chubby model works well in one common case. You have several instances of a process or service, and one of them must be chosen as the leader, or primary. If the leader fails, another node should take over. This is useful for single-leader databases. It is also useful for job schedulers and similar stateful systems.

Another example is a partitioned resource, such as a database, message streams, file storage, or a distributed actor system. You need to decide which partition goes to which node. When new nodes join the cluster, some partitions must move from existing nodes to the new ones, to rebalance the load. When nodes are removed or fail, other nodes must take over their work.

These tasks can be done with careful use of atomic operations, ephemeral nodes, and notifications in ZooKeeper. If done correctly, the application can recover from faults automatically, without human intervention. But it is not easy, despite libraries such as Apache Curator, which provide higher-level tools on top of the ZooKeeper client API. Still, it is much better than trying to implement the necessary consensus algorithms from scratch, which has a poor success record.

An application may start on a single node and eventually grow to thousands of nodes. Holding majority votes across thousands of nodes would be terribly inefficient. So ZooKeeper runs on a fixed number of nodes, usually three or five. It performs its majority votes among those few nodes, while supporting a potentially large number of clients. In this way ZooKeeper outsources some of the work of coordinating nodes, such as consensus, operation ordering, and failure detection, to an external service.

The data ZooKeeper manages is normally slow-changing. It holds facts like “the node running on a certain IP address is the leader for partition 7.” Such facts may change over minutes or hours. ZooKeeper is not meant to store the runtime state of an application, which may change thousands or millions of times per second. If application state needs to be replicated from one node to another, other tools such as Apache BookKeeper can be used.

Service Discovery

ZooKeeper, etcd, and Consul are also often used for service discovery. That means finding the IP address you need to connect to in order to reach a particular service. In cloud datacenters, virtual machines constantly come and go, so you often do not know the IP addresses of your services ahead of time. Instead, when a service starts, it registers its network endpoints in a service registry, where other services can find it.

However, it is less clear that service discovery actually needs consensus. DNS is the traditional way to look up the IP address for a service name. It uses several layers of caching to achieve good performance and availability. Reads from DNS are definitely not linearizable, and it is usually not considered a problem if the results of a DNS query are a little stale. It matters more that DNS is reliably available and robust to network interruptions.

So service discovery does not require consensus, but leader election does. If your consensus system already knows who the leader is, it can make sense to use that information to help other services discover the leader. For this purpose, some consensus systems support read-only caching replicas. These replicas receive the log of all decisions asynchronously, but they do not take part in voting. They can serve read requests that do not need to be linearizable.

Membership Services

ZooKeeper and similar tools can be seen as part of a long history of research into membership services, which goes back to the 1980s. Membership services have been important for building highly reliable systems, for example in air traffic control.

A membership service determines which nodes are currently active and live members of a cluster. As Chapter 8 showed, because of unbounded network delays, it is not possible to reliably detect whether another node has failed. But if you couple failure detection with consensus, the nodes can come to an agreement about which nodes should be considered alive.

It can still happen that a node is wrongly declared dead by consensus, even though it is alive. But it is still very useful for a system to agree on which nodes make up the current membership. For example, choosing a leader could mean simply picking the lowest-numbered of the current members. That approach would fail if different nodes had different opinions about who the current members are.

Summary

Summary
  • Linearizability makes replicated data look like a single copy, and makes each operation act atomically. It is appealing because it is easy to understand: it makes a database behave like a variable in a single-threaded program. Its downside is that it is slow, especially when network delays are large.
  • Causality orders events by cause and effect: what happened before what. It is a weaker model than linearizability. Instead of one straight timeline, the version history can branch and merge, because some events are concurrent. Causal consistency avoids the coordination overhead of linearizability and is much less sensitive to network problems.
  • Lamport timestamps capture the causal order using counters and node IDs. But even with causal ordering, some problems cannot be solved this way. Take a username that must be unique, where concurrent registrations must be rejected. A node that accepts a registration must somehow know that no other node is registering the same name at the same time. That problem leads to consensus.
  • Consensus means deciding so that all nodes agree on what was decided, and the decision is irrevocable. Many problems reduce to consensus and are equivalent to each other, in the sense that a solution to one can be turned into a solution for the others:
    • Linearizable compare-and-set registers, which must decide whether to set their value based on the current value.
    • Atomic transaction commit, where a database must decide whether to commit or abort a distributed transaction.
    • Total order broadcast, where the messaging system must decide the order in which to deliver messages.
    • Locks and leases, where, when clients race to grab a lock, the lock decides which one gets it.
    • Membership and coordination, where, given a failure detector such as timeouts, the system must decide which nodes are alive.
    • Uniqueness constraints, where, when transactions concurrently create conflicting records, the constraint must decide which one is allowed.
  • A single node makes all of these easy, or you can give the decision-making power to one node. This is what a single-leader database does. All the power to decide sits with the leader, so it can offer linearizable operations, uniqueness constraints, and a totally ordered replication log. But if the leader fails, or a network problem makes it unreachable, the system cannot make progress. There are three ways to handle that:
    1. Wait for the leader to recover, and accept that the system is blocked in the meantime. Many XA and JTA transaction coordinators choose this. It does not fully solve consensus, because if the leader never recovers, the system can be blocked forever.
    2. Fail over manually, by having people choose a new leader and reconfigure the system. Many relational databases do this. It is a kind of consensus by “act of God,” and it is limited by the speed at which humans can act.
    3. Use an algorithm to choose a new leader automatically. This needs a consensus algorithm, and it is wise to use a proven one that handles bad network conditions correctly.
  • A single leader can provide linearizability without running consensus on every write. But it still needs consensus to maintain its leadership and to change leaders. So having a leader only kicks the can down the road. Consensus is still needed, just in a different place and less often.
  • Coordination tools such as ZooKeeper provide “outsourced” consensus, failure detection, and membership. They are not easy to use. But they are much better than building your own algorithms to withstand every problem from Chapter 8. If you need something that reduces to consensus and must be fault-tolerant, it is wise to use a tool like ZooKeeper.
  • Not every system needs consensus. Leaderless and multi-leader replication usually do not use global consensus. The conflicts they produce are a consequence of having no consensus across leaders. That may be acceptable. Perhaps we simply need to live without linearizability, and learn to work with data that has branching and merging version histories.

The chapter draws on a large body of research in the theory of distributed systems. The theoretical papers and proofs are not always easy to read, and they sometimes make unrealistic assumptions. But they are very valuable. They help us reason about what can and cannot be done, and they reveal the counterintuitive ways in which distributed systems are often flawed. The chapter ends with 110 numbered references. This retelling does not reproduce them, but readers who have the time will find them well worth exploring.

This brings us to the end of Part II. That part covered replication (Chapter 5), partitioning (Chapter 6), transactions (Chapter 7), the failure models of distributed systems (Chapter 8), and finally consistency and consensus (this chapter). With that foundation of theory in place, Part III turns to more practical systems, and to how to build powerful applications from heterogeneous building blocks.

Check yourself

  1. A web server saves a photo to file storage, then puts a resize job on a message queue. The image resizer fetches the photo when it gets the job. If the file storage is not linearizable, why can the thumbnail end up permanently wrong?

    Show answer

    The queue message can arrive before the photo write has reached every replica. The resizer may then fetch an old copy of the photo, or nothing at all, and it resizes the wrong version. The full-size image and the thumbnail stay inconsistent, because nothing rechecks them. The two channels, storage and queue, race with each other.

  2. A single-leader database has its leader in datacenter 1, and the network link to datacenter 2 is cut. Why can clients in datacenter 2 neither write nor read linearizably? Why would a multi-leader setup keep working?

    Show answer

    Writes and linearizable reads must reach the leader, which is across the cut link, so they fail or wait. A multi-leader setup lets each datacenter accept writes locally and queue the replication until the link returns. That keeps the system available, but the behavior is not linearizable. This is the trade-off described by the CAP theorem.

  3. A node’s Lamport counter is 1. It receives a message carrying the maximum counter value 5. What counter does its next operation get, and why must the maximum travel with every message?

    Show answer

    The next operation gets counter 6. On receiving the maximum, the node moves its own counter up to 5, then increments it. Because the maximum travels with every message, every causal dependency produces a larger timestamp, so the ordering stays consistent with causality.

  4. In two-phase commit, a participant has voted yes, and then the coordinator crashes before sending it a commit or abort request. Why can the participant not safely commit or abort on its own?

    Show answer

    A yes vote is a promise to commit if asked, but the participant does not know what the coordinator decided. Another participant may have committed, or may have aborted. Committing on its own could contradict an abort somewhere else, and aborting could contradict a commit. So it must wait for the coordinator to recover and read its decision from its log. The only other option, a heuristic decision, risks breaking atomicity.

Part III

Derived Data

Part III looks at how several data systems with different strengths, such as databases, caches, indexes, and analytics tools, can be combined into one application, starting with batch processing in Chapter 10 and then moving on to streams.

A paraphrase of Kleppmann’s part introduction: most applications need several data systems at once, and separating the system of record from derived data makes the flow of data easy to follow.

Part III · Chapter 10

Batch Processing

The big idea: a batch job reads a fixed set of input files and writes new output files without changing its input. That simple rule makes jobs easy to rerun, debug, and roll back, and the same design ideas that made Unix tools work scale up to thousands of machines.

Parts I and II looked at one database at a time, and then at distributed databases, always assuming that the application had only one of them. Real systems are rarely that simple. A large application often needs to access and process the same data in many different ways, and no single database handles all of them well. So it uses a mix of datastores, indexes, caches, and analytics systems, plus code that moves data from one store to another.

Part III studies how to fit those different systems, each with its own data model and access pattern, into one coherent architecture. The book notes that this work is often overlooked, especially by vendors who promise that their product meets all of your needs. In practice, connecting disparate systems is one of the most important jobs in any serious application.

Systems of Record and Derived Data

Systems that store and process data fall into two broad groups.

A system of record, also called the source of truth, holds the authoritative version of the data. When new data comes in, for example as user input, it is written here first. Each fact is represented exactly once, usually in a normalized form (split into tables that avoid repeating information). If another system disagrees with the system of record, the system of record is correct by definition.

A derived data system holds data that was produced by taking existing data from another system and transforming or processing it. If you lose derived data, you can rebuild it from its source. A cache is the classic example. The application reads from the cache when it can, and falls back to the underlying database when the cache does not have what it needs. Denormalized values (copies of data arranged for faster reads), indexes, and materialized views (results computed in advance and stored) are also derived data. In a recommendation system, the predicted summaries are often derived from logs of user activity.

Derived data is redundant, because it repeats information that already exists. It is still essential for fast read queries, and it is often denormalized. You can derive several different datasets from one source, which lets you look at the same data from several points of view.

Not every system draws a clear line between systems of record and derived data, but the distinction is very helpful. It shows which parts of the system have which inputs and outputs, and how they depend on each other. The book also points out that most databases, storage engines, and query languages are not inherently one or the other. A database is just a tool. How your application uses it decides which role its data plays.

Key idea

The line between a system of record and derived data depends on how you use the tool, not on the tool itself. Being clear about which data is derived from which other data brings order to a confusing architecture.

Overview of Chapters

The book’s roadmap for Part III is short. Chapter 10 starts with batch-oriented dataflow systems such as MapReduce, and shows the tools and principles they offer for building large-scale data systems. Chapter 11 takes the same ideas to data streams, which let you do similar work with lower delays. Chapter 12 closes the book by asking how we might use these tools to build reliable, scalable, and maintainable applications in the future.

Chapter 10 opens with a quote from Donald Knuth. In short, a system cannot succeed if one person has too much influence over it, because the real test comes when many people with different viewpoints run their own experiments.

Much of modern software works in a request and response style. You ask for something, or send an instruction, and some time later the system gives you an answer. Databases, caches, search indexes, and web servers all work this way. The web and many HTTP-based APIs have made this style so common that it is easy to forget it is only one option. The book distinguishes three types of system.

  • Services (online systems) wait for a request from a client, handle it as quickly as possible, and send a response. Response time is the main measure of performance, and availability matters a lot, because a client that cannot reach the service shows its user an error.
  • Batch processing systems (offline systems) take a large amount of input data, run a job over it, and produce output data. Jobs can take anywhere from a few minutes to several days, so no user is waiting for one to finish. They are often scheduled to run regularly, for example once a day. Their main measure is throughput, which is how long it takes to get through an input of a given size.
  • Stream processing systems (near-real-time systems) sit between the two. Like batch systems, they consume input and produce output rather than answering requests. But they work on events shortly after those events happen, instead of on a fixed set of data. That gives them lower latency. Because stream processing builds on batch processing, Chapter 11 covers it.

Batch processing is an important building block for reliable, scalable, and maintainable applications. MapReduce, a batch processing algorithm published in 2004, was called, perhaps over-enthusiastically, “the algorithm that makes Google so massively scalable.” It was later implemented in open source systems such as Hadoop, CouchDB, and MongoDB.

MapReduce is a fairly low-level programming model compared with the parallel processing systems that data warehouses had used for years. But it was a major step forward in the scale of processing that commodity hardware could handle. The book says MapReduce is now declining in importance, yet it is still worth understanding, because it gives a clear picture of why and how batch processing is useful.

Batch processing is also very old. Before programmable computers existed, punch card tabulating machines, such as the Hollerith machines used in the 1890 US Census, did a semi-mechanized form of batch processing to compute totals from large inputs. MapReduce also resembles the electromechanical IBM card-sorting machines that businesses used in the 1940s and 1950s. History, as the book puts it, has a tendency to repeat itself.

The chapter starts with Unix tools. The ideas and lessons from Unix carry over to large, mixed distributed data systems, so they are a good place to begin.

Batch Processing with Unix Tools

Let’s start with a simple example. Suppose a web server appends a line to a log file every time it serves a request. With the default nginx access log format, one line looks like the example below. The book broke it across several lines for readability. In the file, it is one line.

216.58.210.78 - - [27/Feb/2015:17:55:11 +0000] "GET /css/typography.css HTTP/1.1"
200 3377 "http://martin.kleppmann.com/" "Mozilla/5.0 (Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X
10_9_5) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/40.0.2214.115
Safari/537.36"

To interpret that line, you need the definition of the log format, which is:

$remote_addr - $remote_user [$time_local] "$request"
$status $body_bytes_sent "$http_referer" "$http_user_agent"
Example

Reading the sample line field by field tells you the following:

  • The client’s IP address is 216.58.210.78.
  • The user was not logged in, so the remote user field is a hyphen.
  • The request arrived on 27 February 2015 at 17:55:11 UTC.
  • The request asked for the file /css/typography.css.
  • The response status was 200, which means success, and the response was 3,377 bytes.
  • The page that referred the browser was http://martin.kleppmann.com/, so the browser loaded the stylesheet because that page used it.
  • The browser was Chrome 40, on a Mac.

Simple Log Analysis

Various tools can turn log files into pretty reports about website traffic. For the sake of the exercise, let’s build our own with basic Unix tools. Say you want to find the five most popular pages on your site. In a Unix shell you can do it like this:

cat /var/log/nginx/access.log |
awk '{print $7}' |
sort |
uniq -c |
sort -r -n |
head -n 5

Each command does one small step:

  1. cat reads the log file. (Some people point out that cat is not strictly needed, since awk could read the file directly. The book keeps it because the pipeline then reads clearly from left to right.)
  2. awk splits each line into fields separated by whitespace, and prints only the seventh field, which is the requested URL. For the sample line, that is /css/typography.css.
  3. sort puts the URLs in alphabetical order. If a URL was requested n times, the same URL now appears n times in a row.
  4. uniq -c filters out repeated lines by checking whether two adjacent lines are the same. The -c option adds a counter, so for each distinct URL it reports how many times the URL appeared.
  5. The second sort sorts by that number (-n), in reverse (-r) order, so the largest count comes first.
  6. head -n 5 outputs the first five lines and discards the rest.

The output looks something like this:

4189 /favicon.ico
3631 /2013/05/24/improving-security-of-ssh-private-keys.html
2124 /2012/12/05/schema-evolution-in-avro-protocol-buffers-thrift.html
1369 /
915 /css/typography.css

This command line looks obscure if you do not know Unix tools, but it is very powerful. It processes gigabytes of log files in seconds, and you can change the analysis easily. To leave CSS files out of the report, change the awk argument to '$7 !~ /\.css$/ {print $7}'. To count the top client IP addresses instead of the top pages, change it to '{print $1}'. And so on.

Try it

Using the pipeline above, what single change to the awk argument would give you the top client IP addresses? Then think about the sort and uniq steps. Would they need to change at all, and why?

The book does not have space to explore Unix tools in detail, but they are worth learning. Surprisingly many data analyses can be done in a few minutes with some combination of awk, sed, grep, sort, uniq, and xargs, and the tools perform surprisingly well.

Chain of commands versus custom program

Instead of a chain of Unix commands, you could write a simple program to do the same thing. In Ruby, it might look like this:

counts = Hash.new(0)
File.open('/var/log/nginx/access.log') do |file|
  file.each do |line|
    url = line.split[6]
    counts[url] += 1
  end
end
top5 = counts.map{|url, count| [count, url] }.sort.reverse[0...5]
top5.each{|count, url| puts "#{count} #{url}" }

Read it step by step:

  1. counts is a hash table that keeps a counter for each URL. A counter starts at zero by default.
  2. For each line of the log, the URL is the seventh whitespace-separated field. The index is 6 because Ruby arrays start counting at zero.
  3. The counter for that URL goes up by one.
  4. The table is sorted by counter value, largest first, and the top five entries are kept.
  5. Those five entries are printed.

This program is not as concise as the chain of Unix pipes, but it is fairly readable. Which of the two you prefer is partly a matter of taste. The real difference lies in how they run on a large file.

Sorting versus in-memory aggregation

The Ruby script keeps an in-memory hash table with one entry per URL. The Unix pipeline has no such table. It sorts a list in which every request for a URL is a repeated line, and then counts the repeats that sit next to each other.

Which approach is better depends on how many different URLs you have. For most small and mid-sized websites, every distinct URL and a counter for each can fit in about 1 GB of memory, even on a laptop. The book calls the memory a job needs for random access its working set. Here the working set depends only on the number of distinct URLs. If a single URL appears a million times in the log, the table still holds one entry for it, plus one counter. If that working set is small enough, the in-memory hash table works fine.

When the working set is larger than memory, the sorting approach has the advantage, because it can use disks efficiently. This is the same principle the book described in Chapter 3 for SSTables and LSM-Trees. Chunks of data are sorted in memory and written to disk as segment files, and then several sorted segments are merged into one larger sorted file. Merging reads each file in order, which is a sequential access pattern that disks handle well. Chapter 3 stressed optimizing for sequential I/O, and the same pattern reappears here.

The sort utility in GNU Coreutils, the standard tools on Linux, handles datasets larger than memory by spilling to disk. It also uses several CPU cores automatically. So the simple chain of commands scales to large datasets without running out of memory. The bottleneck is most likely the rate at which the input file can be read from disk.

The Unix Philosophy

It is no coincidence that the log file was easy to analyze with a chain of commands. This was one of the key design ideas of Unix, and it is still remarkably relevant. Doug McIlroy, who invented Unix pipes, first described them in 1964. He compared programs to garden hoses: you screw in another segment when you need to massage the data in another way. The plumbing analogy stuck, and the idea of connecting programs with pipes became part of what is now called the Unix philosophy. In 1978, the philosophy was described with four principles:

  1. Make each program do one thing well. To do a new job, build afresh rather than complicate old programs by adding new features
  2. Expect the output of every program to become the input to another, as yet unknown, program. Do not clutter output with extra information. Avoid strictly columnar or binary input formats. Do not insist on interactive input.
  3. Design and build software, even operating systems, to be tried early, ideally within weeks. Do not hesitate to throw away the clumsy parts and rebuild them.
  4. Use tools in preference to unskilled help to lighten a programming task, even if you have to detour to build the tools and expect to throw some of them out after you have finished using them.

The book notes that this approach, with its automation, rapid prototyping, incremental iteration, friendliness to experimentation, and breaking large projects into manageable chunks, sounds much like today’s Agile and DevOps movements. Surprisingly little has changed in four decades.

The sort tool is a good example of the first principle. It is arguably a better sorting implementation than most programming languages have in their standard libraries, since those usually do not spill to disk or use several threads. Yet sort is barely useful on its own. It becomes powerful only in combination with other tools, such as uniq.

A uniform interface

If the output of one program is to become the input of another, the two programs must agree on a data format. If any program’s output can connect to any other program’s input, every program must use the same input and output interface. In Unix, that interface is a file, or more precisely a file descriptor. A file is an ordered sequence of bytes. Because the interface is so simple, many different things can use it: an ordinary file on disk, a communication channel to another process (a Unix socket, standard input, or standard output), a device driver such as an audio device or a printer, or a TCP connection over the network. These very different things share one interface, so they plug together easily. The book calls this remarkable.

By convention, many (but not all) Unix programs treat that byte sequence as ASCII text. The log analysis used this fact. awk, sort, uniq, and head all treat their input as a list of records separated by the newline character. The choice of newline is somewhat arbitrary. The ASCII record separator character would arguably have been a better choice, since it exists for exactly this purpose. Still, because the programs all agree on the same separator, they can work together.

The web has a similar uniform interface. A URL names a particular resource, and you can link to any URL from any other website, even when the servers belong to unrelated organizations. The book contrasts this with the era of bulletin board systems (BBSs), where each system had its own phone number and modem settings. A reference from one BBS to another had to be written as a phone number and modem configuration. The user had to hang up, dial the other system, and search for the information by hand. You could not link directly to a piece of content inside another BBS.

Parsing each record is less uniform. Unix tools often split a line into fields by whitespace or tab characters, but CSV, pipe-separated, and other encodings are also common. Even a simple tool like xargs has about half a dozen command-line options for controlling how its input is parsed. And the uniform interface is not beautiful. The expression {print $7} to extract a URL is hard to read. In an ideal world it might be something like {print $request_url}. The book returns to this idea later in the chapter.

Even so, the uniform text interface of Unix is still remarkable decades later. Few software tools compose as well. You cannot easily pipe your email and your online shopping history through a custom analysis tool into a spreadsheet and post the results to a social network. Even databases with the same data model often make it hard to move data from one into another. The book calls this lack of integration the Balkanization of data.

Separation of logic and wiring

Another feature of Unix tools is their use of standard input (stdin) and standard output (stdout). By default, stdin comes from the keyboard and stdout goes to the screen. You can also take input from a file or send output to a file. A pipe connects the stdout of one process to the stdin of another, using a small in-memory buffer. The whole intermediate stream is never written to disk.

A program can still read and write files directly when it needs to. But the Unix approach works best when a program ignores particular file paths and simply uses stdin and stdout. The person running the shell then decides how the inputs and outputs are wired together. The program does not know or care where its input comes from or where its output goes. The book calls this loose coupling, late binding, or inversion of control. Separating the wiring from the program logic makes it easier to combine small tools into bigger systems.

You can even write your own programs and join them with the tools that come with the operating system. A program only needs to read stdin and write stdout to take part in a pipeline. In the log example, you could write a tool that turns user-agent strings into sensible browser names, or one that turns IP addresses into country codes, and plug it straight into the pipeline. The sort program does not care whether its neighbor is part of the operating system or code you wrote yourself.

There are limits, though. Programs that need several inputs or outputs are possible but tricky. You cannot pipe a program’s output into a network connection directly. You need a separate tool such as netcat or curl for that. (Unix began by representing everything as files, but the BSD sockets API broke with that pattern. The research systems Plan 9 and Inferno are more consistent, and represent a TCP connection as a file.) If a program opens files itself, starts subprocesses, or opens network connections, it does the wiring itself. It can still be configured through command-line options, but the shell user has less freedom to rewire it.

Transparency and experimentation

Part of what makes Unix tools so successful is that they make it easy to see what is going on. The book lists three reasons:

  • The input files to Unix commands are normally treated as immutable, meaning they are never changed. You can run a command as often as you like, trying different options, without damaging the input.
  • You can end a pipeline at any point, send the output to less, and look at it to check that it has the expected form. That makes debugging easy.
  • You can write the output of one stage to a file and use that file as the input to the next stage. You can then restart the later stage without rerunning the whole pipeline.

Unix tools are quite blunt, simple compared with a relational database’s query optimizer, but they remain amazingly useful for experimentation. Their biggest limitation is that they run on a single machine. That is where tools like Hadoop come in.

MapReduce and Distributed Filesystems

MapReduce is a bit like Unix tools, but distributed across potentially thousands of machines. Like Unix tools, it is a fairly blunt, brute-force approach, yet it is surprisingly effective. A single MapReduce job is comparable to a single Unix process: it takes one or more inputs and produces one or more outputs.

As with most Unix tools, running a MapReduce job normally does not modify its input, and it has no side effects other than producing its output. The output files are written once, sequentially, and no existing part of a file is ever changed after it is written. Where Unix tools use stdin and stdout, MapReduce jobs read and write files in a distributed filesystem. In Hadoop’s implementation, that filesystem is HDFS, the Hadoop Distributed File System. HDFS is an open source reimplementation of Google’s File System (GFS). Other distributed filesystems include GlusterFS and the Quantcast File System (QFS). Object storage services such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and OpenStack Swift are similar in many ways. This chapter uses HDFS as its running example, but the principles apply to any distributed filesystem.

HDFS follows the shared-nothing principle, which the introduction to Part II described. It contrasts with the shared-disk approach of network attached storage (NAS) and storage area networks (SAN). Shared-disk storage is a centralized storage appliance, often built with custom hardware and special network infrastructure such as Fibre Channel. A shared-nothing system needs no special hardware, only computers connected by a normal datacenter network.

HDFS runs a daemon process on each machine. The daemon exposes a network service that lets other nodes access the files stored on that machine. This works because each general-purpose machine in a datacenter has some disks attached to it. A central server called the NameNode keeps track of which file blocks are stored on which machine. HDFS therefore presents one big conceptual filesystem that uses the disk space of every machine running the daemon.

To tolerate machine and disk failures, file blocks are replicated on several machines. Replication can mean simply keeping several copies. It can also mean an erasure coding scheme such as Reed–Solomon codes, which can recover lost data with less storage overhead than full copies. These techniques are similar to RAID, which protects several disks attached to one machine. The difference is that in a distributed filesystem, file access and replication happen over an ordinary datacenter network, with no special hardware.

HDFS has scaled well. At the time of writing, the largest HDFS deployments ran on tens of thousands of machines, with combined storage in the hundreds of petabytes. This became viable because storing and accessing data on HDFS, using commodity hardware and open source software, costs far less than the same capacity on a dedicated storage appliance.

MapReduce Job Execution

MapReduce is a programming framework for writing code that processes large datasets stored in a distributed filesystem like HDFS. The easiest way to understand it is to go back to the web server log example. The data processing pattern is very similar:

  1. Read a set of input files and break them into records. In the log example, each record is one line, so the newline is the record separator.
  2. Call the mapper function to extract a key and a value from each record. In the example, the mapper is awk '{print $7}'. It extracts the URL as the key and leaves the value empty.
  3. Sort all the key-value pairs by key. In the log example, this is done by the first sort command.
  4. Call the reducer function to iterate over the sorted pairs. If the same key appears several times, sorting has made those occurrences adjacent, so they are easy to combine without keeping much state in memory. In the example, the reducer is uniq -c, which counts adjacent records with the same key.

All four steps can be performed by one MapReduce job. Steps 2 (map) and 4 (reduce) are where you write your own data processing code. Step 1, breaking files into records, is handled by the input format parser. Step 3, the sort, is implicit in MapReduce. You never write it, because the mapper output is always sorted before it is given to the reducer.

The log example had a second sort in step 5, which ranked the URLs by how many requests they received. In MapReduce, if you need a second sorting stage, you write a second job and use the output of the first job as the input of the second. Seen this way, the mapper’s role is to prepare the data in a form suitable for sorting, and the reducer’s role is to process the data after it has been sorted.

To create a MapReduce job, you implement two callback functions, the mapper and the reducer. They behave as follows (the book also links this to the MapReduce querying in Chapter 2):

  • Mapper. The mapper is called once for every input record, and its job is to extract the key and value from that record. For each input it may emit any number of key-value pairs, including none. It keeps no state from one record to the next, so each record is handled on its own.
  • Reducer. The framework takes the key-value pairs from the mappers, collects all the values that belong to the same key, and calls the reducer with an iterator over that collection. The reducer can produce output records, such as the number of occurrences of one URL.

In Hadoop MapReduce, the mapper and reducer are each a Java class that implements a particular interface. In MongoDB and CouchDB, they are JavaScript functions. Standard Unix tools can also serve as mappers and reducers in a distributed computation, although that is less common.

Distributed execution of MapReduce

The main difference from a pipeline of Unix commands is that MapReduce can spread a computation across many machines without you writing any code to handle the parallelism. Mappers and reducers work on one record at a time. They do not need to know where their input comes from or where their output goes, so the framework can handle the complicated work of moving data between machines.

Parallelization is based on partitioning. The input to a job is typically a directory in HDFS. Each file, or each block of a large file, is a partition, and a separate map task processes it. The book’s Figure 10-1 shows a job with three mappers and three reducers. The diagram below draws the same idea.

The input files are typically hundreds of megabytes each. The MapReduce scheduler tries to run each mapper on a machine that stores a replica of the input file, provided that machine has enough spare RAM and CPU to run the task. This principle is known as putting the computation near the data. It saves copying the input over the network, which reduces network load and improves locality. In most cases, the application code for the mapper is not yet on the assigned machine, so the framework first copies the code (for example, JAR files for a Java program) to the right machines. Then it starts the map task and passes the input file to the mapper one record at a time. The output of the mapper is a set of key-value pairs.

The reduce side is partitioned too. The number of map tasks is set by the number of input file blocks. The number of reduce tasks is set by the job’s author, and it can differ from the number of map tasks. To make sure that all key-value pairs with the same key end up at the same reducer, the framework hashes the key to decide which reduce task receives each pair.

The pairs must be sorted, but the dataset is usually too large to sort with a normal algorithm on one machine. So the sorting happens in stages. First, each map task partitions its output by reducer, based on the hash of the key. Each partition is written to a sorted file on the mapper’s local disk, using a technique similar to the SSTables discussed in Chapter 3.

When a mapper finishes reading its input and writing its sorted files, the scheduler tells the reducers that they can start fetching that mapper’s output. Each reducer connects to every mapper and downloads the sorted files for its partition. The whole process of partitioning by reducer, sorting, and copying data from the mappers to the reducers is called the shuffle. The book admits this is a confusing name, since unlike shuffling a deck of cards, there is no randomness in MapReduce.

The reduce task takes the files from the mappers and merges them, keeping the sort order. If different mappers produced records with the same key, those records end up next to each other in the merged input. The reducer is called with a key and an iterator that scans all the records with that key. Those records may not all fit in memory, so the iterator reads them incrementally. The reducer can apply any logic, and it can produce any number of output records. These are written to a file in the distributed filesystem, usually with one copy on the local disk of the reducer’s machine and replicas on other machines.

MapReduce workflows

The range of problems you can solve with a single MapReduce job is limited. In the log example, one job can count page views per URL. But finding the most popular URLs requires a second round of sorting. So it is very common to chain MapReduce jobs into workflows, where the output of one job becomes the input of the next.

Hadoop’s MapReduce framework has no special support for workflows. The chaining is done implicitly by directory name. The first job is configured to write its output to a designated directory in HDFS, and the second job is configured to read from that same directory. To the framework, they are two independent jobs.

Chained MapReduce jobs therefore look less like Unix pipelines, which pass output straight to the next process through a small buffer, and more like a sequence of commands where each command writes its output to a temporary file that the next command reads. The book discusses the advantages and disadvantages of this design in the section on materialization, later in the chapter.

A batch job’s output is considered valid only when the job has completed successfully. MapReduce discards the partial output of a failed job. So a job can start only when the jobs that produce its input directories have completed successfully. To manage these dependencies, several workflow schedulers for Hadoop exist, including Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, Airflow, and Pinball. They also provide management features that matter when you maintain a large collection of batch jobs. Workflows of 50 to 100 MapReduce jobs are common when building recommendation systems, and in a large organization many teams may run jobs that read one another’s output. Tool support becomes essential.

Higher-level tools for Hadoop, including Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch, and FlumeJava, also set up workflows of several MapReduce stages and wire them together automatically.

Reduce-Side Joins and Grouping

Chapter 2 discussed joins in the context of data models and query languages, but it did not explain how joins are actually implemented. It is time to pick up that thread.

In many datasets, one record is associated with another. That can be a foreign key in a relational model, a document reference in a document model, or an edge in a graph model. A join is needed whenever some code must access records on both sides of that association. Denormalization can reduce the need for joins, but it generally cannot remove them entirely. The joins discussed in this book are mostly equi-joins, in which a record is associated with other records that have an identical value in a particular field, such as an ID. Some databases also support other kinds of join, but the book does not cover them.

In a database, a query that involves only a few records typically uses an index to find them quickly. If the query involves joins, it may need several index lookups. MapReduce has no concept of indexes in the usual sense. When a MapReduce job is given a set of files as input, it reads the entire content of all those files. A database would call this a full table scan. For reading just a few records, a full scan is outrageously expensive compared with an index lookup. But analytic queries often need aggregates over a large number of records. In that case, scanning the whole input can be a reasonable thing to do, especially if the processing is spread across many machines.

When the book talks about joins in batch processing, it means resolving all occurrences of an association within a dataset.
