For example, a job processes the data for all users at once, rather than looking up the data for one particular user. The second approach would be far more efficient with an index.

Example: analysis of user activity events

Example

The book’s example, shown in its Figure 10-2, has two inputs. On the left is a log of activity events, the clickstream of things that logged-in users did on a website. On the right is a database of users. You can think of this as part of a star schema (see Chapter 3): the log of events is the fact table, and the user database is one of the dimensions.

An analyst may want to correlate activity with profile information. If the profile holds the user’s age or date of birth, the analyst can find which pages are most popular with which age groups. But each activity event holds only a user ID, not the full profile. Embedding the profile in every event would be wasteful, so the events need to be joined with the user database.

The simplest implementation goes through the events one by one and queries the user database on a remote server for each user ID. That is possible, but it performs poorly. Throughput is limited by the round-trip time to the database server. A local cache helps only as much as the distribution of the data allows. Running many such queries in parallel could easily overwhelm the database.

To get good throughput in a batch process, the computation must be as local to one machine as possible. Making random-access requests over the network for every record is too slow. Querying a remote database also makes the batch job nondeterministic, because the data in that database might change while the job runs. A better approach is to take a copy of the user database, for example from a database backup using an ETL (extract, transform, load) process, and put it in the same distributed filesystem as the activity log. Then you have the user database in one set of files and the activity records in another, and MapReduce can bring the relevant records together efficiently.

Sort-merge joins

Recall that the mapper’s job is to extract a key and a value from each input record. In this join, the key is the user ID. One set of mappers goes over the activity events and emits the user ID as the key, with the event as the value. Another set of mappers goes over the user database and emits the user ID as the key, with the date of birth as the value. Figure 3 shows this.

When the framework partitions the mapper output by key and sorts the pairs, the activity events and the user record with the same ID become adjacent in the reducer input. The job can even arrange the sort so that the reducer always sees the user record first, followed by that user’s events in timestamp order. This technique is called a secondary sort.

The reducer then performs the join. Its function is called once for every user ID. Thanks to the secondary sort, the first value is the date-of-birth record from the user database. The reducer stores the date of birth in a local variable, then iterates over the activity events with the same user ID, outputting pairs of viewed URL and viewer age in years. Later MapReduce jobs can calculate the distribution of viewer ages for each URL, and cluster the URLs by age group.

Because the reducer processes all the records for one user ID in one go, it needs to keep only one user record in memory at a time. It never needs to make a network request. This algorithm is called a sort-merge join, because the mapper output is sorted by key, and the reducers then merge the sorted lists of records from both sides of the join.

Bringing related data together in the same place

In a sort-merge join, the mappers and the sorting process make sure that all the data needed for one user ID is brought together in one place: a single call to the reducer. With the data lined up in advance, the reducer can be a simple, single-threaded program that churns through records with high throughput and low memory overhead.

One way to look at this is that the mappers send messages to the reducers. When a mapper emits a key-value pair, the key acts like the destination address for the value. The key is just an arbitrary string, not a network address such as an IP address and port number. But it behaves like an address, because all the pairs with the same key are delivered to the same destination, a call to the reducer.

This model separates the physical network communication (getting the data to the right machine) from the application logic (processing the data once you have it). That contrasts with a typical database use, where a request for data often happens somewhere deep inside a piece of application code. MapReduce handles all of the network communication, so application code does not have to worry about partial failures, such as the crash of another node. The framework transparently retries failed tasks without affecting the application logic.

GROUP BY

Besides joins, another common use of the pattern of bringing related data to the same place is grouping records by some key, like the GROUP BY clause in SQL. All records with the same key form a group. The next step is often to aggregate within each group. Common examples are:

  • Counting the records in each group. In SQL this is a COUNT(*) aggregation, such as counting page views per URL.
  • Adding up the values in one field, as with SUM(fieldname).
  • Picking the top k records according to some ranking function.

The simplest way to implement grouping with MapReduce is to set up the mappers so that their key-value pairs use the grouping key. The partitioning and sorting then bring all records with the same key to the same reducer. This is why grouping and joining look quite similar when built on MapReduce.

Another common use of grouping is sessionization: collecting all the activity events of one user session, to find the sequence of actions that user took. Such analysis can answer whether users who saw a new version of your website are more likely to buy than those who saw the old version (this is A/B testing), or whether a marketing campaign is worth its cost. If you run several web servers, one user’s events are probably spread across several servers’ log files. You can implement sessionization by using a session cookie, user ID, or similar identifier as the grouping key. That brings all of one user’s events together in one place, while spreading different users across different partitions.

Handling skew

The pattern of bringing all records with the same key to the same place breaks down when a very large amount of data is related to a single key. In a social network, most users have a few hundred connections, but a few celebrities may have many millions of followers. Records that are this disproportionately active are called linchpin objects or hot keys.

Watch out

Collecting all the activity about a celebrity, such as the replies to one of their posts, in a single reducer causes skew, also called a hot spot. One reducer ends up with far more records than the others. A MapReduce job is complete only when all of its mappers and reducers have finished, so every later job waits for that slowest reducer.

If a join input has hot keys, there are several algorithms to compensate:

  • Pig’s skewed join first runs a sampling job to find out which keys are hot. When it performs the join, mappers send the records for a hot key to one of several reducers, chosen at random. Normal MapReduce would pick a reducer deterministically from a hash of the key. For the other input, the records for the hot key must be copied to all the reducers that handle that key.
  • Crunch’s sharded join works in a similar way, but requires the hot keys to be specified explicitly rather than found by sampling.
  • Hive’s skewed join requires the hot keys to be named in the table metadata. It stores the records for those keys in separate files from the rest. When joining that table, it uses a map-side join (described below) for the hot keys.

These techniques spread the work for a hot key over several reducers, which parallelizes it better. The cost is that the other join input has to be replicated to several reducers. The randomization idea is the same one used to ease hot spots in partitioned databases, which Chapter 6 covers.

Grouping by a hot key and aggregating can also be done in two stages. The first MapReduce stage sends records to random reducers, so each reducer groups only a subset of the hot key’s records and outputs a more compact partial result. The second MapReduce job then combines the partial results from all the first-stage reducers into one value per key.

Try it

Imagine a reduce-side join in which one key has far more records than all the others put together. Which of the skew techniques above would you choose, and what would it cost the other join input?

Map-Side Joins

The join algorithms in the last section perform the actual join logic in the reducers, so they are called reduce-side joins. The mappers prepare the input: they extract the key and value from each record, assign the pairs to reducer partitions, and sort them by key.

The reduce-side approach has one great advantage. You do not need to make assumptions about the input data. Whatever its properties and structure, the mappers can prepare it for joining. The downside is that all that sorting, copying to reducers, and merging can be quite expensive. Depending on the available memory buffers, the data may be written to disk several times as it passes through the stages of MapReduce.

If you can make certain assumptions about your input, you can make joins faster with a map-side join. This approach uses a cut-down MapReduce job with no reducers and no sorting. Each mapper reads one input file block from the distributed filesystem and writes one output file. That is all.

Broadcast hash joins

The simplest map-side join applies when a large dataset is joined with a small dataset. The small dataset must be small enough to load entirely into memory in each mapper. For example, suppose the user database in Figure 10-2 fits in memory. When a mapper starts, it first reads the user database from the distributed filesystem into an in-memory hash table. Then it scans the activity events and looks up each event’s user ID in that hash table. (This assumes there is exactly one entry for each key, which is probably true for a user database, since a user ID identifies one user. In general a key can have several entries, and the join outputs all the matches.)

There can still be several map tasks, one for each file block of the large input. In Figure 10-2, the activity events are the large input. Each of these mappers loads the small input entirely into memory. This simple but effective algorithm is called a broadcast hash join. The word broadcast reflects that every mapper for a part of the large input reads all of the small input, so the small input is effectively sent to every partition of the large input. The word hash reflects the use of a hash table. Pig supports this join under the name replicated join. Hive calls it MapJoin, and Cascading, Crunch, and the Impala query engine also use it.

Instead of loading the small input into an in-memory hash table, an alternative is to store it in a read-only index on the local disk. The frequently used parts of that index stay in the operating system’s page cache, so lookups can be almost as fast as an in-memory hash table. This works without requiring the whole dataset to fit in memory.

Partitioned hash joins

If the inputs to a map-side join are partitioned in the same way, the hash join can be applied to each partition independently. For Figure 10-2, you could partition both the activity events and the user database by the last decimal digit of the user ID, giving 10 partitions on each side. Then mapper 3 first loads all users whose ID ends in 3 into a hash table. It then scans all the activity events for users whose ID ends in 3.

If the partitioning is done correctly, every record that might be joined lies in the same numbered partition. So each mapper needs to read only one partition from each input dataset. This has the advantage that each mapper loads a smaller amount of data into its hash table.

This approach works only if both inputs have the same number of partitions, with records assigned to partitions by the same key and the same hash function. If the inputs were generated by earlier MapReduce jobs that already performed this grouping, that can be a reasonable assumption. Hive calls these bucketed map joins.

Map-side merge joins

Another variant applies when the input datasets are not only partitioned in the same way but also sorted on the same key. In that case it does not matter whether the inputs are small enough to fit in memory. A mapper can perform the same merge that a reducer would normally do. It reads both input files incrementally, in ascending key order, and matches the records with the same key.

If a map-side merge join is possible, earlier MapReduce jobs probably produced the inputs in this partitioned and sorted form. In principle, the join could have been done in the reduce stage of that earlier job. But it may still be worth running the merge join as a separate map-only job, for example if the partitioned and sorted datasets are needed for other purposes as well.

MapReduce workflows with map-side joins

When the output of a MapReduce join is used by later jobs, the choice of map-side or reduce-side join changes the structure of the output. The output of a reduce-side join is partitioned and sorted by the join key. The output of a map-side join is partitioned and sorted in the same way as the large input. This is because one map task starts for each file block of the join’s large input, whether the join is partitioned or broadcast.

Map-side joins also make more assumptions about the size, sorting, and partitioning of their inputs. So when you optimize join strategies, you must know the physical layout of the datasets in the distributed filesystem. It is not enough to know the encoding format and the directory name. You must also know the number of partitions, and the keys by which the data is partitioned and sorted. In the Hadoop ecosystem, this metadata is often kept in HCatalog and the Hive metastore.

Trade-offs
Join methodWhat it needsGood atCosts
Sort-merge (reduce-side)Nothing special about the inputsWorks on any inputs, however they are structuredSorting, copying, and merging every record across the network, with data possibly written to disk several times
Broadcast hash (map-side)One input small enough to fit in memory in each mapperNo sort and no reduce stage. The large input is read where it sitsThe small input is copied to every mapper. The method breaks down if the small side does not fit
Partitioned hash (map-side)Both inputs partitioned the same way, with the same key, hash function, and number of partitionsEach mapper loads only one slice of each inputThe partitioning must be correct in advance, usually set up by earlier jobs
Map-side merge (map-side)Both inputs partitioned and sorted on the same keyA map-only job, with no sorting and no reducers. Input size does not matterThe sorted, partitioned inputs must already exist, which usually means an earlier job produced them

The Output of Batch Workflows

The chapter has covered the algorithms for running workflows of MapReduce jobs, but it has not yet asked an important question. What is the result of all that processing, once it is done? Why run these jobs in the first place?

For database queries, the book distinguishes transaction processing (OLTP) from analytic purposes. OLTP queries generally look up a small number of records by key, using indexes, in order to show them to a user, for example on a web page. Analytic queries often scan a large number of records, group and aggregate them, and produce a report. The report might be a graph of a metric over time, a top 10 ranking, or a breakdown of a quantity into subcategories. Its consumer is often an analyst or a manager who needs to make business decisions.

Where does batch processing fit? It is neither transaction processing nor analytics, though it is closer to analytics, because a batch process typically scans large parts of its input. But a workflow of MapReduce jobs is not the same as an SQL query used for analysis. The output of a batch process is often not a report at all. It is some other kind of structure.

Building search indexes

Google’s original use of MapReduce was to build indexes for its search engine, and that work was a workflow of 5 to 10 MapReduce jobs. Google later moved away from MapReduce for this purpose, but it still helps to understand MapReduce through the lens of building a search index. Even today, Hadoop MapReduce remains a good way to build indexes for Lucene and Solr.

Chapter 3 described briefly how a full-text search index such as Lucene works. It is a file, called the term dictionary, in which you can efficiently look up a keyword and find a list of all the document IDs containing it, called the postings list. The book calls this a very simplified view. A real index also needs more data to rank results by relevance, correct misspellings, resolve synonyms, and so on. The principle still holds.

If you need to run a full-text search over a fixed set of documents, a batch process is a very effective way to build the indexes. The mappers partition the set of documents as needed, each reducer builds the index for its partition, and the index files are written to the distributed filesystem. Building document-partitioned indexes, which Chapter 6 covers, parallelizes very well.

Querying a search index by keyword is a read-only operation, so the index files are immutable once they have been created. If the set of documents changes, one option is to rerun the entire indexing workflow periodically and replace the old index files wholesale with the new ones when it is done. That can be computationally expensive if only a few documents changed. But the approach is easy to reason about: documents in, indexes out. The other option is to build the index incrementally. As Chapter 3 discussed, when you add, remove, or update documents in Lucene, it writes new segment files and asynchronously merges and compacts segment files in the background. Chapter 11 covers more on incremental processing.

Key-value stores as batch process output

Search indexes are only one example of the output of a batch workflow. Another common use of batch processing is to build machine learning systems, such as classifiers for spam filters, anomaly detection, and image recognition, and recommendation systems that suggest people you may know, products you may be interested in, or related searches. The output of those jobs is often a database. For example, one database can be queried by user ID to get suggested friends for that user. Another can be queried by product ID to get a list of related products.

These databases must be queried by the web application that handles user requests, which is usually separate from the Hadoop infrastructure. So how does the output get back into a database the web application can query?

The most obvious choice is to use the client library of your favorite database directly inside a mapper or reducer, and write from the batch job straight to the database server, one record at a time. This can work, provided your firewall rules allow direct access from the Hadoop environment to your production databases. But the book calls it a bad idea, for several reasons:

  1. As discussed for joins, making a network request for every single record is orders of magnitude slower than the normal throughput of a batch task. Even if the client library supports batching, performance is likely to be poor.
  2. MapReduce jobs often run many tasks in parallel. If they all write to the same output database at the rate a batch process can produce, the database can be overwhelmed, and its performance for queries suffers. That can cause operational problems in other parts of the system.
  3. Normally, MapReduce gives a clean all-or-nothing guarantee for job output. If the job succeeds, the result is the output of running every task exactly once, even if some tasks failed and were retried. If the whole job fails, no output is produced. But writing to an external system creates side effects that cannot be hidden this way. Partial results from an unfinished job may be visible to other systems. You also have to deal with the complexities of Hadoop task attempts and speculative execution, where a second copy of a slow task may be started.
Key idea

A much better solution is to build the new database inside the batch job and write it out as files in the job’s output directory, just like the search indexes. The files are immutable once written, and they can be loaded in bulk into servers that handle read-only queries.

Several key-value stores support building database files inside MapReduce jobs. They include Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB, and HBase bulk loading. Building these files suits MapReduce well. A mapper extracts a key, and sorting by that key is already much of the work needed to build an index. Most of these key-value stores are read-only once loaded, since the files can be written only by a batch job and are then immutable. That means their data structures can be quite simple. For example, they do not need a write-ahead log (WAL), the log of changes that databases use to recover from crashes.

When loading data into Voldemort, the server keeps serving requests from the old data files while the new files are copied from the distributed filesystem to the server’s local disk. When the copy is complete, the server atomically switches over to querying the new files. If anything goes wrong, it can easily switch back to the old files, because they are still there and immutable.

Philosophy of batch process outputs

The Unix philosophy encourages experimentation by making the dataflow very explicit. A program reads its input and writes its output. The input is left unchanged, any previous output is completely replaced, and there are no other side effects. You can rerun a command as often as you like, tweaking or debugging it, without messing up the state of your system.

MapReduce follows the same philosophy. By treating inputs as immutable and avoiding side effects such as writes to external databases, batch jobs achieve good performance and are much easier to maintain:

  • Rolling back bugs. If you introduce a bug and the output is wrong or corrupted, you can roll back to an earlier version of the code and rerun the job. The output will be correct again. Or, even simpler, keep the old output in a different directory and switch back to it. A read-write database does not offer this. If buggy code wrote bad data into the database, rolling back the code does nothing to fix the data. The book calls the ability to recover from buggy code human fault tolerance.
  • Faster development. Because mistakes are easy to undo, feature development can move faster than in an environment where mistakes could cause irreversible damage. The book links this principle of minimizing irreversibility to Agile software development.
  • Automatic retries. If a map or reduce task fails, the framework reschedules it and runs it again on the same input. If the failure is caused by a bug, the task keeps crashing and the job eventually fails after a few attempts. If the failure is transient, the fault is tolerated. Automatic retry is only safe because the inputs are immutable and the outputs of failed tasks are discarded.
  • Shared inputs. The same set of files can be the input for many different jobs. That includes monitoring jobs that calculate metrics and check whether a job’s output has the expected characteristics, for example by comparing it with the output of the previous run.
  • Logic separate from wiring. Like Unix tools, MapReduce jobs separate logic from wiring, which means configuring the input and output directories. That separation of concerns makes code reusable. One team can focus on a job that does one thing well, while other teams decide where and when to run it.

Unix and Hadoop also differ in some ways. Most Unix tools assume untyped text files, so they must do a lot of input parsing. The log example used {print $7} to extract the URL. On Hadoop, some of those low-value syntactic conversions are avoided by using more structured file formats. Avro and Parquet are often used. Avro provides efficient schema-based encoding and allows the schema to evolve over time, as Chapter 4 discusses. Parquet is a column-oriented format, covered in Chapter 3.

Comparing Hadoop to Distributed Databases

Hadoop is somewhat like a distributed version of Unix. HDFS is the filesystem, and MapReduce is a quirky implementation of a Unix process that always runs the sort utility between its map phase and its reduce phase. The earlier sections showed how to implement join and grouping operations on top of these primitives.

When the MapReduce paper was published, its ideas were not new in one sense. The processing and parallel join algorithms discussed in the last few sections had already been implemented in massively parallel processing (MPP) databases more than a decade earlier. The Gamma database machine, Teradata, and Tandem NonStop SQL were pioneers in this area.

The biggest difference is in focus. MPP databases concentrate on parallel execution of analytic SQL queries on a cluster of machines. The combination of MapReduce and a distributed filesystem offers something much more like a general-purpose operating system that can run arbitrary programs.

Diversity of storage

Databases require you to structure data according to a particular model, such as relational or document. Files in a distributed filesystem are just byte sequences, which can be written using any data model and any encoding. They might be collections of database records, but they could equally be text, images, videos, sensor readings, sparse matrices, feature vectors, genome sequences, or any other kind of data.

The book puts it bluntly: Hadoop made it possible to dump data indiscriminately into HDFS and work out how to process it later. MPP databases typically require careful up-front modeling of the data and of the query patterns, before the data is imported into the database’s proprietary storage format. From a purist’s point of view, this careful modeling is desirable, because the users of the database get better-quality data. In practice, though, simply making data available quickly, even in a raw and awkward format, is often more valuable than deciding on the ideal data model in advance.

This is similar to a data warehouse, where bringing data from many parts of a large organization into one place is valuable, because it enables joins across datasets that were previously separate. The careful schema design that an MPP database requires slows down that central collection. Collecting data in its raw form and worrying about the schema later speeds up collection. This idea is sometimes called a data lake or enterprise data hub.

Indiscriminate data dumping shifts the burden of interpreting the data. Instead of forcing the producer of a dataset to convert it into a standardized format, the interpretation becomes the consumer’s problem. This is the schema-on-read approach, which Chapter 2 discussed in connection with the document model. It can be an advantage when the producer and the consumers are different teams with different priorities. There may not even be one ideal data model. Different views of the data may suit different purposes, and dumping data in its raw form allows several such transformations. The book calls this the sushi principle, meaning that raw data is better.

Hadoop has therefore often been used for ETL. Data from transaction processing systems is dumped into the distributed filesystem in some raw form. MapReduce jobs then clean up that data, transform it into a relational form, and import it into an MPP data warehouse for analysis. Data modeling still happens, but it is a separate step, decoupled from data collection. That decoupling works because a distributed filesystem accepts data in any format.

Diversity of processing models

MPP databases are monolithic, tightly integrated pieces of software. They take care of storage layout on disk, query planning, scheduling, and execution. Because all these components can be tuned for the needs of the database, the system as a whole can perform very well on the kinds of queries it was designed for. The SQL query language also allows expressive queries and clean semantics without writing any code, which makes it accessible to graphical tools used by business analysts, such as Tableau.

Not all processing can sensibly be expressed as SQL queries. If you are building machine learning or recommendation systems, full-text search indexes with relevance ranking models, or image analysis, you most likely need a more general model of data processing. These kinds of processing are often very specific to an application. Examples include feature engineering for machine learning, natural language models for machine translation, and risk estimation functions for fraud prediction. They inevitably require writing code, not just queries.

MapReduce gave engineers the ability to run their own code easily over large datasets. If you have HDFS and MapReduce, you can build a SQL query execution engine on top of them, and that is what the Hive project did. But you can also write many other kinds of batch process that do not lend themselves to being expressed as a SQL query.

Later, people found that MapReduce was too limiting and too slow for some types of processing, so other processing models were developed on top of Hadoop. Two processing models, SQL and MapReduce, were not enough, and more were needed. Thanks to Hadoop’s openness, it was feasible to implement a whole range of approaches that would not have fit within the confines of a monolithic MPP database.

All of these processing models can run on a single shared-use cluster of machines, all accessing the same files in the distributed filesystem. There is no need to import the data into several specialized systems for different kinds of processing. The system is flexible enough to support a diverse set of workloads within the same cluster. Not having to move data around makes it much easier to derive value from it, and much easier to experiment with new processing models.

The Hadoop ecosystem includes both random-access OLTP databases, such as HBase (see the SSTables and LSM-Trees discussion in Chapter 3), and MPP-style analytic databases, such as Impala. Neither HBase nor Impala uses MapReduce, but both use HDFS for storage. They are very different ways of accessing and processing data, yet they can coexist and be integrated in the same system.

Designing for frequent faults

Two more differences in design stand out when comparing MapReduce with MPP databases: how each handles faults, and how each uses memory and disk. Batch processes are less sensitive to faults than online systems. A fault does not immediately affect users, and the job can always be run again.

If a node crashes while a query is executing, most MPP databases abort the entire query. They either let the user resubmit the query or run it again automatically. Queries normally run for seconds or minutes at most, so this way of handling errors is acceptable, because retrying is not too expensive. MPP databases also prefer to keep as much data as possible in memory, for example by using hash joins, to avoid the cost of reading from disk.

MapReduce can tolerate the failure of a map or reduce task without affecting the job as a whole, because it retries work at the granularity of an individual task. It is also very eager to write data to disk. That is partly for fault tolerance, and partly because it assumes the dataset will be too big to fit in memory anyway.

The MapReduce approach suits larger jobs: jobs that process so much data, and run for so long, that they are likely to suffer at least one task failure along the way. In that case, rerunning the entire job because of a single task failure would be wasteful. Even if recovery at the granularity of a task makes fault-free processing slower, it can still be a reasonable trade-off when the rate of task failures is high enough.

But how realistic are these assumptions? In most clusters, machine failures do occur, but they are rare, so most jobs will not experience a machine failure. Is it really worth paying significant overhead for fault tolerance?

To understand MapReduce’s careful use of memory and its task-level recovery, look at the environment it was designed for. Google ran mixed-use datacenters, where online production services and offline batch jobs ran on the same machines. Every task had a resource allocation (CPU cores, RAM, disk space, and so on) enforced by containers. Every task also had a priority. If a higher-priority task needed more resources, lower-priority tasks on the same machine could be terminated, or preempted, to free them up. Priority also set the price of computing resources. Teams had to pay for what they used, and higher-priority processes cost more.

This architecture allows non-production, low-priority resources to be overcommitted, because the system knows it can reclaim them when needed. Overcommitting lets machines be used more fully, and it is more efficient than systems that keep production and non-production work apart. But MapReduce jobs run at low priority, so they risk being preempted at any time when a higher-priority process needs their resources. Batch jobs effectively use whatever computing resources remain after the high-priority processes have taken what they need.

At Google, a MapReduce task that runs for an hour has an approximately 5% risk of being terminated to make room for a higher-priority process. That rate is more than an order of magnitude higher than the rate of failures from hardware problems, machine reboots, or other causes. At that rate, a job with 100 tasks that each run for 10 minutes has a risk greater than 50% that at least one task will be terminated before it finishes.

This is why MapReduce is designed to tolerate frequent, unexpected task termination. It is not because the hardware is especially unreliable. It is because the freedom to terminate processes at any time allows better resource utilization across the cluster.

Among open source cluster schedulers, preemption is less widely used. YARN’s CapacityScheduler supports preemption to balance resources between queues. But general priority preemption was not supported in YARN, Mesos, or Kubernetes at the time the book was written. In an environment where tasks are not often terminated, MapReduce’s design decisions make less sense. The next section looks at some alternatives that make different decisions.

Beyond MapReduce

MapReduce became very popular and received a lot of hype in the late 2000s. But it is just one of many possible programming models for distributed systems. Depending on the volume of data, its structure, and the type of processing, other tools may be more appropriate for expressing a computation.

The chapter has spent a lot of time on MapReduce because it is a useful learning tool. It is a fairly clear and simple abstraction on top of a distributed filesystem. It is simple in the sense that you can understand what it is doing, not in the sense of being easy to use. Implementing a complex processing job with the raw MapReduce APIs is actually quite hard and laborious. For instance, you would have to implement any join algorithm from scratch.

In response, higher-level programming models such as Pig, Hive, Cascading, and Crunch were created on top of MapReduce. If you understand how MapReduce works, they are fairly easy to learn, and their higher-level constructs make many common batch tasks much easier to implement.

However, there are also problems with the MapReduce execution model itself, which are not fixed by adding another layer of abstraction. They show up as poor performance for some kinds of processing. MapReduce is very robust. You can use it to process almost arbitrarily large amounts of data on an unreliable, multi-tenant system with frequent task terminations, and it will still get the job done, albeit slowly. Other tools, on the other hand, are sometimes orders of magnitude faster for some kinds of processing.

The rest of this chapter looks at some of those alternatives. Chapter 11 moves on to stream processing, which can be regarded as another way of speeding up batch processing.

Materialization of Intermediate State

Every MapReduce job is independent of every other job. The main contact points of a job with the rest of the world are its input and output directories in the distributed filesystem. If you want the output of one job to be the input of a second job, you must set the second job’s input directory to be the same as the first job’s output directory. An external workflow scheduler must then start the second job only once the first has completed.

This setup is reasonable when the output of the first job is a dataset you want to publish widely within your organization. Then other jobs, including jobs written by other teams, can refer to it by name and reuse it. Publishing data to a well-known location allows loose coupling, so that jobs do not need to know who produces their input or who consumes their output.

In many cases, however, you know that the output of one job is only ever used as the input of one other job, and both are maintained by the same team. Then the files on the distributed filesystem are just intermediate state: a means of passing data from one job to the next. In complex workflows of 50 or 100 MapReduce jobs, used to build recommendation systems, there is a lot of this intermediate state.

The process of writing this intermediate state to files is called materialization. The term also appears with materialized views in Chapter 3. It means eagerly computing the result of an operation and writing it out, rather than computing it on demand when someone asks for it.

The log analysis at the start of the chapter used Unix pipes to connect one command’s output to the next command’s input. Pipes do not fully materialize the intermediate state. They stream the output to the input incrementally, using only a small in-memory buffer. MapReduce’s approach of fully materializing intermediate state has three downsides compared with Unix pipes:

  • A MapReduce job can start only when all the tasks in the preceding jobs that generate its inputs have completed. Processes connected by a Unix pipe all start at the same time, and each consumes output as soon as it is produced. Skew, or uneven load on different machines, means that a job often has a few straggler tasks that take much longer than the rest. Waiting for all of the preceding job’s tasks slows down the whole workflow.
  • Mappers are often redundant. They just read back the file that a reducer has just written, and prepare it for the next stage of partitioning and sorting. In many cases, the mapper’s work could be part of the previous reducer. If reducer output were partitioned and sorted the same way as mapper output, reducers could be chained together directly, without interleaved mapper stages.
  • Storing intermediate state in a distributed filesystem means the files are replicated across several nodes. For temporary data that is often overkill.

Dataflow engines

To fix these problems with MapReduce, several new execution engines for distributed batch computations were developed. The best known are Spark, Tez, and Flink. They differ in design, but they share one idea: they handle an entire workflow as one job, rather than breaking it into independent subjobs.

Because these systems explicitly model the flow of data through several processing stages, they are known as dataflow engines. Like MapReduce, they work by repeatedly calling a user-defined function to process one record at a time on a single thread. They parallelize work by partitioning their inputs, and they copy the output of one function over the network to become the input of another.

Unlike in MapReduce, these functions do not have to take the strict roles of alternating map and reduce. They can be assembled in more flexible ways. The book calls them operators. A dataflow engine offers several options for connecting one operator’s output to another’s input:

  • Repartition and sort the records by key, as in the MapReduce shuffle. This enables sort-merge joins and grouping, in the same way as MapReduce.
  • Take several inputs, partition them in the same way, but skip the sorting. This saves effort for partitioned hash joins. The order of records does not matter there, because building the hash table randomizes it anyway.
  • For broadcast hash joins, send the same output from one operator to all partitions of the join operator.

This style of processing engine is based on research systems called Dryad and Nephele. It has several advantages over the MapReduce model:

  • Expensive work such as sorting needs to be performed only where it is actually required. It does not happen by default between every map and reduce stage.
  • There are no unnecessary map tasks. The work of a mapper can often be folded into the preceding reduce operator, because a mapper does not change how a dataset is partitioned.
  • Because all joins and data dependencies in a workflow are declared explicitly, the scheduler has an overview of what data is needed where. It can therefore make locality optimizations. For example, it can place the task that consumes some data on the same machine as the task that produces it, so the data can pass through a shared memory buffer instead of being copied over the network.
  • Intermediate state between operators can be kept in memory or written to local disk. That needs less I/O than writing it to HDFS, where it must be replicated to several machines and written to disk on each replica. MapReduce already uses this trick for mapper output, and dataflow engines apply it to all intermediate state.
  • Operators can start executing as soon as their input is ready. There is no need to wait for the entire preceding stage to finish.
  • Existing Java Virtual Machine (JVM) processes can be reused to run new operators. This reduces startup overhead, whereas MapReduce launches a new JVM for each task.

You can use dataflow engines to implement the same computations as MapReduce workflows, and they usually execute significantly faster because of these optimizations. Since operators are a generalization of map and reduce, the same processing code can run on either engine. Workflows written in Pig, Hive, or Cascading can be switched from MapReduce to Tez or Spark with a simple configuration change, without modifying the code.

Tez is a fairly thin library that relies on the YARN shuffle service to copy data between nodes. Spark and Flink are big frameworks. They include their own network communication layer, scheduler, and user-facing APIs, which the chapter returns to shortly.

Fault tolerance in dataflow engines

An advantage of fully materializing intermediate state to a distributed filesystem is that the state is durable. That makes fault tolerance fairly easy in MapReduce. If a task fails, it can be restarted on another machine, and it can read the same input again from the filesystem.

Spark, Flink, and Tez avoid writing intermediate state to HDFS, so they take a different approach. If a machine fails and the intermediate state on that machine is lost, the lost data is recomputed from other data that is still available. The framework uses a prior intermediate stage if one is available. Otherwise it goes back to the original input data, which is normally in HDFS.

To make recomputation possible, the framework must keep track of how each piece of data was computed. That means which input partitions it used and which operators were applied to it. Spark uses the resilient distributed dataset (RDD) abstraction to track the ancestry of data. Flink checkpoints operator state, so that it can resume an operator that ran into a fault while it was running.

Recomputation depends on determinism. Given the same input data, do the operators always produce the same output? This question matters when some lost data has already been sent to downstream operators. If the operator is restarted and the recomputed data differs from the original lost data, it becomes very hard for the downstream operators to resolve the contradiction between the old and new data. The solution for nondeterministic operators is normally to kill the downstream operators as well, and run them again on the new data.

To avoid such cascading faults, it is better to make operators deterministic. But nondeterminism can creep in by accident. Many programming languages do not guarantee any particular order when you iterate over the elements of a hash table. Many probabilistic and statistical algorithms rely on random numbers. Any use of the system clock or of external data sources is also nondeterministic. These causes must be removed to recover reliably from faults. One way is to generate pseudorandom numbers from a fixed seed, so that the same sequence comes out every time.

Recovering by recomputation is not always the right answer. If the intermediate data is much smaller than the source data, or if the computation is very CPU-intensive, it is probably cheaper to materialize the intermediate data to files than to recompute it.

Discussion of materialization

Return to the Unix analogy. MapReduce is like writing the output of each command to a temporary file. Dataflow engines look much more like Unix pipes. Flink in particular is built around pipelined execution, which means passing the output of an operator incrementally to other operators, without waiting for the input to be complete before starting to process it.

A sorting operation inevitably needs to consume its entire input before it can produce any output. The very last input record might be the one with the lowest key, and so it must be the very first output record. Any operator that requires sorting therefore has to accumulate state, at least temporarily. But many other parts of a workflow can run in a pipelined manner.

When the job completes, its output needs to go somewhere durable, where users can find and use it. Most likely it is written to the distributed filesystem again. So when you use a dataflow engine, the materialized datasets on HDFS are still usually the inputs and the final outputs of a job. As with MapReduce, the inputs are immutable and the output is completely replaced. The improvement over MapReduce is that you no longer have to write all the intermediate state to the filesystem as well.

Graphs and Iterative Processing

Chapter 2 discussed using graphs to model data, and graph query languages to traverse their edges and vertices. That discussion focused on OLTP-style use, quickly running queries that find a small number of vertices matching certain criteria.

It is also interesting to look at graphs in a batch context, where the goal is an offline process or analysis of an entire graph. This need often arises in machine learning, for example in recommendation engines and ranking systems. One of the most famous graph algorithms is PageRank, which estimates the popularity of a web page based on which other pages link to it. It is part of the formula that determines the order in which search engines present their results.

There is a naming trap here. Dataflow engines such as Spark, Flink, and Tez arrange the operators in a job as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). That is not the same as graph processing. In a dataflow engine, the flow of data from one operator to another is structured as a graph, but the data itself is usually relational-style tuples. In graph processing, the data itself has the form of a graph. The book calls this another unfortunate naming confusion.

Many graph algorithms work by traversing one edge at a time. They join one vertex with an adjacent vertex to propagate some information, and they repeat until a condition is met. For example, the algorithm might stop when there are no more edges to follow, or when some metric converges. Chapter 2 gave an example of this, which made a list of all the locations in North America in a database by repeatedly following edges that say which location is within which other location. This kind of algorithm is called a transitive closure.

You can store a graph in a distributed filesystem, as files containing lists of vertices and edges. But the repeat until done idea cannot be expressed in plain MapReduce, because MapReduce performs only a single pass over the data. So this kind of algorithm is often implemented in an iterative style:

  1. An external scheduler runs a batch process to calculate one step of the algorithm.
  2. When the batch process completes, the scheduler checks whether the algorithm has finished, based on the completion condition. For example, there are no more edges to follow, or the change since the last iteration is below some threshold.
  3. If it has not finished, the scheduler goes back to step 1 and runs another round.

This approach works, but implementing it with MapReduce is often very inefficient. MapReduce does not understand that the algorithm is iterative. It always reads the entire input dataset and produces a completely new output dataset, even if only a small part of the graph changed since the last iteration.

The Pregel processing model

As an optimization for batch processing of graphs, the bulk synchronous parallel (BSP) model of computation has become popular. It is implemented by Apache Giraph, by the GraphX API in Spark, and by the Gelly API in Flink. It is also known as the Pregel model, because Google’s Pregel paper popularized this approach for graph processing.

Recall that in MapReduce, mappers conceptually send a message to a particular call of the reducer, because the framework collects together all the mapper outputs with the same key. Pregel works on a similar idea. One vertex can send a message to another vertex, and typically the messages travel along the edges of the graph. In each iteration, a function is called for each vertex and given all the messages sent to it, much like a call to a reducer. The difference is that in the Pregel model, a vertex remembers its state in memory from one iteration to the next. So the function only needs to process the new incoming messages. If no messages are being sent in some part of the graph, no work needs to be done there.

The model is somewhat like the actor model, the distributed actor frameworks discussed earlier in the book, if you think of each vertex as an actor. But there are differences. Vertex state and messages between vertices are fault-tolerant and durable. Communication also proceeds in fixed rounds. At every iteration, the framework delivers all the messages sent in the previous iteration. Actors normally have no such timing guarantee.

Fault tolerance in Pregel

Vertices can communicate only by passing messages, not by querying each other directly. This helps performance, because messages can be batched and there is less waiting for communication. The only waiting happens between iterations. Since Pregel guarantees that all messages sent in one iteration are delivered in the next, the previous iteration must completely finish, and all of its messages must be copied over the network, before the next one can start.

The underlying network may drop, duplicate, or arbitrarily delay messages, as discussed in the unreliable networks section of Chapter 8. Even so, Pregel implementations guarantee that messages are processed exactly once at their destination vertex in the following iteration. As with MapReduce, the framework transparently recovers from faults, which simplifies the programming model for algorithms built on Pregel.

This fault tolerance comes from checkpointing. At the end of an iteration, the state of all vertices is periodically written to durable storage. If a node fails and its in-memory state is lost, the simplest solution is to roll the whole graph computation back to the last checkpoint and restart from there. If the algorithm is deterministic and messages are logged, it is also possible to recover only the lost partition, as discussed for dataflow engines.

Parallel execution

A vertex does not need to know which physical machine it is running on. When it sends messages to other vertices, it simply sends them to a vertex ID. The framework decides which vertex runs on which machine, and how to route messages over the network so that they arrive in the right place.

Because the programming model deals with one vertex at a time, sometimes described as thinking like a vertex, the framework can partition the graph in arbitrary ways. Ideally, vertices that communicate heavily would be colocated on the same machine. But finding such an optimized partitioning is hard. In practice, the graph is often partitioned simply by an arbitrarily assigned vertex ID, with no attempt to group related vertices together.

As a result, graph algorithms often have a lot of cross-machine communication overhead. The intermediate state, the messages sent between nodes, is often bigger than the original graph. The overhead of sending messages over the network can significantly slow down distributed graph algorithms.

For this reason, if your graph fits in memory on a single computer, a single-machine algorithm, perhaps even a single-threaded one, will quite likely outperform a distributed batch process. Even if the graph is bigger than memory but fits on the disks of one computer, single-machine processing with a framework such as GraphChi is a viable option. If the graph is too big for one machine, a distributed approach such as Pregel is unavoidable. Efficiently parallelizing graph algorithms is an area of ongoing research.

High-Level APIs and Languages

Over the years since MapReduce became popular, the execution engines for distributed batch processing have matured. The infrastructure is now robust enough to store and process many petabytes of data on clusters of more than 10,000 machines. Physically operating batch processes at that scale is considered more or less solved. Attention has turned to other areas: improving the programming model, improving the efficiency of processing, and broadening the set of problems these technologies can solve.

As discussed earlier, higher-level languages and APIs such as Hive, Pig, Cascading, and Crunch became popular because programming MapReduce jobs by hand is laborious. When Tez emerged, these languages gained the extra benefit of running on the new dataflow engine without rewriting job code. Spark and Flink also include their own high-level dataflow APIs, often inspired by FlumeJava.

These dataflow APIs generally use relational-style building blocks to express a computation. You can join datasets on the value of a field, group tuples by key, filter by a condition, and aggregate tuples by counting, summing, or other functions. Internally, these operations are carried out by the join and grouping algorithms that this chapter described.

Besides requiring less code, high-level interfaces allow interactive use. You can write analysis code incrementally in a shell and run it frequently to see what it is doing. This style of development helps a lot when exploring a dataset and trying different ways to process it. It also resembles the Unix philosophy. These interfaces make the people using the system more productive, and they also improve the efficiency of job execution at the machine level.

The move toward declarative query languages

Specifying joins as relational operators, rather than spelling out the code that performs the join, has an advantage. The framework can analyze the properties of the join inputs and decide automatically which join algorithm suits the task. Hive, Spark, and Flink have cost-based query optimizers that do this. They can even change the order of joins so that the amount of intermediate state is minimized.

The choice of join algorithm can make a large difference to the performance of a batch job, and it is convenient not to have to understand and remember all the join algorithms in this chapter. That works when joins are declared in a declarative way. The application states which joins it needs, and the query optimizer decides how to execute them best. Chapter 2 introduced this idea in its discussion of query languages for data.

In other ways, MapReduce and its dataflow successors differ from the fully declarative model of SQL. MapReduce was built around callback functions. For each record or group of records, a user-defined function, the mapper or reducer, is called, and it is free to run arbitrary code to decide what to output. The advantage is that you can draw on a large ecosystem of existing libraries for parsing, natural language analysis, image analysis, and numerical or statistical algorithms.

The freedom to run arbitrary code is what has long distinguished batch systems of MapReduce heritage from MPP databases. Databases have facilities for user-defined functions, but they are often cumbersome to use and not well integrated with the package managers and dependency systems that most programming languages use, such as Maven for Java, npm for JavaScript, and RubyGems for Ruby.

Dataflow engines have also found advantages in adding declarative features in areas beyond joins. If a callback function contains only a simple filtering condition, or just selects a few fields from a record, calling the function on every record has a real CPU cost. If such simple filtering and mapping are declared in a declarative way, the query optimizer can take advantage of column-oriented storage layouts and read only the columns it needs from disk. Hive, Spark DataFrames, and Impala also use vectorized execution. This means iterating over data in a tight inner loop that is friendly to CPU caches and avoids function calls. Spark generates JVM bytecode for this, and Impala uses LLVM to generate native code for those inner loops.

By adding declarative aspects to their high-level APIs, and by having query optimizers that can use them, batch processing frameworks begin to look more like MPP databases, and they can reach comparable performance. Because they can still run arbitrary code and read data in arbitrary formats, they keep their flexibility advantage.

Specialization for different domains

The ability to run arbitrary code is useful, but many common processing patterns recur. So it is worth having reusable implementations of the common building blocks. MPP databases have traditionally served business intelligence analysts and business reporting. But that is just one of many domains in which batch processing is used.

Statistical and numerical algorithms are increasingly important, because machine learning applications such as classification and recommendation systems need them. Reusable implementations are emerging. For example, Mahout implements machine learning algorithms on top of MapReduce, Spark, and Flink. MADlib implements similar functionality inside a relational MPP database, Apache HAWQ.

Spatial algorithms are also useful. The book gives k-nearest neighbors as an example. It searches for the items that are close to a given item in some multi-dimensional space, which is a kind of similarity search. Approximate search matters for genome analysis too, where algorithms must find strings that are similar but not identical.

As batch engines gain built-in functions and declarative operators, and as MPP databases become more programmable and flexible, the two are beginning to look more alike. In the end, they are all systems for storing and processing data.

Summary

Summary
  • Unix lessons. The chapter started with awk, grep, sort, and uniq. Their design ideas carry into MapReduce and newer dataflow engines. Inputs are immutable, outputs are meant to become the input of some later program, and complex problems are solved by composing small tools that each do one thing well.
  • The interface. In the Unix world, the uniform interface that lets one program compose with another is files and pipes. In MapReduce, it is a distributed filesystem. Dataflow engines add pipe-like transport so that intermediate state does not have to be written to the filesystem. The initial input and final output of a job are still usually HDFS.
  • Partitioning. In MapReduce, mappers are partitioned by input file block. Their output is repartitioned, sorted, and merged into a configurable number of reducer partitions, so that related data (all records with the same key) ends up in the same place. Dataflow engines avoid sorting unless it is needed, but they take a broadly similar approach to partitioning.
  • Fault tolerance. MapReduce writes to disk often. That makes it easy to recover one failed task without restarting the job, but slows execution when nothing fails. Dataflow engines materialize less and keep more in memory, so when a node fails they must recompute more. Deterministic operators reduce the amount of data that must be recomputed.
  • Join algorithms. Sort-merge joins have each input pass through a mapper that extracts the join key, then partition, sort, and merge so that all records with the same key reach the same reducer call. Broadcast hash joins load one small input into a hash table in every mapper. Partitioned hash joins apply the hash table approach to each matching partition of two inputs. Most of these are also used inside MPP databases and dataflow engines.
  • A restricted model. Batch callback functions are assumed to be stateless and to have no externally visible side effects other than their designated output. That lets the framework retry tasks safely and discard the output of failed tasks. The framework can guarantee that the final output is the same as if no faults had occurred. These guarantees are much stronger than those of online services that write to databases as a side effect of handling a request.
  • Bounded input. A batch job reads input and produces output without modifying the input. The input is bounded, meaning it has a known, fixed size, such as a set of log files at one point in time or a snapshot of a database. So the job knows when it has finished and eventually completes. Chapter 11 turns to stream processing, where the input is unbounded, so a job is never complete.

The chapter ends with a numbered References list of 81 sources, including the MapReduce paper, the Hadoop and Spark books, and the Pregel paper. This retelling does not reproduce that list.

Check yourself

  1. The Ruby program and the Unix pipeline give the same top five pages. When is the sort-based pipeline the better choice?

    Show answer

    When the working set is larger than memory, such as a site with very many distinct URLs. The sort utility spills to disk, sorts chunks, and merges them with sequential reads, so it keeps working where a hash table would run out of memory.

  2. In the reduce-side sort-merge join, why does the reducer need to hold only one user record in memory at a time, and why does the secondary sort help?

    Show answer

    The reducer is called once per user ID, and with a secondary sort the user record arrives first. The reducer can keep that one date of birth in a variable and stream through the user’s events. It never needs another record in memory or any network request.

  3. Why is it a bad idea for a batch job to write its results one record at a time into the production database, and what does the book suggest instead?

    Show answer

    Each record costs a slow network request, many parallel writers can overwhelm the database, and side effects on an external system cannot be hidden if the job fails. The book suggests building the new database files inside the job, writing them to the output directory, and loading them in bulk into read-only servers.

  4. A dataflow engine recovers from a lost machine by recomputing its data instead of reading an HDFS copy. Why must the operators be deterministic?

    Show answer

    If a recomputed result differs from the lost one that was already sent downstream, the downstream operators face contradictory data. Making operators deterministic avoids that, so only the lost data needs to be recomputed.

Part III · Chapter 11

Stream Processing

The big idea: a stream is data that never stops arriving. Once you treat changes as a log of events, a database, a cache, and a search index can all be kept current from that one log, and a process that runs forever needs its own tools for time, joins, and recovery.

The chapter opens with a line from John Gall’s book Systemantics: a complex system that works is invariably found to have grown out of a simple system that worked, and a complex system designed from scratch never works. Keep that in mind, because the chapter builds up a fairly complicated set of ideas one step at a time.

Chapter 10 covered batch processing. A batch job reads a set of input files and writes a new set of output files. Its output is derived data, which means it can be recreated at any time by running the job again. Batch processing was used to build search indexes, recommendation systems, and analytics.

Chapter 10 made one big assumption, though. It assumed the input is bounded, meaning it has a known, finite size. Because of that, the batch job knows when it has read everything and can finish. This matters more than it sounds. Take sorting, which is central to MapReduce. A sort must read its entire input before it can write any output, because the very last record might have the lowest key and so has to come first. You cannot start writing early.

In reality, a lot of data is unbounded. It arrives gradually. Your users produced data yesterday and today, and they will produce more tomorrow. Unless the business shuts down, the dataset is never complete in any meaningful sense. So batch systems have to cut the endless flow into chunks of fixed length, such as one day’s data at the end of each day, or one hour’s data at the end of each hour.

The trouble is that a daily batch run means a change in the input shows up in the output only a day later. That is too slow for impatient users. You can shorten the chunks, for example processing each second’s data at the end of every second. Or you can drop the chunks altogether and process every event as soon as it happens. That second option is the idea behind stream processing.

In general, a stream is data that is made available bit by bit over time. The idea shows up in many places: the standard input and output of Unix programs, lazy lists in some programming languages, file APIs such as Java’s FileInputStream, TCP connections, and the delivery of audio and video over the internet.

The chapter treats event streams as a way of managing data. An event stream is the unbounded, step-by-step counterpart of the batch data from the last chapter. It covers three things. First, how streams are represented, stored, and sent over a network. Second, how streams relate to databases. Third, how to process streams continually and what applications can be built from that.

Transmitting Event Streams

In the batch world, the inputs and outputs of a job are files, perhaps on a distributed filesystem. What is the streaming equivalent?

When the input is a file, the first step is usually to parse it into a sequence of records. In streaming, a record is more often called an event. It is essentially the same thing: a small, self-contained, unchangeable object that holds the details of something that happened at a point in time. An event usually carries a timestamp, taken from a time-of-day clock, that says when it happened.

The thing that happened might be an action a user took, such as viewing a page or making a purchase. It might come from a machine, such as a temperature reading from a sensor or a CPU usage measurement. The web server log lines from the batch chapter were events too.

An event can be encoded as text, as JSON, or in a compact binary form, as Chapter 4 discussed. That encoding lets you store the event, for example by appending it to a file, inserting it into a relational table, or writing it to a document database. It also lets you send the event over a network to another machine for processing.

In batch processing, a file is written once and may then be read by many jobs. In streaming, the same pattern is described with new words. An event is produced once by a producer, which is also called a publisher or sender. It can then be processed by many consumers, also called subscribers or recipients. In a filesystem, a file name groups related records together. In a streaming system, related events are grouped into a topic or a stream.

In principle, a file or a database is enough to connect producers and consumers. The producer writes every event to the datastore. Each consumer polls the datastore from time to time to see whether new events have appeared since it last looked. That is exactly what a batch job does when it runs once a day.

When you want continual processing with low delays, polling becomes expensive, unless the datastore was designed for it. The more often you poll, the smaller the share of requests that return anything new, and the higher the overhead. It is better for consumers to be notified when new events arrive. Relational databases have triggers, which can react to a change such as a new row, but the book says they are very limited and have long been something of an afterthought. Specialized tools were built to deliver event notifications instead.

Messaging Systems

A common way to notify consumers is a messaging system. A producer sends a message, which contains the event, and the system pushes that message to the consumers. The chapter had already touched on this in its section on message-passing dataflow in Chapter 4, and here it goes into more detail.

The simplest messaging system is a direct channel, such as a Unix pipe or a TCP connection between producer and consumer. But pipes and TCP connect exactly one sender to one recipient. A messaging system goes further. It lets many producers send messages to the same topic, and it lets many consumers receive the messages in that topic.

Within this publish and subscribe model, systems take many different approaches, and none of them is right for every purpose. The book suggests two questions that tell the systems apart.

  1. What happens when producers send messages faster than consumers can handle them? There are three basic options. The system can drop messages. It can buffer them in a queue. Or it can apply backpressure, also called flow control, which means blocking the producer from sending more until the consumer catches up. Unix pipes and TCP use backpressure. They have a small, fixed-size buffer, and when it fills up the sender is blocked until the receiver takes data out. If a system buffers messages in a queue, you need to know what happens when the queue no longer fits in memory. Does the system crash, or does it write messages to disk? And how does that disk access affect performance?

  2. What happens if nodes crash or go offline? Are any messages lost? Durability, the promise that accepted data is kept, usually requires writing to disk, replicating to other machines, or both. Each of these has a cost. If you can afford to lose some messages, you can often get higher throughput and lower latency from the same hardware.

Whether losing messages is acceptable depends on the application. Take sensor readings and metrics that are sent regularly. One missing data point is usually harmless, because a newer value follows soon. But if many messages are dropped, the metrics may be wrong without anyone noticing. If you are counting events, the picture is different. Every lost message means a wrong counter, so reliable delivery matters a great deal.

Chapter 10’s batch systems had a useful property here. They give a strong reliability guarantee. Failed tasks are retried automatically, and the partial output of a failed task is thrown away. So the output looks as if no failure happened, which keeps the programming model simple. Later in this chapter the book looks at how to get similar guarantees in a streaming setting.

Direct messaging from producers to consumers

Some messaging systems skip any middleman and send messages directly between producers and consumers. The book lists several examples.

  • UDP multicast is widely used in finance for feeds such as stock market prices, where low latency matters most. UDP on its own is unreliable, so the application protocol must recover lost packets. The producer has to remember the packets it sent so it can resend them on request.
  • Brokerless libraries such as ZeroMQ and nanomsg take a similar approach. They implement publish and subscribe over TCP or IP multicast, without a central server.
  • StatsD and Brubeck collect metrics from every machine on a network using unreliable UDP messages. In the StatsD protocol, counters are only correct if every message arrives. Because UDP can lose messages, the counts are at best approximate.
  • Webhooks are a pattern where a service registers a callback URL with another service. Whenever an event happens, the second service makes a request to that URL. This is a direct push from producer to consumer, usually over HTTP or RPC.

These systems work well in the situations they were built for. But they generally require the application code to be aware that messages can be lost. The faults they tolerate are limited. Even when the protocol detects and resends packets that the network lost, these systems assume that producers and consumers are online all the time. If a consumer is offline, it misses the messages sent while it was unreachable. Some protocols let the producer retry failed deliveries, but that breaks down if the producer crashes and loses the buffer of messages it was going to retry.

Message brokers

A widely used alternative is a message broker, also called a message queue. A broker is essentially a database that has been optimized for handling message streams. It runs as a server, and producers and consumers connect to it as clients. Producers write messages to the broker, and consumers read them from the broker.

Because the data is kept in one central place, the broker can handle clients that come and go, connecting, disconnecting, and crashing, more easily. Durability moves to the broker. Some brokers keep messages only in memory. Others, depending on configuration, write them to disk so they survive a broker crash. When consumers are slow, most brokers allow the queue to grow without limit, rather than dropping messages or applying backpressure. This choice may also depend on configuration.

This leads to a consequence. Consumers are usually asynchronous. When a producer sends a message, it normally waits only for the broker to confirm that it has stored the message. It does not wait for consumers to process it. Delivery to a consumer happens at some later point. That is often within a fraction of a second, but it can take much longer if the queue has a backlog.

Message brokers compared to databases

Some message brokers can take part in two-phase commit protocols using XA or JTA, the transaction standards covered in Chapter 9. That makes them similar in nature to databases. But the book points out four practical differences.

  • Lifetime of data. Databases keep data until someone explicitly deletes it. Most brokers delete a message automatically once it has been delivered successfully. That makes them unsuitable for long-term storage.
  • Size of the working set. Because brokers delete messages quickly, they assume their working set is small and their queues are short. If consumers are slow and the broker must buffer a lot, perhaps spilling messages to disk, each message takes longer to handle and overall throughput can drop.
  • Ways of selecting data. Databases often support secondary indexes and many ways to search. Brokers often let a consumer subscribe to the topics that match a pattern. The mechanisms differ, but both let a client choose the part of the data it cares about.
  • Queries and notifications. A database query returns the result as of one moment. If another client changes the data later, the first client is not told that its result is now stale, unless it asks again or polls. Brokers do not support arbitrary queries, but they do notify clients when new messages arrive.

This is the traditional view of message brokers. It is captured in standards such as JMS (Java Message Service) and AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol). It is implemented in software such as RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, Qpid, TIBCO Enterprise Message Service, IBM MQ, Azure Service Bus, and Google Cloud Pub/Sub.

Multiple consumers

When several consumers read from the same topic, two main patterns are used. Figure 11-1 in the book shows both.

  • Load balancing. Each message is delivered to one of the consumers, so the consumers share the work. The broker may assign messages to consumers in any way. This pattern is useful when each message is expensive to process, because you can add consumers to process more in parallel. In AMQP, several clients consume from the same queue to get this effect. JMS calls it a shared subscription.
  • Fan-out. Each message is delivered to all of the consumers. Several independent consumers can each tune in to the same broadcast without affecting one another. This is the streaming version of several batch jobs reading the same input file. JMS provides it through topic subscriptions, and AMQP through exchange bindings.

The two patterns can be combined. Two groups of consumers might each subscribe to the same topic. Each group as a whole receives every message, but within each group only one node gets each message.

Acknowledgments and redelivery

Consumers can crash at any time. So a broker might deliver a message to a consumer that never finishes it, or finishes only part of it before crashing. To make sure a message is not lost, brokers use acknowledgments, usually shortened to acks. A consumer must explicitly tell the broker when it has finished processing a message. Only then does the broker remove the message from the queue.

If the connection to a consumer closes, or times out, before the broker gets an ack, the broker assumes the message was not processed. It then delivers the message again, to another consumer. The book points out a subtle case. The message may have been fully processed, but the ack was lost on the network. Handling that case needs an atomic commit protocol, which the chapter on distributed transactions covers.

Redelivery has a surprising side effect on ordering. Here is how the book describes it.

Example

Producer 1 sends messages m3, m4, and m5 in that order, to a topic with two consumers. The consumers normally handle messages in the order they were sent.

  1. Consumer 2 receives m3 and starts processing it.
  2. At the same moment, consumer 1 is processing m4.
  3. Consumer 2 crashes before it acknowledges m3.
  4. The broker, seeing no ack, redelivers m3 to consumer 1 later on.
  5. Consumer 1 therefore handles the messages in the order m4, m3, m5.
