The result is that m3 and m4 are no longer processed in the order the producer sent them. Figure 11-2 in the book draws this sequence.

Even if the broker tries to keep messages in order, which the JMS and AMQP standards both ask it to do, load balancing combined with redelivery inevitably reorders messages. One way to avoid it is to use a separate queue for each consumer, so no load balancing happens. Reordering does not matter when messages are fully independent. It does matter when there are causal dependencies between messages, as the chapter shows later.

Partitioned Logs

Sending a packet over a network, or making a request to a network service, is usually a short-lived action that leaves no lasting record. You could record it with packet capture and logging, but nobody normally thinks of it that way. Even message brokers that write messages to disk quickly delete them after delivery. They are built around a transient view of messaging.

Databases and filesystems take the opposite view. Anything written to a database or a file is expected to stay recorded, until someone deliberately deletes it. This difference in mindset has a large effect on how derived data is produced.

A key property of batch jobs, from Chapter 10, is that you can run them again and again, trying out different processing steps, without any risk to the input, because the input is read-only. That does not hold for AMQP- and JMS-style messaging. Receiving a message is destructive if the acknowledgment deletes it from the broker. You cannot run the same consumer again and expect the same result.

Adding a new consumer to a messaging system also has a limit. A new consumer normally receives only the messages sent after it registered. Earlier messages are already gone. A new client of a file or database, by contrast, can read data written at any time in the past, as long as the application has not overwritten or deleted it.

So the question becomes: why not combine the two? You could have the durable storage of a database together with the low-latency notification of a messaging system. This is the idea behind log-based message brokers.

Using logs for message storage

A log is an append-only sequence of records on disk. The earlier chapters met logs in log-structured storage engines and write-ahead logs (Chapter 3), and in replication (Chapter 5). The same structure can carry messages. A producer sends a message by appending it to the end of the log. A consumer reads messages by moving through the log in order. When a consumer reaches the end, it waits to be notified that another message has been appended. The Unix tool tail -f, which watches a file and prints new lines as they are added, works in much this way.

To go beyond what one disk can handle, the log can be partitioned, using the partitioning idea from Chapter 6. Each partition is a separate log, and different partitions can live on different machines. Each can be read and written independently of the others. A topic is then a group of partitions that all carry messages of the same type. Figure 1 shows the idea.

Within each partition, the broker gives every message a number that always goes up, called an offset. The offset is a sequence number. Because a partition is append-only, the messages in it are in a single, fixed order. There is no ordering guarantee across different partitions.

Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams, and Twitter’s DistributedLog are log-based message brokers that work this way. Google Cloud Pub/Sub is built along similar lines, but it offers a JMS-style interface rather than a log interface. These brokers write every message to disk, yet they reach throughputs of millions of messages per second. They do it by spreading partitions across many machines, and they get fault tolerance by replicating messages to other machines.

Logs compared to traditional messaging

The log-based approach makes fan-out easy. Several consumers can read the log independently, and reading a message does not delete it. Load balancing works differently. Instead of handing out individual messages, the broker assigns whole partitions to the nodes in a consumer group. Each consumer then reads all the messages in its partitions, usually in order and on a single thread.

This coarse form of load balancing has two downsides, which the book describes.

  • The number of nodes that can share the work of a topic is at most the number of partitions in that topic. Messages in one partition always go to the same node.
  • If one message is slow to process, it holds up every message behind it in the same partition. This is the head-of-line blocking described earlier in Chapter 1.

The book notes a workaround. Two consumers can share one partition if both read the full set of messages but one handles only the even-numbered offsets and the other only the odd ones. Another option is a thread pool inside one consumer. But the book prefers single-threaded processing of each partition, because a thread pool makes it harder to track consumer offsets. Parallelism is then increased by adding more partitions.

Which style is better depends on the work. The table below sums up the trade-off.

Trade-offs
StyleGood atCosts
AMQP or JMS-style brokerExpensive messages handled in parallel, one at a time, when order matters less. Good for task queues.Messages can be reordered after a redelivery. Messages are deleted once acknowledged, so they cannot be replayed.
Log-based brokerHigh throughput with fast messages where order matters. Many independent readers. Replaying old messages.Parallelism within a consumer group is capped by the partition count. One slow message holds up the rest of its partition.

Consumer offsets

Reading a partition in order makes it easy to see what has been processed. Every message with an offset below a consumer’s current offset has been handled. Every message with a higher offset has not been seen yet. So the broker does not need to track an acknowledgment for every single message. It only needs to record each consumer’s offset from time to time. Less bookkeeping means more room for batching and pipelining, which helps throughput.

The book notes that this offset is very like the log sequence number used in database replication. In replication, the sequence number lets a follower reconnect to its leader after a disconnection and carry on without skipping writes. The same idea is used here. The broker plays the part of a leader database, and each consumer plays the part of a follower.

If a consumer node fails, another node in the group is assigned the failed consumer’s partitions. It starts reading from the last offset that was recorded. Any messages the failed consumer had processed after its last recorded offset will be processed a second time. The chapter comes back to how to deal with that later.

Disk space usage

If a log only ever grows, it will eventually run out of disk space. So the log is split into segments. From time to time, old segments are deleted or moved to archive storage. A more refined way of freeing space comes later in the chapter.

This has a consequence for slow consumers. If a consumer falls so far behind that its offset points to a segment that has been deleted, it will miss messages. In effect, the log is a bounded buffer that throws away the oldest messages when it is full. This is known as a circular buffer or ring buffer. Because the buffer lives on disk, it can still be very large.

Example

The book does a quick estimate. At the time of writing, a typical large hard drive held 6 TB and could write at 150 MB per second. If messages arrive as fast as the disk can take them, the drive fills in about 11 hours. After that, it starts overwriting the oldest messages.

  1. Take 6 TB, which is about 6,000,000 MB.
  2. Divide by 150 MB per second. That is 40,000 seconds.
  3. 40,000 seconds is roughly 11 hours.

This ratio stays the same whether you use one drive or many machines. In practice, deployments rarely use the full write speed of the disk, so a log can typically keep several days, or even weeks, of messages.

The throughput of a log stays roughly constant no matter how much history it keeps, because every message is written to disk anyway. That is different from messaging systems that keep messages in memory and only write to disk when the queue gets too long. Those systems are fast while queues are short, but they slow down sharply once they start spilling to disk. Their throughput depends on how much history they hold.

When consumers cannot keep up with producers

Earlier, the chapter listed three things a system can do when consumers fall behind: drop messages, buffer them, or apply backpressure. A log-based broker is a form of buffering, with a large buffer. The buffer is fixed in size, but it is limited only by available disk space.

If a consumer falls so far behind that the messages it needs are older than what the disk retains, it cannot read them. The broker has effectively dropped the messages that were older than the buffer can hold. You can watch how far each consumer is behind the head of the log, and raise an alert when the gap grows too large. Because the buffer is large, a human operator usually has plenty of time to fix a slow consumer and let it catch up before any messages are lost.

Only the slow consumer is affected when it falls behind. It does not disturb the service for other consumers. The book calls this a big operational advantage. You can read a production log experimentally, for development, testing, or debugging, without much risk to production. When a consumer shuts down or crashes, it stops using resources. The only thing left behind is its offset.

Traditional message brokers work differently. There, you must be careful to delete any queue whose consumer has shut down. Otherwise the queue keeps filling with messages and takes memory away from the consumers that are still running.

Replaying old messages

With AMQP- and JMS-style brokers, processing and acknowledging a message is destructive, because it deletes the message. A log-based broker is different. Consuming from a log is more like reading a file. It is read-only and does not change the log. The only side effect, apart from whatever output the consumer writes, is that the consumer’s offset moves forward. And the consumer controls its own offset, so it can be moved on purpose.

For example, you can start a copy of a consumer using yesterday’s offsets and send its output to a different place. That way it reprocesses the last day’s messages. You can repeat this as many times as you like, changing the processing code each time. This makes log-based messaging look more like the batch processing of the last chapter, where derived data is kept separate from the input by a repeatable transformation. That makes experiments easier, and it makes recovery from errors and bugs easier too. The book calls this a good tool for connecting data flows across an organization.

Try it

Suppose a bug in your consumer wrote wrong totals for the past three days. With a message queue that deletes on acknowledgment, what would you have to do? With a log that keeps a week of history, how would you fix it? Which design gives you more room to experiment?

Databases and Streams

The chapter has compared message brokers with databases several times, and found them different in many ways. Yet the log-based brokers borrowed ideas from databases, and the relationship runs in the other direction too. Ideas from messaging and streams can be applied to databases.

The earlier sections said that an event is a record of something that happened at a point in time. That something may be a user action, such as typing a search query. It may be a sensor reading. It may also be a write to a database. The fact that something was written to a database is itself an event, and it can be captured, stored, and processed. This suggests that the link between databases and streams goes deeper than the physical storage of logs on disk. It is a basic relationship.

Look at the replication log from Chapter 5. It is a stream of database write events, produced by the leader as it processes transactions. Followers apply that stream of writes to their own copy of the database, and so they end up with an accurate copy of the same data. The events in the replication log describe the changes to the data.

Chapter 9 also introduced the principle of state machine replication. It says that if every event is a write to the database, and every replica processes the same events in the same order, then all the replicas end up in the same final state. This assumes that processing an event is deterministic, meaning the same input always gives the same result. It is another case of event streams.

The rest of this section first looks at a problem that arises in systems built from several different data stores. Then it shows how bringing ideas from event streams into databases can solve that problem.

Keeping Systems in Sync

No single system can satisfy every need for storing, querying, and processing data. Most real applications combine several technologies. A typical setup might use an OLTP database (a database that handles many small reads and writes from users), a cache to speed up common requests, a full-text index to answer search queries, and a data warehouse for analytics. Each one holds its own copy of the data, in a format chosen for its own purpose.

When the same data sits in several places, the copies have to be kept in step. If an item is updated in the database, it must also be updated in the cache, the search index, and the warehouse. For a data warehouse, this synchronization is usually done by ETL processes (extract, transform, and load, covered in Chapter 3). ETL often takes a full copy of the database, transforms it, and bulk-loads it into the warehouse. That is a batch process. The book also notes that search indexes and recommendation systems are often built the same way, with batch jobs.

If full copies every day are too slow, teams sometimes turn to dual writes. The application code writes to each system directly when the data changes. For example, it first writes to the database, then updates the search index, then invalidates the cache entries. Or it does the writes at the same time.

Dual writes have serious problems. The first is a race condition, which the book illustrates in Figure 11-4. Here is the example, step by step.

Example

Two clients try to update the same item, X. Client 1 wants to set it to A. Client 2 wants to set it to B. Both clients first write to the database, then write to the search index. Bad timing interleaves their requests.

  1. The database first receives client 1’s write, which sets X to A.
  2. Then it receives client 2’s write, which sets X to B. The final value in the database is B.
  3. The search index first receives client 2’s write, which sets X to B.
  4. Then it receives client 1’s write, which sets X to A. The final value in the search index is A.

The two systems now disagree with each other, permanently. No error was raised anywhere.

Unless you have some extra mechanism for detecting concurrent writes, such as the version vectors discussed in Chapter 5, you will not even notice that the writes overlapped. One value silently overwrites the other.

The second problem is that one of the two writes can fail while the other succeeds. That is a fault-tolerance problem rather than a concurrency problem. But it also leaves the two systems inconsistent. Making sure that both writes succeed or both fail is an instance of the atomic commit problem, which is expensive to solve (Chapter 9).

The third problem is structural. If you have one replicated database with a single leader, that leader sets the order of writes, so state machine replication works among the database replicas. In the example above, though, there is no single leader. The database has a leader, and the search index has a leader, but neither follows the other. So conflicts can happen (Chapter 5 covers multi-leader replication). The situation would be much better if there were one leader, the database, and the search index were simply a follower of it. Is that possible in practice? The next section says yes, with some work.

Watch out

Writing to two systems at once, without coordination, can leave them permanently different, with no error. Ordering problems and partial failures both cause this.

Change Data Capture

The problem with most databases’ replication logs is that they have long been treated as an internal detail of the database, not as a public interface. Clients are meant to query the database through its data model and its query language. They are not meant to read the replication log and pull data out of it.

For decades, many databases had no documented way to get the log of changes written to them. So it was hard to take every change made in a database and copy it to another storage system, such as a search index, a cache, or a data warehouse.

More recently, interest has grown in change data capture, usually shortened to CDC. CDC means observing all the data changes written to a database and extracting them in a form that can be copied to other systems. It is especially useful when the changes are published as a stream, immediately as they are written.

For example, you can capture the changes in a database and apply the same changes, in the same order, to a search index. If the changes are applied in the same order they were written, the data in the search index will match the data in the database. The search index and any other derived data system are then just consumers of the change stream. Figure 11-5 in the book shows this layout.

Implementing change data capture

The source database becomes the leader, from which the changes are captured. The other systems become followers. A log-based message broker is a good way to carry the change events, because it keeps messages in order. That avoids the reordering problem shown in Figure 11-2. The derived data systems are called derived because their data is a view onto the data in the system of record, which is the authoritative source.

There are several ways to capture changes. One is a database trigger, which is a small piece of logic that runs on every change to a table. The triggers write a matching entry to a changelog table. Chapter 5 described this as trigger-based replication. The book says triggers tend to be fragile and to add significant overhead. A more robust option is to parse the database’s replication log. That also has challenges, such as handling schema changes.

Several large companies have built CDC systems this way. LinkedIn’s Databus, Facebook’s Wormhole, and Yahoo!’s Sherpa all use the idea at large scale. Some open source tools do the same for individual databases. Bottled Water decodes PostgreSQL’s write-ahead log. Maxwell and Debezium parse MySQL’s binlog. Mongoriver reads MongoDB’s oplog. GoldenGate provides similar facilities for Oracle.

Like message brokers, CDC is usually asynchronous. The source database does not wait for the change to be applied to the consumers before it commits. This is good for operations, because adding a slow consumer does not hurt the source database much. The downside is that all the problems of replication lag apply (Chapter 5).

Initial snapshot

If you have the complete log of every change ever made to a database, you can rebuild the whole state by replaying the log from the start. In most cases, though, keeping every change forever would take too much disk space, and replaying it would take too long. So the log has to be cut short, or truncated.

That creates a problem for new derived systems. Building a new full-text index, for example, needs a full copy of the entire database. Applying only the recent changes is not enough, because items that were not changed recently would be missing from the index. So if you no longer have the full log history, you have to start from a consistent snapshot of the database. Chapter 5 described this for setting up new followers.

The snapshot must match a known position, or offset, in the change log. That tells you where to start applying changes once the snapshot has been loaded. Some CDC tools include this snapshot step. Others leave it as a manual task.

Log compaction

If you can keep only a limited amount of log history, you must take a new snapshot every time you want to add a derived system. Log compaction offers a better option. Chapter 3 discussed the idea in connection with hash indexes and log-structured storage engines, and Figure 3-2 in the book shows an example.

The principle is simple. The storage engine regularly looks for log records that share a key, throws away the older duplicates, and keeps only the most recent update for each key. The compaction and merging run in the background. In a log-structured storage engine, a special update with a null value, called a tombstone, marks a key as deleted. Compaction removes the key when it sees the tombstone. As long as a key is not overwritten or deleted, it stays in the log forever.

The space a compacted log needs depends only on the current contents of the database, not on how many writes have ever happened. If the same key is overwritten many times, its old values are eventually garbage-collected, and only the latest value stays.

The same idea works for log-based message brokers and CDC. If every change has a primary key, and every update for a key replaces the previous value for that key, then keeping only the most recent write per key is enough. You can then rebuild a derived system, such as a search index, by starting a new consumer at offset 0 of the compacted topic and reading every message in order. The log is guaranteed to hold the most recent value for every key, and it may also hold some older values. So you get a full copy of the database without taking another snapshot of the source database.

Apache Kafka supports this log compaction feature. The book points out that this makes the message broker usable for durable storage, not only for transient messaging.

API support for change streams

Databases are increasingly offering change streams as a first-class interface, rather than leaving CDC to be retrofitted and reverse-engineered. The book gives several examples. RethinkDB lets a query subscribe to notifications when its results change. Firebase and CouchDB provide data synchronization based on a change feed that applications can also read. Meteor uses the MongoDB oplog to subscribe to data changes and update the user interface.

VoltDB lets transactions export data continuously as a stream. The database exposes an output stream as a special table that transactions can insert rows into, but that table cannot be queried. The stream is the log of rows that committed transactions wrote to this table, in commit order. External consumers read it asynchronously and use it to update derived systems. Kafka Connect is an effort to bring CDC tools for many database systems together with Kafka. Once the change events are in Kafka, they can update search indexes and feed stream processors.

Event Sourcing

There are parallels between the ideas above and event sourcing. Event sourcing was developed in the domain-driven design (DDD) community. It is worth discussing because it has some useful ideas for streaming systems.

Like CDC, event sourcing stores every change to the application state as a log of change events. The main difference is the level of abstraction at which the idea is applied.

  • In CDC, the application uses the database in a mutable way. It updates and deletes records as it likes. The log of changes is pulled out of the database at a low level, such as by parsing the replication log. That keeps the order of the extracted writes the same as the order in which they were actually made, which avoids the race in Figure 11-4. The application writing to the database does not need to know that CDC is happening.
  • In event sourcing, the application logic is built directly on immutable events written to an event log. The event store is append-only, and updates or deletes are discouraged or forbidden. The events are designed to describe things that happened in the application, not low-level changes to stored state.

The book calls event sourcing a powerful technique for data modeling. From the application’s point of view, it is more meaningful to record what the user did as immutable events, rather than recording the effect of those actions on a mutable database. Event sourcing makes applications easier to change over time. It helps debugging, because it is easier to see afterwards why something happened. It also guards against application bugs, as discussed later in the chapter.

Example

Consider an event that records a student cancelling their course enrollment. That event clearly states the intent of one action in a neutral way.

Compare it with recording the side effects instead: one entry was deleted from the enrollments table, and a cancellation reason was added to the student feedback table. The side effects carry many assumptions about how the data will be used later. If a new feature arrives, such as offering the freed place to the next person on the waiting list, the event-sourcing version can attach that new step directly to the existing cancellation event. The side-effect version has already decided what happens to the data.

Event sourcing is similar to the chronicle data model, and an event log resembles the fact table in a star schema (Chapter 3). Specialized databases such as Event Store have been built for applications that use event sourcing. But the approach does not depend on any particular tool. A conventional database or a log-based message broker can also be used to build applications in this style.

Trade-offs
ApproachWhat is loggedWhat it makes easier
Change data captureChanges to rows, pulled from a mutable database at a low level, with the application unawareKeeping other systems in step with an existing database. Log compaction can discard older versions of each row.
Event sourcingImmutable application events that describe user intent, written by the application itselfEvolving the app, reasoning about past behavior, and recovering from bugs. Full history must be kept, so compaction works differently.

Deriving current state from the event log

An event log on its own is not very useful, because users usually want the current state of a system, not a list of every change ever made. On a shopping site, a customer expects to see what is in the cart now, not an append-only history of every change to the cart.

So an application that uses event sourcing must take the event log and turn it into application state that is suitable for showing to users. This transformation can use any logic, but it should be deterministic. That way you can run it again and get the same application state from the same event log.

Replaying the event log lets you rebuild the current state, as with CDC. But log compaction must be handled differently in the two cases.

  • A CDC event for an update usually contains the entire new version of the record. So the current value for a primary key is fully determined by the most recent event for that key, and compaction can discard earlier events for the same key.
  • With event sourcing, events are modeled at a higher level. An event usually expresses the intent of a user action, not the mechanics of the state change that resulted. Later events do not override earlier ones. So you need the full history of events to rebuild the final state, and compaction in the same way is not possible.

Event-sourced applications usually also store snapshots of the current state derived from the log, so they do not have to reprocess the full log each time. But the snapshots are only a performance optimization, to speed up reads and recovery after crashes. The intention is that the system can store all raw events forever and reprocess the whole log whenever needed. The book returns to this assumption in its discussion of limitations.

Commands and events

Event sourcing separates commands from events. When a request from a user first arrives, it is a command. At this stage it can still fail, for example because an integrity rule would be broken. The application must first check that it is allowed to carry out the command. If the check passes and the command is accepted, it becomes an event, which is durable and cannot be changed.

Consider a user who wants to register a username, or to reserve a seat on a plane or in a theater. The application must first check that the username or the seat is not already taken. This is the example the book used earlier, when discussing fault-tolerant consensus (Chapter 9). Once the check succeeds, the application can create an event saying that a particular username was registered by a particular user ID, or that a particular seat was reserved for a particular customer.

Once the event has been created, it is a fact. Suppose the customer later decides to change or cancel the reservation. The fact that they held a reservation for that seat stays true. The change or cancellation is a separate event, added to the log later.

A consumer of the event stream cannot reject an event. By the time a consumer sees it, the event is an immutable part of the log, and other consumers may already have read it. So any checking of a command has to happen before the command becomes an event. One way is to use a serializable transaction that checks the command and publishes the event as one atomic step. Another way is to split the request into two events. The first is a tentative reservation. The second is a separate confirmation event, written once the reservation has been validated. This split lets the validation run in an asynchronous process, as Chapter 9 described for linearizable storage built on total order broadcast.

Example

A theater seat is requested through the split approach.

  1. A customer asks for seat C5. The application writes a command, not yet an event.
  2. The application checks whether C5 is free and, if so, appends a tentative reservation event for that customer.
  3. A separate process validates the tentative reservation against the current state of the seat map.
  4. If it is valid, the process appends a confirmation event. The seat is now held for the customer.
  5. If the customer later cancels, a new cancellation event is appended. The reservation event is never edited or removed.

State, Streams, and Immutability

Chapter 10 showed that batch processing benefits from the immutability of its input files. You can experiment with a job on existing input without fear of damaging it. This principle is also what makes event sourcing and CDC so powerful.

We normally think of databases as storing the current state of the application. That representation is optimized for reads, and it is usually the most convenient one for answering queries. Because state changes, databases support updating and deleting data as well as inserting it. How does that fit with immutability?

Any state that changes is the result of the events that changed it over time. The list of seats still available is the result of the reservations processed so far. The current balance of an account is the result of the credits and debits on it. The response-time graph for a web server is an aggregation of the individual response times of all the requests. No matter how the state changes, there was always a sequence of events that caused those changes. Even when things are done and then undone, the events still happened.

So mutable state and an append-only log of immutable events do not contradict each other. They are two sides of the same coin. The log of all changes, which the book calls the changelog, records how the state evolved over time.

The book offers a mathematical comparison. Application state is what you get when you integrate an event stream over time. A change stream is what you get when you differentiate the state with respect to time. The comparison has limits: the second derivative of state does not seem to have a clear meaning. But it is a useful starting point for thinking about data.

If you store the changelog durably, the state can always be reproduced from it. If you treat the log of events as the system of record, and any mutable state as derived from it, the flow of data through the system is easier to reason about. Pat Helland puts the idea this way: “The truth is the log.” The book also notes that log compaction is one way to bridge the gap between the log and database state, because it keeps only the latest version of each record and discards overwritten ones.

Advantages of immutable events

Immutability is an old idea in databases. Accountants have used it for centuries in financial bookkeeping. When a transaction happens, it is recorded in an append-only ledger, which is essentially a log of events describing money, goods, or services that changed hands. Accounts such as the profit and loss statement or the balance sheet are derived from the ledger by adding up the transactions.

If a mistake is made, an accountant does not erase or change the incorrect entry. Instead, another transaction is added that compensates for the mistake. For example, a wrong charge is corrected by a refund. The incorrect transaction stays in the ledger forever, because it may matter for audits. If figures based on the incorrect ledger were already published, the figures for the next accounting period include a correction. The book says this process is entirely normal in accounting.

Auditability is especially important in financial systems, but it helps many other systems too. As discussed in Chapter 10, if buggy code accidentally writes bad data to a database, recovery is much harder when the code can overwrite data destructively. With an append-only log of immutable events, it is much easier to work out what happened and to recover.

Immutable events also capture more than the current state. Take a shopping site. A customer adds an item to the cart, then removes it again. For order fulfillment, the second event cancels out the first. But for analytics, it may be useful to know that the customer considered that item and then decided against it. They might buy it later, or they might have found a substitute. This information is recorded in an event log, but a database that deletes the item when it is removed from the cart would lose it.

Deriving several views from the same event log

Separating mutable state from the immutable event log has another benefit. You can derive several different read-oriented views from the same events. This works like having several consumers of one stream, as in Figure 11-5. The book gives examples. The analytic database Druid ingests data directly from Kafka this way. Pistachio, a distributed key-value store, uses Kafka as its commit log. Kafka Connect sinks can export data from Kafka to a variety of databases and indexes. The book argues that many other storage and indexing systems, such as search servers, could take their input from a distributed log in the same way.

An explicit translation step from an event log into a database also makes it easier to change an application over time. Suppose you want a new feature that shows your existing data in a new way. You can use the event log to build a separate, read-optimized view for that feature. It runs alongside the existing systems without changing them. Running the old and new systems side by side is often easier than a complicated schema migration in an existing database. Once the old system is no longer needed, you shut it down and reclaim its resources.

Storing data is quite straightforward if you do not have to worry about how it will be queried and accessed. Many of the complications of schema design, indexing, and storage engines come from supporting certain query and access patterns (Chapter 3). So you gain a lot of flexibility by separating the form in which data is written from the form in which it is read, and by allowing several different read views. This idea is sometimes called command query responsibility segregation, or CQRS.

The book argues that the traditional approach to database design rests on a mistake: that data must be written in the same form in which it will be queried. Debates about normalization and denormalization (Chapter 2) become largely irrelevant if you can translate data from a write-optimized event log into a read-optimized application state. It is perfectly reasonable to denormalize the read-optimized views, because the translation process keeps them consistent with the event log.

Twitter’s home timelines, from Chapter 1, are another example. Each timeline is a cache of recent tweets from the people a user follows, a kind of mailbox. It is highly denormalized, because each tweet is copied into the timelines of all the followers. The fan-out service keeps this duplicated state in step with new tweets and new follow relationships, which keeps the duplication manageable.

Concurrency control

The biggest downside of event sourcing and change data capture is that the consumers of the event log are usually asynchronous. A user can write to the log, then read from a view derived from it, and find that their own write is not in the view yet. Chapter 5 covered this problem as reading your own writes.

One fix is to update the read view at the same time as appending the event. That needs a transaction, so both writes happen as one unit. Either the log and the view must live in the same storage system, or you need a distributed transaction across the two systems. The book mentions a second option, covered in Chapter 9: building linearizable storage on top of total order broadcast.

On the other hand, deriving current state from an event log makes some concurrency control easier. Much of the need for multi-object transactions (Chapter 7) comes from one user action that must change data in several places. With event sourcing, you can design an event to be a self-contained description of the user action. The action then needs only one write, appending the events to the log, and a single write is easy to make atomic.

If the event log and the application state are partitioned the same way, a simple single-threaded log consumer needs no concurrency control for writes. By construction, it handles one event at a time, which is the same idea as the actual serial execution in Chapter 7. The log removes the unpredictability of concurrency by defining a serial order of events within each partition. If one event touches several state partitions, more work is needed, and Chapter 12 discusses that.

Limitations of immutability

Many systems that do not use event sourcing still rely on immutability. Various databases use immutable data structures or several versions of the data internally, so they can take point-in-time snapshots (Chapter 7). Version control systems such as Git, Mercurial and Fossil also rely on immutable data to keep the history of files.

Can you keep an immutable history of every change forever? That depends on how much churn the data has. Some workloads mostly add data and rarely update or delete it, and those are easy to keep immutable. Others update and delete a lot of data within a small dataset. There, the history can grow too large, fragmentation can become a problem, and compaction and garbage collection become essential for the system to run reliably.

Sometimes data must be deleted for administrative reasons, even in an immutable system. Privacy rules may require deleting a user’s personal information after they close an account. Data protection law may require removing wrong information. An accidental leak of sensitive data may need to be contained. In those cases, appending a “deleted” event is not enough. You want to rewrite history so that the data looks as if it was never written. Datomic calls this feature excision, and the Fossil version control system has a similar feature called shunning.

Truly deleting data is surprisingly hard, because copies can live in many places. Storage engines, filesystems and SSDs often write to a new location instead of overwriting in place, and backups are often made deliberately immutable to prevent accidental deletion or corruption. Deletion is therefore less about making data impossible to retrieve and more about making it hard to retrieve. Sometimes you have to try harder, which the book returns to in Chapter 12, when it discusses legislation and self-regulation.

Processing Streams

So far the chapter has covered where streams come from (user activity, sensors, and writes to databases) and how they travel (direct messaging, message brokers, and event logs). The remaining question is what you can do with a stream once you have it. In broad terms there are three options.

  1. Take the data in the events and write it to a database, cache, search index, or similar store, where other clients can query it later. As Figure 11-5 showed, this keeps a database in step with changes made elsewhere. It works best when the stream consumer is the only client writing to that database. Writing to a store this way is the streaming version of the batch outputs in Chapter 10.
  2. Push the events to people, for example as email alerts, push notifications, or a live dashboard. Here a human is the final consumer of the stream.
  3. Process one or more input streams to produce one or more output streams. A stream can go through a pipeline of several such stages before it ends up at option 1 or option 2.

The rest of the chapter focuses on option 3, processing streams to make other, derived streams. A piece of code that does this is called an operator or a job. It is close to the Unix processes and MapReduce jobs from Chapter 10. The dataflow pattern is similar. A stream processor reads its input streams without changing them, and writes its output to another place in an append-only way.

The patterns for partitioning and parallelizing stream processors are very similar to those in MapReduce and the dataflow engines of Chapter 10, so the book does not repeat them. Basic operations such as transforming and filtering records also work the same way.

Key idea

The one crucial difference from batch jobs is that a stream never ends. That changes two things. Sorting stops making sense, so sort-merge joins cannot be used. And restarting after a failure is no longer simple.

Sorting does not make sense for a dataset with no end, because you can never know that you have seen the whole thing. So the sort-merge joins from Chapter 10 cannot be used. Fault tolerance changes too. A batch job that has run for a few minutes can be restarted from the beginning when a task fails. A stream job that has been running for years may not be able to restart from the beginning after a crash. The book handles this in the last section of the chapter.

Uses of Stream Processing

Stream processing has long been used for monitoring, where an organization wants to be alerted when certain things happen. The book gives four examples.

  • Fraud detection checks whether the usage pattern of a credit card has suddenly changed, and blocks the card if it seems to have been stolen.
  • Trading systems examine price changes in a financial market and execute trades according to set rules.
  • Manufacturing systems watch the status of machines in a factory, and quickly find the cause if one malfunctions.
  • Military and intelligence systems track the activity of a possible aggressor and raise the alarm if there are signs of an attack.

These uses need quite sophisticated pattern matching and correlation. Over time, other uses of stream processing also emerged. The next few sections compare some of them.

Complex event processing

Complex event processing, or CEP, is an approach developed in the 1990s. It analyzes event streams and is aimed at applications that search for particular patterns of events. It works like a regular expression. A regular expression lets you search a string for a pattern of characters. CEP lets you write rules that search a stream for a pattern of events.

CEP systems often use a high-level declarative query language, such as SQL, or a graphical interface, to describe the event patterns to detect. The queries are submitted to a processing engine. The engine consumes the input streams and keeps an internal state machine that does the matching. When a match is found, the engine emits a complex event, which gives the details of the pattern that was detected.

In CEP the roles of queries and data are reversed compared with a normal database. A database stores data for a long time and treats queries as temporary. A query arrives, the database searches for matching data, and then it forgets the query. A CEP engine does the opposite. Queries are stored for a long time, and events flow past them continuously, looking for a query that matches.

The book lists implementations including Esper, IBM InfoSphere Streams, Apama, TIBCO StreamBase, and SQLstream. Distributed stream processors such as Samza are also gaining SQL support for declarative queries over streams.

Stream analytics

Stream processing is also used for analytics. The line between CEP and stream analytics is blurry. As a general rule, analytics cares less about finding specific sequences of events, and more about aggregations and statistics across a large number of events. Typical examples are:

  • measuring how often an event of some type occurs in each time interval;
  • calculating a rolling average of a value over some period;
  • comparing current statistics with earlier time intervals, for example to spot a trend, or to flag a metric that is unusually high or low compared with the same time last week.

Such statistics are usually computed over fixed time intervals. You might want the average number of queries per second to a service over the last 5 minutes, along with the 99th percentile response time during that period. Averaging over a few minutes smooths out small fluctuations from one second to the next. It still gives a timely picture of changes in traffic. The time interval over which you aggregate is called a window. Windows are covered in more detail later in the chapter.

Stream analytics systems sometimes use probabilistic algorithms. Bloom filters, which Chapter 3 met, test set membership. HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct values there are. Other algorithms estimate percentiles (Chapter 1). These produce approximate answers, but they need much less memory in the processor than exact methods. Some people conclude from this that stream processing is always lossy and inexact. The book says that is wrong. Nothing about stream processing is inherently approximate. Probabilistic algorithms are just an optimization.

Many open source frameworks are built with analytics in mind, including Apache Storm, Spark Streaming, Flink, Concord, Samza, and Kafka Streams. Hosted services include Google Cloud Dataflow and Azure Stream Analytics.

Maintaining materialized views

The earlier section on change streams showed that a stream of database changes can keep derived systems, such as caches, search indexes, and data warehouses, up to date. These can all be seen as special cases of maintaining materialized views. A materialized view is an alternative view of a dataset, stored so that it can be queried quickly. It is updated whenever the underlying data changes. Chapter 3 covered materialized views in the context of data cubes.

Event sourcing works the same way. The application state is maintained by applying a log of events, so the application state is also a kind of materialized view.

There is one difference from stream analytics. For analytics, it is often enough to consider events inside a time window. Building a materialized view usually needs all events over an arbitrary period, possibly all the way back to the beginning. The only exception is obsolete events that log compaction discards. In effect, you need a window that stretches back to the beginning of time.

In principle, any stream processor could maintain materialized views. But many analytics frameworks assume that they work on windows of limited length, so keeping events forever runs against their design. Samza and Kafka Streams support this kind of use. They build on Kafka’s support for log compaction.

Search on streams

CEP looks for patterns made of several events. Sometimes you need something simpler: searching for individual events that match complex criteria, such as a full-text query. For example, media monitoring services subscribe to feeds of news articles and broadcasts. They search every item for mentions of companies, products, or topics of interest. The search query is written in advance, and each news item is matched against it as it arrives. Real estate websites offer a similar feature. A user can ask to be notified when a new property matching their criteria comes on the market. Elasticsearch has a feature called the percolator that supports this kind of stream search.

A normal search engine first indexes the documents and then runs queries against the index. Searching a stream reverses this. The queries are stored, and the documents flow past them, as in CEP. In the simplest version, you test every document against every query. That gets slow when there are many queries. To speed it up, you can index the queries as well as the documents, and so narrow down which queries might match a document.

Message passing and RPC

Chapter 4 described message-passing systems as an alternative to RPC. In these systems, services communicate by sending messages, as in the actor model. Although they are based on messages and events, the book does not normally think of them as stream processors. There are three reasons.

  • Actor frameworks are mainly a way to manage concurrency and distributed execution of modules that talk to each other. Stream processing is mainly a way to manage data.
  • Communication between actors is often temporary and one-to-one. Event logs are durable and can have many subscribers.
  • Actors can communicate in any pattern, including cycles of requests and responses. Stream processors are usually set up as acyclic pipelines, where each stream is the output of one particular job and is derived from a well-defined set of input streams.

There is some overlap, though. Apache Storm has a feature called distributed RPC. It sends user queries to a set of nodes that also process event streams. The queries are mixed in with events from the input streams, and the results are aggregated and sent back to the user. It is also possible to process streams using actor frameworks. But many actor frameworks do not guarantee that messages are delivered if a node crashes. So processing is not fault-tolerant unless you add your own retry logic.

Reasoning About Time

Stream processors often have to deal with time, especially when they are used for analytics. Analytics often uses time windows, such as the average over the last five minutes. It might seem obvious what that means. It is surprisingly tricky.

In a batch process, the tasks crunch quickly through a large collection of historical events. If the data needs to be broken down by time, the batch job looks at the timestamp inside each event. It does not matter what time the job itself runs, because that time has nothing to do with when the events happened. A batch job may read a year of historical events in a few minutes. The timeline that matters is the year of history, not the few minutes of processing. Using the timestamps in the events also makes the job deterministic. Running it again on the same input gives the same result (Chapter 10).

Many stream processing frameworks take a different route. They use the local system clock on the processing machine to decide windows. This is called processing time. It is simple, and it is reasonable when the delay between creating an event and processing it is negligible. But it breaks down when there is significant lag, meaning the processing happens noticeably later than the event actually occurred.

Event time versus processing time

Processing can be delayed for many reasons. These include queueing, network faults (Chapter 8), performance problems that cause contention in the message broker or the processor, a restart of the stream consumer, and reprocessing of past events while recovering from a fault or after fixing a bug.

Message delays can also make messages arrive in an unpredictable order. Here is the book’s example.

Example
  1. A user makes one web request, which is handled by web server A.
  2. The user then makes a second request, which is handled by web server B.
  3. Servers A and B each emit an event describing the request they handled.
  4. Event B reaches the message broker before event A does.
  5. The stream processor therefore sees event B first and event A second, even though the requests happened in the opposite order.

The book offers an analogy. The Star Wars films came out in one order: Episode IV in 1977, Episode V in 1980, and Episode VI in 1983. Episodes I, II, and III came out later, in 1999, 2002, and 2005. Episode VII came out in 2015. If you watch them in release order, the order you process them in does not match the story order. The episode number is like an event timestamp. The date you watch the film is like the processing time. People cope with such jumps easily, but stream processing algorithms have to be written specifically to handle timing and ordering problems like these.

Confusing event time with processing time leads to bad data. Imagine a stream processor that measures the rate of requests, counting how many arrive each second. If you redeploy the processor, it may be stopped for a minute and then process the backlog of events when it comes back. If you measure the rate by processing time, the backlog looks like a sudden spike in requests. In fact the real rate of requests was steady. Figure 11-7 in the book shows this artifact.

Knowing when you’re ready

A tricky problem with event-time windows is that you can never be sure you have received all the events for a window. There may always be more to come.

Suppose you group events into one-minute windows so that you can count requests per minute. You have counted some events whose timestamps fall in the 37th minute of the hour. Time has moved on, and most of the new events now fall in the 38th and 39th minutes. When should you declare the window for the 37th minute finished, and output its count?

You could time out, and declare the window ready after no new events have arrived for a while. But some events may still be stuck in a buffer on another machine, delayed by a network problem. So you need a way to handle stragglers, which are events that arrive after their window has been declared complete. The book gives two options.

  1. Ignore the stragglers. They are probably a small share of events in normal conditions. Track how many are dropped as a metric, and raise an alert if a significant amount of data starts being dropped.
  2. Publish a correction. Output an updated value for the window that includes the stragglers. You may also need to retract the previous output.

In some systems, a special message can announce that no more messages with a timestamp earlier than some time t will arrive. Consumers can use that message to trigger their windows. But if several producers on different machines each generate events with their own minimum timestamps, the consumer has to track each producer separately. Adding and removing producers then becomes more complicated.

Whose clock are you using, anyway?

Assigning timestamps to events is harder when events can sit in buffers at several points in the system. Take a mobile app that reports usage events to a server. The app may be used while the device is offline. It stores the events locally and sends them when a connection returns, which may be hours or even days later. To any consumer, those events look like extremely late stragglers.

Ideally, the timestamp should be the time the user did the action, according to the device’s clock. But a device the user controls is not a trustworthy clock. It may be set to the wrong time by accident or on purpose (Chapter 8 covers clock accuracy). The time at which the server received the event, according to the server’s clock, is more likely to be accurate, because you control the server. But it says less about the user’s actual action.

To correct for a wrong device clock, the book suggests logging three timestamps.

  1. The time the event occurred, according to the device clock.
  2. The time the event was sent to the server, according to the device clock.
  3. The time the event was received by the server, according to the server clock.

Subtract the second timestamp from the third to estimate the offset between the device clock and the server clock. This assumes the network delay is negligible compared with the accuracy you need. Then apply that offset to the event timestamp, which gives an estimate of when the event really occurred. This also assumes the device’s clock offset did not change between the event happening and the event being sent.

The book notes that this problem is not unique to stream processing. Batch processing has exactly the same issues when it reasons about time. They are just more noticeable in streaming, where you are more aware of time passing.

Types of windows

Once you know how an event’s timestamp should be determined, the next step is to decide how windows over time should be defined. A window can be used for aggregations, such as counting events or averaging values inside it. The book describes four common types.

  • Tumbling window. A tumbling window has a fixed length, and every event belongs to exactly one window. For a 1-minute tumbling window, events timestamped from 10:03:00 to 10:03:59 form one window, events from 10:04:00 to 10:04:59 form the next, and so on. You can build one by rounding each event’s timestamp down to the nearest minute.
  • Hopping window. A hopping window also has a fixed length, but windows can overlap, which gives some smoothing. A 5-minute window with a hop size of 1 minute contains events from 10:03:00 to 10:07:59. The next window covers 10:04:00 to 10:08:59, and so on. You can build it by first computing 1-minute tumbling windows, then combining several adjacent ones.
  • Sliding window. A sliding window contains all the events that occur within some interval of each other. A 5-minute sliding window would cover events at 10:03:39 and 10:08:12, because they are less than 5 minutes apart. Tumbling and hopping 5-minute windows would not put these two events together, because they have fixed boundaries. A sliding window can be built by keeping a buffer of events sorted by time and removing old events as they expire.
  • Session window. A session window has no fixed length. It groups together all the events for the same user that happen close together in time. The window ends when the user has been inactive for some time, for example when there have been no events for 30 minutes. Sessionization is a common need in website analytics (Chapter 10 discusses GROUP BY).
Trade-offs
WindowLengthOverlapGood for
TumblingFixedNone. Each event is in one window.Simple per-minute or per-hour counts.
HoppingFixedYes, windows overlap by the hop size.Smoothed, regularly updated averages.
SlidingSet by the gap between eventsYes, one window per eventPairs of events that are close together, however their clock times fall.
SessionEnds after a quiet gapNot applicableGrouping one user’s activity into visits.
Try it

Take the two example events at 10:03:39 and 10:08:12. Which window types would put them in the same window? Now change the second event to 10:08:45. Does your answer change for the sliding window, and why?

Stream Joins

Chapter 10 showed how batch jobs can join datasets by key, and how those joins are an important part of data pipelines. Stream processing turns data pipelines into continuous, incremental processing of unbounded datasets. So there is exactly the same need for joins on streams.

New events can appear on a stream at any time, though, which makes stream joins harder than batch joins. The book distinguishes three types of join: stream-stream joins, stream-table joins, and table-table joins. Each is illustrated below.

Stream-stream join (window join)

Suppose your website has a search feature, and you want to spot recent trends in the URLs people search for. Each time someone types a query, you log an event with the query and the results shown. Each time someone clicks a result, you log a second event recording the click. To calculate the click-through rate for each URL in the results, you need to bring together the search events and the click events. They are linked by a shared session ID. Advertising systems have similar analyses.

The click may never come, if the user gives up on the search. Even when it does come, the gap between search and click can vary widely. It is often a few seconds, but it could be days or weeks, if someone runs a search, forgets the tab, and clicks a result later. Because of network delays, the click event can even arrive before the search event. So you choose a window for the join. For example, you might join a click with a search if they happened at most one hour apart.

It is tempting to skip the join and just put the details of the search inside the click event. But that is not equivalent. It would tell you only about the searches where the user clicked a result. It would miss the searches where they clicked nothing. To measure search quality you need accurate click-through rates, and that requires both kinds of event.

To run this join, the stream processor must keep some state. It holds all the events from the last hour, indexed by session ID. When a search or click event arrives, the processor adds it to the matching index. It also checks the other index to see whether an event for the same session has already arrived. If a match is found, it emits an event saying which search result was clicked. If a search event expires from the window without a matching click, it emits an event saying that none of the results were clicked.

Stream-table join (stream enrichment)

Chapter 10 had a batch job that joined user activity events with a database of user profiles. It is natural to think of the activity events as a stream, and to run the same join continuously in a stream processor. The input is a stream of activity events, each with a user ID. The output is a stream in which each user ID has been expanded with profile information. This is called enriching the activity events with information from the database.

For each event, the processor looks up the user ID in the database and adds the profile to the event. The lookup could query a remote database. But, as Chapter 10 explained, remote queries are slow and risk overloading the database. Another approach is to load a copy of the database into the stream processor, so it can be queried locally without a network round trip. This is very similar to the hash joins from Chapter 10. The local copy might be an in-memory hash table, if it is small enough, or an index on local disk.

A batch job reads a point-in-time snapshot of the database. A stream processor runs for a long time, and the database is likely to change while it runs. So the local copy must be kept up to date. Change data capture solves this. The stream processor subscribes to the changelog of the user profile database, as well as to the stream of activity events. When a profile is created or changed, the processor updates its local copy. The result is a join between two streams: the activity events and the profile updates.

A stream-table join is very similar to a stream-stream join. The main difference is the window. For the changelog of the table, the join uses a window that reaches back to the beginning of time, and newer versions of a record overwrite older ones. For the stream input, the join might not keep a window at all.

Table-table join (materialized view maintenance)

Chapter 1 described Twitter’s home timelines. When a user opens their home timeline, it is too expensive to look up everyone they follow, find their recent tweets, and merge them. So the system keeps a timeline cache, a per-user inbox to which tweets are written as they are sent. Reading a timeline then takes a single lookup. Keeping that cache up to date requires four kinds of event processing.

  1. When user u sends a new tweet, the tweet is added to the timeline of every user who follows u.
  2. When a user deletes a tweet, it is removed from every user’s timeline.
  3. When user u1 starts following user u2, the recent tweets by u2 are added to u1’s timeline.
  4. When user u1 unfollows user u2, the tweets by u2 are removed from u1’s timeline.

To do this in a stream processor, you need streams of events for tweets (sending and deleting) and for follow relationships (following and unfollowing). The processor also has to keep a database of the followers of each user, so it knows which timelines to update when a new tweet arrives.

Another way to see this is that the stream processor maintains a materialized view for a query that joins two tables, tweets and follows. The book writes it as something like this.

SELECT follows.follower_id AS timeline_id,
  array_agg(tweets.* ORDER BY tweets.timestamp DESC)
FROM tweets
JOIN follows ON follows.followee_id = tweets.sender_id
GROUP BY follows.follower_id

The join of the two streams corresponds directly to the join of the two tables in that query. The timelines are effectively a cache of the query’s result, and they are updated every time the underlying tables change. In a footnote, the book notes that this matches the product rule from calculus. A change to the joined result comes from a change to either input, joined with the current state of the other input. So any new tweet is joined with the current followers, and any change to followers is joined with the current tweets.

Time-dependence of joins

The three types of join have a lot in common. Each requires the stream processor to keep some state based on one join input, such as search and click events, user profiles, or follower lists. It then queries that state when messages arrive from the other input.

The order of events that build that state matters. It matters whether you first follow someone and then unfollow them, or the other way round. In a partitioned log, the order of events within one partition is kept. But there is usually no ordering guarantee across different streams or partitions.

That raises a question. If events on different streams happen at about the same time, in what order are they processed? In the stream-table join, suppose a user updates their profile. Which activity events are joined with the old profile, because they were processed before the update, and which are joined with the new one? Put another way: if state changes over time and you join with that state, which point in time do you use for the join?

This time dependence shows up in many places. Suppose you sell products. You must apply the right tax rate to each invoice. That rate depends on the country or state, the type of product, and the date of the sale, because tax rates change from time to time. When you join sales with a table of tax rates, you usually want the rate in force at the time of the sale. That may differ from the current rate if you are reprocessing historical data.

If the order of events across streams is not fixed, the join becomes nondeterministic. That means you cannot rerun the same job on the same input and necessarily get the same result, because the events may interleave differently the second time.

In data warehouses this is known as a slowly changing dimension. It is often handled by giving each version of the joined record a unique identifier. Each time the tax rate changes, it gets a new identifier, and each invoice records the identifier of the rate in force at the time of sale. This makes the join deterministic. But it has a cost: every version of the records must be kept, so log compaction is not possible.

Trade-offs
Join typeInputsState keptTypical example
Stream-stream (window join)Two activity streamsEvents inside a time window, indexed by keyMatching searches with clicks in the same session within an hour
Stream-table (enrichment)An activity stream and a changelog of a tableA local copy of the table, kept current from its changelogAdding user profile fields to each activity event
Table-table (view maintenance)Two changelogsBoth tables, so each change can be joined with the other side’s latest stateKeeping home timeline caches up to date
Try it

You are joining sales events with tax rates. A tax rate changes while some sales from last month are still in the stream. Should the join use the rate in force on the sale date or the current rate? What would you need to store so that reprocessing gives the same answer every time?

Fault Tolerance

The last part of the chapter asks how stream processors can tolerate faults. Chapter 10 showed that batch frameworks handle faults fairly easily. If a task in a MapReduce job fails, it can simply be started again on another machine, and the failed task’s output is discarded. Transparent retry works because input files are immutable, each task writes its output to a separate file, and output becomes visible only when a task completes successfully.

So the output of a batch job is the same as if nothing had gone wrong, even when some tasks did fail. It looks as though every input record was processed exactly once. No record is skipped, and none is processed twice in the visible result. Restarted tasks may process some records more than once, but the visible effect is as if each was processed once. The book calls this exactly-once semantics, and notes that effectively-once would be a more accurate name.

Stream processing faces the same problem but handles it less directly. You cannot wait until a task finishes before making its output visible, because a stream never finishes. Waiting is not an option.

Microbatching and checkpointing

One solution is to cut the stream into small blocks and treat each block like a miniature batch job. This is called microbatching, and Spark Streaming uses it. The batch size is typically around one second. That is a performance compromise. Smaller batches mean more scheduling and coordination overhead. Larger batches mean a longer delay before the results of the stream processor become visible.

Microbatching also gives you a tumbling window equal to the batch size, windowed by processing time rather than by event timestamps. Jobs that need larger windows must explicitly carry state over from one microbatch to the next.

A variant used in Apache Flink is to take rolling checkpoints of the state at regular intervals and write them to durable storage. If a stream operator crashes, it restarts from its most recent checkpoint. It discards any output produced between that checkpoint and the crash. The checkpoints are triggered by barriers, which are markers that flow through the message stream, similar to the boundaries between microbatches. But checkpoints do not force a particular window size.

Within the stream processing framework, microbatching and checkpointing give the same exactly-once semantics as batch processing. But the moment output leaves the stream processor, the framework can no longer discard it. Examples include writing to a database, sending messages to an external broker, or sending emails. If a failed task is restarted, the external side effect happens twice. Microbatching or checkpointing alone cannot prevent this.

Atomic commit revisited

To give the appearance of exactly-once processing when faults occur, all the outputs and side effects of processing an event must take effect if and only if the processing succeeds. These include any messages sent to downstream operators or to external messaging systems (including email and push notifications), any database writes, any changes to operator state, and any acknowledgment of input messages. For a log-based broker, that last item means moving the consumer offset forward.

All of these must either happen together, or none of them must happen. They must not fall out of step with each other. This should sound familiar, because Chapter 9 discussed the same idea under exactly-once message processing, in the context of distributed transactions and two-phase commit.

Chapter 9 also described the problems with traditional distributed transaction implementations, such as XA. In more restricted environments, though, an atomic commit facility can be implemented efficiently. Google Cloud Dataflow and VoltDB do this, and there are plans to add similar features to Apache Kafka. Unlike XA, these implementations do not try to provide transactions across different technologies. They keep the transactions inside the stream processing framework, managing both state changes and messaging there. The cost of the transaction protocol can be spread out by processing several input messages within a single transaction.

Idempotence

The goal is to discard the partial output of any failed task, so that it can be safely retried without taking effect twice. Distributed transactions are one way to reach that goal. The other way is to rely on idempotence.

An idempotent operation is one you can perform several times with the same effect as performing it once. Setting a key in a key-value store to a fixed value is idempotent. Writing the value again just overwrites it with the same value. Incrementing a counter is not idempotent, because doing it again adds one more.

Even an operation that is not naturally idempotent can often be made idempotent with a little extra metadata. When you consume messages from Kafka, each message has a persistent, always-increasing offset. When you write a value to an external database, you can store along with the value the offset of the message that caused the last write. Then you can tell whether an update has already been applied, and skip it if so.

Example

The book describes the idea in general terms. Here is one way the check can work.

  1. A message at offset 42 arrives and updates a value in the external database. The database also stores the number 42 alongside the value.
  2. The consumer crashes, and after a restart the broker delivers the message at offset 42 again.
  3. The consumer reads the stored number. It is already 42, so the update was applied before, and the consumer skips it.

The state handling in Storm’s Trident is based on a similar idea. Relying on idempotence brings several assumptions. Restarting a failed task must replay the same messages in the same order, which a log-based broker does. The processing must be deterministic. And no other node may update the same value at the same time. When failing over from one processing node to another, fencing may be needed, to stop a node that is believed to be dead but is actually alive from interfering (Chapter 8 covers this with the leader and the lock). Despite these conditions, idempotent operations can be an effective way to get exactly-once semantics with only a small overhead.

Rebuilding state after a failure

Any stream process that keeps state must be able to recover that state after a failure. This includes windowed aggregations, such as counters, averages, and histograms, and any tables and indexes used for joins.

One option is to keep the state in a remote datastore and replicate it there. But querying a remote database for each message can be slow, as discussed in the stream-table join section. The other option is to keep the state local to the stream processor, and replicate it periodically. When the processor recovers from a failure, the new task reads the replicated state and carries on without losing data.

Different systems do this in different ways. Flink periodically captures snapshots of operator state and writes them to durable storage such as HDFS. Samza and Kafka Streams replicate state changes by sending them to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction, in a way similar to change data capture. VoltDB replicates state by processing each input message redundantly on several nodes, as described in the section on actual serial execution in Chapter 7.

Sometimes the state does not need to be replicated at all, because it can be rebuilt from the input streams. If the state consists of aggregations over a fairly short window, it may be fast enough to replay the input events for that window. If the state is a local copy of a database kept up to date by change data capture, the copy can be rebuilt from the log-compacted change stream.

All of these trade-offs depend on how fast the underlying infrastructure is. In some systems, network delay is lower than disk access time, and network bandwidth is comparable to disk bandwidth. There is no universally ideal trade-off. The merits of local versus remote state may also shift as storage and networking technology change.

Trade-offs
ApproachHow it worksCosts
MicrobatchingSmall blocks, about one second each, processed like mini batch jobsScheduling overhead when batches are small. Latency when batches are large. Larger windows need state carried between batches.
CheckpointingPeriodic snapshots of state, triggered by barriers, restored after a crashWriting checkpoints to durable storage. Output after the last checkpoint is discarded and recreated, and external side effects still need care.
Atomic commitOutputs, state changes, and offsets all take effect together, or not at allTransaction overhead, which can be spread by batching several input messages per transaction. Works best inside one framework.
Idempotent writesWrites that can be repeated safely, often by storing the input offset with the valueRequires deterministic processing, a replayable input order, and no concurrent writers to the same value.
Rule of thumb

No mechanism is free. Choose the one that matches the cost of repeated effects in your system. Where effects leave the stream processor, idempotent writes or careful external commits are usually needed, because the framework cannot undo them.

Summary

Summary
  • Streams are unbounded. Batch jobs chop endless data into fixed chunks, which delays results. Stream processing handles each event as it happens. A stream is data that becomes available bit by bit over time.
  • Events and transport. An event is a small, immutable record of something that happened, usually with a timestamp. Producers send events, and consumers read them. Messaging systems can drop, buffer, or backpressure messages, and they can lose messages on crashes unless they write to disk or replicate.
  • Two broker styles. AMQP and JMS-style brokers assign single messages to consumers, who acknowledge each one. Acknowledged messages are deleted, which suits asynchronous task queues. A log-based broker assigns all the messages in a partition to one consumer, keeps them in order, and lets consumers track their position with offsets. It keeps messages on disk, so consumers can go back and reread old ones. Parallelism comes from partitions.
  • Databases as streams. The changes made to a database can be captured as a stream, either implicitly through change data capture or explicitly through event sourcing.
