Log compaction lets the stream keep a full copy of the database contents. Derived systems such as search indexes, caches, and analytics systems can be kept current by consuming the change log. New views can be built by starting from the beginning of the log.
  • State and replay. Keeping state as a stream and replaying messages is the basis for stream joins and fault tolerance. Stream processing covers complex event processing (searching for event patterns), stream analytics (windowed aggregations), and materialized views (derived data kept up to date).
  • Time is hard. Stream processors must separate processing time from event timestamps. Stragglers that arrive after a window is closed can be ignored and counted, or handled with corrections. Device clocks can be wrong, so the book suggests logging the send and receive times to estimate the offset.
  • Three joins. Stream-stream joins match related events within a window of time. Stream-table joins enrich an event stream with a locally kept copy of a table. Table-table joins maintain a materialized view of the join of two changing tables. Each join depends on the order of events, and when that order is not fixed, a join can give different results on a rerun.
  • Fault tolerance. Stream processors need the same exactly-once effect that batch jobs get from discarding failed output. Microbatching, checkpointing, atomic commits, and idempotent writes all achieve it in different ways. External side effects are the hard part, because a framework cannot discard what has already left it.

The chapter ends with about 100 references to papers, blog posts, and talks that support its claims. This retelling does not reproduce that list. The book notes that an event touching several state partitions needs more work, and leaves that topic to Chapter 12.

Check yourself

  1. Two clients write to the same item at nearly the same time, and the database and the search index receive those writes in opposite orders. Why does this leave the two systems permanently different, even though no error happened?

    Show answer

    Each system applied the writes in the order it received them. The database ends with the value from the write it saw last, and the search index ends with the value from the write it saw last, which are different. Without a single leader or version detection to order the writes, nothing notices the conflict.

  2. A topic has 4 partitions, and a consumer group has 6 consumers. How many of the consumers can do useful work at the same time, and why?

    Show answer

    Only 4. Messages in one partition always go to the same consumer, so each partition can be given to at most one consumer in the group. The other 2 consumers have nothing to read. More parallelism needs more partitions.

  3. A 5-minute tumbling window and a 5-minute sliding window both see events. Events arrive at 10:03:39 and 10:08:12. Why are the two events in the same sliding window but not in the same tumbling window?

    Show answer

    The events are 4 minutes 33 seconds apart, which is less than 5 minutes, so a sliding window can cover both. Tumbling windows have fixed boundaries, and 10:03:39 and 10:08:12 fall in different fixed 5-minute windows, so they are not grouped together.

  4. A batch job that fails can simply be restarted from the beginning, but a stream job that has run for years may not be able to. What do stream processors use instead, and why does it matter if output has already left the processor?

    Show answer

    They use mechanisms such as microbatching, checkpoints, atomic commits, and idempotent writes, which allow recovery from a recent known point without starting over. If output has already been sent to an outside system, such as a database or an email service, the processor cannot discard it. A restart can then repeat that side effect unless the external write is idempotent or otherwise coordinated.

Part III · Chapter 12

The Future of Data Systems

The big idea: no single tool does everything well, so good systems combine several tools. Data flows from one tool to the next as an ordered log of changes, which keeps every copy correct and easy to rebuild. The author also argues that the people building these systems must weigh what the systems do to the people whose data they hold.

The book has mostly described things as they are. This last chapter looks forward and asks how things should be. The author proposes ideas that, in his view, could improve how applications are designed and built. Predictions are a matter of opinion, so he writes in the first person whenever he is giving his own view. You are free to disagree. The ideas are meant as a starting point for discussion, and as a way to clear up terms that people often mix up.

The goal of the book, set out in Chapter 1, was to explore how to build applications that are reliable, scalable, and maintainable. This chapter brings those themes together. Fault-tolerance algorithms improve reliability, partitioning improves scalability, and mechanisms for evolution and abstraction improve maintainability. The aim now is to design applications better than today’s: robust, correct, easy to change, and in the end good for people.

The chapter opens with a quote from St. Thomas Aquinas about a ship’s captain. The captain’s final aim is not to keep the ship safe in harbor, because a ship exists to sail. The book gives the quote as an epigraph and does not explain it at length. A reasonable reading is that a system should be judged by what it is for, not by how well it avoids change.

Data Integration

A theme that has run through the book is that every problem has several solutions, each with its own pros, cons, and trade-offs. Chapter 3 compared log-structured storage, B-trees, and column-oriented storage. Chapter 5 compared single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless replication. If your problem is simply storing some data and looking it up again later, there is no single right answer. Each approach suits a different set of circumstances.

A piece of software usually has to commit to one approach. Making one code path robust and fast is hard enough, and trying to do everything in one program almost guarantees that it will do each job poorly. So the right tool depends on the circumstances. Even a so-called general-purpose database is designed for a particular pattern of use.

That creates two challenges. The first is knowing which products fit which circumstances. Vendors are reluctant to describe the workloads their software handles badly, so you have to read between the lines, using the trade-off questions from earlier chapters. The second challenge is that complex applications use the same data in several different ways. No single program suits all of those uses. You usually end up combining several pieces of software to deliver one application’s features. The book calls this the data integration problem.

Combining Specialized Tools by Deriving Data

A common example is combining an OLTP database with a full-text search index. OLTP stands for online transaction processing, the workload of many small reads and writes that most application databases handle. A full-text index lets users search for arbitrary keywords in text. Some databases, PostgreSQL among them, include a basic full-text feature that is enough for simple applications. More sophisticated search needs dedicated information retrieval tools. Search indexes, however, are generally poor systems of record, meaning the authoritative place where the data is kept. So many applications need two tools: one to store the data reliably, and one to search it well.

The integration problem grows with each new representation of the data. Besides the database and the search index, you may need to:

  • keep copies in analytics systems, such as data warehouses or batch and stream processing systems;
  • maintain caches, or denormalized versions (copies that repeat data in a shape that makes reads faster) of objects derived from the original data;
  • pass the data through machine learning, classification, ranking, or recommendation systems;
  • send notifications when the data changes.

The author has heard engineers claim that 99% of people need only some small subset of a technology’s features. He thinks such claims say more about the speaker’s experience than about the real usefulness of a technology. What looks obscure to one person can be a central requirement for another. The need for integration usually becomes visible only when you zoom out and look at the dataflows across a whole organization.

Reasoning about dataflows. When the same data must live in several storage systems to serve different access patterns, you need to be clear about inputs and outputs. Where is the data written first? Which representations are derived from which sources? And how does each change reach every place it belongs, in the right format?

Take the database and search index example. You can write the data first to a system-of-record database, then capture the changes made to that database. This is change data capture, or CDC, which means reading the database’s change log and sending each change onward. Those changes are then applied to the search index in the same order. If CDC is the only way the index gets updated, the index is entirely derived from the database, and so it is consistent with it, barring bugs in the software. Writing to the database is then the only way new input enters the system.

The alternative is to let the application write directly to both the database and the search index. That creates the problem the book illustrates in its Figure 11-4, described in the next paragraph.

The dual-writes problem. Suppose two clients concurrently send conflicting writes to the same record. The application writes to the database and to the search index, one after the other. The two systems may process the writes in different orders. The database may apply client 1’s write first and client 2’s second, while the search index applies them the other way round. Neither system is in charge of deciding the order, so they can make contradictory decisions and stay permanently inconsistent with each other.

Try it

Two clients write conflicting values through an app that updates a database and a search index directly. Name one design change that would make a single system decide the order of writes. Then say what you give up with it, thinking about the extra delay and the new bottleneck.

Deciding on one total order. If every user input passes through a single system that decides one order for all writes, the problem goes away. Other representations can then be derived by processing the writes in that same order. This is the state machine replication approach from Chapter 9, in which every copy applies the same operations in the same sequence. The author says it matters less whether you use CDC or an event sourcing log (a log that records every change as the permanent history) than that you decide on a total order. Updating a derived system from an event log can also be made deterministic and idempotent. Deterministic means the same input always gives the same output, and idempotent means running a step twice has the same effect as running it once. Both properties make recovery from faults much easier.

Derived data versus distributed transactions. The classic way to keep several data systems consistent is a distributed transaction, which is one transaction spanning more than one system that succeeds or fails as a unit. How does using derived data compare?

At an abstract level, both aim at the same goal by different means. Distributed transactions decide the order of writes using locks, which stop two transactions from touching the same data at the same time. Logs decide order by recording events in sequence. Distributed transactions use atomic commit, a protocol that makes a change take effect everywhere or nowhere, so each change takes effect exactly once. Log-based systems rely on deterministic retries and idempotence instead, so a repeated step does no extra harm.

The biggest difference is timing. Transaction systems usually provide linearizability, a strong guarantee that once a write completes, every later read sees it. That gives useful properties such as reading your own writes: after you save something, your next read shows it. Derived data systems are usually updated asynchronously, meaning the update happens a little later and the sender does not wait. So they do not offer the same timing guarantees by default.

Distributed transactions have been used successfully in limited environments that accept their cost. The author, however, thinks XA, a standard for distributed transactions across different products, has poor fault tolerance and performance, which severely limits its usefulness. A better protocol might be possible, but getting it widely adopted and built into existing tools would be hard and is unlikely soon. Until then, he believes log-based derived data is the most promising way to integrate systems. He does not think it helps to tell everyone that eventual consistency (copies agree only after some delay) is unavoidable and that they should simply live with it, at least not without good guidance on how. The chapter returns to this when it discusses aiming for correctness, where it looks at building stronger guarantees on top of asynchronous systems.

The limits of total ordering. For small systems, building one totally ordered event log is easy. Single-leader databases do exactly that, since their replication log is a total order of writes. As systems grow to bigger and more complex workloads, limits appear:

  • A total order usually requires all events to pass through one leader node that decides the order. If the event rate is more than one machine can handle, the log must be split into partitions across machines. The order between two partitions is then undefined.
  • Servers spread across datacenters, for example to survive a whole datacenter going offline, usually have a leader in each one. Network delays make coordinating every write across datacenters too slow, so events that start in two datacenters have no defined order.
  • In microservices, each service often keeps its own durable state, with no state shared between services. Events from different services then have no defined order.
  • Some applications update client-side state immediately, and even work offline. Clients and servers are then likely to see events in different orders.

Deciding on a total order of events is called total order broadcast, and it is equivalent to consensus, the problem of getting several nodes to agree on one value. Most consensus algorithms assume that one node can handle the whole stream of events, and they offer no way for multiple nodes to share the ordering work. The author says that designing consensus algorithms that scale beyond one node’s throughput and work well across the globe is still an open research problem.

Ordering events to capture causality. When two events have no causal link, the lack of a total order does not matter, because concurrent events can be ordered in any way. Some cases are easy. If several updates touch the same object, you can route all updates for that object ID to the same log partition, which keeps them in order. Causal dependencies can also appear in subtler ways, and then the order matters.

Example

The unfriend and the message. Two former partners on a social network have just broken up. One removes the other as a friend, and then posts a complaint about the ex-partner to the rest of their friends. The poster’s intention is that the ex-partner should not see it, since the post was sent after the friendship ended. But suppose friend status is stored in one place and messages in another. Then the order between the two events can be lost. A service that sends notifications about new messages could process the message before the unfriend event. It would then notify the ex-partner by mistake.

The notifications here are effectively a join between messages and the friend list, so this is a timing problem with joins, the kind discussed earlier in the book. The author says there is no simple answer. Starting points include:

  • Logical timestamps, which give a total order without coordination, so they can help where total order broadcast is not feasible. But recipients must then handle events that arrive out of order, and extra metadata must travel with the events.
  • Logging an event that records the state the user saw before deciding, and giving that event a unique ID. Later events can then refer to that ID to record the dependency. The book returns to this idea in the section on reads being events.
  • Conflict resolution algorithms, which help when events arrive in an unexpected order. They help maintain state, but not when an action has an external side effect, such as sending a notification.

The author hopes that patterns will emerge that capture causal dependencies efficiently and keep derived state correct, without forcing every event through the bottleneck of total order broadcast.

Batch and Stream Processing

The goal of data integration is simple to state: data should end up in the right form, in all the right places. Getting there means consuming inputs, transforming them, joining them, filtering and aggregating them, training models, evaluating results, and writing the outputs. Batch and stream processors are the tools for this work. Their outputs are derived datasets, such as search indexes, materialized views (precomputed query results stored as data), recommendations for users, and aggregate metrics.

Chapters 10 and 11 showed that batch and stream processing share many principles. The main difference is that stream processors work on unbounded datasets, which never end, while a batch job reads an input of known, finite size. The engines are built differently, and those differences are starting to blur. Spark does stream processing on top of a batch engine by cutting the stream into small batches called microbatches. Apache Flink does batch processing on top of a stream engine. In principle each style can be imitated with the other, but performance differs. Microbatching, for example, may perform poorly with hopping or sliding windows, which are time windows that overlap.

Maintaining derived state. Batch processing has a strong functional flavor, even when the code is not written in a functional language. It favors deterministic, pure functions. A pure function’s output depends only on its inputs, and it has no side effects beyond its explicit outputs. Inputs are treated as immutable (never changed), and outputs are append-only (only added to). Stream processing follows the same style, but adds managed, fault-tolerant state, which the framework keeps safe across crashes.

Pure functions are good for fault tolerance, because rerunning them is safe. They also make the dataflows of an organization easier to reason about. Whether the derived data is a search index, a statistical model, or a cache, it helps to think of data pipelines that derive one thing from another. A state change in one system passes through application functions, and its effects are applied to the derived systems.

In principle, derived systems could be updated synchronously, in the same way a relational database updates a secondary index (an extra lookup structure on a column, kept apart from the main table) within the same transaction as the table write. The book argues that asynchrony is what makes log-based systems robust. It lets a fault in one part stay contained locally. Distributed transactions, by contrast, abort if any one participant fails, so they tend to spread a failure to the rest of the system.

Partitioned systems with secondary indexes face a related issue. Chapter 6 showed that a secondary index often crosses partition boundaries. If the index is term-partitioned, meaning the index is split by the indexed value, writes must go to several partitions. If it is document-partitioned, meaning each partition indexes its own documents, reads must go to all partitions. Either way, the cross-partition communication is most reliable and scalable when the index is maintained asynchronously.

Reprocessing data for application evolution. Stream processing lets changes in the input appear in derived views with low delay. Batch processing lets you reprocess large amounts of accumulated history to derive new views from existing data. Both are useful for maintaining derived data.

Reprocessing is also a good way to evolve a system so it supports new features and requirements. Without it, schema evolution (changing the structure of stored data) is limited to simple changes, such as adding a new optional field or a new type of record. That holds whether the database checks the schema when data is written or only when it is read. With reprocessing, you can restructure a whole dataset into a completely different model that suits the new requirements.

Example

Schema migrations on railways. The book notes that large migrations also happen outside computing. In the early days of railway building in nineteenth-century England, there were competing track gauges, the distance between the two rails. A train built for one gauge could not run on track of another, which limited how the network could connect. A single standard gauge was decided on in 1846, but the other tracks then had to be converted. Shutting a line for months or years was not an option.

The solution was to convert the track first to dual or mixed gauge by adding a third rail. Trains of both gauges could then run on the line, using two of the three rails. Once every train had been converted to the standard gauge, the nonstandard rail could be removed. Reprocessing the old track this way, with old and new side by side, let the change happen gradually over years. It is still expensive, which is why some nonstandard gauges survive. The BART system in the San Francisco Bay Area, for example, uses a different gauge from most of the US.

Derived views allow gradual evolution. To restructure a dataset, you do not need a sudden switch. You can keep the old schema and the new schema as two independently derived views of the same underlying data. Start by routing a small number of users to the new view, to test its performance and find bugs, while most users stay on the old one. Then increase the share of users on the new view, and eventually drop the old one. Every stage can be reversed if something goes wrong, because a working system is always there to go back to. The author says that reducing the risk of irreversible damage makes teams more confident, so they can move faster.

The lambda architecture. If batch processing reprocesses history and stream processing handles recent updates, how do you combine the two? The lambda architecture is a proposal that attracted a lot of attention. Its core idea is that incoming data is recorded by appending immutable events to an ever-growing dataset, similar to event sourcing. Read-optimized views are derived from those events. The lambda architecture runs two systems in parallel: a batch system, such as Hadoop MapReduce, and a separate stream system, such as Storm.

The two layers cooperate in a specific way. The stream processor consumes events quickly and produces an approximate update to the view. Later, the batch processor consumes the same events and produces a corrected version of the derived view. The reasoning is that batch processing is simpler and less prone to bugs, while stream processors were thought to be less reliable and harder to make fault-tolerant. The stream side can also use fast approximate algorithms, while the batch side uses slower exact ones.

The author says the lambda architecture improved data systems, mainly by popularizing the principle of deriving views from streams of immutable events and reprocessing those events when needed. But he sees several practical problems:

  • Running the same logic in both a batch framework and a stream framework is a lot of extra work. Libraries such as Summingbird let one computation run in either context, but the operational complexity of debugging, tuning, and maintaining two systems remains.
  • The two pipelines produce separate outputs, and those must be merged to answer user requests. The merge is fairly easy for a simple aggregation over a tumbling window, which is a fixed, non-overlapping time slice. It becomes much harder with joins, with sessionization (grouping a user’s events into sessions), or when the output is not a time series.
  • Reprocessing all history is expensive on large datasets. So the batch side is often set up to process incremental batches, such as an hour of data at the end of each hour. That raises the timing problems discussed in the book’s section on reasoning about time, such as stragglers (events that arrive late) and windows that cross batch boundaries. Making the batch job incremental makes it more like the streaming layer, which goes against the goal of keeping the batch layer simple.

Unifying batch and stream processing. Newer work lets you have the benefits of the lambda architecture without its downsides. It runs both batch computations, which reprocess history, and stream computations, which handle events as they arrive, in the same system. The author names three features that make this possible, and says they are becoming widely available:

  • The ability to replay historical events through the same engine that handles recent events. Log-based message brokers can replay messages, and some stream processors can read input from a distributed filesystem such as HDFS.
  • Exactly-once semantics for stream processors. This means the output is the same as if no faults had happened, even if some did. As in batch processing, this requires discarding the partial output of any failed tasks.
  • Windowing by event time instead of processing time. Event time is when something actually happened. Processing time is when the system handled it. Processing time is meaningless when you replay old events. Apache Beam provides an API for such computations, which can run on Apache Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow.

Unbundling Databases

At the most abstract level, databases, Hadoop, and operating systems do the same basic job. They store some data, and they let you process and query it. A database stores records in some data model, such as rows in tables, documents, or vertices in a graph. An operating system’s filesystem stores data in files. At their core, both are information management systems. Chapter 10 noted that the Hadoop ecosystem is somewhat like a distributed version of Unix. There are real practical differences. Many filesystems cope poorly with a directory holding 10 million small files, while a database holding 10 million small records is ordinary. Even so, comparing the two is useful.

Unix and relational databases took very different philosophies. Unix aimed to give programs a logical but fairly low-level view of the hardware. Relational databases aimed to give application programmers a high-level abstraction that hides the complexity of on-disk data structures, concurrency, crash recovery, and more. Unix offered pipes and files that are simply sequences of bytes. Databases offered SQL and transactions.

Which is better depends on what you want. In one sense Unix is simpler, since it is a thin wrapper around the hardware. In another sense relational databases are simpler. A short declarative query, which says what result you want rather than how to compute it, can draw on a great deal of machinery, such as query optimization, indexes, join methods, concurrency control, and replication, without the author of the query needing to know the details. Both Unix and the relational model appeared in the early 1970s, and the tension between them has lasted for decades. The author reads the NoSQL movement as an attempt to apply the Unix style of low-level abstractions to distributed OLTP storage. He says he will try to reconcile the two philosophies, to combine the best of both.

Composing Data Storage Technologies

Across the book we have looked at many features that databases provide. There are secondary indexes, which let you find records quickly by the value of a field. There are materialized views, which are precomputed caches of query results. There are replication logs, which keep copies of the data on other nodes up to date. And there are full-text search indexes, which some relational databases include. Chapters 10 and 11 showed similar themes: building full-text indexes in batch jobs, maintaining materialized views in stream processing, and replicating changes from a database to derived systems through CDC.

So there are parallels between the features built into databases and the derived systems people build with batch and stream processors. The author draws several of them out.

Creating an index. Consider what happens when you run CREATE INDEX on a relational database. The database scans a consistent snapshot of the table (a frozen view of the table as it was at one moment) and picks out the values of the field being indexed. It sorts them and writes out the index. Then it processes the backlog of writes made since the snapshot, because the table was not locked and writes could continue. From then on, it keeps the index up to date on every write.

That process is remarkably like setting up a new follower replica, which takes a snapshot, catches up on changes, and then keeps following along. It is also very like starting CDC in a streaming system, which begins with an initial snapshot. So running CREATE INDEX reprocesses the existing dataset and derives the index as a new view on it. The existing data may be a snapshot of the current state rather than a full log of past changes, but the two are closely related.

The meta-database of everything. The author suggests that the dataflow across a whole organization starts to look like one huge database. Whenever a batch job, a stream job, or an ETL process (extract, transform, and load: copying data from one system into another in a reshaped form) moves data from one place and form to another, it is doing what a database does internally when it keeps indexes or materialized views up to date. Seen this way, batch and stream processors are elaborate versions of database triggers (code that runs automatically when data changes), stored procedures (code kept and run inside the database), and materialized view maintenance routines. The derived systems they maintain are like different index types. A relational database may support B-tree indexes, hash indexes, and spatial indexes. In the emerging architecture, those facilities are not features of one integrated product. They are supplied by different pieces of software, on different machines, run by different teams.

The author starts from the premise that no single data model or storage format suits every access pattern. He then speculates that there are two ways different storage and processing tools can still be composed into a cohesive system.

Federated databases: unifying reads. You can provide a unified query interface over many underlying storage engines and processing methods. This is called a federated database, or polystore. PostgreSQL’s foreign data wrapper feature follows this pattern, for example. Applications with a specialized data model or query interface can still reach the underlying engines directly. People who need to combine data from scattered places can do it easily through the federated interface. A federated query interface follows the relational tradition of one integrated system with a high-level language and elegant semantics, but its implementation is complicated.

Unbundled databases: unifying writes. Federation addresses read-only querying across several systems. It has no good answer for keeping writes in sync across them. Inside a single database, creating a consistent index is a built-in feature. When you compose several storage systems, you need the same guarantee: every data change must end up in every right place, even when faults happen. Making it easier to plug storage systems together reliably, for example through CDC and event logs, is like unbundling a database’s index-maintenance features so they can synchronize writes across different technologies. This follows the Unix tradition of small tools that each do one thing well, communicate through a uniform low-level interface (pipes), and can be composed with a higher-level language, the shell.

Making Unbundling Work

Federation and unbundling are two sides of one coin: composing a reliable, scalable, and maintainable system out of diverse parts. Read-only federated querying requires mapping one data model onto another. That takes thought, but it is ultimately a manageable problem. The author thinks keeping writes in sync across several storage systems is the harder engineering problem, so he focuses on it.

The traditional approach to synchronizing writes uses distributed transactions across heterogeneous storage systems, meaning systems of different kinds. The author thinks that is the wrong solution. Transactions within one storage or stream system are feasible. But when data crosses the boundary between technologies, he believes an asynchronous event log with idempotent writes is a far more robust and practical approach.

Stream processors already use distributed transactions internally to reach exactly-once semantics, and that can work well. But when a transaction must involve systems written by different groups of people, such as a stream processor writing to a distributed key-value store or a search index, the lack of a standard transaction protocol makes integration much harder. An ordered log of events, consumed by idempotent consumers, is a much simpler abstraction, and much more feasible to build across different systems.

Log-based integration gives loose coupling between components. That shows up in two ways.

  1. At the system level, asynchronous event streams make the whole system more robust to outages or slowdowns in one component. If a consumer runs slowly or fails, the log buffers messages, and the producer and other consumers keep running. The faulty consumer catches up once it is fixed, so it misses no data, and the fault stays contained. By contrast, the synchronous coupling of distributed transactions tends to turn a local fault into a large-scale failure.
  2. At the human level, unbundling lets different teams develop, improve, and maintain different components independently. Each team can focus on doing one thing well, with well-defined interfaces to other teams’ systems. Event logs are powerful enough to capture strong consistency properties, because events are durable and ordered. They are also general enough to apply to almost any kind of data.

Unbundled versus integrated systems. If unbundling does become the way of the future, it will not replace databases in their current form. Databases are still needed to maintain state inside stream processors, and to serve queries over the output of batch and stream jobs. Specialized query engines will also stay important. The query engines of massively parallel processing (MPP) data warehouses, for example, are optimized for exploratory analytic queries and handle that workload very well.

Running several kinds of infrastructure has costs. Each piece has a learning curve, configuration issues, and operational quirks, so it is worth deploying as few moving parts as possible. A single integrated product may also deliver better and more predictable performance on the workloads it was designed for, compared with a system of several tools joined by application code. The author repeats a point from the preface: building for scale you do not need is wasted effort, and it can lock you into an inflexible design. In effect, it is a form of premature optimization.

The goal of unbundling is therefore not to beat individual databases on performance for particular workloads. The goal is to combine several databases so you get good performance across a much wider range of workloads than any single product offers. It is about breadth, not depth. This is the same idea as the diversity of storage and processing models in the Hadoop comparison earlier in the book. If one technology does everything you need, you are most likely best off using it rather than rebuilding it from lower-level parts. Composition pays off only when no single product meets all your requirements.

Trade-offs
OptionGood atCosts
One integrated databaseOne product to run, and predictable performance on the workloads it was built forYou get only what that product offers. Unusual combinations of needs can be poorly served.
Unbundled compositionBreadth: each part can be the best tool for its job, across many kinds of workloadMany moving parts, each with its own learning curve and quirks. You must write and maintain the glue code between them.

What’s missing? Tools for composing data systems are getting better, but the author says one major piece is still missing. We do not yet have an unbundled-database equivalent of the Unix shell, meaning a high-level language for composing storage and processing systems in a simple, declarative way.

He would love to be able to declare something like mysql | elasticsearch, by analogy with a Unix pipe. This would be the unbundled version of CREATE INDEX. It would take all the documents in a MySQL database and index them in an Elasticsearch cluster. Then it would keep capturing every change to the database and apply it to the search index automatically, without custom application code. The author thinks this kind of integration should be possible with almost any storage or indexing system.

Caches could be maintained more easily in a similar way. A materialized view is essentially a precomputed cache. So you could imagine creating a cache by declaratively specifying materialized views for complex queries. Those queries might include recursive queries over graphs (queries that follow links through a network of connected records) and even application logic. The author notes early research in this area, such as differential dataflow, and hopes these ideas will reach production systems.

Designing Applications Around Dataflow

The approach of unbundling a database, by composing specialized storage and processing systems with application code, is sometimes called the database inside-out approach. The name comes from the title of a 2014 conference talk the author gave. He says calling it a new architecture would be too grand. He sees it as a design pattern and a starting point for discussion, and gives it a name so that people can talk about it more easily.

The ideas are not his own. They are a blend of other people’s work, and there is a lot of overlap with dataflow programming languages such as Oz and Juttle, with functional reactive programming (FRP) languages such as Elm, and with the logic language Bloom. The term unbundling, in this context, was proposed by Jay Kreps.

Spreadsheets already have dataflow programming that is well ahead of most mainstream languages. You place a formula in one cell, such as the sum of the cells in another column. Whenever an input to the formula changes, the result updates automatically. That is exactly what we want at the data-system level. When a database record changes, any index on it should update, and any cached views or totals that depend on it should refresh. You should not have to manage the mechanics. You should be able to trust that the refresh happens correctly.

The author thinks most data systems can still learn from VisiCalc, a spreadsheet program from 1979. Today’s data systems differ from spreadsheets in important ways. They must be fault-tolerant, scalable, and durable. They must also integrate technologies written by different groups of people over time, and reuse existing libraries and services. It is unrealistic to expect all software to be written in one language, with one framework or tool. The rest of this section explores ways to build applications around unbundled databases and dataflow.

Application Code as a Derivation Function

When one dataset is derived from another, a transformation function turns one into the other. The book gives several examples:

  • A secondary index is a derived dataset with a simple transformation. For each row or document in the base table, it picks out the values of the indexed columns or fields, and sorts by them. For a B-tree or SSTable index, which are sorted by key as Chapter 3 described, that sort is the index.
  • A full-text search index is built by applying natural language processing first. That includes language detection, word segmentation (splitting text into words, which matters in languages without spaces), stemming or lemmatization (reducing words to a base form, such as running to run), spelling correction, and synonym identification. Then it builds a structure for fast lookups, such as an inverted index, which maps each word to the documents that contain it.
  • In a machine learning system, a model is derived from training data through feature extraction and statistical analysis. When the model is applied to new input, its output is derived from the input and the model, and so indirectly from the training data.
  • A cache often holds data aggregated in the form the user interface will display. Filling it requires knowing which fields the interface uses. If the interface changes, the way the cache is filled may need to change too, and the cache must be rebuilt.

The derivation for a secondary index is so common that many databases build it in, so you can invoke it by saying CREATE INDEX. Basic linguistic features for common languages may be built into a database’s full-text search, but the more sophisticated features often need domain-specific tuning. In machine learning, feature engineering, which means choosing the input signals a model uses, is notoriously specific to the application. It often depends on detailed knowledge of how users interact with the app.

When the function that creates a derived dataset is not a standard, cookie-cutter function like a secondary index, custom code is needed to handle the application’s specific needs. This is where many databases struggle. Relational databases support triggers, stored procedures, and user-defined functions, which can run application code inside the database. But these have mostly been an afterthought in database design.

Separation of Application Code and State

In theory, a database could be a deployment environment for arbitrary application code, the way an operating system is. In practice, databases have proved poorly suited to the job. They do not fit the needs of modern application development, such as dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, evolvability, monitoring, metrics, calls to network services, and integration with external systems. Tools for running clusters, such as Mesos, YARN, Docker, and Kubernetes, were designed specifically to run application code. By doing one thing well, they do it much better than a database that runs user-defined functions as one feature among many.

So the author thinks it makes sense for some parts of a system to specialize in durable data storage, and other parts to specialize in running application code. The two can interact while staying independent.

Most web applications today are deployed as stateless services. Any user request can be routed to any application server, and the server forgets everything about the request once it has sent the response. That makes servers easy to add or remove, but the state has to live somewhere, usually in a database. The trend has been to keep stateless application logic separate from state management: no application logic inside the database, and no persistent state inside the application. The author jokes that the functional programming community likes to say it believes in the separation of Church and state. The joke is a pun on Alonzo Church, the mathematician who created the lambda calculus, which has no variables that can be overwritten, so mutable state sits apart from his work.

In this typical model, the database acts as a shared mutable variable that the application reads and updates synchronously over the network. The database takes care of durability, some concurrency control, and fault tolerance. But in most programming languages you cannot subscribe to changes in a variable. You can only read it. Readers are not notified when it changes, unlike a spreadsheet cell. You can build such notification yourself with the observer pattern, but most languages do not have it built in. Databases have inherited this passive approach. To find out whether data has changed, you often have to poll, meaning repeat your query on a timer. Subscribing to changes is only just starting to appear as a feature.

Dataflow: Interplay Between State Changes and Application Code

Thinking about applications as dataflow changes the relationship between application code and state management. Instead of treating the database as a passive variable that the application manipulates, you focus on the interplay between state, state changes, and the code that processes them. Application code responds to a state change in one place by triggering a state change in another.

The book has met this idea before. Chapter 11 treated the log of database changes as a stream of events you can subscribe to. Message-passing systems such as actors, which Chapter 4 covered, also respond to events through messages. In the 1980s, tuple spaces explored describing distributed computations as processes that observe state changes and react to them. Inside a database, the same thing happens when a trigger fires on a data change, or when a secondary index is updated to reflect a change in its table. Unbundling takes this idea and applies it outside the primary database, to create derived datasets such as caches, full-text search indexes, machine learning models, and analytics systems. Stream processing and messaging systems can do this work.

The author stresses that maintaining derived data is not the same as asynchronous job execution, which messaging systems were traditionally built for. Two differences matter:

  • Order matters. If several views are derived from one event log, they must process events in the same order to stay consistent with each other. Many message brokers do not preserve that order when they redeliver unacknowledged messages. Dual writes are also ruled out.
  • Fault tolerance is essential. Losing a single message leaves the derived dataset permanently out of sync with its source. So both message delivery and derived state updates must be reliable. Many actor systems keep actor state and messages in memory by default, so they are lost if the machine running the actor crashes.

Stable message ordering and reliable processing are demanding requirements. But they are much less expensive and more operationally robust than distributed transactions. Modern stream processors can provide these guarantees at scale, and they let application code run as stream operators. Such operators can do the arbitrary processing that built-in derivation functions usually cannot. Like Unix tools chained by pipes, stream operators can be composed into large systems. Each operator takes streams of state changes as input, and produces other streams of state changes as output.

Stream Processors and Services

The fashionable style of application development splits functionality into services that talk through synchronous network requests, such as REST APIs. Compared with one large application, the main advantage of this service-oriented approach is organizational scalability through loose coupling. Different teams can work on different services, which reduces coordination effort between teams, as long as each service can be deployed and updated independently.

Composing stream operators into dataflow systems shares many traits with the microservices approach. The underlying communication mechanism is very different, though. Dataflow uses one-directional, asynchronous message streams rather than synchronous request and response. Besides the advantages listed earlier in the book, such as better fault tolerance, dataflow systems can also achieve better performance. The book gives an example. A customer buys an item priced in one currency but paid for in another. To convert the currency, the system needs the current exchange rate. There are two ways to do that.

Example

Exchange rates in a purchase. In the microservices approach, the code that processes the purchase queries an exchange-rate service or database for the current rate each time. In the dataflow approach, the purchase code subscribes ahead of time to a stream of exchange-rate updates. Whenever a rate changes, it records the current rate in a local database. When a purchase arrives, it queries only that local database.

The second approach has replaced a synchronous network request to another service with a query to a local database, which may be on the same machine or even in the same process. The book adds that the microservices team could avoid the network call by caching rates locally. But to keep that cache fresh, they would have to poll for updated rates or subscribe to a stream of changes, which is exactly what the dataflow approach does.

The dataflow approach is faster, and it is more robust to another service failing. The fastest and most reliable network request is no network request at all. Instead of an RPC call, meaning one program invoking a function on another over the network, the system now performs a stream join between purchase events and exchange-rate update events. The join is time-dependent. If the purchase events are reprocessed later, the exchange rate will have changed. To rebuild the original output, you need the historical rate from the time of purchase. Whether you query a service or subscribe to a stream, you have to handle this time dependence.

There are still open questions, such as how to handle time-dependent joins. But the author believes that building applications around dataflow is a very promising direction. Subscribing to changes, instead of querying the current state whenever you need it, brings us closer to a spreadsheet model of computation: when some piece of data changes, anything derived from it can be updated swiftly.

Observing Derived State

The dataflow systems in the last section give a process for creating derived datasets, such as search indexes, materialized views, and predictive models, and keeping them up to date. The book calls this process the write path. Whenever information is written, it may pass through several stages of batch and stream processing, and eventually every derived dataset is updated to include it. The book’s Figure 12-1 shows the idea with a search index, where document updates on one side meet queries on the other.

But why create the derived dataset in the first place? Most likely because you want to query it later. That is the read path. When a user request arrives, you read from the derived dataset, perhaps do more processing on the results, and construct the response. Together, the write path and the read path cover the whole journey of the data, from the point where it is collected to the point where it is consumed, probably by another person. The write path is the part that is precomputed as soon as data comes in, whether or not anyone has asked to see it. The read path happens only when someone asks. If you know functional programming, you may notice that the write path is like eager evaluation, and the read path is like lazy evaluation.

The derived dataset is the place where the write path and the read path meet. It represents a trade-off between the amount of work done at write time and the amount done at read time.

Materialized Views and Caching

A full-text search index is a good example. The write path updates the index, and the read path searches it for keywords. Both sides do work. Writes update the index entries for every term that appears in a document. Reads look up each word in the query and apply Boolean logic to find matching documents. An AND query needs every word to match. An OR query accepts any synonym of each word.

Without an index, a search would have to scan all documents, the way the grep command scans files. That gets very expensive with many documents. No index means less work on the write path, since there is nothing to update, but much more work on the read path.

You could go the other way and precompute the results for every possible query. Then reads would only fetch ready answers, with no Boolean logic at all. But the write path would become far too expensive. The set of possible queries is effectively infinite, so precomputing all of them would need unlimited time and storage. The author adds a footnote: the set of distinct queries with nonempty results is finite if the collection is finite, but it grows exponentially with the number of terms, which is still bad news.

A middle path is to precompute results only for a fixed set of the most common queries, so they can be served quickly without going to the index. Uncommon queries are still served from the index. This is generally called a cache of common queries. It could also be called a materialized view, because it must be updated when new documents appear that belong in the results of one of the common queries.

So an index is not the only possible boundary between the write path and the read path. You can cache common search results, or scan without an index when there are only a few documents. Caches, indexes, and materialized views all shift the boundary. They let you do more work on the write path, by precomputing results, in order to save effort on the read path.

This shift was the subject of the Twitter example at the start of the book. Chapter 1 gave the numbers. Posting a tweet averaged 4.6k requests per second, with a peak above 12k. Viewing a home timeline ran at 300k requests per second. A typical tweet reached about 75 followers, but some users had over 30 million.

Example

The Twitter timeline, revisited. The book returns to this example to show how the boundary can be drawn differently for different users.

  1. Ordinary users: work at write time. When an ordinary user posts a tweet, the system looks up their followers and copies the tweet into each follower’s home timeline cache. At an average of about 75 followers, 4.6k tweets per second become roughly 345k timeline writes per second.
  2. Reading is then cheap. When a follower opens their timeline, the read path is a lookup in that cache. The work was already done when the tweet was posted.
  3. Celebrities: work at read time. A user with over 30 million followers would cause over 30 million writes for one tweet if fanned out. So their tweets are not copied into every timeline. They are stored once. When a user reads their timeline, the tweets of any celebrities they follow are fetched and merged in at read time, the way the read-time approach works.
  4. The result. Most of the work for ordinary users happens at write time, where reads are fast, and celebrities avoid the write storm by doing a little more work when the timeline is read. The book says this hybrid gives consistently good performance, and that after 500 pages the book has come full circle.

Stateful, Offline-Capable Clients

The author finds the idea of a boundary between the write path and the read path useful beyond databases. It is worth looking at it in another setting: the clients, meaning the programs that run on end users’ devices.

Web applications have long been built on the client/server model, in which clients are largely stateless and servers hold the authority over the data. The model is so common that we almost forget anything else exists. Technology keeps moving, though. Traditionally, web browsers were stateless clients that were useful only while connected. About the only thing you could do offline was scroll through a page you had loaded earlier. Recent single-page JavaScript apps have gained stateful powers, including client-side interaction and persistent local storage. Mobile apps can keep much state on the device and skip the round trip to a server for most actions.

This has renewed interest in offline-first applications. They do as much as possible using a local database on the same device, without an internet connection, and they sync with remote servers in the background when a connection is available. Mobile connections are often slow and unreliable. So it is a big advantage for users when the interface does not wait for network requests, and the app mostly works offline.

When state lives on end-user devices, new options appear. You can think of the on-device state as a cache of state on the server. The pixels on the screen are a materialized view onto the model objects in the client app. The model objects are a local replica of state held in a remote datacenter.

Pushing state changes to clients. In a typical web page, if the data changes on the server after you load the page, the browser does not find out until you reload. The browser reads the data at one point in time, assumes it is static, and does not subscribe to updates. So the state on the device is a stale cache, which is never refreshed unless you poll for changes. RSS feeds, too, are really a basic form of polling.

Newer protocols go beyond the basic request and response pattern of HTTP. Server-sent events, using the EventSource API, and WebSockets let a browser keep an open TCP connection to a server. While the connection stays open, the server can push messages to the browser whenever it has something to say. That lets the server inform the client about changes to its state, which reduces how stale the client’s state gets.

In terms of the write and read paths, actively pushing state changes all the way to client devices extends the write path to the end user. A client still uses a read path to get its initial state. After that, it can rely on a stream of state changes from the server. The ideas of stream processing and messaging are not limited to a datacenter. They can be extended all the way to end-user devices.

Devices will sometimes be offline and unable to receive changes. But the book says this problem is already solved. Chapter 11 described how a consumer of a log-based message broker can reconnect after failing or disconnecting, and still not miss any messages that arrived while it was away. The same technique works for individual users, where each device is a small subscriber to a small stream of events.

End-to-end event streams. Tools for building stateful clients and user interfaces, such as the Elm language and Facebook’s React, Flux, and Redux toolchain, already manage client-side state by subscribing to a stream of events. The events represent user input or responses from a server, and the structure is similar to event sourcing. It would be natural to extend this model so that a server can push state-change events into the same client-side pipeline. State changes could then flow end to end. An action on one device would pass through event logs and several derived data systems and stream processors, and reach the user interface of a person watching on another device. The author suggests such changes could arrive with low delay, under one second from end to end.

Some applications, such as instant messaging and online games, already have this kind of real-time architecture, meaning one where interactions have low delay. The book notes this is a different sense of real-time from the response time guarantees discussed earlier. So why do we not build all applications this way? The challenge is that the assumption of stateless clients and request and response interactions is deeply built into our databases, libraries, frameworks, and protocols. Many datastores support reads and writes where one request gets one response. Far fewer let you subscribe to changes, meaning a request that returns a stream of responses over time. To extend the write path all the way to the user, we would need to rethink many of these systems, moving away from request and response and toward publish/subscribe dataflow, where producers publish events and interested parties subscribe to them. The author believes the gains in responsive interfaces and offline support would be worth the effort. He hopes designers will keep subscribing to changes in mind as an option, not only querying the current state.

Reads Are Events Too

When a stream processor writes derived data to a store, and user requests query that store, the store is the boundary between the write path and the read path. The store allows random-access reads to the data, which would otherwise require scanning the whole event log.

Often the data storage is separate from the streaming system. But stream processors also need to maintain state to perform aggregations and joins, as Chapter 11 described. That state is usually hidden inside the processor. Some frameworks let outside clients query it, which turns the stream processor into a simple database.

The author wants to take the idea further. So far, writes go through an event log, while reads are transient network requests sent directly to the nodes that hold the data. That is reasonable, but it is not the only option. Reads can also be represented as streams of events. Both read events and write events can then be sent through a stream processor, which answers each read event by emitting the result to an output stream. When writes and reads are both events, routed to the same stream operator, you are in fact performing a stream-table join between the stream of read queries and the database. A read event must be sent to the database partition that holds the data, just as batch and stream processors must put inputs with the same key together when they join.

This correspondence between serving requests and performing joins is fundamental. A one-off read request passes through the join operator, gets its answer, and is forgotten. A subscribe request is a persistent join, with past and future events on the other side of the join producing results over time.

Recording a log of read events also helps track causal dependencies and data provenance (where data came from and how it was derived) across a system. It lets you reconstruct what the user saw before making a decision. In an online shop, for example, the predicted shipping date and the inventory status shown to a customer may affect whether they buy. To study that connection, you need a record of what the customer was shown. Writing read events to durable storage improves causal tracking, but it adds storage and I/O cost, and reducing that overhead is still an open research problem. If you already log read requests for operational purposes, as a side effect of processing them, then making that log the source of the requests is not a big change.

Multi-Partition Data Processing

For a query that touches a single partition, sending it through a stream and collecting a stream of responses may be overkill. But the idea opens up distributed execution of complex queries that combine data from several partitions. It reuses the message routing, partitioning, and joining infrastructure that stream processors already provide. Storm’s distributed RPC feature supports this pattern. It has been used, for example, to count how many people have seen a URL on Twitter. That count is the union of the follower sets of everyone who tweeted the URL. Because the set of users is partitioned, computing it requires combining results from many partitions.

Fraud prevention is another example. To judge whether a purchase is fraudulent, you can examine the reputation scores of the user’s IP address, email address, billing address, shipping address, and so on. Each of those reputation databases is itself partitioned. So collecting the scores for one purchase needs a sequence of joins with differently partitioned datasets.

The internal query execution graphs of MPP databases have similar characteristics. The author says that if you need this kind of multi-partition join, it is probably simpler to use a database that provides the feature than to build it on a stream processor. Still, treating queries as streams offers a way to build large-scale applications that run up against the limits of conventional off-the-shelf solutions.

Aiming for Correctness

A stateless service that only reads data is not a big risk. If something goes wrong, you fix the bug, restart the service, and everything returns to normal. Stateful systems such as databases are different. They are designed to remember things more or less forever, so the effects of a mistake can also last forever. That calls for more careful thought.

We want applications that are reliable and correct, meaning programs whose behavior is well defined and understood, even when faults occur. For about four decades, the transaction properties of atomicity, isolation, and durability, covered in Chapter 7, have been the tools of choice for building correct applications. The author says those foundations are weaker than they seem. The confusion around weak isolation levels is one example. In some areas, transactions are being abandoned entirely in favor of models that offer better performance and scalability but much messier semantics. Leaderless replication is one example. Consistency is often discussed but poorly defined. Some people say we should accept weak consistency for the sake of better availability, without a clear idea of what that means in practice.

Engineering methods are also less solid than they should be. It is very difficult to tell whether a particular application is safe at a particular isolation level or replication setup. Simple solutions often appear to work when concurrency is low and nothing fails, then turn out to have many subtle bugs under heavier conditions. Kyle Kingsbury’s Jepsen experiments have highlighted stark gaps between some products’ claimed safety guarantees and their actual behavior during network problems and crashes. Even if the infrastructure were perfect, application code would still have to use its features correctly. That is error-prone when the configuration is hard to understand, as with weak isolation levels and quorum configurations, which are rules about how many nodes must agree on a read or write.

The trade-off is clear. If your application can tolerate occasionally corrupting or losing data in unpredictable ways, life is much simpler, and you might get away with hoping for the best. If you need stronger assurances, serializability and atomic commit are established approaches. But they come at a cost. They typically work only within a single datacenter, which rules out geographically distributed architectures, and they limit the scale and fault tolerance you can achieve.

The author believes the traditional transaction approach is not going away, but it is not the last word on making applications correct and resilient to faults. The rest of this section suggests ways of thinking about correctness in dataflow architectures.

The End-to-End Argument for Databases

Using a data system with strong safety properties, such as serializable transactions, does not guarantee that your application is free from data loss or corruption. If an application has a bug that writes incorrect data, or deletes data, serializable transactions will not save you.

This may sound obvious, but the author says application bugs and human mistakes happen, so it is worth taking seriously. He used this point earlier, in the discussion of immutability, to argue for append-only data. It is easier to recover from mistakes if faulty code cannot destroy good data. Immutability is not a cure-all, though, and a subtler kind of corruption can still occur.

Exactly-once execution of an operation. Earlier the book met the idea of exactly-once, or effectively-once, semantics. If something goes wrong while processing a message, you can give up, which drops the message and loses data, or you can try again. If you try again, there is a risk that the operation actually succeeded the first time, and you simply did not find out. Then the message is processed twice. Processing twice is a form of corruption. It is undesirable to charge a customer twice for one service, or to increment a counter twice and overstate a metric. Here, exactly-once means arranging the computation so that its final effect is the same as if no faults had occurred, even if the operation was retried.

One of the most effective approaches is to make the operation idempotent, so that it has the same effect whether it runs once or many times. But making an operation that is not naturally idempotent into one takes effort and care. You may need extra metadata, such as the set of operation IDs that have already updated a value. You must also ensure fencing when failing over from one node to another, which means making sure an old node cut off from the cluster cannot keep writing.

Duplicate suppression. The same need to suppress duplicates appears in many places besides stream processing. TCP uses sequence numbers on packets to put them in order at the recipient, and to detect whether packets were lost or duplicated. Lost packets are retransmitted, and duplicates are removed, before the data reaches the application. But this only works within one TCP connection.

Imagine the TCP connection is a client’s connection to a database, currently running a transaction. In many databases, a transaction is tied to a client connection, so the database knows that several queries sent on the same connection belong to one transaction. If the client suffers a network interruption and a timeout after sending COMMIT, but before hearing back from the database, it does not know whether the transaction committed or aborted.

Example

A transfer that is not safe to retry. The book’s Example 12-1 moves $11 from one account to another inside one transaction. It is the standard textbook illustration of atomicity:

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 11.00 WHERE account_id = 1234;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 11.00 WHERE account_id = 4321;
COMMIT;
Example

Walk through what happens when the connection fails:

  1. The client sends the transaction. The database adds $11 to account 1234 and takes $11 from account 4321.
  2. The database commits. Before the reply reaches the client, the connection times out.
  3. The client does not know whether the transfer happened. It reconnects and retries the same transaction.
  4. If the first attempt did commit, the retry moves another $11. The transfer that was meant to move $11 has moved $22.

The transaction is not idempotent, so a retry can do the damage twice. The author notes that although Example 12-1 is a standard example of atomicity, it is not actually correct, and real banks do not work like this.

Two-phase commit protocols break the one-to-one link between a TCP connection and a transaction. They must let a transaction coordinator reconnect to a database after a network fault and tell it whether to commit or abort an in-doubt transaction (one whose outcome is not yet known). Is that enough to ensure the transaction runs only once? Unfortunately not. The network between the end user’s device and the application server is still a problem. If the client is a web browser, it probably sends an instruction with an HTTP POST request. A user on a weak cellular connection may succeed in sending the POST, but lose the signal before the response arrives. They will probably see an error and may retry manually. Browsers ask whether you are sure you want to submit the form again, and the user says yes, because they wanted the operation to happen. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern avoids that warning in normal operation, but it does not help when the POST times out. From the web server’s point of view, the retry is a separate request. From the database’s point of view, it is a separate transaction. The usual deduplication mechanisms do not help.

Operation identifiers. To make an operation idempotent across several hops of network communication, relying on a transaction mechanism inside the database is not enough. You need to consider the end-to-end flow of the request. For example, you could generate a unique identifier for each operation, such as a UUID, and include it as a hidden form field in the client application. Or you could calculate a hash of all the relevant form fields to derive the operation ID. If the browser submits the POST twice, both requests carry the same operation ID. You can pass that ID all the way through to the database, and check that only one operation with that ID ever executes.

Example

Suppressing duplicates with a request ID. Example 12-2 is the book’s version of the same transfer, with a request ID stored in a table that has a uniqueness rule:

ALTER TABLE requests ADD UNIQUE (request_id);
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO requests
  (request_id, from_account, to_account, amount)
  VALUES('0286FDB8-D7E1-423F-B40B-792B3608036C', 4321, 1234, 11.00);
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 11.00 WHERE account_id = 1234;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 11.00 WHERE account_id = 4321;
COMMIT;
Example

Walk through the retry in Example 12-2:

  1. The unique constraint on request_id tells the database that no two rows may share that ID.
  2. The first attempt inserts a row with the ID, then updates both balances, and commits.
  3. The retry sends the same request ID. The INSERT fails because the ID already exists. That aborts the transaction, so the balances are not touched a second time.

Relational databases can generally maintain a uniqueness constraint correctly, even at weak isolation levels. An application-level check-then-insert, by contrast, can fail under nonserializable isolation, as discussed earlier in the book. The author also notes that the requests table acts as a kind of event log, which points toward event sourcing. The balance updates do not have to happen in the same transaction as the insert. They are redundant, since they could be derived from the request event in a downstream consumer, provided that event is processed exactly once. That too can be enforced with the request ID.

The end-to-end argument. Suppressing duplicate transactions is one example of a more general principle, which Saltzer, Reed, and Clark articulated in 1984. In essence, the principle says that a function can be implemented completely and correctly only with the knowledge and help of the applications at the two endpoints of a communication system. So providing that function as a feature of the communication system itself is not possible. An incomplete version provided inside the system may still be useful as a performance boost.

In this example, the function was duplicate suppression. TCP suppresses duplicate packets within a connection. Some stream processors provide exactly-once semantics at the message level. But neither is enough to stop a user from submitting a duplicate request when the first one timed out. Solving the problem requires an end-to-end solution: a transaction identifier that is passed all the way from the end-user client to the database.

The same argument applies to checking data integrity. Checksums built into Ethernet, TCP, and TLS can detect corruption of packets in the network. They cannot detect corruption caused by bugs in the software at either end of the connection, or corruption on the disks where data is stored. If you want to catch every possible source of corruption, you also need end-to-end checksums.

A similar argument applies to encryption. The password on your home WiFi network protects against people snooping on your WiFi traffic, but not against attackers elsewhere on the internet. TLS or SSL between your client and the server protects against network attackers, but not against a compromised server. Only end-to-end encryption and authentication protect against all of these.

Low-level features, such as TCP duplicate suppression, Ethernet checksums, and WiFi encryption, cannot provide the end-to-end properties by themselves. But they are still useful, because they reduce the probability of problems at higher levels. HTTP requests would often be mangled if TCP did not put packets back in the right order. The point is only that low-level reliability is not sufficient on its own to ensure end-to-end correctness.

Applying end-to-end thinking in data systems. This brings the argument back to the author’s original thesis. Just because an application uses a data system with comparatively strong safety properties does not mean the application is guaranteed to be free from data loss or corruption. The application itself needs to take end-to-end measures, such as duplicate suppression. The author calls that a shame, because fault-tolerance mechanisms are hard to get right. Low-level reliability mechanisms, such as those in TCP, work quite well, so the remaining higher-level faults are fairly rare.

It would be nice to wrap the remaining high-level fault-tolerance machinery in an abstraction, so that application code need not worry about it. But the author fears the right abstraction has not been found yet. Transactions have long been seen as a good abstraction. They take a wide range of possible problems, such as concurrent writes, constraint violations, crashes, network interruptions, and disk failures, and collapse them into two outcomes: commit or abort. That is a huge simplification of the programming model, but he fears it is not enough.

Transactions are expensive, especially across heterogeneous storage technologies. When we refuse to use distributed transactions because they cost too much, we end up reimplementing fault-tolerance mechanisms in application code. The book has shown that reasoning about concurrency and partial failure is difficult and counterintuitive. So the author suspects that most application-level mechanisms do not work correctly, and the consequence is lost or corrupted data. He therefore thinks it is worth exploring fault-tolerance abstractions that make it easy to provide application-specific, end-to-end correctness properties, while keeping good performance and operational characteristics in a large distributed environment.

Enforcing Constraints

Let us think about correctness in the context of unbundled databases. We saw that end-to-end duplicate suppression works with a request ID that is passed from the client to the database that records the write. What about other kinds of constraints?

Uniqueness constraints are the focus here. Earlier chapters gave several examples of applications that must enforce uniqueness. A username or email address must identify one user. A file storage service cannot hold two files with the same name. Two people cannot book the same seat on a flight or in a theater. Other constraints are similar. An account balance must never go negative. You must not sell more items than the warehouse holds. A meeting room must not have overlapping bookings. Techniques that enforce uniqueness can often be used for these as well.

Uniqueness constraints require consensus. Chapter 9 showed that in a distributed setting, enforcing a uniqueness constraint requires consensus.
