If several concurrent requests want the same value, the system must somehow decide which operation is accepted and reject the others. The most common way to reach that agreement is to make one node the leader and let it make all the decisions. That works as long as you do not mind funneling all requests through a single node, even when the client is on the other side of the world, and as long as that node does not fail. If you need to tolerate the leader failing, you are back at the consensus problem.

Uniqueness checking can be scaled out by partitioning on the value that must be unique. If you need uniqueness by request ID, you can route all requests with the same ID to the same partition. If you need usernames to be unique, you can partition by a hash of the username. Asynchronous multi-leader replication is ruled out, however. Different leaders could concurrently accept conflicting writes, and then the values would no longer be unique. If you want to reject any write that would violate the constraint immediately, synchronous coordination is unavoidable.

Uniqueness in log-based messaging. A log ensures that all consumers see messages in the same order. That guarantee is total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus. In the unbundled approach with log-based messaging, a very similar method can enforce uniqueness constraints. A stream processor consumes all the messages in a log partition sequentially, on a single thread. If the log is partitioned by the value that must be unique, the stream processor can decide, without ambiguity and deterministically, which of several conflicting operations came first.

Example

Several users claim the same username. The book describes the following steps:

  1. Every request for a username is encoded as a message, and appended to a partition determined by the hash of the username.
  2. A stream processor reads the requests in the log in order. It uses a local database to keep track of which usernames are taken. For a name that is available, it records the name as taken and emits a success message to an output stream. For a name that is already taken, it emits a rejection message.
  3. The client that requested the username watches the output stream and waits for the success or rejection that matches its request.

Because all requests for one username go to the same partition, and each partition is handled one message at a time, the first request for a name is the one that wins. The author notes that this is basically the same algorithm as implementing linearizable storage using total order broadcast, which the book covered earlier. It scales to a large request volume by adding partitions, since each partition is processed independently.

The approach works not only for uniqueness constraints but for many other kinds of constraints. Its basic principle is that any writes that may conflict are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially. What counts as a conflict depends on the application, and the stream processor can use arbitrary logic to validate a request. The author says this is similar to an approach pioneered by Bayou in the 1990s.

Multi-partition request processing. Making an operation atomic while satisfying constraints becomes more interesting when several partitions are involved. In Example 12-2 there are potentially three partitions: one holding the request ID, one holding the payee’s account, and one holding the payer’s account. There is no reason those three things should share a partition, since they are independent of each other.

In the traditional database approach, this transaction would need an atomic commit across all three partitions. That forces it into a total order with respect to every other transaction touching those partitions. Because the partitions now coordinate, they can no longer be processed independently, and throughput is likely to suffer. The book says equivalent correctness can be reached with partitioned logs and without an atomic commit.

Example

Transferring money across partitions. The steps are:

  1. The client gives the request to transfer money from account A to account B a unique request ID. It appends the request to a log partition chosen by that ID.
  2. A stream processor reads the log of requests. For each request, it emits two messages to output streams: a debit instruction for payer A, partitioned by A, and a credit instruction for payee B, partitioned by B. The original request ID goes into both.
  3. Further processors consume the streams of credit and debit instructions, deduplicate them by request ID, and apply the changes to the account balances.

The first two steps matter. If the client sent the credit and debit instructions directly, it would need an atomic commit across the two partitions, so that either both happen or neither does. Instead, the request is first logged as a single message, and the credit and debit instructions are derived from that message. Single-object writes are atomic in almost all data systems, so the request either appears in the log or it does not. No multi-partition atomic commit is needed.

If the stream processor in step 2 crashes, it resumes from its last checkpoint, which is a saved position in the log. It does not skip any request. But it may process some requests more than once, and produce duplicate credit and debit instructions. Because it is deterministic, it produces the same instructions again. The processors in step 3 can then deduplicate them by the end-to-end request ID.

If you also want to ensure the payer is not overdrawn by the transfer, you can add a stream processor, partitioned by payer account number, that maintains account balances and validates transactions. Only valid transactions would then be placed in the request log in step 1.

By breaking the multi-partition transaction into two differently partitioned stages, and using the end-to-end request ID, the system achieves the same correctness property. Every request is applied exactly once to both the payer and the payee accounts, even in the presence of faults, and without an atomic commit protocol. The author notes that the idea of several differently partitioned stages is similar to the multi-partition data processing discussed earlier.

Timeliness and Integrity

A convenient property of transactions is that they are typically linearizable. A writer waits until the transaction commits, and afterward its writes are immediately visible to all readers. That is not the case when an operation is spread across several stages of stream processing. Consumers of a log are asynchronous by design, so a sender does not wait until its message has been processed. A client can still choose to wait for a message to appear on an output stream, which is what the username example did when it checked whether a uniqueness constraint was satisfied.

In that example, the correctness of the uniqueness check does not depend on whether the sender waits. Waiting only informs the sender, synchronously, whether the check succeeded. That notification can be decoupled from the effects of processing the message.

The author says the term consistency combines two different requirements, which are worth considering separately.

  • Timeliness means ensuring that users observe the system in an up-to-date state. If a user reads from a stale copy of the data, they may see an inconsistent state. But that inconsistency is temporary, and it resolves itself if you wait and try again. The CAP theorem uses consistency in the sense of linearizability, which is a strong way of achieving timeliness. Weaker timeliness properties, such as read-after-write consistency (seeing your own writes), can also be useful.
  • Integrity means absence of corruption: no data loss, and no contradictory or false data. If some derived dataset is maintained as a view onto underlying data, the derivation must be correct. A database index must correctly reflect the contents of the database. An index in which some records are missing is not very useful. If integrity is violated, the inconsistency is permanent. Waiting and retrying will not fix corruption in most cases, so explicit checking and repair are needed. In the context of ACID transactions, consistency is usually understood as an application-specific notion of integrity, and atomicity and durability are important tools for preserving it.

In slogan form, violations of timeliness are eventual consistency, whereas violations of integrity are perpetual inconsistency.

The author asserts that in most applications integrity is much more important than timeliness. Violations of timeliness can be annoying and confusing. Violations of integrity can be catastrophic. Take a credit card statement. It is not surprising if a purchase made within the last 24 hours is not yet on it, because banks reconcile and settle transactions asynchronously, and timeliness is not very important there. But it would be very bad if the statement balance did not equal the previous balance plus the transactions, which would be an error in the sums. It would also be bad if you were charged for a purchase that was never paid to the merchant, which is disappearing money. Those are violations of integrity.

Key idea

Waiting fixes timeliness problems, but it cannot fix integrity problems. Integrity matters more than timeliness in most applications, and it is the property you must protect first.

Correctness of dataflow systems. ACID transactions usually provide both timeliness, such as linearizability, and integrity, such as atomic commit. So if you approach correctness from the point of view of ACID transactions, the distinction between the two is fairly unimportant. Event-based dataflow systems, however, decouple them. When event streams are processed asynchronously, there is no guarantee of timeliness unless you build consumers that wait for a message to arrive before returning. Integrity, though, is central to streaming systems. Exactly-once, or effectively-once, semantics is a mechanism for preserving integrity. If an event is lost, or takes effect twice, the integrity of the data system can be violated. So fault-tolerant message delivery and duplicate suppression, for example through idempotent operations, are important for maintaining integrity.

Reliable stream processing can preserve integrity without distributed transactions or an atomic commit protocol. That means it can potentially reach comparable correctness with much better performance and operational robustness. The author says this integrity comes from a combination of mechanisms:

  • The content of a write is represented as a single message, which can be written atomically. This fits event sourcing well.
  • All other state updates are derived from that message using deterministic functions, similar to stored procedures.
  • A client-generated request ID is passed through all levels of processing, which enables end-to-end duplicate suppression and idempotence.
  • Messages are immutable, and derived data can be reprocessed from time to time, which makes it easier to recover from bugs.

The author sees this combination as a very promising direction for building fault-tolerant applications.

Loosely interpreted constraints. Enforcing a traditional uniqueness constraint requires consensus, typically implemented by funneling all events in a partition through a single node. That is unavoidable for the strict form of the constraint, and stream processing cannot avoid it. But many real applications can get by with much weaker notions of uniqueness:

  • If two people concurrently register the same username, or book the same seat, you can send one of them a message apologizing and asking them to choose something different. Correcting a mistake in this way is called a compensating transaction.
  • If customers order more items than you have in the warehouse, you can order more stock, apologize for the delay, and offer a discount. That is the same as what you would have to do if a forklift truck ran over some of the items, leaving you with fewer than you thought. So the apology workflow already has to be part of your business processes, and a linearizable constraint on stock may be unnecessary.
  • Many airlines overbook flights, expecting some passengers to miss theirs. Many hotels overbook rooms, expecting some guests to cancel. The rule of one person per seat is deliberately broken for business reasons, and compensation, such as refunds, upgrades, or a room at a neighboring hotel, handles the cases where demand exceeds supply. Even without overbooking, flights are cancelled because of weather or staff strikes, and recovering from that is a normal part of the business.
  • If someone withdraws more money than they have, the bank can charge an overdraft fee and ask them to pay back what they owe. By limiting total withdrawals per day, the bank bounds its risk.

In many business contexts it is acceptable to violate a constraint temporarily, and fix it afterward by apologizing. The cost of the apology, in money or reputation, varies, but it is often low. You cannot unsend an email, but you can send a follow-up correction. If you accidentally charge a credit card twice, you can refund one charge, and the cost to you is processing fees and perhaps a complaint. Once money has come out of an ATM, you cannot directly get it back, although in principle you could send debt collectors after an overdrawn customer who will not pay.

Whether the cost of an apology is acceptable is a business decision. If it is, the traditional model of checking all constraints before writing any data is unnecessarily restrictive. It can be reasonable to write optimistically and check the constraint afterward. You can still make sure validation happens before anything expensive to reverse, but that does not imply validating before every write. These applications do require integrity. You would not want to lose a reservation, or have money disappear through mismatched credits and debits. What they do not require is timeliness in enforcing the constraint. If you have sold more items than you have in the warehouse, you can patch up the problem afterward by apologizing. This is similar to the conflict resolution approaches discussed earlier in the book.

Coordination-avoiding data systems. The author makes two observations. First, dataflow systems can maintain integrity guarantees on derived data without atomic commit, linearizability, or synchronous cross-partition coordination. Second, although strict uniqueness constraints require timeliness and coordination, many applications are fine with loose constraints that may be temporarily violated and fixed up later, as long as integrity is preserved throughout.

Taken together, these mean dataflow systems can provide data management for many applications without requiring coordination, while still giving strong integrity guarantees. Such coordination-avoiding data systems have a lot of appeal, because they can achieve better performance and fault tolerance than systems that need synchronous coordination. For example, a system could run across several datacenters in a multi-leader configuration, replicating asynchronously between regions. Any one datacenter could keep operating independently, because no synchronous cross-region coordination is required. Such a system would have weak timeliness. It could not be linearizable without adding coordination. But it could still have strong integrity.

In that kind of system, serializable transactions are still useful for maintaining derived state, but they can run at a small scope where they work well. Heterogeneous distributed transactions, such as XA, are not required. Synchronous coordination can still be introduced where it is needed, for example to enforce a strict constraint before an operation from which recovery is not possible. But there is no need for everything to pay the cost of coordination if only a small part of the application needs it.

The author offers one more way to see the trade-off. Coordination and constraints reduce the number of apologies you have to make because of inconsistencies. But they can also reduce performance and availability, which can increase the number of apologies you have to make because of outages. You cannot reduce apologies to zero. The aim is to find the sweet spot where there are neither too many inconsistencies nor too many availability problems.

Trade-offs
ApproachGood atCosts
Distributed transactions across systems (such as XA)Strong timeliness and atomic changes across systems. Readers see committed writes right away.Poor fault tolerance and performance. A failure in one participant can stall or abort the rest, and the protocol must be supported by every system involved.
Log-based derived data with idempotent consumersLoose coupling. Faults stay contained, teams work independently, and the design works across different products.Updates are asynchronous, so there is no timeliness guarantee by default. You must handle stale reads and build idempotence yourself.
Check constraints after the fact, and apologize when neededNo coordination on the write path, so writes are fast and the system stays available during partitions.Violations are visible to users. Apologies and compensation cost money or reputation, and the business must have a process for them.

Trust, but Verify

The discussion so far has assumed that certain things might go wrong, and other things will not. These assumptions form the system model. For example, we assume processes can crash, machines can lose power suddenly, and networks can delay or drop messages. We also assume that data written to disk is not lost after an fsync (a command that forces data onto disk), that data in memory is not corrupted, and that the multiplication instruction of a CPU always returns the correct result.

Those assumptions are reasonable. They are true most of the time, and it would be hard to get anything done if we constantly worried about computers making mistakes. Traditionally, system models take a binary view of faults: some things can happen, and other things never can. In reality, it is a question of probabilities. Some things are more likely and others less likely. The real question is whether violations of our assumptions happen often enough that we will meet them in practice.

Data can become corrupted while it sits untouched on disk. Corruption on the network can sometimes slip past TCP checksums. Maybe this deserves more attention than it gets. The author describes an application he once worked on, which collected crash reports from clients. Some reports could only be explained by random bit flips in the memory of those devices. That seems unlikely, but if you have enough devices running your software, even very unlikely things happen. Besides random memory corruption from hardware faults or radiation, certain memory access patterns can flip bits even in memory that has no faults. This effect, known as rowhammer, has been used to break security mechanisms in operating systems. Once you look closely, hardware is not the perfect abstraction it may seem.

The author adds that random bit flips are still very rare on modern hardware. He only wants to point out that they are not beyond the realm of possibility, and so they deserve some attention.

Maintaining Integrity in the Face of Software Bugs

Besides hardware problems, there is always the risk of software bugs. Such bugs can get past lower-level network, memory, or filesystem checksums. Even widely used database software has bugs. The author has personally seen MySQL fail to maintain a uniqueness constraint correctly. He has also seen PostgreSQL’s serializable isolation level show write skew anomalies, where two transactions each read data that the other changes, and both commit. MySQL and PostgreSQL are robust, well-regarded databases that many people have battle-tested for years. Less mature software is likely to be worse. Despite careful design, testing, and review, bugs creep in. They are rare, and they eventually get found and fixed, but there is a period during which they can corrupt data.

Application code gets far less review and testing than database code, so the author assumes many more bugs there. Many applications do not even use the database features that preserve integrity correctly, such as foreign key or uniqueness constraints. ACID consistency is based on the idea that a database starts in a consistent state, and each transaction moves it to another consistent state. That only makes sense if the transaction is free from bugs. If the application uses the database incorrectly, for example by relying on a weak isolation level unsafely, the integrity of the database cannot be guaranteed.

Don’t Just Blindly Trust What They Promise

With both hardware and software falling short of the ideal, the author says corruption is inevitable sooner or later. So we should at least have a way of finding out whether data has been corrupted, so that we can fix it and track down the source of the error. Checking the integrity of data is called auditing. As Chapter 11 showed in its discussion of immutable events, auditing is not just for financial applications. But auditability is especially important in finance, precisely because everyone knows mistakes happen, and everyone accepts the need to be able to detect and fix problems.

Mature systems usually plan for unlikely things going wrong. Large storage systems such as HDFS and Amazon S3 do not fully trust their disks. They run background processes that continually read files back, compare them with other replicas, and move files from one disk to another, to reduce the risk of silent corruption. The lesson for everyone is the same. If you want to be sure your data is still there, you have to actually read it and check. Most of the time it will be. But if it is not, you really want to find out sooner rather than later. By the same argument, you should try restoring from your backups from time to time. Otherwise you may find out that a backup is broken only when it is too late and you have already lost data. Do not just blindly trust that everything is working.

A Culture of Verification

Systems like HDFS and S3 still have to assume that disks work correctly most of the time. That is a reasonable assumption, but it is not the same as assuming they always work. Few systems have this trust-but-verify approach of continually auditing themselves. Many assume that correctness guarantees are absolute, and make no provision for the possibility of rare data corruption. The author hopes that in the future we will see more self-validating and self-auditing systems that continually check their own integrity, rather than relying on blind trust.

He fears that the culture of ACID databases has led developers to build applications on blind trust in technology, such as a transaction mechanism, and to neglect auditability along the way. The technology worked well enough most of the time, so auditing did not seem worth the investment. Then the database landscape changed. Weaker consistency guarantees became the norm under the NoSQL banner, and less mature storage technologies came into wide use. Because audit mechanisms had not been developed, applications kept running on blind trust, which had become more dangerous than before. That is the reason to think carefully about designing for auditability.

Designing for Auditability

If a transaction changes several objects in a database, it is hard to tell afterward what that transaction meant. Even if you capture the transaction logs through CDC, the inserts, updates, and deletes across various tables do not necessarily show why those changes were made. The application logic that decided on the changes was transient, and it cannot be reproduced.

Event-based systems can provide better auditability. In event sourcing, user input is recorded as a single immutable event, and all resulting state updates are derived from that event. The derivation can be made deterministic and repeatable. So running the same log of events through the same version of the derivation code results in the same state updates. The book’s earlier discussion of batch outputs stressed being explicit about dataflow, and that makes the provenance of data much clearer, which makes integrity checking much more feasible. For the event log, you can use hashes to check that the event storage has not been corrupted. For any derived state, you can rerun the batch and stream processes that derived it from the event log, to check whether you get the same result. You can even run a redundant derivation in parallel.

A deterministic, well-defined dataflow also makes it easier to debug and trace a system, to find out why it did something. If something unexpected happened, it is valuable to reproduce the exact circumstances that led to it. The author calls this a kind of time-travel debugging capability.

The End-to-End Argument Again

If we cannot fully trust that every component is free from corruption, with every disk fault-free and every program bug-free, then we must at least check the integrity of our data periodically. If we do not check, we will not find out about corruption until it has caused downstream damage, and by then it is much harder and more expensive to track down. Checking integrity is best done end to end, as discussed earlier. The more systems an integrity check includes, the fewer opportunities there are for corruption to go unnoticed at some stage. If you can check that an entire derived data pipeline is correct from end to end, then every disk, network, service, and algorithm along the path is implicitly included in the check.

Continuous end-to-end integrity checks give you more confidence that your systems are correct, and that lets you move faster. Like automated testing, auditing increases the chances that bugs are found quickly, which reduces the risk that a change to the system, or a new storage technology, will cause damage. If you are not afraid of making changes, you can evolve an application much more easily to meet changing requirements.

Tools for Auditable Data Systems

At present, few data systems make auditability a top-level concern. Some applications implement their own audit mechanisms, for example by logging all changes to a separate audit table. But guaranteeing the integrity of both the audit log and the database state is still difficult. A transaction log can be made tamper-proof by periodically signing it with a hardware security module (a tamper-resistant device that holds signing keys). That does not guarantee, though, that the right transactions went into the log in the first place.

The author suggests that cryptographic tools might prove the integrity of a system in a way that is robust to a wide range of hardware and software issues, and even to malicious actions. Cryptocurrencies, blockchains, and distributed ledger technologies such as Bitcoin, Ethereum, Ripple, and Stellar have appeared to explore this. The author is not qualified to judge them as currencies or as ways to agree on contracts. From a data systems point of view, though, they contain interesting ideas. Essentially, they are distributed databases with a data model and a transaction mechanism, in which different replicas can be hosted by organizations that do not trust each other. The replicas continually check each other’s integrity, and use a consensus protocol to agree on which transactions to execute.

He is somewhat skeptical of the Byzantine fault tolerance aspects, which deal with nodes that lie or act maliciously. He finds the proof-of-work technique, such as Bitcoin mining, extraordinarily wasteful. Bitcoin’s transaction throughput is also rather low, mainly for political and economic reasons rather than technical ones. The integrity-checking aspects, however, are interesting.

Cryptographic auditing and integrity checking often rely on Merkle trees, which are trees of hashes that can efficiently prove that a record appears in some dataset, among other things. Outside the hype around cryptocurrencies, certificate transparency is a security technology that relies on Merkle trees to check the validity of TLS/SSL certificates. The author can imagine integrity-checking and auditing algorithms, like those of certificate transparency and distributed ledgers, becoming more widely used in data systems. Some work would be needed to make them as scalable as systems without cryptographic auditing, and to keep the performance penalty low. But he thinks it is an interesting area to watch.

Doing the Right Thing

In the final section, the author steps back. Throughout the book we have examined a wide range of architectures for data systems, weighed their pros and cons, and explored techniques for building reliable, scalable, and maintainable applications. But we have left out an important and fundamental part of the discussion, and he wants to fill that gap now.

Every system is built for a purpose, and every action has intended and unintended consequences. The purpose may be as simple as making money, but the consequences for the world can reach far beyond it. Engineers building these systems have a responsibility to consider those consequences carefully, and to decide consciously what kind of world they want to live in.

We talk about data as an abstract thing. But many datasets are about people: their behavior, their interests, and their identity. We must treat that data with humanity and respect. Users are people too, and human dignity is paramount.

Software development increasingly involves making important ethical choices. Guidelines exist to help engineers, such as the ACM’s Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice. But they are rarely discussed, applied, and enforced in practice. As a result, engineers and product managers sometimes take a cavalier attitude toward privacy and the potential negative consequences of their products.

A technology is not good or bad in itself. What matters is how it is used and how it affects people. That is true for a software system such as a search engine, in much the same way as it is true for a weapon. The author thinks it is not enough for software engineers to focus only on the technology and ignore its consequences. The ethical responsibility is theirs to bear too. Reasoning about ethics is difficult, but it is too important to ignore.

Predictive Analytics

Predictive analytics is a major part of the big data hype. Using data analysis to predict the weather, or the spread of a disease, is one thing. Predicting whether a convicted person is likely to reoffend, whether a loan applicant is likely to default, or whether an insurance customer is likely to make expensive claims is another. Those predictions directly affect individual people’s lives.

Payment networks want to prevent fraudulent transactions. Banks want to avoid bad loans. Airlines want to avoid hijackings. Companies want to avoid hiring ineffective or untrustworthy people. From their point of view, the cost of a missed business opportunity is low, but the cost of a bad loan or a problematic employee is much higher. So it is natural for organizations to be cautious. If in doubt, they are better off saying no.

However, as algorithmic decision-making becomes more widespread, someone who has been labeled risky by an algorithm, accurately or falsely, may suffer a large number of those no decisions. Being systematically excluded from jobs, air travel, insurance, rental housing, financial services, and other key parts of society is a large constraint on personal freedom. The book cites the term algorithmic prison for this situation. In countries that respect human rights, the criminal justice system presumes innocence until guilt is proven. Automated systems can exclude a person from participating in society without any proof of guilt, and with little chance of appeal.

Bias and discrimination. Decisions made by an algorithm are not necessarily better or worse than those made by a human. Every person has biases, even if they actively try to counteract them, and discriminatory practices can become culturally institutionalized. There is hope that basing decisions on data, rather than on subjective and instinctive judgments, could be fairer and give a better chance to people who are often overlooked by the traditional system.

But when we develop predictive analytics systems, we are not merely automating a human’s decision by writing the rules for when to say yes or no. We are leaving the rules themselves to be inferred from data. The patterns these systems learn are opaque. Even if there is some correlation in the data, we may not know why. If there is a systematic bias in the input, the system will most likely learn that bias and amplify it in its output.

Anti-discrimination laws in many countries prohibit treating people differently based on protected traits such as ethnicity, age, gender, sexuality, disability, or beliefs. Other features of a person’s data may be analyzed, but what happens if they are correlated with protected traits? In racially segregated neighborhoods, a person’s postal code, or even their IP address, is a strong predictor of race. It seems ridiculous to believe that an algorithm could take biased data as input and produce fair and impartial output. Yet that belief is often implied by proponents of data-driven decision making. One satirical description of the attitude compares machine learning to money laundering for bias.

Predictive analytics systems merely extrapolate from the past. If the past was discriminatory, they codify that discrimination. If we want the future to be better than the past, moral imagination is required, and that is something only humans can provide. Data and models should be our tools, not our masters.

Responsibility and accountability. Automated decision making raises the question of who is responsible and who can be held to account. If a human makes a mistake, they can be held accountable, and the person affected can appeal. Algorithms make mistakes too, but who is accountable when they go wrong? When a self-driving car causes an accident, who is responsible? If an automated credit-scoring algorithm systematically discriminates against people of a particular race or religion, is there any recourse? If a decision made by your machine learning system comes under judicial review, can you explain to the judge how the algorithm reached its decision?

Credit rating agencies are an old example of collecting data to make decisions about people. A bad credit score makes life difficult. But a credit score is normally based on relevant facts about a person’s actual borrowing history, and any errors in the record can be corrected, although the agencies often do not make this easy. Scoring algorithms based on machine learning typically use a much wider range of inputs, and they are much more opaque. That makes it harder to understand how a particular decision came about, and whether someone is being treated unfairly.

A credit score summarizes how you behaved in the past. Predictive analytics often works on a different basis: who is similar to you, and how did people like you behave? That draws parallels with other people’s behavior, which implies stereotyping, for example based on where you live, a close proxy for race and socioeconomic class. What about people who get put in the wrong bucket? And if a decision is incorrect because the data was erroneous, recourse is almost impossible.

Much data is statistical in nature. Even if the probability distribution as a whole is correct, individual cases may well be wrong. If the average life expectancy in your country is 80 years, that does not mean you are expected to die on your 80th birthday. From the average and the distribution, you cannot say much about how long one particular person will live. Similarly, the output of a prediction system is probabilistic, and it may well be wrong in individual cases.

A blind belief in the supremacy of data for making decisions is not only delusional, the author says. It is dangerous. As data-driven decision making spreads, we will need to make algorithms accountable and transparent, to avoid reinforcing existing biases, and to fix them when they inevitably make mistakes. We will also need to prevent data from being used to harm people, and to realize its positive potential instead. Analytics can reveal the financial and social characteristics of people’s lives. On one hand, that power could focus aid on the people who most need it. On the other hand, it is sometimes used by predatory businesses that look for vulnerable people to sell them risky products, such as high-cost loans and worthless college degrees.

Feedback loops. Even predictive applications with less immediately far-reaching effects, such as recommendation systems, raise difficult issues. When services become good at predicting what content users want to see, they may end up showing people only opinions they already agree with. That can create echo chambers, in which stereotypes, misinformation, and polarization breed. The author notes that we are already seeing the impact of social media echo chambers on election campaigns.

When predictive analytics affects people’s lives, self-reinforcing feedback loops can cause especially pernicious problems. Consider employers who use credit scores to evaluate potential hires. You may be a good worker with a good credit score, and then suddenly find yourself in financial difficulty because of a misfortune outside your control. As you miss payments, your score suffers, and you become less likely to find work. Joblessness pushes you toward poverty, which further worsens your score, making it even harder to find employment. The author calls it a downward spiral, driven by poisonous assumptions hidden behind a camouflage of mathematical rigor and data.

We cannot always predict when feedback loops will form. But many consequences can be foreseen by thinking about the entire system, not just its computerized parts, but also the people who interact with it. The book calls this systems thinking. We can try to understand how a data analysis system responds to different behaviors, structures, or characteristics. Does it reinforce and amplify existing differences between people, making the rich richer or the poor poorer? Or does it try to combat injustice? Even with the best intentions, we must beware of unintended consequences.

Privacy and Tracking

Besides the problems of predictive analytics, which uses data to make automated decisions about people, there are ethical problems with data collection itself. What is the relationship between the organizations collecting data and the people whose data is being collected?

When a system only stores data that a user explicitly entered, because they want the system to store and process it in a certain way, the system is performing a service for the user, and the user is the customer. But when a user’s activity is tracked and logged as a side effect of other things they do, the relationship is less clear. The service no longer just does what the user tells it to do. It takes on interests of its own, which may conflict with the user’s interests.

Tracking behavioral data has become important for user-facing features of many online services. Tracking which search results are clicked helps improve their ranking. Recommending that people who liked X also liked Y helps users discover interesting things. A/B tests and user flow analysis help show how an interface might be improved. These features require some tracking, and users benefit from them.

However, depending on the company’s business model, tracking often does not stop there. If a service is funded through advertising, the advertisers are the actual customers, and users’ interests take second place. Tracking becomes more detailed, analyses reach further, and data is kept for a long time to build detailed profiles of each person for marketing. The relationship between the company and the user then starts to look quite different. The user is given a free service and coaxed into engaging with it as much as possible. The tracking serves the advertisers who fund the service more than the individual. The author argues that this relationship is best described with a word that has more sinister connotations: surveillance.

Surveillance. As a thought experiment, replace the word data with surveillance and see whether common phrases still sound good. Try: our surveillance-driven organization collects real-time surveillance streams, stores them in a surveillance warehouse, and uses surveillance scientists to derive new insights. The author admits this is an unusually polemic tone for this book, but he thinks strong words are needed to make the point.

In our attempts to make software eat the world, we have built the greatest mass surveillance infrastructure the world has ever seen. Rushing toward the Internet of Things, we are rapidly approaching a world in which every inhabited space contains at least one internet-connected microphone. The devices include smartphones, smart TVs, voice-controlled assistants, baby monitors, and even children’s toys that use cloud-based speech recognition. Many of these devices have a terrible security record.

Even the most totalitarian and repressive regimes could only dream of putting a microphone in every room, and forcing every person to carry a device that tracks their location and movements. Yet we apparently throw ourselves into this world of total surveillance, voluntarily and even enthusiastically. The difference is that the data is collected by corporations rather than government agencies.

Not all data collection is surveillance, but thinking of it that way helps us understand our relationship with the data collector. Why are we seemingly happy to accept surveillance by corporations? One reason is the belief that you have nothing to hide. The author points out that this assumes you are fully in line with existing power structures, are not a marginalized minority, and need not fear persecution, and not everyone is so fortunate. Another reason is that the purpose seems benign. It is not overt coercion and conformance, but merely better recommendations and more personalized marketing. Combined with the discussion of predictive analytics, though, that distinction seems much less clear.

Car insurance premiums are already linked to tracking devices in cars, and some health insurance coverage depends on wearing a fitness tracker. When surveillance is used to determine things that hold sway over important parts of life, such as insurance coverage or employment, it starts to look much less benign. Data analysis can also reveal surprisingly intrusive things. The movement sensor in a smartwatch or fitness tracker can be used to work out what you are typing, such as passwords, with fairly good accuracy. And analysis algorithms are only going to get better.

Consent and freedom of choice. One argument is that users voluntarily choose to use a service that tracks their activity. They have agreed to its terms of service and privacy policy, so they consent to the data collection. Some add that users receive a valuable service in return for their data, and that tracking is necessary to provide that service. Social networks, search engines, and other free online services are indeed valuable to users. But there are problems with this argument.

Users have little knowledge of what data they are feeding into the databases, or how it is retained and processed. Most privacy policies do more to obscure than to illuminate. Without understanding what happens to their data, users cannot give any meaningful consent. Often, data from one user also says things about other people who are not users of the service and have not agreed to any terms. The derived datasets discussed in this part of the book, in which data from the entire user base is combined with behavioral tracking and external data sources, are precisely the kind of data that users cannot have any meaningful understanding of.

Moreover, data is extracted from users through a one-way process, not a relationship with true reciprocity and not a fair value exchange. There is no dialog, and no option for users to negotiate how much data they provide in return for what service. The relationship is very asymmetric. The terms are set by the service, not by the user.

For a user who does not consent to surveillance, the only real alternative is not to use the service. But this choice is not free either. If a service is so popular that most people regard it as essential for basic social participation, then it is not reasonable to expect people to opt out. Using it is in effect mandatory. In most Western social communities, it has become the norm to carry a smartphone, use Facebook for socializing, and use Google for finding information. Especially when a service has network effects, meaning it becomes more useful as more people join, there is a social cost to choosing not to use it.

Declining to use a service because of its tracking is an option only for the small number of people who are privileged enough to have the time and knowledge to understand its privacy policy, and who can afford to miss out on the social participation or professional opportunities that might have come from using it. For people in a less privileged position, there is no meaningful freedom of choice. Surveillance becomes inescapable.

Privacy and use of data. Sometimes people claim that privacy is dead, on the grounds that some users are willing to post all sorts of things about their lives to social media, some of them mundane and some deeply personal. The author says this claim is false, and it rests on a misunderstanding of the word privacy. Having privacy does not mean keeping everything secret. It means having the freedom to choose which things to reveal to whom, what to make public, and what to keep secret. The right to privacy is a decision right. It enables each person to decide where they want to be on the spectrum between secrecy and transparency in each situation. It is an important aspect of a person’s freedom and autonomy.

When data is extracted from people through surveillance infrastructure, privacy rights are not necessarily eroded. They are transferred to the data collector. Companies that acquire data are in effect asking users to trust them with it. The right to decide what to reveal and what to keep secret moves from the individual to the company.

The companies in turn keep much of the outcome of this surveillance secret, because revealing it would seem creepy and would harm a business that relies on knowing more about people than other companies do. Intimate information about users is revealed only indirectly, for example in tools that target advertisements at specific groups, such as people suffering from a particular illness. Even if a particular user cannot be personally identified from the group an ad targets, they have lost their agency over the disclosure of intimate information, such as whether they suffer from an illness. It is not the user who decides what is revealed to whom. It is the company, exercising the privacy right to maximize its profit.

Many companies aim to avoid being seen as creepy. They focus on managing user perceptions rather than asking how intrusive their data collection actually is. Even those perceptions are often managed poorly. Something can be factually correct and still, if it triggers painful memories, the user may not want to be reminded of it. With any kind of data, we should expect that it may be wrong, undesirable, or inappropriate in some way, and we need to build mechanisms for handling those failures. Whether something is undesirable or inappropriate is a matter of human judgment. Algorithms are oblivious to such notions unless we explicitly program them to respect human needs. As engineers of these systems, we must be humble and plan for these failings.

Privacy settings that let a user of an online service control which aspects of their data other users can see are a starting point for handing some control back to users. However, regardless of the setting, the service itself still has unfettered access to the data, and can use it in any way the privacy policy permits. Even if the service promises not to sell the data to third parties, it usually grants itself unrestricted rights to process and analyze the data internally, often going much further than what is visible to users.

This large-scale transfer of privacy rights from individuals to corporations is historically unprecedented. Surveillance has always existed, but it used to be expensive and manual, not scalable and automated. Trust relationships have always existed too, such as between a patient and their doctor, or between a defendant and their attorney. But in those cases, the use of data has been strictly governed by ethical, legal, and regulatory constraints. Internet services have made it much easier to amass huge amounts of sensitive information without meaningful consent, and to use it at massive scale without users understanding what is happening to their private data.

Data as assets and power. Since behavioral data is a byproduct of users interacting with a service, it is sometimes called data exhaust, which suggests that it is worthless waste. Seen that way, behavioral and predictive analytics recycle material that would otherwise be thrown away. The author suggests the reverse view is more accurate. If targeted advertising is what pays for a service, then behavioral data about people is the service’s core asset. The application the user interacts with is merely a means of luring users into feeding more and more personal information into the surveillance infrastructure. The delightful human creativity and social relationships that find expression in online services are, in this view, cynically exploited by a data extraction machine.

The claim that personal data is a valuable asset is supported by the existence of data brokers. This is a shady industry, operating in secrecy, that buys, aggregates, analyzes, infers, and resells intrusive personal data, mostly for marketing. Startups are often valued by their user numbers, which really means their surveillance capabilities.

Because the data is valuable, many people want it. Companies want it, which is why they collect it. Governments want it too, through secret deals, coercion, legal compulsion, or simply stealing it. When a company goes bankrupt, the personal data it has collected is one of the assets that get sold. The data is also difficult to secure, so breaches happen disconcertingly often.

Critics have called this data a toxic asset, or at least hazardous material. Even if we think we are capable of preventing abuse, whenever we collect data we must balance the benefits against the risk of it falling into the wrong hands. Computer systems may be compromised by criminals or hostile foreign intelligence services. Data may be leaked by insiders. The company may fall into the hands of unscrupulous management that does not share our values. The country itself may be taken over by a regime that has no qualms about compelling us to hand over data.

So when we collect data, we need to consider not just today’s political environment, but all possible future governments. There is no guarantee that every government elected in the future will respect human rights and civil liberties. Installing technology that could someday help build a police state is poor civic hygiene, as one commentator has put it. The author also cites the old adage that knowledge is power. To watch others while avoiding being watched oneself is one of the most important forms of power. That is why totalitarian governments want surveillance: it gives them power to control the population. Today’s technology companies are not overtly seeking political power. But the data and knowledge they have accumulated still gives them a great deal of power over our lives, much of it hidden from public oversight.

Remembering the Industrial Revolution

Data is the defining feature of the information age. The internet, data storage, processing, and software-driven automation have a major impact on the global economy and human society. As our daily lives and social organization have changed over the past decade, and will probably change radically in the decades ahead, comparisons to the Industrial Revolution come to mind.

The Industrial Revolution came about through major technological and agricultural advances, and in the long run it brought sustained economic growth and much better living standards. It also brought serious problems. Pollution of the air, from smoke and chemical processes, and of the water, from industrial and human waste, was dreadful. Factory owners lived in splendor, while urban workers often lived in very poor housing and worked long hours in harsh conditions. Child labor was common, including dangerous and poorly paid work in mines.

Safeguards took a long time to arrive. They included environmental protection regulations, safety protocols for workplaces, the outlawing of child labor, and health inspections for food. The cost of doing business rose once factories could no longer dump their waste into rivers, sell tainted food, or exploit their workers. But society as a whole benefited hugely, and few of us would want to return to the time before those rules.

Just as the Industrial Revolution had a dark side that had to be managed, the transition to the information age has major problems that we must confront and solve. The author believes the collection and use of data is one of them. He quotes Bruce Schneier, who calls data “the pollution problem of the information age,” and says that protecting privacy is the environmental challenge. Almost all computers produce information, and it stays around, festering. How we contain it and dispose of it is central to the health of the information economy. Later generations, Schneier suggests, will judge us for how we handled data collection and misuse, just as we now judge early industrialists who ignored pollution. The author ends by hoping that we will make them proud.

Legislation and self-regulation. Data protection laws might help preserve individuals’ rights. For example, the 1995 European Data Protection Directive says that personal data must be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes, and not further processed in ways incompatible with those purposes. It also says the data must be adequate, relevant, and not excessive for those purposes.

The author doubts that this kind of legislation is effective in today’s internet context. These rules run directly counter to the philosophy of big data, which is to maximize data collection, combine it with other datasets, and experiment to generate new insights. Exploration means using data for purposes nobody foresaw, which is the opposite of the specific, explicit purposes for which a user gave consent, if we can meaningfully speak of consent at all. Updated regulations are now being developed.

Companies that collect lots of data about people oppose regulation as a burden and a hindrance to innovation. To some extent the author thinks that opposition is justified. When sharing medical data, for example, there are clear risks to privacy, but there are also real opportunities. How many deaths could be prevented if data analysis helped with better diagnostics or better treatments? Over-regulation may prevent such breakthroughs. It is difficult to balance those opportunities against the risks.

Fundamentally, the author thinks the tech industry needs a culture shift with regard to personal data. We should stop regarding users as metrics to be optimized, and remember that they are humans who deserve respect, dignity, and agency. We should self-regulate our data collection and processing to establish and maintain the trust of the people who depend on our software. And we should take it upon ourselves to educate end users about how their data is used, rather than keeping them in the dark.

We should allow each individual to maintain their privacy, meaning their control over their own data, and not steal that control from them through surveillance. Our individual right to control our data is like the natural environment of a national park. If we do not explicitly protect and care for it, it will be destroyed. That would be a tragedy of the commons, and we would all be worse off for it. Ubiquitous surveillance is not inevitable. We are still able to stop it.

How exactly we might achieve this is an open question. To begin with, the author says we should not retain data forever. We should purge it as soon as it is no longer needed. Purging runs counter to the idea of immutability, but that issue can be solved. A promising approach he sees is to enforce access control through cryptographic protocols, rather than merely by policy. Overall, culture and attitude changes will be necessary.

Summary

Summary
  • Data integration. No single tool serves every use, so applications combine several. The approach in this chapter designates some systems as systems of record, and derives other data from them through transformations. That is how indexes, materialized views, machine learning models, and statistical summaries are maintained. Making these derivations asynchronous and loosely coupled stops a problem in one area from spreading into unrelated parts of the system.
  • Evolving dataflows. Expressing dataflows as transformations from one dataset to another helps applications evolve. If you want to change a processing step, such as the structure of an index or cache, you can rerun the new transformation code over the whole input to rederive the output. If something goes wrong, you can fix the code and reprocess the data to recover. The chapter recasts these dataflow applications as an unbundled database, a set of loosely coupled components that together do what a database does internally.
  • Observing change. Derived state can be updated by observing changes in the underlying data, and the derived state can itself be observed by downstream consumers. The dataflow can extend all the way to the end user’s device, so interfaces update as data changes and keep working offline.
  • Correctness. Strong integrity can be implemented at scale with asynchronous event processing. End-to-end operation identifiers make operations idempotent, and constraints are checked asynchronously. Clients either wait for the check to pass, or go ahead without waiting and risk having to apologize for a violation. This is more scalable and robust than distributed transactions, and it fits how many business processes work in practice.
  • Auditing. Audits verify the integrity of data and detect corruption. End-to-end checks cover every component of a pipeline at once, including the disks, networks, services, and algorithms along the path.
  • Ethics. Data can be used to do good, but it can also do significant harm. It can drive decisions that seriously affect people’s lives and are hard to appeal, lead to discrimination and exploitation, normalize surveillance, and expose intimate information. Breaches and unintended consequences are real risks even for well-meant uses. Engineers have a responsibility to work toward a world that treats people with humanity and respect.

The chapter ends with a numbered list of references to papers, talks, and posts that support its claims, and this retelling does not reproduce that list.

Check yourself

  1. Two clients write conflicting values to the same record. One write goes to the database and the other goes straight to a search index. Why can the two systems end up permanently different, and what single change fixes the problem?

    Show answer

    Neither system decides the order of the writes, so the two may process them in different orders and finish with different values. The fix is to send all input through one system that decides a total order, and to derive the index from that ordered stream of changes, for example with CDC or an event log.

  2. In Example 12-1, a client retries a transfer after losing the reply to its COMMIT. Why can $22 move instead of $11, and how does Example 12-2 prevent it?

    Show answer

    The first attempt may have committed, so the retry repeats the transfer. In Example 12-2, each transfer carries a request ID under a uniqueness rule. The retry’s INSERT fails because the ID already exists, which aborts the repeat. The request ID is an end-to-end operation identifier, so it recognizes the same logical operation across every retry.

  3. An overbooked flight can be fixed with an apology, but a bank statement that does not add up cannot. Explain the difference using the book’s two requirements, timeliness and integrity.

    Show answer

    Overbooking is a timeliness or constraint problem. It is a temporary breach that a business process can fix by compensating, such as a refund or an upgrade. A statement whose sums are wrong is an integrity violation. It is permanent unless someone explicitly detects and repairs it, and waiting does not help. The book argues integrity matters more than timeliness in most applications.

  4. A predictive model is trained on past loan decisions. Why can the model not be called fair just because it is built from data? Give two reasons from the chapter.

    Show answer

    Any two of these: the model learns the patterns in its input, including systematic bias, and it amplifies them. Proxies such as postal code can stand in for protected traits like race. The learned patterns are opaque and the output is probabilistic, so individual decisions can be wrong and hard to explain or appeal. Feedback loops can also turn one bad decision into a downward spiral.

Back matter

Glossary

The big idea: this is a plain-English version of the book’s glossary. Each term gets a short meaning and a pointer to the chapter where the book explains it in full. The book warns that its own definitions are short, so use the pointers when you need more detail.

TermWhat it means
asynchronousNot waiting for something to finish, such as data sent to another machine over the network. The sender makes no assumption about how long it will take. See Chapter 5 on synchronous and asynchronous replication, and Chapter 8 on networks and on the system model.
atomicTwo meanings. For operations running at the same time, an operation that looks as if it happens at one instant, so no other process sees it half finished. See isolation. For transactions, a group of writes that must all be saved or all be undone, even if a fault happens. See Chapter 7 on atomicity, and Chapter 9 on atomic commit and two-phase commit.
backpressureMaking the sender of some data slow down because the receiver cannot keep up. Also called flow control. See Chapter 11 on messaging systems.
batch processA computation that reads a fixed, usually large, set of input data and produces new output, without changing the input. See Chapter 10.
boundedHaving a known upper limit or size. The book uses it for network delay (see Chapter 8 on timeouts and unbounded delays) and for datasets (see the start of Chapter 11).
Byzantine faultA node that misbehaves in any arbitrary way, for example by sending contradictory or malicious messages to other nodes. See Chapter 8 on Byzantine faults.
cacheA component that remembers recently used data so that future reads of the same data are faster. It is usually not complete. If an item is missing, it must be fetched from the slower storage underneath, which holds the full copy.
CAP theoremA result that is widely misunderstood and, the book says, not useful in practice. See Chapter 9 on the CAP theorem.
causalityThe link between events where one thing happens before another, and the later one responds to, builds on, or must be understood in light of the earlier one. See Chapter 5 on the happens-before relationship and concurrency, and Chapter 9 on ordering and causality.
consensusGetting several nodes to agree on something, such as which node should lead a database cluster. It is much harder than it looks at first. See Chapter 9 on fault-tolerant consensus.
data warehouseA database that combines data from several OLTP systems (see OLTP below) and prepares it for analysis. See Chapter 3 on data warehousing.
declarativeDescribing the result or properties you want, without spelling out the exact steps to get it. For queries, a query optimizer (the part of the database that picks how to run a query) decides the steps. See Chapter 2 on query languages.
denormalizeAdding some duplication to a normalized dataset (one with no duplication), usually as a cache or index, to speed up reads. A denormalized value is a precomputed query result, similar to a materialized view. See Chapter 7 on single-object and multi-object operations, and Chapter 11 on deriving several views from the same event log.
derived dataA dataset made from other data by a repeatable process that you could run again if needed. It is usually made to speed up one kind of read. Indexes, caches, and materialized views are examples. See the introduction to Part III.
deterministicDescribing a function that always gives the same output for the same input. So it cannot depend on random numbers, the time of day, network communication, or other unpredictable things.
distributedRunning on several nodes connected by a network. Such systems have partial failures: one part can be broken while others still work, and the software often cannot tell exactly what is broken. See Chapter 8 on faults and partial failures.
durableStoring data so that you believe it will not be lost, even when various faults happen. See Chapter 7 on durability.
ETLExtract–Transform–Load. The process of pulling data out of a source database, reshaping it so it suits analytic queries, and loading it into a data warehouse or batch processing system. See Chapter 3 on data warehousing.
failoverIn a system with a single leader, moving the leader role from one node to another, for example when the current leader goes down. See Chapter 5 on handling node outages.
fault-tolerantAble to recover automatically when something goes wrong, such as a machine crashing or a network link failing. See Chapter 1 on reliability.
flow controlAnother name for backpressure. See backpressure above.
followerA replica (a copy of the data on another node) that accepts no writes from clients. It only applies the data changes it gets from the leader. Also called a secondary, slave, read replica, or hot standby. See Chapter 5 on leaders and followers.
full-text searchSearching text by any keyword, often with extras such as matching similar spellings or synonyms. A full-text index is a kind of secondary index that supports these searches. See Chapter 3 on full-text search and fuzzy indexes.
graphA data structure made of vertices (things you can refer to, also called nodes or entities) and edges (connections from one vertex to another, also called relationships or arcs). Here “node” means a point in the graph, not a machine. See Chapter 2 on graph-like data models.
hashA function that turns an input into a random-looking number. The same input always gives the same number. Different inputs almost always give different numbers, but sometimes two inputs give the same number, which is called a collision. See Chapter 6 on partitioning by hash of key.
idempotentDescribing an operation that is safe to retry. If it runs more than once, the effect is the same as if it ran only once. See Chapter 11 on idempotence.
indexA data structure that lets you quickly find all the records that have a particular value in a particular field. See Chapter 3 on the data structures that power your database.
isolationIn transactions, how far transactions running at the same time can interfere with each other. Serializable isolation gives the strongest guarantees, but weaker levels are also used. See Chapter 7 on isolation.
joinBringing together records that have something in common. Most often one record refers to another (through a foreign key, a document reference, or an edge in a graph), and a query needs the record it points to. See Chapter 2 on many-to-one and many-to-many relationships, and Chapter 10 on reduce-side joins and grouping.
leaderWhen data or a service is copied across several nodes, the leader is the one replica allowed to make changes. A leader can be picked by a protocol or chosen by an administrator. Also called the primary or master. See Chapter 5 on leaders and followers.
linearizableBehaving as if the system has only one copy of the data, which is updated by atomic operations (operations that take effect all at once). See Chapter 9 on linearizability.
localityA performance trick: putting pieces of data in the same place when they are needed at the same time. See Chapter 2 on data locality for queries.
lockA mechanism that lets only one thread, node, or transaction use something at a time. Anyone else who wants it must wait until the lock is released. See Chapter 7 on two-phase locking, and Chapter 8 on the leader and the lock.
logAn append-only file, meaning records are only ever added to the end. A write-ahead log helps a storage engine recover from crashes. A log-structured storage engine uses logs as its main storage format. A replication log copies writes from a leader to its followers. An event log can represent a data stream. See Chapter 3 on making B-trees reliable and on SSTables and LSM-trees, Chapter 5 on leaders and followers, and Chapter 11 on partitioned logs.
materializeTo do a computation ahead of time and write out its result, instead of working it out when someone asks. See Chapter 3 on aggregation, data cubes and materialized views, and Chapter 10 on materialization of intermediate state.
nodeAn instance of some software running on a computer, which talks to other nodes over a network to get a task done.
normalizedStructured so there is no redundancy or duplication. In a normalized database, when a piece of data changes, you change it in one place only. See Chapter 2 on many-to-one and many-to-many relationships.
OLAPOnline analytic processing. An access pattern where queries add up or average (count, sum, average) over a large number of records. See Chapter 3 on transaction processing or analytics.
OLTPOnline transaction processing. An access pattern where queries are fast and read or write a small number of records, usually found by their key. See Chapter 3 on transaction processing or analytics.
partitioningSplitting a dataset or computation that is too big for one machine into smaller parts, and spreading them across several machines. Also called sharding. See Chapter 6.
percentileA way to describe how values are spread out, by counting how many fall above or below a threshold. For example, the 95th percentile response time is the time t at which 95% of requests in that period finish in less than t, and 5% take longer. See Chapter 1 on describing performance.
primary keyA value, usually a number or a string, that uniquely identifies a record. In many applications the system generates it when the record is created, often in sequence or at random, rather than the user setting it. See also secondary index.
quorumThe minimum number of nodes that must vote on an operation before it counts as successful. See Chapter 5 on quorums for reading and writing.
rebalanceMoving data or services from one node to another so the load is spread fairly. See Chapter 6 on rebalancing partitions.
replicationKeeping a copy of the same data on several nodes (replicas), so that the data stays accessible if one node becomes unreachable. See Chapter 5.
schemaA description of the structure of some data, including its fields and their datatypes. You can check whether data matches a schema at various points in its life, and a schema can change over time. See Chapter 2 on schema flexibility in the document model, and Chapter 4 on how data and schemas change over time.
secondary indexAn extra data structure kept alongside the main data, which lets you efficiently search for records that match a certain kind of condition. See Chapter 3 on other indexing structures, and Chapter 6 on partitioning and secondary indexes.
serializableA guarantee that if several transactions run at the same time, they behave the same as if they had run one at a time, in some order. See Chapter 7 on serializability.
shared-nothingAn architecture in which independent nodes, each with their own CPUs, memory, and disks, are connected by a normal network. This contrasts with shared-memory or shared-disk designs. See the introduction to Part II.
skewTwo meanings. (1) Uneven load across partitions, so some have many requests or lots of data and others have little. Also called hot spots. See Chapter 6 on skewed workloads and relieving hot spots, and Chapter 10 on handling skew. (2) A timing oddity that makes events appear in an unexpected order. See Chapter 7 on read skew and write skew, and Chapter 8 on clock skew.
split brainA situation where two nodes both believe they are the leader at the same time, which may break the system’s guarantees. See Chapter 5 on handling node outages, and Chapter 8 on the truth being defined by the majority.
stored procedureA way of writing the logic of a transaction so that it runs entirely on the database server, without going back and forth with the client while the transaction runs. See Chapter 7 on actual serial execution.
stream processA computation that keeps running, taking an endless stream of events as input and deriving some output from them. See Chapter 11.
synchronousThe opposite of asynchronous: waiting for something to complete before moving on.
system of recordA system that holds the main, authoritative version of some data, also called the source of truth. Changes are written here first, and other datasets are derived from it. See the introduction to Part III.
timeoutOne of the simplest ways to detect a fault: if no response arrives within some time, assume something is wrong. But a timeout cannot tell whether the remote node has a problem or the network does. See Chapter 8 on timeouts and unbounded delays.
total orderA way of comparing things, such as timestamps, that always says which of two is greater and which is smaller. An ordering where some things cannot be compared is called a partial order. See Chapter 9 on the causal order not being a total order.
transactionGrouping several reads and writes into one logical unit, to simplify error handling and concurrency issues. See Chapter 7.
two-phase commit (2PC)An algorithm that makes sure several database nodes either all commit a transaction (save it) or all abort it (cancel it). See Chapter 9 on atomic commit and two-phase commit.
two-phase locking (2PL)An algorithm for serializable isolation. A transaction takes a lock on all the data it reads or writes, and holds those locks until the transaction ends. See Chapter 7 on two-phase locking.
unboundedHaving no known upper limit or size. The opposite of bounded.

Summary of Designing Data-Intensive Applications: The Big Ideas Behind Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems by Martin Kleppmann (O’Reilly Media, 2017). Independent summary, not affiliated with the author or publisher.
